VIII. ENGINEER-PROCURE-CONSTRUCT 	49
EPC is similar to design-build in that an owner contracts with a single entity for the entire project.
Thus, the EPC contractor assumes the project’s corresponding business risk. The parties to an EPC
contract must consider the same issues that apply to design-build contracts.
EPC is widely used in industrial projects (that is, major utilities projects and manufacturing
facilities) and is being used often in large infrastructure developments, including airports, ports,
water-treatment facilities, railways, and telecommunications systems. Because these projects may
take several years to complete, scheduling and sequencing are critical to the success of an EPC
project. The owner normally contracts with a consultant and the EPC contractor. Generally, the
EPC contractor self-performs most of the construction work while subcontracting some of the trade
construction work. The EPC contractor then contracts with material suppliers for the major equip-
ment purchases. In some cases, the EPC contractor is a major equipment supplier that in turn subcon-
tracts the construction and equipment installation work. There are no generally accepted form EPC
contracts. The contract forms from the International Federation of Consulting Engineers (FIDIC)
are gaining in popularity, but are still not widely used. As a result, contracts for each EPC project
are different and must be carefully negotiated to arrive at a middle ground. EPC contractors should
be aware that owner-provided EPC contracts will undoubtedly favor the owner. The EPC contrac-
tor should review the owner-generated contract carefully to ensure that the contractor does not take
on unnecessary risk. Early discussions and agreements finalizing the design scope are critical to a
successful EPC experience.
Often, the owner will contract with the EPC contractor for a turnkey project delivery, meaning
the EPC contractor will be the single point of contact for all steps in the project and will be required
to meet certain performance benchmarks or design criteria. This shifts traditional owner risks to the
EPC contractor in return for a theoretical higher fee for the EPC contractor. EPC contractors entering
into a lump-sum or fixed-price turnkey project should be especially careful because such agreements
can result in unlimited liability for the EPC contractor. Performance requirements provide the key
difference between a design-build project and an EPC project. The technical scope of work and the
project definition provide the primary risks associated with an EPC project. Many owners address
the risks associated with the scope of work by using performance specifications or output/throughput
criteria that require the EPC contractor to achieve certain performance standards through any means
or process selected by the EPC contractor. EPC projects and design-build projects share many of the
same contractual issues. But because of the high-tech nature of EPC projects—and thus the height-
ened importance of performance requirements—two contract risks are influenced more heavily by
such performance requirements: limitations of liability and liquidated damages. EPC contracts also
present unique issues related to changes to the work.
A. 	Limitations of Liability
Most EPC contractors will not risk their company’s entire net worth on an owner’s project. Although
this is perplexing to owners who have been sold on an EPC contractor’s abilities based on its proposal,
glossy brochures, business-development materials, portfolio of successful projects, and, most likely,
financial resources, it is understandable that an EPC contractor in a position to earn a reasonable
profit on a project does not want to have a downside risk that far exceeds its upside potential.
Limitation-of-liability clauses are commonplace and expected by most experienced owners. A
reasonable limitation-of-liability clause does not diminish an EPC contractor’s commitment to the
project, nor does it represent an attempt to evade its project responsibilities. Rather, it represents
an arm’s-length negotiated cap on the potential downside risk of the project. Owners are certainly
willing and eager to negotiate an EPC contractor’s fee down, so it is not unreasonable to look at the
entire risk spectrum and negotiate reasonable limitations that afford each party appropriate protection
on the project.

-- 87 of 771 --

50 	CHAPTER 3 ALTERNATIVE CONTRACTING METHODS
Often the limitation of liability is tied to limits of applicable insurance coverage 52 or to a
percentage of the contract price or the EPC contractor’s fee. In addition, EPC contractors commonly
negotiate a limitation of their obligations in the event of design errors or omissions. Insurance
policies are also increasingly available to EPC contractors for design-related coverage.53 Most
of these clauses derive from the design professional’s agreement that often limits the obligation
to perform redesign work. While many contractors will not enter into an EPC contract without a
limitation-of-liability clause, the validity of such a clause needs to be determined under the applicable
state law. 54
B. 	Liquidated Damages
Liquidated damages (LDs) are the primary way an owner may minimize the risks associated with the
scope of work. Liquidated damages clauses are common to construction contracts as a way for the
owner to fairly approximate its actual damages if the contractor fails to timely deliver the completed
project (see Chapter 13). Liquidated damages may be tied to a variety of criteria. In the EPC con-
tract, the two most common criteria for imposing LDs are project delivery date(s) and performance
guarantees.
• Time-Related LDs. In EPC projects, time is money and money is time. High-tech owners sim-
ply do not have the time to complete the design, procure the contractor and materials, and then
construct the project in a linear sequence. The time savings—or perceived time savings—often
creates the greatest risk on the project. For example, every day that a power plant is not gen-
erating electricity, the owner loses revenue. It is incredibly important that the EPC contractor
hit the project delivery date so the owner can begin generating revenue. Most owners will
put teeth into the EPC contract by including a very strict liquidated damages provision for
a delay. The owner may go so far as to include a clause that allows the owner to termi-
nate the EPC contractor and obtain an assignment of all subcontracts and purchase orders
for the project in the event the EPC contractor is extremely late in performing or completing
the work.
• Project Performance-Related LDs. Owners also may tie liquidated damages to the project’s
performance specifications. Often the EPC contractor has no choice but to deliver a project
that is operating at less than 100 percent of the performance specifications called for in the
EPC contract. There are myriad reasons that performance specifications are not met. In the
vast majority of cases, the owner finds the completed project perfectly acceptable, but oper-
ating at a lower efficiency than expected. In those cases, it would be far too costly to tear out
and replace the offending materials or machinery. Liquidated damages for decreased perfor-
mance are a common way to compensate an owner for a project that does not meet 100 percent
of the performance guarantees the EPC contractor promised but is otherwise operational and
acceptable.
52 Examples of insurance include: (1) force majeure coverage, which protects against labor disputes, war, acts of terror, and
changes in the law; (2) liquidated damages coverage, which protects the EPC contractor from liquidated damages or penalties
related to late completion; (3) cost overrun coverage, which protects the owner from cost overruns; and (3) project-specific
policies such as OCIP, CCIP, and Subguard.
53 Because of the increased use of EPC contracting, as well as the prevalence of design-build contracting, insurance companies
have created new Enhanced Professional Liability coverage for contractors with design responsibilities. While the exact terms
of the policies differ, the policies often include coverage for third-party professional liability, first-party professional liability,
and coverage for both direct damages and economic loss associated with the alleged design deficiency.
54Compare Blaylock Grading Co. v. Smith, 658 S.E.2d 680 (N.C. App. 2008) (clause valid) with Lanier at McEver, L.P. v.
Planners & Eng’rs Collaborative, Inc., 663 S.E.2d 240 (Ga. 2008) (clause invalid); see also Mistry Prabhudas Manji Eng.
PVT, Ltd. v. Raytheon Engineers & Constructors, Inc., 213 F. Supp. 2d 20 (D. Mass. 2002).

IX. BUILDING INFORMATION MODELING 	51
The prudent EPC contractor, when reviewing a liquidated damages clause, needs to make sure
that these damages take the place of, and are not in addition to, actual damages that the owner might
incur. Likewise, the EPC contractor would be well served to include contract terms that expressly
avoid (or waive) consequential damages. If the liquidated damages truly are a fair approximation
of the damages that an owner will incur as a result of the EPC contractor’s failure to timely deliver
the work or to deliver the work at the specified performance levels, then these should be the only
damages for such delays or inefficiencies.
C. 	Design Changes
Design changes are virtually inevitable on any project, so EPC contracts allow for owner changes
or variations during performance. Issues arise, however, about which party is ultimately responsible
for the change’s incurred cost and impacts. Due to the unique burden-shifting associated with EPC
contracting, determining which party should be held responsible for the cost of the change is not as
straightforward as in the more traditional design-bid-build model. Instead, both parties face additional
proof requirements for changes. The parties may, however, proactively avoid many of these disputes.
One popular method for addressing the changes problem is for the owner and EPC contractor
to work together in basic design-review sessions. Any comments or revisions made during these
sessions are then included in the basic design documents. The parties then, in writing, approve the
changes and assign any applicable additional costs. Another method is to establish a contingency in
the contract price to cover any changes that arise after the basic design documents are issued.
If a claim does arise from changes, EPC contractors face additional burdens of proof. With
EPC contracts, the EPC contractor should immediately start tracking the individual cost and sched-
ule impacts associated with the change using individual cost/activity codes. These impacts should
include labor, equipment, materials, and all other allocable costs. Failure to track these costs may
result in the EPC contractor’s waiving or greatly reducing its claim.
IX. 	BUILDING INFORMATION MODELING
Another computer-based communications trend sweeping the construction industry affects the plan-
ning, design, and construction of a project from the outset, throughout the project’s duration, and
beyond. Through such a process, the owner and other members of the project-delivery team, such as
the design professional, the contractor, major trade subcontractors, and suppliers, use virtual design
and construction concepts, or building information modeling (BIM), to interactively model project
design and construction. Multiple software programs currently on the market offer BIM capabilities.
Industry leaders include Autodesk’s Revit, Graphisoft’s ArchiCAD, Bentley’s AECOsim Building
Designer, and VectorWorks Architect.
Various models or processes can be broadly categorized as BIM. The Associated General Con-
tractors of America (AGC) offers this definition:
Building Information Modeling is the development and use of a computer software model to
simulate the construction and operation of a facility. The resulting model, a Building Informa-
tion Model, is a data-rich, object-oriented, intelligent and parametric digital representation of
the facility, from which views and data appropriate to various users’ needs can be extracted and
analyzed to generate information that can be used to make decisions and improve the process
of delivering the facility. 55
55The Contractor’s Guide to BIM, 2nd ed. (2010) (Associated General Contractors of America, Inc.). Information on BIM
education and training offered by AGC is available at https://www.agc.org/learn/education-training/building-information-
modeling-education-program.

-- 89 of 771 --

52 	CHAPTER 3 ALTERNATIVE CONTRACTING METHODS
Another industry organization categorizes BIM as “a digital representation of physical and func-
tional characteristics of a facility … a shared knowledge resource for information about a facility
forming a reliable basis for decisions during its life-cycle; defined as existing from earliest concep-
tion to demolition. A basic premise of BIM is collaboration by different stakeholders at different
phases of the life cycle of a facility to insert, extract, update or modify information in the BIM to
support and reflect the roles of that stakeholder.”56 The remainder of this section focuses on BIM’s
collaborative process and the related issues that construction project delivery team members should
understand.
A. 	Collaborative Uses of BIM
In its simplest form, BIM represents a means of interactively sharing project design and construction
data to more economically and timely achieve the finished project that meets the owner’s objectives.
More specifically, BIM allows the project delivery team to achieve this goal in a number of ways,
including the following:
• Design visualization and comprehension
• Space utilization
• Structural analysis
• Energy analysis
• Preparation of design drawings
• Systems (for example, mechanical, electrical, and plumbing) coordination
• Interference or conflict identification and resolution
• Constructability reviews
• Communication
• Integration of various players’ models
• Multidimensional modeling (XD) 57
• Work scheduling and sequencing
• Site planning and utilization
• Cost estimating
• Layout and fieldwork
• Prefabrication of materials and equipment
• Safety analysis and management
• Operations and maintenance 58
Members of the project-delivery team collaborate to provide the information necessary to achieve
these goals. Ideally, this collaboration serves to achieve a desired finished construction project more
quickly and economically than more conventional methods, such as paper RFIs, by which project
members would collaborate and communicate.
56See “What is a BIM?” at https://www.nationalbimstandard.org/faqs#faq1 (last accessed 1/7/19).
57 From a modeling standpoint, BIM offers users the ability to view facility design and construction in three dimensions (3D).
Most modeling software also allows the user to integrate other “dimensions” into the modeling, such as time (4D), costs (5D),
and beyond (XD).

As with any model, BIM is useful only if it is implemented effectively, which typically involves
what is known as a BIM Execution Plan (BxP or BEP). A BEP is described as follows:
The intent of the BIM Execution Plan (BEP) is to define a foundational framework to ensure
successful deployment of advanced design technologies on your BIM enabled project. The
BEP is about optimizing work and model flow across the project, as contrasted with optimizing
siloed interests. The key is good planning of the design-to-engineering-to-construction process
to minimize downstream surprises, rework, redundancies or gaps in the flow of (model-based)
information. 59
B. 	BIM’s Legal Implications
Given the recent development of BIM and the contract documents implementing its use, it is
difficult to predict all of the legal issues that might be presented by this data-sharing technique.
Needless to say, such sharing of information would give rise to intellectual-property issues such as
copyright and ownership—that is, who owns the collaborative work product. The most effective
way to resolve such an issue is to address it in the parties’ contract. Beyond that, any further
discussion of intellectual property issues exceeds the scope of this book. Other, more “traditional”
construction-law questions or issues that might arise using this collaborative method include the
following:
• If there is a contract addendum or specification addressing BIM, does it clearly define key
concepts or terms?
• If the owner is seeking competitive proposals addressing the use of BIM in the design and
construction of the project, what level of detail is required in the proposal? How costly will
that effort be?
• Does the BIM model become a contract document once it is completed? If there are differ-
ences between the final BIM model and the owner’s original statement of requirements or
specifications, which controls?
• Who is responsible for project design, and, by collaborating in such design, does one assume
added risk or liability for such design?
• Who is responsible for project submittals, such as shop drawings and material samples, and,
by collaborating in such submittals, does one assume added risk or liability?
• Who is responsible for delays in design or submittals?
• What affect, if any, does participation in this collaborative process have on the recognized
standards of care for design and construction?
• If there is a serious construction failure involving property damage or physical injury, can each
party’s responsibility be clearly traced? If the responsibility is mixed, does the contract address
the allocation or sharing of that risk? Does the contract address responsibility for economic
losses?
• If multiple contracts contemplate collaboration by multiple parties in the BIM process, does a
party’s responsibility for losses or damages extend to those with whom it does not have a direct
contractual relationship?
• Do potential insurance-coverage gaps exist between traditional coverage under comprehensive
general liability policies and errors and omissions policies?
59 https://www.gsa.gov/real-estate/design-construction/3d4d-building-information-modeling/guidelines-for-bim-software/
document-guides/bim-execution-plan.

-- 91 of 771 --

54 	CHAPTER 3 ALTERNATIVE CONTRACTING METHODS
• Are there any statutory limitations of risk transfer applicable where the project is located?
• Who is responsible if there are any software errors?
Ultimately, the goal of such a collaborative project design, construction, and management system
should be to reduce risks and liabilities. The legal issues just mentioned are not unique to BIM. They
arise in other contexts, as discussed throughout this book. As in those cases, to avoid these risks, the
parties need to understand how they manifest during the project and attempt to address and mitigate
them from the outset. This can be accomplished in careful drafting of the contract documents.
Various organizations, such as the U. S. Army Corps of Engineers, the federal government’s
General Services Administration (GSA), the AIA, and ConsensusDocs have published specifications
or addenda addressing the use of BIM. There can be significant differences in these organizations’
use of BIM. For example, EJCDC C-800 Supplementary Conditions briefly mentions BIM in the
guidance notes for Section 2.06,60 whereas the GSA has extensive information on using BIM for
government contracts 61 and AIA offers the following documents specific to BIM:
• AIA Document E203 – 2013 Building Information Modeling and Digital Data Exhibit. This
document must be attached as an exhibit to an existing agreement, such as the AIA Document
B101 – 2007 Standard Form of Agreement Between Owner and Architect or A101 – 2007
Agreement Between Owner and Contractor. Its purpose is to establish the parties’ expectations
for the use of digital data and BIM on the project and to provide a process for developing
the detailed protocols and procedures that will govern the development, use, transmission and
exchange of digital data and BIM on the project.
• AIA Document G201 – 2013 Project Digital Data Protocol is used to document the agreed-upon
protocols and procedures that will govern the transmission, use, and exchange of digital data
on a project, such as electronic project communications, submittals, contract document, and
payment document.
• AIA Document G202 – 2013 Project BIM Protocol is for use with AIA Document E203 – 2013
Building Information Modeling and Digital Data Protocol Exhibit. It is used to document the
agreed-upon protocols and procedures that will govern the development, transmission, use,
and exchange of building information models on a project. It establishes the requirements for
model content at five levels of development, and the authorized uses of the model content
at each level of development. Through a table completed for each project, AIA Document
G202 – 2013 assigns authorship of each model element by project milestone. G202 defines the
extent to which model users may rely on model content, clarifies model ownership, and sets
forth building information modeling standards and file formats.

➣ 	POINTS TO REMEMBER
• The traditional approach to construction of design-bid-build has many strengths, but also weak-
nesses that have prompted pursuit of other construction-process approaches.
• To avoid unanticipated problems and disputes, pay careful attention to how alternative con-
tracting methods divert from clearly defined and accepted practices and roles.
• Multiprime (or parallel prime) contracting, particularly when employed with fast-track con-
struction, can reduce the time and cost of construction.
• All parties to a multiprime project must recognize that with the elimination of the general
contractor, another party with appropriate power should be designated to assume the coordi-
nation responsibilities traditionally fulfilled by the general contractor. Without some express
disclaimer, the owner assumes the duty to coordinate in the multiprime setting.
• Construction management generally entails involving an entity with diverse expertise in design,
construction, and management in the design and construction process. The precise role of a
construction manager on any project, however, can be determined only by specific contract
language.
• The role of the construction manager can range from that of a traditional general contractor,
which provides some estimating and constructability input during the design phase but is still
required to guarantee time and price of performance, to a traditional design firm, which simply
provides a higher level of construction administration and scheduling services for a fixed fee,
without any guarantee of time or cost of performance.
• Design-build contracting represents the most radical departure from the traditional approach to
construction by vesting all design and construction responsibilities, and resulting liabilities, in
one party. The dramatic alteration of the traditional roles of the parties in design-build requires
special attention to make certain the contract sets out the mutually understood and specific
rights and responsibilities of each party.
• There are many customizable variants to the design-build model, which allows the owner to tai-
lor the contract arrangement to best suit the owner’s needs. One emerging method is ECI, which
facilitates communication and problem-solving by involving the contractor at the beginning of
the design process.
• Even in the traditional build-to-design approach, contractors can assume discrete design liabil-
ity as the result of performance specifications, the shop drawing process, and where secondary
design review responsibility is imposed by standard contract clauses.
• Many states have passed laws allowing alternative methods of project delivery. Design profes-
sionals, contractors, and subcontractors should still check state laws governing licensing and
the formation of business entities before signing the contract.
• EPC contracting is gaining in popularity, particularly in industrial construction. There are no
widely accepted form contracts, so the EPC contractor should review carefully any proposed
EPC contract.
• Performance requirements are very important in EPC contracts. Performance requirements will
influence two major areas of contract negotiation in EPC contracts: limitations of liability and
liquidated damages.

4
PUBLIC-PRIVATE
PARTNERSHIPS
In the early years of the United States, private entities built the majority of the infrastructure of
North America. The original ports, ferries, bridges, transcontinental railroads, trolley and cable car
systems, and local water systems were almost exclusively private endeavors or, in some instances,
public-private partnerships where the only public involvement was a grant of permission to proceed
or maybe a land grant.
In the past one hundred years, the public sector has largely assumed the role of planning, design-
ing, financing, and executing large municipal and infrastructure projects. The massive public works
projects of the 1930s (Works Project Administration) and the Interstate Highway System, officially
the Dwight D. Eisenhower National System of Interstate and Defense Highways, created after World
War II, are two major examples of massive public infrastructure spending. Along with this transfor-
mation evolved the concept of entrusting the government with oversight of public projects. Many
consider this “public trust” very important.
In the past decade, the financial impact of a lengthy, worldwide recession, the accompanying
growing public-debt crisis, an increasing size and complexity of many public projects, and a desire
to better evaluate and optimize life-cycle costs have caused the tide to shift toward a mixture of
private and public financing for many large public projects.
The public-private partnership (P3) delivery method allows private entities to become more
involved in these projects, typically as the concessionaire or developer, whereby they become
responsible for the design, finance, construction, and long-term operation and maintenance of public
facilities. These include so-called “horizontal projects,” such as bridges, roadways, pipelines, and
rail and mass transit, as well as “vertical projects,” including government office buildings, student
housing, schools, police and fire stations, hospitals, and courthouses.
The National Council for Public-Private Partnerships defines a public-private partnership as:
[a] contractual agreement between a public agency (federal, state or local) and a private sector
entity. Through this agreement, the skills and assets of each sector (public and private) are
shared in delivering a service or facility for the use of the general public. In addition to the
sharing of resources, each party shares in the risks and rewards potential in the delivery of the
service or facility.1
1 National Council for Public-Private Partnerships, “7 Keys to Success,” www.ncppp.org/ppp-basics/7-keys.
56

-- 94 of 771 --

I. THE P3 ALTERNATIVE 	57
One of the core attributes of a P3 project is the partial or total private financing of the project
through private debt and equity. Another is long-term operation and maintenance of the facilities by
private operators. Within these general confines, the P3 project delivery method is readily adaptable
to a wide variety of project types, sizes, and objectives.
The previous chapter addressed a number of alternate contracting methods such as CM at
risk, design-build, ECI (early contractor involvement), or EPC (engineer, procure, and construct).
Long-term alternative project delivery methods include design-build and operate or design-build-
operate-maintain. A P3 project is different from all of these alternative delivery methods because
the project financing is also added to the private sector or contractor’s side of the equation. The
shifting or sharing of the financial risks with the private sector on projects that, for the last century,
were thought of as public projects entrusted to federal, state, or local government entities is key to
every P3 project.
A significant number of recent P3 projects in the United States have been “mega-sized” highway,
bridge, and transportation projects. However, the vast majority of P3 projects accomplished in the
past 30 years have been water, wastewater, and bio-waste facilities, which have been much smaller
in physical scope and financial commitment. Canada has long used P3s as a major way to finance the
development and construction of its government healthcare facilities and other government build-
ings. P3 models have also been used in Europe and elsewhere.
P3 projects entail unique attributes, risks, and contract terms. They present distinct risks to par-
ticipants who have not undertaken these types of projects in the past. Their attributes are far more
familiar to those organizations that have done private development or large design-build projects.
The complex contracts and security arrangements for these projects are often driven by the needs and
dictates of the private financial community—equity holders, financiers, brokers, and banks—which
requires a high degree of quality assurance and financial security ensuring that the project will be
completed and go into operation as originally budgeted and scheduled, so the expected revenue
stream will begin, as planned, to service the project debt.
P3 projects also create significant new questions under state and local contracting law, which
is geared to the traditional design-bid-build approach. Almost all of these projects require some
sort of enabling P3 legislation. In addition, a wide variety of potential pitfalls or traps arise in the
P3 process through the interplay of new statutes, unfamiliar project roles, and complex, uniquely
written contracts.
This chapter looks at each of the following issues:
• What are key prerequisites to a successful P3 project?
• Who are the P3 key participants?
• What are the P3 financing strategies or methods?
• What are the unique P3 risk allocations?
• What, if any, performance and payment protections are in place?
I. 	THE P3 ALTERNATIVE
A. 	The Emergence of P3 Projects
Federal, state, and local governments normally do not pay for capital improvements using ordinary
operating revenues. Traditionally, they raised money from tax revenues or borrowed money through
the public bond markets, used outside designers, sought competitive bids/proposals, and awarded to
the lowest cost responsive and responsible contractor. Once projects were built and accepted, public
employees maintained the completed projects and facilities.

-- 95 of 771 --

58 	CHAPTER 4 PUBLIC-PRIVATE PARTNERSHIPS
However, the tax receipts and borrowing capacity of U.S. public agencies, especially at the state
and local levels, has been under increasing pressure for several decades and was sharply reduced after
the economic upheavals that began in 2008. Those financial pressures also caused public owners to
revisit the subject of project life-cycle costing in a desire to design projects that were sustainable,
maintainable, and operable by the facility users.
As a result, a growing number of community leaders at the state and local levels now look to P3s
as an additional method of creating, financing, and maintaining public infrastructure by assigning
greater roles to private investors and developers. It takes careful stewardship of public funds to meet
the essential public needs of transportation, clean water, education, law enforcement, and healthcare.
The public trusts its elected officials to act in the public’s best interest. P3 projects present an oppor-
tunity to stretch limited public funds further by recognizing the true costs of public projects and
using the financing tools available to private industry to deliver services efficiently to the citizens.
The private capital markets dwarf the public finance sector. This pool of capital is global, mobile,
and robust, and is quickly attracted to long-term opportunities for moderate to high returns on
low-risk projects. P3 projects must promise a desirable return on investment to make them attrac-
tive to private entities. These private sources of capital require a higher return than the buyers of
municipal bonds, who accept a very low rate of return (usually tax-free), but expect virtually no
investment risk.
Private funds will be increasingly called upon to upgrade the country’s aging and deteriorating
infrastructure and supplement shrinking government budgets for such projects. The expertise and
financial incentives of P3s can optimize the long-term operation and maintenance costs of infras-
tructure projects. Those long-term costs are borne by the P3 developer who has a strong incentive to
design and build the project to keep the facility running with low operational costs.
In most cases, the developer (or concessionaire) gets a fixed monthly availability payment that
varies with the degree the facility is constantly available and operating at peak performance. This
gives the public the assurance of a predictable cost for the life of a reliable and cost-effective project.
In some sectors, such as water and wastewater, the global investment and sophisticated engineer-
ing and management skills of P3 teams can result in technically effective and efficiently controlled
end-use technology for the community—often years before local agencies would be able to imple-
ment such solutions.
Over the last decade, all of these factors have combined to increase use of the P3 option. P3s are
especially suited for situations where the project would not be built for many years to come without
the private initiative, capital, or technical expertise.
As it turns out, P3 offers the nation a once-in-a-century revolution in reexamining the contract-
ing strategies that can be used to accomplish public projects. State legislatures are acknowledging
the public’s demand for reliable infrastructure and effective control of the costs of government ser-
vices. Local governments are facing an era of limited budgets for infrastructure projects. Therefore,
many public entities are expanding the range of contracting strategies to include consideration of
public-private partnerships.
B. 	Considerations for a P3 Project
A P3 procurement process typically includes the following:
• A sponsoring government agency with statutory authority to enter into a long-term P3 contract.
• The development of a public solicitation known as a request for qualifications (RFQ) or request
for proposals (RFP). (In a number of states, the enabling P3 legislation allows private sector
entities to make an unsolicited proposal or bid for a P3 project to the public agency. See the
table in Section D, “P3 Enabling Legislation”).

-- 96 of 771 --

I. THE P3 ALTERNATIVE 	59
• The selection of a short list of potential developers to prepare project submittals in response to
the RFQ.
• Extensive effort by each of the short-listed candidates to develop a comprehensive plan for all
aspects of the P3 project.
• The award to a successful developer who arranges for the financing of the project (construction
and permanent), as well as the design, construction, procurement, startup, commissioning, and,
thereafter, the operation and maintenance of a project for 20, 30, or more years.
• All aspects of the P3 project are typically covered in a single complex agreement between the
public owner and the developer; all lower-tier contract relationships with the developer flow
down from this “master agreement.”
P3 projects tend to be awarded on a best-value basis where the competitiveness of the monthly
revenue or availability payment required is a major, but far from the only, factor in the selection.
A P3 project is typically bid and awarded using a life-cycle costing model, so that long-term
energy costs, maintenance, operational expenses, and financing are included in the bid and, as a
result, are optimized during the design process. This is in contrast to a traditional design-bid-build
project, where the architects and engineers prepare the plans and specifications and may have no
further involvement with the project. The general contractor similarly has no long-term obligation
to minimize future operations or maintenance costs, so long as they build pursuant to the plans and
specifications. They have little incentive to improve upon the design to achieve overall project goals.
Their value-engineering efforts are rarely rewarded beyond reducing immediate construction costs
and typically do not address long-term savings to the user group.
The P3 project model is intended to bind the developer to the performance standards set forth in
the RFQ and the designers and contractors to the developer for the agreed-upon price for the job.
Similarly, the operation and maintenance contractor on the overall development team is bound to its
long-term bid for operation and maintenance.
Of course, that “long view” business model works only if the public agency, developer, and
design-builder work cooperatively (in true partnership) within the spirit of the contract and for the
best interests of the project as a whole. If either party tries to take advantage of the other, the entire
delivery method is subject to compromise, delays, and increased costs.
The public sector’s emphasis on long-term operating costs comes at a critical time. Historically,
long-term operating costs were not well analyzed, disclosed, or planned for as integral to the cost of
new construction. According to a Brookings Institute report, operation and management (O&M) has
represented only eight percent of total federal grants since 2000.2 But O&M represents more than
half of the total spending on infrastructure, and in some areas, such as mass transit and aviation, the
proportion is two-thirds or greater. 3 So local governments previously had a greater incentive to build
new infrastructure, even if they did not have all of the necessary technical capability or financial
resources to operate or maintain the infrastructure in a safe or efficient manner for its expected
usable life.
C. 	Traditional Barriers to P3 Projects
The principal barriers to P3 projects have been traditional state and local procurement statutes that
require the award of a project to the lowest responsible and responsive bidder after competitive
bidding. This was how the government agency protected the public trust and the public dollar.
2 Barry Bosworth and Sveta Milusheva, Innovations in U.S. Infrastructure Financing: An Evaluation, pp. 3–4 (The Brookings
Institution 2011).
3Id.

60 	CHAPTER 4 PUBLIC-PRIVATE PARTNERSHIPS
In the established public works model, a government agency establishes the concept, design,
financing, and operational characteristics of the project. The bidding statutes require qualified private
contractors to competitively bid on a set of complete plans and specifications prepared by the agency
or a third-party designer. In the traditional model, the private contractor with the lowest responsive
and responsible bid receives the contract. The contractor puts up payment and performance bonds to
assure it will complete construction and pay all its subcontractors and suppliers. Upon completion
of the work, the public agency then operates the facility until it becomes obsolete and needs to be
replaced by another project.
Congress implemented the federal competitive-bidding statutes during the Civil War in response
to concerns over graft and favoritism of procurement contracts. The legislation required “all
purchases and contracts for supplies and services” to be advertised and competitively bid. 4 As
applied to construction contracts, the legislation governing competitive bidding evolved to separate
design-services contracts from construction contracts.5 The procurement of construction services
required approved plans and specifications before competitive bidding. 6 These construction
contracts were awarded to the lowest responsive bidder.7
The Brooks Act 8 mandates selection of design professionals on the basis of qualifications, not
only price, and many states passed “mini Brooks” acts. Thus, a request for bids could not combine
design and construction services because the award criteria differed. In addition, design services are
generally awarded based upon fixed fees or hourly rates, not upon the efficiency or maintainability
of the final designs or construction.
Although not intended to prevent P3 projects, statutes requiring approved plans and specifications
prior to award of a construction contract prevent P3 project delivery. The emphasis on accepting
the low responsive construction bid further limits the scope of the competition for the project to
construction cost alone. The long-term operations costs are generally ignored in this process.
These barriers are being dismantled across the country by statutory authorizations that encourage
proposals to solve critical infrastructure problems with innovative solutions, allow direct investment
in government properties, and authorize private parties to compete for long-term services to the pub-
lic traditionally performed by government employees already stretched by existing responsibilities.
Such statutes are typically described as “enabling legislation.”
D. 	P3 Enabling Legislation
The majority of states now have authorization for P3 projects.
While generalizations are difficult to make, the statutes typically permit award on a best-value
basis when taking into account life-cycle costing and anticipate and authorize a long-term contract
relationship between the public owner and the developer. The expected variation in responses sub-
mitted in response to a P3 request for proposals containing performance specifications is generally
considerable, so a public entity needs the discretion of using best-value criteria to decide between
alternatives with very different technical approaches and attributes.
Table 4.1 indicates whether a state has enabling legislation for three types of P3 projects and
whether the state allows for unsolicited bids for P3 projects. Building construction P3 means verti-
cal construction such as schools or courthouses and is sometimes referred to as social P3 projects.
Transportation and utility P3s are often referred to as horizontal projects or infrastructure P3s. In a
state where unsolicited bids or proposals are allowed, a private developer can initiate the process for
a P3 project it believes is needed and viable by following the specified process to do so.

64 	CHAPTER 4 PUBLIC-PRIVATE PARTNERSHIPS
It is important to be extremely familiar with any particular state’s laws before planning a P3
project because, for example, a state may allow some types of transportation projects to be done
as P3s but not others. Also, keep in mind that just because a state does not have specific enabling
legislation, it does not mean a P3 project is absolutely impossible in that state.
These enabling statutes have not been without their opponents, such as government watch dog or
oversight groups or, in some instances, state or local public employee unions. As an example, the
California Professional Engineers in Government filed a lawsuit to enjoin the implementation of a
California statute to empower the California Department of Transportation (Caltrans) to contract with
private developers to construct and operate tollway facilities under lease agreements with the State. 57
The statute in question arose from a legislative determination that “public sources of revenues to
provide an efficient transportation system have not kept pace with California’s growing transporta-
tion needs, and alternative funding sources should be developed to augment or supplement available
public sources of revenue.”58 In Professional Engineers in California Government v. Department
of Transportation, 59 the court considered agreements between Caltrans and the private developers
to evaluate the union’s challenge to the P3 procurement. The court found that where letting of any
service contract or franchise might open the door to potential abuses, the legislature can adopt other
measures to prevent such abuse. Further, the court found that to discourage this type of experimenta-
tion would denigrate a key purpose of the civil-service mandate to promote efficiency and economy
in state government.60
Similarly, in Professional Engineers in California Government v. Kempton, the California
Supreme Court upheld the contracting out provisions of enabling legislation allowing private pro-
curement of engineering services and held it impliedly repealed prior and inconsistent regulations
and statutes that previously restricted such private awards of engineering services. 61
The attitude in some public-employee union circles is that P3 projects will actually create gov-
ernmental jobs involving the consideration, award, and oversight of these projects—specifically
endeavors that would never come to fruition without the private financing and cost assurances of
a P3 project.
II. 	P3 PROJECT PARTICIPANTS
The participants on any P3 project will be a unique set of government concerns and individual
entities, companies, or consortiums. Typically, a P3 project will have the key participants that are
described in the next sections.
A. 	Sponsoring Government Agency or Owner
It is the responsibility of the lead, sponsoring governmental agency to determine the viability of
constructing a public facility or infrastructure work as a P3 project. Typically, the lead agency can
select the P3 delivery approach only if, and as authorized by, an enabling legislative act as discussed
above.
The lead public agency will serve as the lead agency during the Environmental Impact State-
ment (EIS) or similar state environmental decision-making process. It will manage the RFQ or RFP
57 98 C.A.B. 680 (1989–1990 Sess.), Stats. 1989, Ch. 107 pp. 1017–19, eff. July 10, 1989.
58Id. at § 1.
59 13 Cal. App. 4th 585 (1993) (cited by dissenting opinion at Professional Engineers v. Department of Transportation, 15 Cal.
4th 543 (1997)).
60 98 C.A.B. 680 (1989–1990 Sess.), Stats. 1989, Ch. 107 pp. 1017–1019, eff. July 10, 1989.
61 40 Cal. 4th 1016 (2007).

II. P3 PROJECT PARTICIPANTS 	65
selection process for the developer and negotiate the project contracts, as well as participate in early
design approvals, depending on the structure of the contractual relationships. The lead agency typi-
cally also maintains the contract relationship with the developer for the life of the P3 project.
The public owner should have realistic expectations with respect to its level of control over the
design and day-to-day operations. The price of a P3 has the potential to be lower in part because
the concessionaire is granted the authority to exercise its discretion to identify and take advantage
of cost-saving opportunities while satisfying the contract’s general performance requirements.
The public owner gives up subjective preferences in the design process and certainly in the con-
struction process. The public owner may pay for changes to make subjective design choices, but as
the project proceeds, the owner has less and less influence over the outcome and changes become
progressively more expensive. From a contracting perspective, the owner’s best opportunity to make
design choices and set operational standards is almost exclusively during the RFP and negotiation
process, prior to awarding the P3 contract.
B. 	Construction Manager/Owner Consultants
A construction manager (CM) may assist the lead public entity in developing the RFQ; assist in cre-
ating the selection process for the developer; perform extensive reviews of the developer’s expertise
and proposals; develop and administer the contracts; provide expertise on schedule and constructabil-
ity; manage relationships with funding and oversight agencies; and provide a system of communi-
cations, public information, emergency response, and policy advice for the owner. The CM can also
manage the independent design checkers, cost estimators, and testing firms working directly for the
public entity to ensure that the public owner is getting what it contracted for. In a traditional infras-
tructure P3 project, the public entity, or government owner, frequently assigns a CM to also track,
review, compute, and approve availability payments.
In addition to a CM, sponsoring agencies may have other consultants including a financial or
accounting firm to review the financial proposals submitted in response to an RFQ and legal counsel
to prepare the multifaceted master agreement with the developer. Typically, each lead public agency
creates a team of supporting consultants and advisors to help it assure that the public trust is protected
throughout the life of the P3 project.
C. 	Developer or Concessionaire
The developer or concessionaire is responsible for the financing, design, construction, delivery, and
O&M of the project as a whole. Often the developer is a limited corporate entity created for the sole
purpose of acting as the private entity to administer all aspects of a specific P3 project (also known
as a special or single-purpose entity). All of its obligations to the public owner are spelled out in
a comprehensive, complex master agreement. The developer may have assurances or guarantees of
performance by other business entities, such as parent companies. The developer is likely to assign
all project-development responsibilities prior to substantial completion to a single design-build con-
tractor, who will provide the designer and contracting skills. This creates a single source of both the
design and construction, which provides the developer with a single price up front and allows for
design and construction to proceed in tandem. However, depending on the project, the P3 master
contract and the design-build contract may leave many residual responsibilities with the developer.
The developer may have separate agreements with lenders or a financial entity for both construc-
tion and long-term financing. The developer may also have independent agreements with a different
entity or group of companies for long-term operation and maintenance of the project once it is up
and running. As just described, each P3 project typically generates numerous contract relationships
within the private sector, all flowing down from the master agreement between the lead public entity
and the developer.

-- 103 of 771 --

66 	CHAPTER 4 PUBLIC-PRIVATE PARTNERSHIPS
D. 	Design-Build Entity
The design-builder is the legal entity or partnership that will often supply the design and construction
services for the project. In the event that the developer assigns the design-build entity responsibility
for all tasks prior to substantial completion, this may include permitting and project development
where the design-build entity may need to obtain additional expertise.
The design-build entity is not in contractual privity with the public owner, so it is imperative that
the design-build entity work to ensure it has open lines of communication with the owner and other
stakeholders through the developer who is in contractual privity with the owner.
P3 project costs may be lower because of the working relationship between designers and con-
tractors established from the beginning of the project. This may lead to the incorporation of more
economical design features and the application of cost-saving construction methods. It is important
to understand that P3 contracts are like any other agreement; if one party breaches, there will be
claims and disputes, albeit on a more limited basis. Remember that the developer will expect the
design-build entity to resolve virtually all internal design and construction disputes within itself.
Projects may proceed more efficiently because designers and constructors are members of
the same “team.” The interface between designer and constructor, often adversarial within
design-bid-build systems, may become more open and foster a cooperative exchange of ideas to
produce a profitable project. Construction efficiency may be improved because design efficiencies
can be woven throughout the construction process and because the designer, as a member of
the design-build team, can participate directly in resolving design issues that surface during
construction.
An owner frequently has a less-adversarial role in P3 projects, particularly when it is satisfied with
the original design specifications and allows the P3 concessionaire and its design-build contractor to
accomplish the project within those parameters. The P3 design-builder has a greater chance of seeing
critical flaws early in the design stage when they can be avoided or mitigated. These flaws comprise a
broad array of design, construction, and operational risks that a design-build team is better prepared
to address than is a designer alone. A design-build team can react faster and with more clarity when
design flaws are identified or when ambiguities arise. In the traditional design-bid-build approach,
the response to design flaws or ambiguities is often defensive and hostile. The design-build team
must react immediately since it owns the problem and must therefore correct it promptly.
Operational efficiencies can be identified during the design process. Over the duration of opera-
tions, even small improvements in daily operations or efficiencies can yield substantial savings.
Fast-track procedures allow certain elements of construction to proceed concurrently with the
design process. This method allows work on one element of a project to proceed prior to the design
for the structure being finalized. Fast-track procedures can overlap and compress the design and
construction phases. Thus, the total time from conception to completion can be greatly reduced.
The design-build entity may actually be a consortium itself. There could be several construction
companies working together under an agreement, and the designer may be a combination of multiple
design firms, each with a specific field of specialization. In addition, the design-builder may have
dozens of subcontracts for portions of the work.
E. 	Designer or Engineer of Record
Typically, P3 contracts place a high degree of responsibility and liability for design on the engineer
of record (EOR) identified by the developer.
A consequence of shifting design risks and liabilities onto the developer is that the owner must
give up some control over the details of the ultimate design. If there are a number of acceptable ways

-- 104 of 771 --

II. P3 PROJECT PARTICIPANTS 	67
of building a bridge, the developer should have the ability to choose the least expensive method that
its designer will design.
However, where the public owner insists on taking over the design process, the legal allocation
of design liability can become very blurred. Fundamental to P3 procurement is a clear definition of
overall design responsibility, a process by which the public agency is kept aware of the advancement
of design, and a mechanism for insisting upon and paying for discretionary design changes.
The EOR is typically an engineering firm or individual licensed engineering professional who
takes independent responsibility for the design’s adequacy. State law usually makes the EOR legally
responsible for errors and omissions in the construction plans it signs. Some states require that the
EOR stamp all of the project drawings, even those prepared by other design teams that are outside
of the EOR’s specialty.
F. 	Operation and Maintenance Contractors
On many P3 projects the developer creates, or contracts with, a separate entity or entities to oper-
ate the facility for the life of the facility. Sometimes the operator has the maintenance obligations
and other times those are set out in separate contracts with the developer. The O&M contract(s)
start upon completion of the project, at the “ribbon cutting,” so to speak. Because the payment
schedule or revenue stream from the public owner on many P3 projects is tied to availability or
operational criteria, keeping the facility open, properly maintained, and fully operational are all key
to the developer. Therefore, careful attention is paid to long-term operational considerations during
the conceptual-design phase of the project.
G. 	Other Project Stakeholders
There are often a number of parties that do not have a direct contract with the public owner, the devel-
oper, the design-build entity, or anyone else. However, they still consider themselves stakeholders,
or watchdogs, over a P3 project. Below are some examples.
1. 	Third-Party Government Stakeholders
Significant new public project construction inevitably affects existing government projects and exist-
ing regulatory structures maintained by other government agencies. New highways cross over exist-
ing highways, rail lines, and aqueducts and may require temporary or permanent easements on land
owned by other entities. They may alter traffic patterns in local communities. Potential issues cre-
ated by these interactions are resolved by the lead public agency emphasizing the project vision to
the other affected government entities and negotiating mitigation steps to enhance their cooperation.
The lead agency is often looked at as the public sponsor or champion, 62 in part because of the need
to work with other agencies to resolve any problems that arise and keep the focus on the positive
aspects of the finished project.
The lead agency and other governmental stakeholders should agree upon: (1) compensation to the
affected stakeholders; (2) technical standards, preliminary configurations, and a process for review-
ing final designs; (3) a detailed process for utility relocation; (4) scope and betterment limitations;
(5) dispute resolution; and (6) cost, indemnity, and insurance requirements. Agreements between
government agencies and other governmental stakeholders will ideally be executed and given to
potential developers during the RFP process. By doing so, the lead public agency helps drive down
the total project cost and expedites placing the new project in service.
62 National Council for Public-Private Partnerships, “7 Keys to Success,” www.ncppp.org/ppp-basics/7-keys.

-- 105 of 771 --

68 	CHAPTER 4 PUBLIC-PRIVATE PARTNERSHIPS
2. 	Community Stakeholders
Community organizations can have a strong voice in supporting or opposing public projects. Meeting
with the community and identifying their concerns early in the development of a project concept is a
critical task of both the lead public agency and the P3 developer. Properly allowing continuing com-
munity involvement in the affairs of local agencies with oversight of a P3 project will also enhance
the opportunities for project success.
3. 	Permit Jurisdictions
Many states and the federal government have statutes regulating the impact of projects on public
health, the environment, water quality, air quality, fish and wildlife, and similar issues of public
concern. These statutes and the established agencies and committees that address them have a sig-
nificant influence on the outcome of a P3 infrastructure project. Agencies with permit authority over
projects may often exercise “go” or “no go” authority over the project and thus their early granting
of approvals is essential to a successful and timely P3 project.
These agencies may also attempt to impose expensive and time-consuming requirements and
conditions upon P3 projects where they believe they have the leverage to do so. The lead agency
must manage these expectations and mitigate the impact of these third-party agencies.
4. 	Quality Assurance and Environmental Monitors
A public entity may feel a loss of control over a P3 project, including the ability to control the
design, construction, inspection, testing, and operations. These problems can be overcome with a
set of explicit inspection and testing requirements or criteria for the project, as well as an efficient
review process that allows the developer to exercise creativity and skill but gives the public agency
reasonable project oversight.
The actual construction can be monitored against the approved drawings through independent
third-party construction inspectors, environmental monitors, and safety professionals retained by
the public entity.
III. 	P3 FINANCING STRATEGIES
A. 	Project Financing: Traditional versus P3
Traditional project delivery requires significant up-front payments by the government. These include
preliminary studies, site investigation, property acquisition, and design preparation. Then the gov-
ernment pays as construction work is completed. At project completion, the government pays public
employees to service the facilities. Tax revenues or municipal bond financing most commonly pays
the ultimate construction costs; however, 100 percent of the construction cost has to be available by
the time the project is operational or the project cannot proceed.
Infrastructure planners face stark political realities that often determine whether an agency can
raise funds for infrastructure projects. In California, state bonds require a simple majority of voter
approval to pass, while local bonds require 55 percent or a two-thirds “supermajority.” (Other govern-
ment funding mechanisms for infrastructure include municipal bonds, certificates of participation,
traditional revenue bonds, sales tax allocations, grants, and redevelopment bonds.)
Instead, by turning to a combination of public and private sector financing, the financing of a P3
can reimburse some of the government’s initial costs, and then spread government payments over

-- 106 of 771 --

III. P3 FINANCING STRATEGIES 	69
the life of the project—20 years, 30 years, or longer—to repay the private investment of funds. The
repayment from the public owner for project financing may include “milestone” payments at the
completion of construction or “availability” payments during the operations period. These funds are
paid by the public entity directly to the concessionaire. It is common that no payments whatsoever
are owed until either substantial completion or operational readiness is achieved.
B. 	Public and Private Funding Sources for Construction and Long-Term Financing
A cornerstone of P3 projects is partial or complete private financing. The developer arranges for the
construction and design cost, secures those funds, spends them to get the project operational, and
then, over the life of the P3 project agreement, receives repayment from an agreed-upon combina-
tion of payments from the public or the public owner. This section considers the types of financing
or funding sources developers often use. The repayment methods are discussed in a subsequent
section.
1. 	Transportation Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act (TIFIA)
Private entities can, with public-owner cooperation, apply for TIFIA credit assistance in the form of
secured loans, loan guarantees, and standby lines of credit for qualifying transportation P3 projects.
The private entity can be the borrower for the loan. It is available for transportation projects eligible
for grant assistance under Chapter 53 of Title 49 of the United States Code. 63 The loan period can
be as long as 35 years after substantial completion of the project.
Lenders will have specific reserve account requirements based upon the risks of the particular
project, such as seismic risks or maintenance costs. Security for the loan may include project rev-
enues such as availability payments. The amount of federal credit assistance through TIFIA may not
exceed 33 percent of total reasonably anticipated eligible project costs, so other sources of funding,
such as equity, must also be in place.
2. 	Private Activity Bonds (PABs)
PABs are bonds to finance a variety of business projects, including public infrastructure. Eligible
infrastructure projects, termed “exempt facilities,” include airports, wharves, water-supply projects,
wastewater facilities, and transportation projects.
Governmental authorities must issue PABs; the authority sells the bond and provides the proceeds
to the concessionaire as a loan. Interest paid to bondholders is exempt from taxes. Security for the
loan can include the TIFIA loan and letters of credit.64
3. 	Private Equity
Investments are typically made through special-purpose investment vehicles. The investor provides
equity in exchange for a percentage of future revenues. Many P3 projects require some percentage of
developer equity (5 to 20 percent is common). The developer may require its design-build contractor,
or even its O&M contractor, to provide some portion of that equity. While contractors are not used
to contributing equity to a project, many feel that by doing so the construction company has a better
seat at the table, so to speak, for all aspects of the project.
63 More information on TIFIA can be found on the U.S. Department of Transportation-FHWA-Innovative Project Delivery
website at www.fhwa.dot.gov/ipd/.
64 Internal Revenue Code, Exempt facility bond, 26 U.S.C. § 142.

-- 107 of 771 --

70 	CHAPTER 4 PUBLIC-PRIVATE PARTNERSHIPS
4. 	Contingency Fund
A liquid contingency fund, or cushion, is necessary to handle unexpected costs without violating
financing terms. Unexpected costs could include the financing charges of an excused delay or con-
struction cost overruns.
5. 	Construction Loan
Some P3 projects may be financed with construction loans. The developer commits approximately
20 percent equity into the project’s design and construction costs. The construction loan is secured
by the developer’s equity, future revenue, and individual or corporate guarantees of one or more
companies on the developer’s team. After substantial completion, a lower-rate permanent loan pays
off the construction loan and interest accumulated during construction.
A construction loan can be a particularly vulnerable component of a P3 project, as discussed in a
court opinion involving a project in New York State. Syracuse, New York contributed $170 million
to a P3 project for an 850,000 square-foot shopping mall expansion that combined research, retail,
entertainment, dining, hospitality, and tourism. The private partner, Destiny USA, contributed
$40 million to initiate the project. Citigroup committed to loan $155 million. 65 When the project was
90 percent complete, Citigroup—perhaps motivated by external market pressures in 2008—asserted
that the loan was out of balance and stopped funding the construction draws. Construction halted
and the project was boarded up.
The mall was completed after the courts sided with the contractor. The courts rejected Citigroup’s
claim that the contractor was in breach of the “deficiency” provision, which required that comple-
tion costs did not exceed the amount of the loan yet to be advanced. The court concluded that the
deficiency provision was a clearly defined formula and Citigroup’s interpretation was unreasonable.
After the contractor posted a $15 million bond to the court, payments resumed, and the project was
successfully completed.
6. 	WIFIA and other Federal Funding
In 2014, bipartisan support for P3 projects for water supply and treatment projects resulted in the
enactment of the federal Water Resources Reform and Development Act. A key provision of this
legislation is the Water Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act (WIFIA), a five-year pilot program
modeled on TIFIA, discussed previously, that authorizes the EPA to provide credit assistance (loans
or loan guarantees) for a range of drinking water and wastewater projects and to provide similar
assistance to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers for water-resource projects, such as flood control or
hurricane and storm damage reduction.
The act authorized appropriations of $175 million over five years to both the EPA and the
Corps (beginning with $20 million for each agency in FY2015 and increasing to $50 million in
FY2019). Project costs must generally be $20 million or larger to be eligible for credit assistance.
In rural areas (defined by WIFIA as populations of 25,000 or less), project costs must be $5 million
or more. 66
Numerous other sources of federal funding can be found for the right project, like the federal
“green bonds” intended for green building projects authorized by the American Jobs Creation Act
of 2004, included in the IRS code with PABs discussed above.67 These funds tend to have strings
65Destiny USA Holdings, LLC v. Citigroup Global Markets Realty Corp. 889 N.Y.S.2d 793 (N.Y. App. Div. 2009).
66See Water Infrastructure Financing: The Water Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act (WIFIA) Program, Updated
September 26, 2018; https://fas.org/sgp/crs/misc/R43315.pdf.
67 Internal Revenue Code, Exempt facility bond, 26 U.S.C. § 142.

attached; if a recipient of the green bonds substantially fails to comply with the act, the recipient
may lose its security and be forced to pay a higher interest rate to investors to pay the taxes on the
now-taxed bonds.
7. 	Land Transfers to Developer
A creative funding source used particularly in dense urban areas is “land swaps.” Public owners
transfer land (through full title transfer or long-term leases, such as 99-year leases) to the project
developer, often with improved zoning, and the developer is entitled to develop and sell or lease to
private buyers. The future sales act as security for and ultimately fund the public improvements.
A land swap was carefully orchestrated with numerous other funding sources to raise funds for
the $2.3 billion (phase 1 only) San Francisco Transbay Terminal when state-owned property became
nonproductive after an earthquake-damaged highway was dismantled. The state gave certain land
parcels to the city, which sold the parcels to third-party developers and is using the revenue to pay
off the terminal bonds. 68
Another example is in Lake Tahoe, where public recreational areas have been landlocked by dense
private development. The Tahoe Regional Planning Agency initially transferred certain property
rights to a private developer. With the revenue from the public contribution, the developer constructed
a bike path through a residential area that linked landlocked recreation areas. 69 The project was
challenged and temporarily derailed by environmental litigation, but has since blossomed into a
comprehensive system of bike paths.
The City of El Paso, Texas, funded a minor league ballpark with a public-private partnership.
The city’s contribution to the project included the land underneath the city hall. A former mayor
led an attempt to stop the project with a ballot initiative and corresponding lawsuit, protesting
the demolition of city hall. The lawsuit was dismissed on procedural grounds and construction
proceeded.70
A variation on a land swap permitted a redevelopment project in Camden, New Jersey. In
exchange for investing in a vast office park, Campbell Soup was authorized to demolish a historic
Sears building that was funded with public and private funds. The project proceeded after a lawsuit
around the building’s historic status. 71
A variety of P3 projects is described and tracked on the website of the United States Department
of Transportation Federal Highway Administration’s Center for Innovative Finance Support. 72
C. 	P3 Payment Mechanisms from the Public Owner
On a large P3 project, the developer may have expended hundreds of millions of dollars to get the
project up and operational. How will the public or public owner repay that cost, plus a reasonable
rate of return to the investors? The most common methods of public-owner payments are discussed
in the next sections.

1. 	Availability Payments
Availability payments are fixed compensation paid periodically by the public owner to the developer
based on the availability of the completed infrastructure. The “maximum” availability payment is
subject to reductions based on penalties for performance deficiencies or downtime.
Availability payments can be selected even for projects where services are paid for by individual
users. For example, if needed, availability payments to supplement toll revenue may reduce uncer-
tainty of future revenue for the private investors or financiers over the 20 or more years of operations.
This method appears to be a common repayment choice, probably because developers are assumed
to substantially discount the value of future user payments to account for uncertainties. The owner
can alternatively structure affordable payments, while toll road operators expect exclusivity if they
shoulder demand risk.
Lease-Leaseback is a form of availability payment that typically describes office space or public
buildings such as a courthouse. 73 For consideration as little as one dollar, the public entity provides a
long-term lease, such as 20 to 30 years, on public property. The developer builds a public-use facility
on the property and the public entity leases back the completed facility. The rent paid by the public
entity pays the developer’s costs and profits.
2. 	User Fees/Tolls
In this approach, the developer is granted an exclusive right to collect fees from the users of the
facility or service. Traditional examples are toll roads and water and wastewater systems that bill
for gallons of water delivered or treated. If there is no other financial commitment from the public
owner, the developer is at risk on these types of projects. Several P3 projects have been unsuccessful
in the transportation area where user projections for tolls were higher than actual usage. The projects
failed from a financial standpoint. P3 agreements may include limitations or guidelines on increasing
toll rates or other user fees.
There are other types of user fees, including airport fees under the FAA’s “Airport Privatization
Pilot Program.” Under the program, an airport can be sold or leased to a private entity and the private
entity can receive the airport fees from carriers. 74
3. 	Milestone Payments
Milestone payments reward the developer for interim progress on the infrastructure project before it
is operational and earning other types of revenue.75
Milestone payments are tied to job progress and are logical from the construction contractor’s
standpoint. However, they are independent of time, unlike debt service. This may be a consideration
in the private-partner agreements and insurance.
D. 	P3 Project Long-Term Cost-Benefit Analysis—A Final Financial Note
The comparison of the overall procurement cost between a P3 project and a traditional
design-bid-build project is called a “value for money analysis” or a “public sector comparator.” The
Federal Highway Administration published an introduction to the method in 2012. 76
