IV. P3 RISK ALLOCATION 	73
Some agencies have published their project-specific analyses, which can be educational.
The outcomes are driven by assumptions about discount rates and equitable allocations
of risk. 77
Historically, public agencies often described projects using just the “construction cost.” This is a
deceptive way of portraying the actual project costs. The so-called “soft” expenses, which include
very real expenditures such as agency administration, project management, design and engineering,
inspection and testing, software installation and maintenance, startup and performance testing, and
related expenses, can meet or exceed construction costs. These are illuminated in a public-sector
comparator.
It is lamentably rare for a public agency to disclose to the public the realistic, long-term costs of
a project. It seems appropriate in an era of desired transparency and openness in government and
the public markets that the public be given a realistic estimate of the overall costs of major public
decisions for the life of the project. Such public disclosure is vital when comparing the various types
of project delivery systems.
IV. 	P3 RISK ALLOCATION
A. 	Risk Shifting to the Developer
In traditional contracts, the contractor is entitled to additional payment for “extra work,” which is
defined as work not covered by any of the bid items. The contractor is responsible only for the
work it reasonably expected from the scope of the work described in the plans and specifications
(bid documents). The owner takes responsibility for extra work. In a P3 project, the bulk of the
design risk is transferred from the public entity to the developer. Not only does the developer assume
the risk for design errors, but it becomes responsible for an array of differing site conditions and
other contingencies. Some risks on P3 projects are not readily insurable; if they are allocated to the
developer, it must assume those risks. Changes in the labor market, schedule risks, and construction
cost overruns are examples of risks frequently assumed by developers. Such cost increases must be
built into the contingency.
The public owner is better situated to retain certain responsibilities and attendant risks, such as
necessary permits or procurement items with long lead times. For example, a proposed project sub-
ject to the National Environmental Policy Act and that requires exhaustive environmental studies
and public comment is likely to experience permitting delays, a risk that a developer may not be
able to assume efficiently. That risk can be nearly cost-free for the public owner who can pace
the award of the P3 project with the progress of governmental approvals. Such risks are therefore
typically mitigated by the public owner by delaying advertisement of a project until those project
requirements are understood, governmental approvals are fully obtained, and the critical permits
obtained.
The contractor must carefully review the contract for the risks associated with permitting delays.
In Bell/Heery v. United States, the contractor sued the owner, the Federal Bureau of Prisons (FBP),
claiming that delays in obtaining certain permits from the New Hampshire Department of Envi-
ronment Services should have been borne by the FBP because the FBP had a duty to intervene in
the permitting process but did not. 78 The court ruled that the contractor assumed and was solely
responsible for that risk because the contract stated that the contractor was responsible for comply-
ing with all state laws, regulations, and permitting requirements “without additional expense to the
77See, e.g., Commonwealth of Virginia, Office of Public-Private Partnerships, PPTA Risk Management Guidance (September
2015) available at www.p3virginia.org/ppta-resources/.
78 106 Fed. Cl. 300 (2012).

-- 111 of 771 --

74 	CHAPTER 4 PUBLIC-PRIVATE PARTNERSHIPS
Government.”79 The court found that the contractor did not adequately complain to the government
agency that its delays and lack of cooperation were delaying the ability of the contractor to obtain
the required local government permits.
P3 contracts may categorize potential delays and cost escalations within a series of definitions
described as relief events. The public owner specifies the unexpected events for which it will bear
the risk and the developer is assumed to take responsibility for every conceivable risk outside of
that list.
Some typical compensable events that may be relief events are discussed elsewhere in this book
and include:
• Force majeure event
• Change in law
• Owner breach of contract
• Discovery of hazardous materials
• Discovery of endangered animals or historic ruins or artifacts within the project boundaries
• Owner-caused delay
• Unreasonable delays by permitting entities
• Owner changes
• Differing site conditions
However, the courts and common law will not allow a public owner to hide known or suspected
risks behind such disclaimer language or be immune from liability for lack of good faith or cooper-
ation during the project.
B. 	Redesign Risk and Changes
When the developer is heavily involved in planning and design from the early stages of the project,
it will have little recourse for the costs of redesign due to errors, except against its own designer or
its design-build entity.
Following the policy that risks are allocated to the party best positioned to manage the particular
risk, designers may take responsibility for quantity overruns when their preliminary designs are
used in bid preparation. This is a contractually assumed risk that the developer should build into the
design contract so that the designer is liable to the developer for design defects. Errors and omissions
coverage will typically not insure this risk, so designers need to be aware of this limitation when
negotiating their contract with the developer.
When the developer is responsible for design, the public owner must realize it is giving up some
ability to control design choices. There is no point to having the developer and design-build entity
assume complete legal and cost responsibility for design and at the same time allow the public agency
to remain so deeply involved in the design process that the developer is left with no choices. Under
that circumstance, the public owner may end up bearing the costs of its excessive design involvement
and the resulting extra costs and schedule delays.
After the P3 agreement is signed, the question should no longer be what the owner or third-party
agencies want the project to look like, but whether the developer’s design choices satisfy the
project’s operational or performance criteria and design specifications. Particularly with perfor-
mance specifications, the question of design adequacy becomes solely whether the design meets the
79Id. at 304.

-- 112 of 771 --

IV. P3 RISK ALLOCATION 	75
P3 criteria and the industry standard of care. Once again, this underscores the importance of using
care in defining the original design criteria.
The architect/engineer (A/E) or EOR will be subject to the professional negligence standard of
care unless the contract provides for a higher standard. 80 The public owner may want to require a
higher standard, such as that provided in the following provision excerpted from a public design
contract drafted by a city attorney:
The architect shall perform the professional services in accordance with the highest profes-
sional standards of those architects practicing in the [designated locale] area and engaged in
providing [designated type of services] design and construction services.
However, because such standards go beyond the traditional common law standard of care, they
may not be insurable under customary malpractice insurance policies available to design profession-
als. (See Chapter 9.)
Shifting responsibility for the design onto the developer can reduce the number of change orders.
The developer will be responsible for any design-related change orders from contractors, subcon-
tractors, and suppliers. By delegating project development to an independent third party, the owner
eliminates from its portfolio a huge and costly source of risk and litigation in the form of subse-
quent change orders. However, where the owner insists on design changes, modifications, and style
changes to suit the public agency staff’s desires, the owner should expect to pay for those increased
costs and delay expenses.
C. 	Design Approvals by Stakeholders
As noted, many stakeholders with influence over projects do not have a direct contract with
the developer. As an example, negotiations of right-of-way agreements with other authorities
having jurisdiction (AHJ) need to address the agreed-upon scope of the project and the process of
incorporating final comments from government entities with whom the developer does not have
a direct contractual relationship. Such agreements must incorporate clear scope, standards, time
limits, and a rapid binding dispute-resolution process of design issues with the AHJ. Otherwise,
the developer may sustain delays and liquidated damages while the AHJ is unapologetically
uncooperative.
One solution is to define AHJ delays as a relief event to the developer and excuse those delays
that are out of the developer’s control. Another solution is to grant the developer the right to enforce
the right-of-way agreement of the public entities against the AHJ in court (perhaps by identifying
the owner’s developer as a third-party beneficiary).
D. 	Permits and Governmental Approvals
P3 contracts may involve a higher level of developer responsibility for governmental approvals
and permitting. Owners will often attempt to transfer this risk to the developer using language
such as “developer shall be solely responsible for compliance with the requirements of the Gov-
ernmental Approvals.” The better approach is to have the developer initiate those discussions and
efforts, but allow a safety-valve handoff to the public agency when those efforts stall or are unduly
delayed.
80Gagne v. Bertran, 275 P.2d 15 (Cal. 1954).

-- 113 of 771 --

76 	CHAPTER 4 PUBLIC-PRIVATE PARTNERSHIPS
E. 	Taxes
Real property taxes should be kept in mind when structuring a P3 project. Typically, property taxes
are not paid on government-owned property. However, when land swaps or long-term leases are used,
the P3 starts looking more like privately owned property subject to property taxes. These taxes could
add to the cost of the project, around two percent of the value of the property per year. Avoiding or
accounting for such cost should be addressed.
As an example of how real property taxes might be avoided, Provident Group—Continuum Prop-
erties, L.L.C., was a nonprofit organization formed to develop, own, and manage student housing on a
private parcel adjacent to the University of Florida. The agreement included turning over the property
to the university, at no cost, at the end of the project term. In Crapo v. Provident Group—Continuum
Properties, L.L.C., the First District Court of Appeal of Florida held that the university was an equi-
table owner of the property and thus the project was exempt from property taxes.81
F. 	Prevailing Wages
Because public entities are by definition involved in P3 projects, the parties must beware of the
potential that the Construction Wage Rate Requirements statute 82 or similar state prevailing-wage
acts may apply.
For the Construction Wage Rate Requirements statute to apply, the public entity must be a party
to the contracts for construction and the project must be a public work. In District of Columbia v.
Department of Labor,83 the Department of Labor’s Administrative Review Board initially determined
that the CityCenterDC development constituted a “public work” within the meaning of the statute
and thus workers should have been paid prevailing wages. The United States Court of Appeals,
District of Columbia Circuit reversed, however, holding that the statute did not apply to construction
of CityCenterDC because the District of Columbia was not a signatory to the construction contracts
and the project was not a public work because: (1) there was no public funding for the project’s
construction; and (2) the government would not own or operate the completed facility (as with a
public highway or a public park) because the lease to the P3 was for 99 years. Thus, the Carpenters’
Union lost their claim for the difference between prevailing wages and wages actually paid by the
contractors who built CityCenterDC.
Would the result have been different if the lease documents had included the construction contract
or if the lease had been of shorter duration, leaving the District of Columbia owning a functional
facility at the end of the lease term? Future cases may answer these and other questions about the
applicability of prevailing-wage laws.
G. 	Increased Risks by Flow Down
Because of the financing component, the developer is the only party with a direct contract relationship
with the public owner. When the public owner puts risks on the developer, the developer flows these
down to its design-build contractor. Many large construction companies find themselves in something
of a subcontractor role to the developer in that regard. If the master agreement prepared by the public
owner and its team of consultants is onerous and pushes all risks over to the developer, that increased
risk profile will flow down to the designers and contractors at all levels.
81Crapo v. Provident Group—Continuum Properties, L.L.C., 238 So.3d 869 (2018).
82 Formerly known as the Davis-Bacon Act.
83District of Columbia v. Department of Labor, 819 F.3d 444 (2016).

V. CONCLUSION 	77
H. 	Lower-Tier Payment Risks
In many respects, P3 projects are still public projects. The public owner enters into a contract with an
entity that includes construction of a public work. Under most traditional public works projects, the
public owner must require that the contractor or entity building the public work provide performance
and payment bonds to guarantee payment for all materials and labor used on the public project. The
delegation of the financing obligation to a private entity on a P3 project blurs this issue.
On a completely private construction project, it is up to the owner to decide if it wants to require
payment and performance bonds. Contractors’ right to payment is typically protected through liens
and stop-payment notices, and owners may protect their property by requiring such bonds. On
P3’s, because the public owns the land, liens are not allowed, and stop-payment notices are use-
less if the financing entity is unable to pay. Some states’ P3 enabling legislation addresses perfor-
mance and payment concerns, but others do not. Additionally, the statutes’ protections are uneven
and inconsistent; within the same state, some P3 projects may be covered, while others are not.
Some require performance but not payment bonds, and some are mandatory while others are sug-
gestive. If the state’s P3 enabling legislation does not expressly require the developer to secure
performance and payment bonds, the public owner often does not include that requirement in the
project’s RFQ.
Performance and payment protection legislation is an evolving area of the law and a consortium
of surety and subcontractor associations is tracking this evolution.84 References to performance and
payment protections legislation have been included in Table 4.1, above.
V. 	CONCLUSION
It is clear that public-private projects are a powerful vehicle for financing, maintaining, and enhanc-
ing the nation’s infrastructure.
As these projects increase in scope and complexity, the public and private sector will find that
the availability of private capital will allow projects to be accomplished that would otherwise have
languished for years, awaiting public grants or financing that may never come.
The acceptability of unsolicited proposals allows community leaders and private entities to pro-
pose, finance, and construct valuable public improvements, such as libraries, bridges, schools, and
hospitals, that the public agencies might not have the will or creativity to bring into being during the
lifetimes of those who need or might enjoy the fruits of such projects.
➣ 	POINTS TO REMEMBER
• A P3 project typically involves four key participants: (1) the sponsoring governmental agency;
(2) the private developer with financing responsibility; (3) a design-build entity; and (4) an
O&M operator.
• The decision as to which of the many P3 approaches will best serve the public’s interests will
depend on factors including, but not limited to, the type of facility being constructed, the rev-
enue flow that the facility will generate, and the structure of the P3 enabling statute governing
the project.

• Inevitably, there will be many project participants and stakeholders and all of their interests

5
INTERNATIONAL
CONSTRUCTION CONTRACTS
What do we mean when we talk about international construction law and contracts? Theoretically,
we should be talking about the law that affects or is applied to construction projects that take place
anywhere in the world. But that definition is not sufficient. Rather, in this context, we are talking
about certain legal considerations and principles that are applied to construction contracts performed
outside the United States. Even with this limitation, to tackle this subject fully would require a
multivolume treatise. We are, however, limited to a single chapter. Consequently, we will limit our
discussion to some key legal issues that should be considered when working on construction projects
abroad.
There is no universally adopted “international law” for construction projects. Instead, the con-
tracting parties are typically at liberty, within certain limits, to adopt the law or laws that they want
to govern their contract and performance. That being said, when determining their risks and respon-
sibilities, the participants will most often look to the contract terms; the law governing the contract;
particular, albeit limited, legal concepts that are recognized in the international community at large;
and the law of the country in which the project is located.
This chapter will: (1) identify some of the unique issues and key risks facing those doing work in
developing countries and areas with a less-established legal system; (2) acknowledge some standard
contract forms that are used for international projects; (3) discuss some international commercial
principles that can be used or to which parties may look for guidance; and (4) address the vehicles
for resolving disputes.
I. 	UNIQUE ISSUES
When performing work abroad, a number of unique issues may arise, depending on the country in
which the work is being performed and the law that governs the contract relationship.
• Currency fluctuation and escalation. This is typically a problem in countries facing severe
inflation or deflation. The problem with currency fluctuation is best addressed in the contract
through the use of formulas designed to adjust payments in light of the fluctuations or by
designating a particular, stable currency to be used.
79

-- 117 of 771 --

80 	CHAPTER 5 INTERNATIONAL CONSTRUCTION CONTRACTS
• Use of different forms of performance security. Letters of credit and bank guarantees are often
used or required in lieu of performance and payment bonds. Letters of credit generally provide
greater security than performance bonds but are less desirable and a greater risk for the party
furnishing the letter of credit.
• Expropriation, seizure, or nationalization by the government in which the project is located.
• Protecting intellectual property rights and technology transfer.
• National and local civil unrest. This can result in supply chain interruptions (for example, fuel,
materials, equipment) and the inability to obtain government approvals or authorizations, all
of which can delay project completion and lead to additional project costs.
• Cultural and religious considerations. For example, the parties may need to account for pro-
longed national and religious holidays when developing work schedules and setting milestones.
• Site security and access to hostile areas. This may include the use of private security forces and
the development of contingency plans for evacuation of project personnel.
• The application of certain human rights and unique health and safety considerations (for
example, disease prevention).
• Delays in obtaining government approvals and permits due to local bureaucratic constriction.
• Changes in government.
• Changes in laws. These can often be extreme, especially if they are in response to a change in
government. Force majeure provisions can address this problem, along with other unforesee-
able events noted here.
• Labor camps and use of foreign labor. For example, obtaining visas can be time consuming
and difficult in many countries.
• The application of World Bank or other development bank standards.
• Force majeure. This term and its application should be defined in detail in the contract and not
be left open to interpretation or to customary practices.
• Stringent or unique lender or financier requirements. This can be particularly important in
projects in high-risk countries or with owners that are considered high risks.
• Requirements that certain documents be certified or otherwise verified officially and unique
obligations to confirm the transmission and receipt of documents by and between the parties.
• Labor unrest and limitations on labor practices or obligations to labor unions.
• Language and translation issues. Contracting parties should realize that not all terms, words, or
phrases can be translated into another language, and important meanings can be lost in trans-
lation. Some governments or owners may require certified translations for certain documents.
• Sustainability and climate-change requirements.
• Export controls that will govern export of materials to certain countries or under certain circum-
stances (for example, the International Traffic in Arms Regulation or the Export Administration
Regulation).
• Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and other anti-corruption laws.
• Taxes, including Value-Added Tax (VAT). Taxes on equipment purchases can be avoided if
the resident project owner purchases the equipment directly. Doing so, however, creates new
issues, such as shifting risks and responsibilities for equipment delivery.
• Import regulations, including tariffs on temporary and permanent equipment.
• Governing law. This not only includes the law stated in the contract, but also the law of the
country in which the project is located, which in some cases can override the law governing
the contract.

-- 118 of 771 --

• Security interests and lien rights and unique problems with insolvent and bankrupt project par-
ticipants. Front-end protective measures may be necessary, such as requiring advance payments
by a project owner or requiring that the owner post an irrevocable standby letter of credit for
certain amounts in order to guard against insolvency or a payment default.
• Unique insurance requirements, such as the obligation to maintain decennial liability insurance.
• Unusual differing site conditions (for example, former war zones, environmental conditions,
unique geological conditions).
• Subcontracting. This may involve laws or regulations requiring the use of local subcontractors
or vendors or design and engineering firms.
Although some of these items will be governed by the law of the country in which the project is
located, most of them can and should be addressed within the contract documents so that there is no
ambiguity as to how they will be handled.
II. 	PROJECT DELIVERY METHODS AND CONTRACT FORMS
Project delivery methods outside of the United States are not dissimilar to those used within U.S.
borders. Smaller projects will often use design-bid-build or basic design-build methods under a lump
sum (fixed price) or cost reimbursable (with or without a guaranteed maximum price) basis for
payment. There is, however, a greater reliance on a variety of turnkey approaches outside the United
States markets. More sophisticated and high-risk project delivery methods, such as Engineer, Procure
& Construct (EPC), Build Operate Transfer (BOT), Build Own Operate (BOO), Build Own Operate
& Transfer (BOOT), Build Own Operate & Maintain (BOOM), and Public-Private Partnerships (P3),
are common, especially for larger projects. Many of these forms of delivery are gaining popularity
due to the need for project financing and difficulties obtaining financing from traditional loan sources.
Contracts for major public and private works are typically bespoke (custom), although they are
often modeled after the forms published by Federation Internationale des Ingenieurs Conseils stan-
dard form contracts, commonly referred to as the FIDIC contracts (www.fidic.org). The following
FIDIC contract forms are available for a variety of project delivery methods:
• The Green Book—Short Form of Contract (1999), recommended for smaller engineering and
construction projects.
• The Red Book—Conditions of Contract for Construction for Building and Engineering Works
Designed by the Employer (2017).
• The Pink Book (MDB edition)—Conditions of Contract for Construction for Building and
Engineering Works Designed by the Employer (2010), for use with Multilateral Development
Banks.
• The Yellow Book—Conditions of Contract for Plant and Design-Build (2017), primarily for
electrical and mechanical plant and for building works designed by the contractor.
• The Orange Book—Conditions of Contract for Design-Build and Turnkey (1995). The Orange
Book has, in large part, become abandoned in favor of the Yellow Book and Silver Book.
• The Silver Book—Conditions of Contract for EPC/Turnkey Projects (2017). This is typically
used on energy and other industrial projects that require procurement of large process equip-
ment or testing and commissioning of complex works.
• The Gold Book (DBO Contract)—Conditions of Contract for Design, Build and Operate
Projects (2008).

-- 119 of 771 --

82 	CHAPTER 5 INTERNATIONAL CONSTRUCTION CONTRACTS
The FIDIC forms are widely used for their Conditions of Contract, which are general contract
terms and conditions governing the works. Each of the FIDIC Conditions typically comes with
sample forms of the letter of tender, contract agreement, performance guarantees, and similar
types of contract documents. The Conditions of Contract are designed to be modified or supple-
mented through the use of specialized Particular Conditions, which are negotiated and drafted by
the parties.
The FIDIC forms are well-recognized throughout the global construction market and, generally,
both owners and contractors are comfortable with them, realizing that they will often need to
be modified extensively to fit particular project requirements and characteristics. From a legal
standpoint, any modifications to the FIDIC forms must be done with the view of making sure
that the revisions accurately reflect the scope of work and allocation of risk that the parties
negotiated and that ambiguities are minimized. The FIDIC forms must also be harmonized with
other contract documents, such as technical specifications and drawings. Modifications to the form
documents should be made to assure consistency with requirements in loan documents, concession
agreements, and other similar obligations that the project owner may have to others. This is
particularly important in project delivery systems using BOOT, BOO, BOOM, and P3 delivery
methods.
The FIDIC forms were traditionally viewed as containing balanced terms and conditions and risk
allocation. Many in the international construction law field, however, believe that this changed with
FIDIC’s introduction of the Silver and Gold Books. The Silver Book particularly demonstrated a
shift of placing most risks (for example, differing site conditions and owner design criteria) on the
contractor. This was consistent with an overall trend in the owner and lender community placing as
much risk as possible on the contractor, especially with larger infrastructure and energy projects.
Thus, contractors finding themselves faced with these forms will want to make sure they review the
terms and conditions carefully and make adjustments through the Particular Conditions, unless they
are willing to accept the proposed risk transfer.
In somewhat of a counter to this trend, some owners and contractors have moved away from
the turnkey approach for larger construction works. The use of EPCM (Engineering, Procurement,
Construction Management) as a project delivery method has gained ground over the past several
years. Under this approach, the contractor avoids contracting with the major construction trades,
which are placed directly under contract with the owner. The positive side to this approach for
project owners is that it reduces multiplier or markup and contingency that contractors use in a
traditional EPC form of delivery to cover the various financial risks. EPCM also allows the owner
to break up large projects into smaller packages that may be more easily managed and that are not
reliant on a single source for delivery. For the contractor, it also offers some benefits, the most basic
being the elimination of risks inherent in turnkey project delivery methods (that is, the contractor
is no longer responsible for the entire project). The downside to this approach is that the owner
assumes several risks, including the overall risk of coordinating the scopes of work and schedules
among the various contractors. Consequently, this approach has often led to the owner facing mul-
tiple claims due to the fact that there is no longer a single point of responsibility to deliver the
entire project.
Although the FIDIC forms are certainly the most common and often used forms in the interna-
tional construction market, 1 they are by no means the only ones. Construction contract forms are
offered by the Joint Contracts Tribunal,2 the Engineering Advancement Association of Japan,3 the
1 A notable exception occurs when parties contract with international financial institutions, such as the World Bank. These
institutional lenders will often resort to standard form contacts published by the FIDIC, but may also incorporate their own
unique terms for contracts and subcontracts that result from their financing.
2 www.jctltd.co.uk.
3 www.enaa.or.jp.

New Engineering Contract (NEC), 4 and the International Chamber of Commerce. 5 Like the FIDIC
forms, most of these forms will require modifications to fit the particular project characteristics and
needs.
Many of the international (that is, non–United States) contract forms use certain terminology
and provisions that may be unfamiliar to those operating primarily within U.S. borders. Terminol-
ogy should not be a major problem because the terms are typically well defined in the contract
documents—for example, the use of the term employer in the FIDIC forms versus the term owner
in the American Institute of Architects forms; or the use of the word tender versus bid, variations
versus change, or programme versus schedule. Parties must understand not only the terminology
and the formal definition of terms, but also how those terms are typically used and understood. The
meaning of a term should never be taken for granted and confusion in terminology can often be
cleared up through careful contract drafting.
Differences with respect to what are considered standard contract provisions can also be a source
of confusion. For instance, the use of payment and performance bonds is not as common on projects
outside of the United States. Instead, the contractor will often furnish a bank guaranty or letter of
credit in order to secure performance. Procuring these instruments can be difficult, especially where
the contractor does not have the requisite financial stability or balance sheet. Advance payments by
the project owner (employer) are also common, especially in developing countries or where large
pieces of equipment must be procured early and vendors require payments up front for the equipment.
This is done to lessen the contractor’s risk of nonpayment during the initial stages of the project.
As already noted above, currency escalation clauses are also frequently used when payment will
be made in a currency subject to large fluctuations. These are merely examples and by no means
exhaustive.
Finally, and most important, when working on a project internationally, the contract terms them-
selves take on more importance than when doing work in the United States or other countries with
well-developed legal systems and precedence. In the United States, when certain contract terms are
absent, ambiguous, or otherwise grossly unfair, there is a body of law to which the parties can turn to
supply the missing terms, interpret the terms, or possibly rectify the unfair terms. This may not be the
case in most other countries. Rather, when determining the parties’ rights, responsibilities, and reme-
dies, it is to the contract that the parties, arbitrators, adjudicators, and judges will turn. This means
that the contract terms must be clear and detailed and address the variety of issues that may be faced
throughout the project cycle. The scope of work must be well defined so that the parties understand
the project and its various facilities that will be delivered. This in turn means that the parties must
spend the time, effort, and money to make certain that the contract documents are complete and leave
no room—or at least as little as possible—for confusion. From defining terminology to accounting
for unusual circumstances and contingencies, the contract will typically be the determining factor
when deciding the rights, responsibilities, risk, and remedies of the parties.
A. 	UNIDROIT Principles of International Commercial Contracts
Despite the fact that there is no universally adopted body of law governing international construction
projects, there have been efforts to develop some standard legal principles. In 1994, the International
Institute for the Unification of Private Law (UNIDROIT) published the UNIDROIT Principles of
International Commercial Contracts (the Principles) with the goal of establishing a consistent body of
4 www.newcontract.com. The current version of NEC’s Engineering and Construction Contract (referred to as NEC3) has

law for international commercial contracts, including service contracts. Its stated goal is to “establish
a balanced set of rules designed for use throughout the world irrespective of the legal traditions
and the economic and political conditions of the countries in which they are to be applied.”6 For
those familiar with contract law as applied in the United States, the Principles are similar to the
Restatement of Contracts and use general contracting principles common to many of the world’s
legal systems.7 Now in its fourth edition (2016), the Principles have proven useful in interpreting
construction contracts across borders. The Principles are applied when: (1) the parties have contrac-
tually agreed to be bound by them; (2) the parties have agreed to be bound by general principles
of law (lex mercatoria); (3) there is no chosen law governing the contract; (4) there is a need to
interpret or supplement international uniform law instruments; and (5) there is a need to interpret or
supplement domestic law.8
As the Principles are nonbinding, parties may use the Principles in whole, in part, or in a
modified form. 9 Unless contracted for by the parties, the Principles will not prevail over mandatory
national, international, or supranational laws, except in certain circumstances.10 Contracts that
infringe on mandatory rules, including statutory provisions and general principles of public
policy, are subject to the effects delineated in those mandatory rules.11 If those rules are silent,
parties may exercise remedies under the contract that are reasonable pursuant to Principle
Article 3.3.1. 12
The Principles currently contains 11 chapters addressing topics from general contracting princi-
ples to performance to set-off and assignment. Some of these warrant a brief discussion here.
1. 	Contract Interpretation/Modification
Pacta sunt servanda (“agreements must be kept”) is a bedrock principle that contracts are binding
on all parties. 13 Contracts are interpreted in accordance with the objective intention of the parties.14
Parties must abide by any agreed upon usages and practices15 and principles of good faith, fair
dealing, 16 and cooperation. 17 Contracts may be modified or terminated upon agreement of all parties
or in the following other circumstances:18
• Breach of obligation of good faith and fair dealing19
• Mistake of law or fact 20
• Fraud21

2. 	Excuses for Nonperformance
Nonperformance may be justified in two situations: hardship26 or force majeure. 27 If one party expe-
riences a hardship, such that there is a “fundamental alteration of the equilibrium of the contract,”
the disadvantaged party is entitled to request renegotiations.28 The request for renegotiation alone,
however, does not allow the disadvantaged party to withhold performance.29 But if renegotiations are
unsuccessful, either party may resort to the courts that then have the power to terminate or adapt the
contract. 30 A hardship must “lead to a fundamental alteration of the equilibrium of the contract” 31
for a party to request a renegotiation of the contract for adaptation to the changed circumstances. 32
If the parties fail to reach an agreement, they may resort to a court or arbitral tribunal, which can
terminate or adapt the contract. 33
Although the term force majeure is widely used in contracts, its meaning in this context is different
because it does not restrict the party not receiving performance from terminating the contract. 34
Instead, when it applies, it excuses the nonperforming party from liability for damages. As is typical
of force majeure clauses, the impediment that causes nonperformance must be one that could not have
reasonably been taken into account at the time of contracting.35 Force majeure may be invoked when
an unforeseeable impediment outside of a party’s control affects the party’s ability to perform. 36 The
party invoking force majeure must provide notice to the other party of its inability to perform within
a reasonable time. 37
3. 	Damages
An aggrieved party is entitled to full compensation for any harm suffered as a result of unexcused
nonperformance38 as long as it can establish the harm “with a reasonable degree of certainty.”39
However, the nonperforming party is only liable for harm that was reasonably foreseeable as an
effect of nonperformance at the conclusion of the contract.40

4. 	Requirement of Good Faith and Fair Dealing
Good faith and fair dealing is essential in international trade and must be observed for the duration of
the contract, including the negotiation process.41 The standard is not applied based on the differing
national legal systems, but on what is generally accepted internationally, viewed in light of the special
conditions of international trade. 42 The principle is considered so important that the parties may not
exclude it.43
5. 	Implied Terms
Implied terms or obligations may arise from four different sources: (1) the nature and purpose of the
contract; (2) practices established between the parties and usages; (3) good faith and fair dealing;
and (4) reasonableness. 44 Some implied terms may be so obvious that they go without saying or they
may stem from what is reasonable in contractual relations.
6. 	Interference with Conditions
If a party acts contrary to the duties of cooperation or good faith and fair dealing to prevent a condition
from being fulfilled or bring about a condition, that party cannot then rely on the nonfulfillment or
fulfillment, respectively, of that condition. 45
7. 	Prevention of Performance
Similar to the principles of Interference with Conditions, a party may not rely on nonperformance
that they cause through act or omission or because of another event for which they bear the risk.46
8. 	Termination
A party may terminate a contract when the nonperformance is fundamental. 47 To determine if the
nonperformance is fundamental, factors that can be considered are: (1) whether the nonperformance
substantially deprives the aggrieved party of what it expected; (2) whether the obligation that has
not been performed is of essence to the contract; (3) whether the nonperformance was intentional
or reckless; (4) whether the nonperformance gives reason to believe that future promises cannot be
relied upon; and (5) whether the aggrieved party will suffer a disproportionate loss as a result of the
nonperformance.48
It is important to note here that the mere fact that there is no universally accepted law governing
international contracts does not mean that laws will always vary greatly from country to country.
In the United States, Canada, England, and Australia, there are a number of similarities in the laws
governing contracts and English law is often adopted as the governing law for projects in Asia,
Africa, and the Middle East. An example of this commonality is seen in the doctrine of prevention
of performance. The law in each of these countries is such that if the project owner prevents the
contractor from completing its work on time by issuing changes to the work, failing to provide critical

B. 	UNCITRAL Model Law on Public Procurement
In 1994, the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL) published
the UNCITRAL Model Law on Procurement of Goods, Construction and Services. 50 In 2011,
UNCITRAL published the UNCITRAL Model Law on Public Procurement, which replaces the 1994
text.51 The UNCITRAL Model Law was created to maximize economy and efficiency; provide fair
and equitable treatment of suppliers and contractors; achieve transparency; and promote competition,
international trade, and the integrity of the public procurement process.52 As a model law it serves as
a template for national governments to reform existing law or introduce laws on public procurement.
1. 	Methods of Procurement
The UNCITRAL Model Law’s primary method of procurement for international construction con-
tracts is open tendering. 53 Tendering (that is, bidding) begins with a solicitation and an invitation
to tender or an invitation to prequalify issued by the procuring entity.54 Tenders are opened at the
deadline for submission, as specified in the solicitation documents, and are announced to all persons
present at the opening. 55 The successful tender is the responsive56 tender with the lowest price or
the lowest evaluated tender based on criteria specified in the solicitation documents.57
While the UNCITRAL Model Law strongly suggests open tendering, it notes alternative methods
of procurement that fall into two categories. The first category is regulated by Article 29 and includes
restricted tendering, requests for quotations, and requests for proposals without negotiation. The
second category is regulated by Article 30 and includes two-stage tendering, requests for proposals
with dialogue, requests for proposals with consecutive negotiations, competitive negotiations, and
single-source procurement.58 Because of the strong preference for open tendering, the model law
requires a justification to use an alternative method. Examples of justifications include the subject
matter of the procurement is highly complex and only a limited number of contractors could perform
the work, 59 the project is time sensitive and open tendering would take too long, 60 and a particular
contractor has exclusive rights in respect of the subject matter of the procurement.61 States may
choose which methods of procurement to use in their national legislation. 62

In addition, if a country decides to use a more restrictive method of procurement than open tender-
ing, it must still do so in a competitive and fair manner in keeping with the purpose of the model law.63
2. 	Review of Tenders
All responsive tenders must be considered in accordance with the solicitation documents.64 This
means that if price was the only award criteria, the tender with lowest price shall be selected unless
certain exceptions apply.65 These rules are designed to promote a fair process of solicitation, tender-
ing, and selection and to eliminate favoritism, bribery, and so on.
Chapters IV and V of the model law explain the additional criteria necessary to properly solicit,
tender, and review the various methods of non-open tendering.
3. 	Challenge Proceedings
a. 	Protest to the Procuring Entity A supplier or contractor may submit to the procuring entity
an application for reconsideration of the terms of the solicitation, prequalification, or preselection at
any time prior to the deadline for submissions. 66 Reconsideration of all other decisions and actions in
the procurement proceedings must be taken before the procurement contract is entered into force.67
Within three working days of receipt of the application, the procuring entity must publish a notice of
the application, decide whether to entertain or dismiss the application, and notify the applicant and
all others in the procurement proceedings of the application and its status. 68 The enacting state may
decide how many working days the procuring entity has to issue a written decision.69 The written
decision must state the reasons for the decision and list remedies or corrective actions taken, if any. 70
b. 	Protest to an Independent Body If the procurement contract has already been entered into
force, a supplier or contractor that wishes to challenge the contract award may submit a complaint
to an independent body within 20 days of the circumstances giving rise to the complaint. 71 The
independent body must notify the procuring entity of the complaint immediately upon receipt. 72
Within 30 days after the submission of the complaint, the independent body must issue a written
decision and explain its decision and remedies granted, if any. 73

lic officials in international business transactions.”74 According to OECD, as of 2018, all thirty-six

also developed its United Nations Convention Against Corruption (UNCAC), which became effec-

anti-corruption laws and cooperate in the prevention of bribery and corruption. The Inter-American
Convention Against Corruption serves a similar purpose. 76 Several countries have put into place
more stringent anti-corruption laws in response to this trend, such as the United Kingdom’s Bribery
Act of 2010. 77
One of the more robust laws, however, is found in the United States under the Foreign Corrupt
Practices Act.
1. 	Foreign Corrupt Practices Act: Anti-Bribery
The Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA), 15 U.S.C. § 78dd-1–3, includes anti-bribery provisions
prohibiting companies from making or promising to make corrupt payments, directly or through a
third party, to foreign officials 78 for purposes of obtaining or retaining business or securing other
favorable treatment both inside and outside of the United States. Corrupt payments include any
offer, promise, or gift of money or anything of value willfully and intentionally used to influence the
actions or decisions of an individual in his official capacity.79 The offer does not need to be accepted
for prosecution under the FCPA.
The anti-bribery provisions of the FCPA conform to the Convention on Combating Bribery of
Foreign Officials in International Business Transactions, or the Anti-Bribery Convention, which was
the culmination of negotiations between the United States and the members of the OECD. 80
a. 	Exceptions to FCPA Prosecution Two exceptions to liability under the FCPA include pay-
ments for “routine governmental action” and situations of extortion or duress.81 Routine govern-
mental actions include nondiscretionary actions performed by foreign officials, such as obtaining
permits and licenses and processing government papers. 82 These actions do not constitute a misuse
of official authority and are therefore not subject to prosecution under the FCPA. 83 Any actions or
decisions made by a foreign official to award a contract to a business or extend a business’ existing
contract would not be a routine governmental function and would be subject to FCPA prosecution.
Extortion and duress occur when a business is compelled to pay a foreign official under threat
of physical harm. 84 As situations of extortion and duress lack the requisite intent to improperly
influence a foreign official, the FCPA does not apply. Extortion is, however, distinguishable from
situations of economic coercion, where a foreign official demands payment in exchange for an

b. 	Affirmative Defenses 	There are two affirmative defenses under the FCPA, including the local
law defense and the reasonable and bona fide business expenditure defense. The burden is on the
alleged offender to prove these affirmative defenses. The local law defense may be used if the defen-
dant can prove that the offer, promise, or gift was lawful under the written laws and regulations of
the recipient’s foreign country at the time of the offense. 87 Lawfulness cannot be inferred from the
absence of written laws or regulations.88 The reasonable and bona fide business expenditure defense
may be used when expenses are incurred for use by a foreign official for the promotion of products
or services or in execution of an existing contract.89
2. 	Corporate Liability for FCPA Violations
a. 	Parent-Subsidiary Liability A parent company may be liable for FCPA violations commit-
ted by its subsidiary if the parent company was directly involved in the misconduct or if an agency
relationship exists between the parent and subsidiary companies.90 When assessing the existence of
an agency relationship, the Department of Justice (DOJ) and Securities and Exchange Commission
(SEC) evaluate the parent’s knowledge and control of the subsidiary’s actions. 91 If the parent com-
pany has the requisite knowledge and control over its subsidiary, it is liable under the doctrine of
respondeat superior for the actions of its agents acting in the scope of their employment and taken
on behalf of the company.92
b. 	Successor Liability Similarly, when a company merges or acquires another company, the suc-
cessor company may be liable for FCPA violations of its predecessor company even if the successor
company had no knowledge of or involvement with the offense.93 The DOJ and SEC, however, have
traditionally declined to prosecute successor companies when they voluntarily disclosed and timely
remedied the violations.94 Therefore, companies considering a merger or acquisition are advised to
perform due diligence on potential predecessor companies and immediately report any violations
discovered post-acquisition.
3. 	FCPA: Accounting Provisions
The FCPA also includes accounting provisions, 15 U.S.C. § 78m(b)(2), that prohibit issuers or
public companies95 from engaging in “off-the-book” accounting.96 Companies are subject to

4. 	FCPA Penalties
Both individuals and companies involved in FCPA violations may be subject to a number of penalties,
including civil penalties, criminal penalties, suspension, or debarment.100 The penalties are based
on the severity of the offense and the facts relating to the crime. 101
Individuals acting on behalf of a company are subject to civil penalties up to $16,000 per
anti-bribery violation102 and up to $160,000 per accounting violation. 103 Criminal penalties for
individuals are up to $250,000 per violation and imprisonment for up to five years for anti-bribery
violations 104 and up to $5 million per violation, and imprisonment for up to 20 years for willful
accounting violations. 105
Companies may be subject to civil penalties up to $16,000 per anti-bribery violation106 and up
to $5,000 per accounting violation.107 Criminal penalties for companies are up to $2 million per
anti-bribery violation108 and up to $25 million per accounting violation. 109
5. 	Developing an Effective Compliance Program
Companies doing business internationally should be aware of potential liability under the FCPA and
establish compliance programs to avoid violations. When assessing potential mergers, acquisitions,
suppliers, or business partners, companies should perform due diligence reviews by researching not
only the company’s history, but also its agents and the country in which the company does business.
The World Bank Listing of Ineligible Firms 110 and Transparency International111 can be used to
assess the company or country’s risk of corruption.
If a company is alerted of a potential FCPA violation, it should conduct a prompt investigation
to determine if a violation exists and the need to self-report. Further, the company should cooperate
with the DOJ or SEC in government investigations, as agencies have discretion to lessen penalties
under the FCPA for timely and voluntary disclosures.

III. 	DISPUTE RESOLUTION
A. 	Methods for Resolving Disputes
Outside of the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia, parties to an international construction
contract usually turn to binding arbitration, often following the use of a nonbinding dispute resolution
board (DRB), a dispute adjudication board (DAB), mediation, or conciliation.
The use of a nonbinding dispute resolution process such as a DRB, DAB, mediation, or concili-
ation can be beneficial, but their requirement or use should be carefully considered. A tremendous
amount of money can be spent on attorneys, experts, and other resources in preparing for and par-
ticipating in these processes, and there is no guarantee that the dispute will be resolved. Instead, the
parties should develop the contract so that these processes are used in the appropriate circumstances
and with some significant restraint on how they will be conducted, when they will be conducted, and
how long they will take.
Arbitration of international construction disputes is still the predominant method or process and
typically the most balanced and fair approach to resolving disputes abroad. There are dozens of
arbitration-administering bodies. Some of the more common are: International Court of Arbitration
of the International Chamber of Commerce; London Court for International Arbitration; China
International Economic and Trade Arbitration Commission; International Arbitral Centre of
the Austrian Federal Economic Chamber; Dubai International Arbitration Centre; Singapore
International Arbitration Centre; Hong Kong International Arbitration Centre; Arbitration Institute
of the Stockholm Chamber of Commerce; Zurich Chamber of Commerce; and American Arbi-
tration Association—International Center for Dispute Resolution. The parties may also choose to
self-administer the arbitration process through use of the UNCITRAL arbitration rules, frequently
referred to as an “ad hoc” arbitration. In such a case, the parties will look solely to the arbitrator(s)
to govern the process, typically at a much-reduced cost because most private administering bodies
have high administrative and filing fees.
Whatever method the parties choose, the conditions and requirements for the arbitration
should be defined in detail in the contract documents. This includes establishing what admin-
istrative organization or process will govern the arbitration, a venue for the hearings (a neutral
country is preferable), the language in which the arbitration will be conducted, limits on the
arbitrators’ jurisdiction or authority, the law governing the arbitration process (if other than the
law governing other aspects of the contract), the arbitrators’ authority to join other parties or
consolidate related arbitrations, the number of arbitrators and how they will be selected, whether
discovery will be allowed and to what extent (for example, exchange of documents), the use
of experts, the timing for hearings, the timing of award, the form of award, and other similar
criteria.
Litigation in countries outside of a limited few is highly risky and can be a frustrating pro-
cess. Problems can be exacerbated when a foreign corporation or entity attempts to litigate
against a party in that party’s home country, especially if that party is a governmental entity or
agency.
B. 	Enforcement of Arbitration Awards
An arbitration award is effective only upon enforcement of the arbitrator’s final decision. When a
party refuses to pay the award, the injured party must seek court recognition and enforcement of the
award. Local court enforcement of the award is dependent on the domestic legal framework of the
country in which the party brings suit and on whether the country is obligated by treaty or convention
to enforce the award.

-- 130 of 771 --

III. DISPUTE RESOLUTION 	93
There are three main conventions that obligate state parties to enforce international arbitration
awards: the United Nations Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral
Awards (the “New York Convention”),112 the Inter-American Convention on International Com-
mercial Arbitration (the “Panama Convention”),113 and the European Convention on International
Commercial Arbitration (the “European Convention”). 114
The New York Convention has been signed and ratified by 159 countries.115 The language of
the New York Convention is mirrored in the two regional conventions, the Panama Convention and
the European Convention. All parties to the regional conventions are also parties to the New York
Convention. 116
While most of the world’s trading nations are obligated to enforce arbitration awards through
ratification of the New York Convention, there are a number of countries that have no such treaty
obligation. Therefore, when writing an arbitration clause into an international construction contract,
parties should ensure that the country in which the arbitration will take place has the domestic legal
framework for enforcing an award and, if possible, an international treaty obligation to enforce an
award.
C. 	Grounds for Refusing to Honor an Arbitration Award
Even if a court is bound by its country’s treaty obligations, it may still refuse to enforce the arbitral
award on seven grounds, as follows:117
• When the parties are incapable or the arbitration agreement is invalid under the laws by which
the contract is governed
• When one party was not given proper notice of the appointment of the arbitrator or the arbitra-
tion proceeding or was unable to present a defense
• When the arbitration is outside the scope of the arbitration clause within the contract
• When the arbitral proceedings or procedure differ from the arbitration clause within the contract
or are not in accordance with the laws in the country where the arbitration took place
• When the arbitration award is not yet binding or has been set aside or suspended by a competent
authority of the country in which the arbitration award was made118
• When the subject of the dispute cannot be arbitrated under the laws of the country where a
party is seeking recognition or enforcement
• When recognition or enforcement is contrary to public policy
As one case study demonstrates, the enforcement of arbitration awards can also be attacked
on multiple procedural fronts.119 Enforcement proceedings were brought in Malaysia, Singapore,
Indonesia, and Hong Kong based on an arbitration award from the Singapore International Arbitra-
tion Centre. Primarily through a series of dubious rulings from Indonesian courts, the losing party

D. 	Enforcing Non-U.S. Judgments in the United States
In addition to arbitration awards, non-U.S. judgments can be enforced in the United States by states,
either through laws adopted based on a uniform act or under principles of comity. There are currently
no federal laws that dictate the enforcement of foreign judgments.
In 1962 the National Conference of Commissioners on Uniform State Laws created the Uniform
Foreign Money Judgments Recognition Act (UFMJRA). 120 The UFMJRA was revised in 2005, and
is now referred to as the Uniform Foreign-Country Money Judgments Recognition Act. It is cur-
rently adopted in 32 states. It is important for anyone attempting to enforce a foreign judgment to
understand how the act applies, if at all, in the state that they are seeking enforcement. Generally,
money judgments are enforceable when the judgment is final, conclusive, and enforceable where
rendered.121 But there are also bars to the enforcement of a money judgment under the UFMJRA,
such as when the judgment was not impartial, when there was no due process, when personal juris-
diction was lacking, or for any other reason that the court chooses (for example, fraud or that the
judgment goes against the public policy of the state). 122 To enforce a foreign judgment in the U.S., it
must first be converted into a U.S. judgment, either through initiating a new action or by some form
of summary proceeding. This will vary from state to state.
Enforcing judgments under principles of comity is very similar to enforcing judgments under the
UFMJRA. Comity is the legal principle that political entities will mutually recognize each other’s
legislative, executive, and judicial acts. For a U.S. court to enforce a foreign judgment, it must be
reasonably sure that the non-U.S. judgment is in line with the U.S. concept of due process of law.
In its most simple form, a non-U.S. judgment has a good chance of being recognized in the U.S.
under principles of comity if the foreign judgment was obtained in a fair and impartial manner that
allowed both parties to present their case fully.
➣ 	POINTS TO REMEMBER
• Although there is no universally accepted “international construction law” governing projects
throughout the world, there are contract and commercial principles that tend to be consistently
applied, regardless of where the project is located.
• A number of unique issues may arise on projects outside the United States and other similar
countries, such as political instability, currency fluctuation, civil unrest, taxes, security, export
controls, and other considerations identified in this chapter. The contracting parties must eval-
uate each project based on the particular risks that may be encountered in the country where
the work will be performed.
• Project delivery in developing countries, especially for large projects, typically includes various
turnkey approaches, often with financing components. This is demonstrated in frequent use of
EPC, BOT, BOOT, BOOM, and other complex contract forms.

121 UFMJRA, Section 2.
122 UFMJRA, Section 4.

• Contractors should be cognizant of how they will be able to obtain payment for their services.
This may include contracting for advance payment or requiring the owner to post a letter of
credit to minimize nonpayment risks.
• UNIDROIT has established a set of commercial principles that contracting parties can use for
construction contracts throughout the world.
• The UNCITRAL Model Law on Procurement of Goods, Construction and Services serves as
a template for governments to use in the procurement of construction services globally.
• Fighting corruption is important in the international construction community. The Organization
for Economic Cooperation and Development drafted its Anti-Bribery Convention to establish
standards to criminalize bribery of foreign public officials in international business transac-
tions.
• The U.S. has enacted the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act to combat bribery of public officials in
the U.S. and abroad. Violation of the Act can result in criminal prosecution and penalties can
include imprisonment and monetary penalties.
• Arbitration is still the preferred method for resolving disputes on construction projects
within and outside the United States. Agreeing to litigate in countries other than those with
well-developed legal systems and established rules of law poses a high financial risk.
• Contracting parties should be careful in selecting the law that will govern their contract and
the organization that will administer the arbitration.
• The contract arbitration provision should be detailed and address issues that could arise during
arbitration, such as location for the arbitration, language to be used in the arbitration hearings,
number of arbitrators, exchange of documents, timing for the hearings, and other similar items.
• Contracting parties should be cognizant of how to enforce arbitration awards and where those
awards can be enforced.

6
WORKING IN A
DIFFERENT STATE
Every construction project presents new challenges and risks in addition to new opportunities. When
a construction company attempts to do business in a different state for the first time, or without
adequate experience in that jurisdiction, the potential stumbling blocks to success are significant. To
meet these challenges, construction firms must arm themselves with information about the political
climate, the labor market, and the laws affecting construction in that new jurisdiction. It is dangerous
to assume that the laws and construction climate in a different state are identical, or even similar, to
those in a contractor’s home state.
This chapter identifies some fundamental issues a contractor should consider before doing busi-
ness in a different state. These guidelines are a first step, not an all-encompassing road map for
avoiding legal landmines when doing business in an unfamiliar jurisdiction.
I. 	QUALIFYING TO DO BUSINESS
Many construction companies perform work in states outside the state in which they are established.
When a company conducts business in another jurisdiction, it is deemed a “foreign” business entity
for purposes of that state’s laws and regulations governing business transactions. For example, if a
Delaware corporation performs work in Florida, that company is considered a foreign corporation
under Florida’s laws. A business entity (such as a corporation, partnership, limited liability company,
or limited liability partnership) that does business—or obtains, possesses, or disposes of property—in
a foreign state must first obtain a certificate of authority from that state. 1 The performance of con-
struction work generally constitutes “doing business” as the term is used in foreign business entity
statutes. 2
By requiring a foreign business entity to obtain a certificate of authority, a state can maintain a
record of the foreign business entity, require the appointment of a registered agent located within
1See, e.g., Ala. Code § 10-2A-15.01; Ga. Code Ann. § 14-2-1501; Haw. Rev. Stat. § 414-431; Ky. Rev. Stat. Ann.
§ 271b.15-010; N.C. Gen. Stat. § 55-15-01; S.C. Code Ann. § 33-15-101; Wis. Stat. Ann. § 180.1501.
2A.H.L. Inc. of Del. v. Star Ins. Co., 10 F. Supp. 2d 1216, 1219 (D. Kan. 1998) (holding “the majority rule is that the per-
formance of construction work by a foreign corporation in a state is generally considered doing business in the state”); S&H
Contractors v. A.J. Taft Coal Co., 906 F.2d 1507, 1510 (11th Cir. 1990) (holding that “a foreign corporation doing construction
work within a state is held to be doing business in that state”).

II. STATE REGISTRATION REQUIREMENTS: BONDS TO SECURE PAYMENT OF TAXES 	97
that state to accept service of legal process, and obtain revenue, generally in the form of taxes. To
ensure compliance with this requirement, most states will not allow a foreign business entity to bring
disputes to that state’s courts until it has obtained the necessary certificate of authority.3 However,
a foreign business entity’s failure to acquire the certificate of authority generally will not invalidate
any contract entered into by the unregistered foreign entity.4
The failure to obtain a certificate of authority is typically curable at any time. Nevertheless, timely
compliance with this statutory requirement is prudent because the need to file a legal action to pre-
serve legal rights may be time sensitive. A foreign company that procrastinates in obtaining the
required certificate of authority does so at its own peril in that a legal right may expire before the
certificate of authority is issued. For example, a foreign contractor may lose its mechanic’s lien rights
if it fails to obtain a certificate of authority before the statutory deadline to foreclose the lien. 5
A certificate of authority is generally not required when the work constitutes an “isolated transac-
tion” in the foreign state. A number of factors are considered when determining whether a contrac-
tor’s work constitutes an “isolated transaction.” As described by the Maryland Court of Appeals,6
the analysis for determining whether a foreign entity is “doing business” in the state does not rest on
a single factor. Rather, it focuses on the nature and extent of the business and activities that occur in
the state. However, because very little business activity is necessary to constitute “doing business,”
most construction work is subject to the certificate of authority requirement rather than the “single
or isolated transaction” exception. 7
II. 	STATE REGISTRATION REQUIREMENTS: BONDS TO SECURE
PAYMENT OF TAXES
A company performing construction work in a foreign jurisdiction should determine whether a bond
must be posted to provide security for any costs or taxes payable to the state. Many states require a
bond from out-of-state contractors to ensure payment of sales and use taxes. The bond requirement
may apply even when the work is performed pursuant to a federal government contract. 8 Although
a state may recover taxes from a contractor that posted a tax bond, it cannot recover taxes from the
federal government. 9
A nonresident contractor’s surety providing a performance bond can also be held liable for sales
and use taxes. 10 This rule was first announced by the United States Supreme Court in 1827 and
remains recognized by a majority of the states.11
The laws regarding the issuance and necessity of tax bonds vary by state. Prior to starting con-
struction work in a foreign jurisdiction, a contractor must identify the specific requirements for a
given jurisdiction. For example, Alabama requires every nonresident contractor to register with the
3St. Paul Fire & Marine v. Paw Paw’s Camper City, Inc., 346 F.3d 153 (5th Cir. 2003).

III. 	STATE LICENSING AND QUALIFICATIONS
In an effort to protect the public from potential problems associated with poor-quality construction,
state and local governments have passed laws and regulations requiring licensure of certain construc-
tion professionals. To ensure strict adherence to these licensing laws, most states’ laws preclude an
unlicensed individual or company from recovering monies owed for services performed. In contrast
to the certificate of authority requirement, the failure to comply with licensing requirements—even
when it is a mistake—is generally not curable. 14
General contractors are not required to be licensed in all states and, in the states where they are,
the procedures for obtaining and retaining a general contractor’s license (including, for example,
whether continuing education is required) vary significantly from state to state. In most states, spe-
cialty contractors engaged in particular trades are also required to be licensed, while a license may
not be required to practice that same trade within a neighboring state or to practice other trades.
While specialty licenses are more frequently required for trades performing work likely to affect life
safety (such as mechanical, electrical, and utility work), it is not prudent to simply assume that a
state does or does not require contractors to be licensed. For example, painting contractors are not
required to be licensed in most states but are required to be licensed in some.
State laws vary as to whether and under what circumstances a licensed trade contractor can act as
a prime contractor (contract directly with the owner of the property) without also holding a general
contractor’s license. State laws also vary as to whether a contractor licensed in its home state must,
in all cases, pass an examination to obtain a license in the foreign state, or whether the state has
reciprocity with some other states that allows a contractor licensed in a reciprocal state to obtain a
license without taking another examination. Given the great variation between the laws of various
states regarding whether a license is required, and the procedure and time required to obtain a license,
this is one of the threshold issues a contractor should thoroughly investigate before embarking upon
a plan to perform work in a new state.
It is imperative that a contractor obtain a proper license in states where a license is required.
Because the licensing process can take months, it is not wise for a contractor to postpone completing
the licensing process until after it is awarded a contract. In fact, some states require that a contractor
be licensed in that state merely to offer to perform work in that state. In some jurisdictions, the failure
to have the required license when a bid is submitted is a violation of the licensing requirements and
can jeopardize the contract award. In addition, a contract entered by an unlicensed contractor may
be deemed invalid or void in some jurisdictions. In California, however, a failure to be licensed at the
time of the contract signing will not invalidate the contract so long as the contractor is fully licensed
at all times during contract performance. 15
Although states have a universal interest in regulating construction companies and professionals,
each state adopts its own unique set of licensing requirements. Not all states require that general

In Florida, general contractors must possess a license, and certain corporations involved in construc-

must obtain a construction license18 and pay an additional fee to perform work in the state.19 The

about the licensing requirements in a foreign jurisdiction because they vary significantly from state

While not all states require that contractors be licensed, all states have laws regulating design pro-
fessionals.21 For example, in West Virginia, architects must register with the West Virginia Board

the unlicensed architect or engineer void and unenforceable.24 Moreover, obtaining a building per-
mit for a construction project generally requires that plans prepared and “sealed” by an architect or
engineer licensed in that state be submitted to the governing building department or other agency for
approval.
Compliance with licensing requirements can be influenced by the subjective interpretations of
those charged with enforcing licensing provisions. Contractors (both general contractors and trade
contractors) are well advised to learn not only the letter of the licensing laws but also how those laws
are applied by a given state’s licensing boards and staff members.
IV. 	PUBLIC-SECTOR CONSTRUCTION
When pursuing or performing work in the public sector (that is, state, local, and federally funded state
and local projects), contractors face additional requirements and considerations that do not apply in
the private sector. The rules governing public construction vary from state to state and possibly even
from county to county within a state. Contractors need to be attuned to these requirements, whether
they are pursuing or performing state, local, or federally funded state or local projects.
For example, statutes governing contracts awarded by state agencies may contain requirements
that add or take away contractual rights even though the contract does not address the particular
issue. A contractor doing business with a state agency, therefore, cannot rely solely on the express
terms of its contract to fully define its contractual rights, obligations, and risks. A prudent contractor
must also examine the statutes and regulations affecting contracts with the contracting state agency.
Contract-award procedures can vary depending on the type of construction and the governmental
entity involved. For example, the Georgia Department of Transportation has its own authority to plan,

Some laws unique to particular states govern the contractor’s conduct in pursuing public work

Over the past several decades, state agencies, counties, and municipalities have begun implement-
ing new procurement methods that offer more options and flexibility in obtaining construction ser-
vices. The trend away from the traditional sealed bidding process is motivated, in part, by increased
pressure on state and local governmental entities to accomplish more with less funding, to complete
projects faster, and to eliminate as much risk as possible. To address these objectives, new procure-
ment rules are giving state and local governmental bodies more discretion in evaluating bids and
proposals. That trend is expected to continue.
To address funding restrictions, states have implemented alternative procurement systems aimed
at lowering project costs or assisting in project financing. Several states have authorized direct nego-
tiation with a low bidder when the low bid exceeds the state agency’s cost estimate. 29 These direct
negotiations allow the public owner to adjust or revise the scope of work in an effort to meet budget
limitations. Although generally unpopular with contractors, a reverse-bid auction is another sys-
tem some states have implemented in an effort to achieve lower prices for public works projects.30
This method for soliciting bids keeps a bidder informed of its relative position among all competing
bidders and allows a firm to adjust its bid price during a designated bidding period.
Some states have also enacted legislation authorizing the use of public-private partnerships
(P3s) 31 to fund infrastructure replacement and new public facilities. This alternative to a competitive
process of sealed bids or sealed proposals allows public entities to consider and accept solicited and,
in some states, unsolicited proposals from private companies. P3 projects allow the private sector
to participate in the development, financing, and operation of public projects and are discussed in
more detail in Chapter 4.
In addition to alternative procurement systems, public owners are authorizing the use of alterna-
tive project delivery methods to meet more aggressive project schedules and to place more risk on
the contractor. Design-build contracts, for example, shift design responsibility (and the correspond-
ing risk) from the owner to the contractor. The Colorado legislature recognized the advantages of
design-build contracts and enacted specific laws to encourage its use for highway construction. 32 In

authority issues that may arise during performance of the work.
