A. 	Creation of an Enforceable Contract Relationship
Promissory estoppel is a fundamental tenet of construction law recognized by court decisions in
many states. Under this legal doctrine, a subcontractor’s or supplier’s quote cannot be changed or
withdrawn when the general contractor or upper-tier subcontractor has reasonably relied on the quote
in preparing its bid to the owner.38 When a firm refuses to honor its quote by providing the goods
and/or services at the quoted price—even if the quote is incorrect because of a mathematical error or
otherwise—the doctrine of promissory estoppel is triggered, and the subcontractor will be required to
honor the quoted price. Application of the doctrine varies depending on the laws of a particular state.
In some states, the law views a subcontractor’s or vendor’s quote as simply an offer to perform work,
not an act that creates a binding contract.39 Accordingly, both general contractors and subcontractors
doing business in a new jurisdiction should understand that state’s view on promissory estoppel and
its application to subcontractor or vendor bids. 40
A common issue involving subcontractor bidding is whether a state has subcontractor-listing
requirements for contractors bidding on a public project. Some states have specific statutes requir-
ing the general contractor to list its intended subcontractors when submitting its bid to the owner.41
Other states, such as Georgia, do not have this statutory requirement. However, it is at the owner’s
discretion to reject a bid that fails to provide this information if the owner’s request for bids or request
for proposals asks that it be provided. 42
B. 	Contract Award Preferences
Some states provide preferential treatment to certain entities when awarding public contracts.
Generally, those qualifying for preferred treatment are selected to further a socioeconomic
or public-policy interest. For example, to reward those contractors who contribute to public-
improvements funding by paying taxes and employing local residents, some states have a stated
preference for bids and proposals from contractors that reside in the state.43 In some jurisdictions,
however, this residency preference has been eliminated by court decisions finding that such
preference violates objectives of competitive bidding and the “privileges and immunities” clause of
the United States Constitution. 44
Because resident-contractor status can provide bid advantages, the standard for determining
whether an entity qualifies as a resident is critical. The standard is not universal and varies from
state to state. For example, states differ as to whether a joint-venture contractor comprised of at
least one nonresident should qualify for the preferential treatment afforded resident contractors. In
Alaska, a joint-venture contractor qualifies for “resident contractor” status as long as one of the
co-venturers is an Alaska resident.45 Louisiana, however, requires that all co-venturers be state
residents.46

V. STATE STATUTES AND POLICIES AFFECTING CONTRACTUAL RELATIONSHIPS AND TERMS 	103
The federal government 47 and some state and local governments 48 provide statutory preferences
for “small business” concerns or other designated categories of contractors. Preferences may take the
form of “set-aside” programs where specific projects are designated for contractors qualifying as a
small business concern. A “small business” is defined by statute or regulation and typically includes
certain entities that fall below specified limitations on the average number of employees or aver-
age annual revenue.49 Similar requirements may exist for other identified categories of contractors
such as firms owned and operated by veterans. A contractor bidding on a contract with a set-aside
provision must determine what percentage of the work must be performed by the firm seeking the
benefit of the set-aside and what constitutes “work” for the purposes of the performance of work
requirement.
State governments may also grant preferences to minority-owned or women-owned enterprises.50
The definition of “minority” varies from state to state, but it typically includes African Americans,
Native Americans, and females.51 States that do not have a specific statutory requirement providing
preferences may encourage the participation of minority-owned or women-owned contractors in
their agencies’ requests for bids and proposals.
Statutory preferences for minority-owned or women-owned businesses have been challenged in
courts across the United States on the basis that they violate federal and state constitutional guar-
antees of equal protection under the law. In an attempt to clarify when and how these preference
policies can be used, the United States Supreme Court 52 set out four requirements that must be met
when formulating these preferences:
1. A high, “strict scrutiny” standard of review must be satisfied in evaluating the constitutionality
of the preference law in question.
2. The preference must be designed to overcome the effects of identified historical discrimination
in the market area of the implementing agency.
3. The governmental entity must have evaluated race-neutral and gender-neutral remedies before
adopting race- and gender-conscious requirements.
4. The plan must be carefully tailored and must be in place only for the amount of time required
to reverse the effects of past discrimination.
Despite this guidance, the debate continues on whether race, ethnicity, and gender should be used
as criteria for awarding contracts.
C. 	Public-Policy Limitations on Contract Clauses
Risk is inherent in any construction project. A well-written contract will address the risks and
clearly allocate them among the contracting parties. Popular risk-shifting provisions include:
(1) no-damages-for-delay clauses; (2) liquidated damages clauses; (3) pay-when-paid and
pay-if-paid clauses; and (4) indemnity provisions. Recognizing that these provisions are often
mandated by the party with superior negotiation leverage, legislatures in various jurisdictions have
limited or nullified the enforceability of these provisions on public-policy grounds. In an effort to
gain the benefit of greater consistency and predictability in the interpretation of an organization’s

contract, subcontract, or purchase order forms, many owners and contractors include provisions
that stipulate that the contract will be interpreted under the laws of a particular state, usually that
organization’s home state. Many states that have nullified contract provisions on public-policy
grounds have also enacted laws addressing choice-of-law clauses.53 Laws limiting choice-of-law
clauses inhibit circumventing the state’s laws limiting risk-shifting provisions.
The no-damages-for-delay clause is a contract provision that precludes a claimant from
recovering monetary damages resulting from project delays. This clause may shift the risk of
owner-caused project delays from the owner to the general contractor (or from the general con-
tractor to the subcontractor). This clause is common in construction contracts and is the subject of
frequent debate. The protection it provides an owner or general contractor will vary by state. For
example, some state legislatures prohibit the use of no-damages-for-delay clauses—at least in some
contracts—because they believe it unfairly shifts a big-dollar construction risk to the other party. 54
Other states, however, adopt a more moderate approach by enforcing the parties’ negotiated contract
terms, even the no-damages-for-delay clause, as long as concealment, misrepresentation, or fraud is
not involved. 55
A delay’s cost to a construction project’s completion may also be addressed through a liqui-
dated damages provision. Typically, this contractual provision will establish a daily rate for delay
damages that accrues after the specified contract completion date has passed. A liquidated damages
provision is enforceable as long as it comports with the standards established in a given jurisdic-
tion. In Colorado, for instance, a liquidated damages clause is enforceable when: (1) it is estab-
lished at a time when the delay damages are difficult to ascertain; (2) it represents an accurate
estimate of the actual costs that may be incurred; and (3) it reflects an agreement by all parties. 56
In South Carolina, a liquidated damages clause is enforceable when a party proves a breach of
contract, 57 but only if the liquidated damages clause is not deemed to serve as a penalty for that
breach. 58
Pay-when-paid and pay-if-paid clauses have long been the topic of heated debate in the construc-
tion industry. (See Chapter 10.) Compared to traditional payment terms, which require payment to
a subcontractor within a defined time period after performance of the work, these clauses attempt
to tie a general contractor’s obligation to pay its subcontractor to the general contractor’s receipt of
payment from the owner. A pay-when-paid clause typically requires that the general contractor pay
the subcontractor within a defined time period after being paid by the owner—or within a reason-
able time if the subcontractor did not assume the risk of owner nonpayment. A pay-if-paid clause
makes payment by the owner to the general contractor an express condition precedent to the general
contractor’s obligation to pay the subcontractor.
General contractors insert these contingent payment clauses into subcontracts to shift to the
subcontractor the risk of an owner’s nonpayment. Because an owner’s refusal to pay the general con-
tractor may be for reasons unrelated to the subcontractor’s work, strict enforcement of these clauses
is viewed with skepticism. Subcontractors, in particular, are critical of these clauses because they
believe a general contractor should not be relieved of its payment obligations when the subcontractor
has satisfactorily completed its work.

V. STATE STATUTES AND POLICIES AFFECTING CONTRACTUAL RELATIONSHIPS AND TERMS 	105
Several states have enacted legislation to ensure that subcontractors are paid timely.59 These statu-
tory provisions define a contractor’s obligation for payment to the subcontractor or vendor (beyond
any obligations contained in the subcontract/purchase order itself) by specifying a time period for
issuing such payments and imposing a penalty for noncompliance. In some states, such as North
Carolina and South Carolina, legislation has been passed making pay-if-paid provisions unenforce-
able, as against public policy. 60 Other states, such as Georgia and Indiana, have no general prohibition
against the enforceability of such provisions, but have statutes making it clear that the presence of
such a subcontract provision does not prohibit a subcontractor from filing a lien for money that would
be due but for the presence of that provision. 61
Some courts have held that particular subcontract language constitutes a pay-when-paid clause
that affords the general contractor a reasonable amount of time to make payment but establishes
an absolute commitment to pay the subcontractor at some point even if the general contractor is
never paid by the owner.62 Other courts, however, have interpreted similar subcontract language to
make payment from the owner an absolute condition precedent to a general contractor’s obligation
to pay its subcontractors if the applicable contract language clearly states this.63 The latter interpre-
tation, making the provision a pay-if-paid clause (as opposed to a pay-when-paid clause), will be
applied only when the court determines that the contract language is clear and unambiguous (for
example, “Subcontractor acknowledges that payments will be made only from money received from
the Owner, and that it relies on the credit of the Owner and not that of the Contractor”).
Other laws also affect the payment rights and obligations of contractors and subcontractors. For
example, some states have enacted “trust fund” statutes to discourage the misuse of payments to the
contractor. 64 Payments received and used for purposes other than the proper payment for construction
services and materials may result in the assessment of civil and criminal penalties on the contrac-
tor. These penalties may also extend to individual representatives of the company who actively or
passively permit the misuse of construction proceeds. 65
A state trust fund statute may provide that if a contractor or subcontractor fraudulently obtains an
“advance” of contract payments with a promise to perform construction work and then fails to do so,
the contractor, or the principals of the contracting firm, may be guilty of larceny. 66 Oklahoma law
provides that managing officers of a corporate contractor can be found guilty of embezzlement for
trust fund statute violations.67 Wisconsin courts have allowed civil suits against officers of corporate
contractors for diverting funds protected by trust fund statutes.68
Subcontractors performing work on federal government projects subject to the Miller Act are
afforded some protection against conditional payment provisions by being able to recover payment
under the Miller Act payment bond, even though the underlying subcontract itself precludes the right

to payment. (See Chapter 16.) This right, however, can be waived by the subcontractor if the waiver
is clear and explicit, in writing, and signed by the subcontractor after the work has started.69 Some
courts have construed this type of waiver provision very narrowly.70
Another risk-shifting provision subject to much debate is the indemnity clause. This provision,
which imposes “hold-harmless” obligations on one of the contracting parties, is common in
construction contracts and can take various forms. Because many indemnity provisions are drafted
very broadly, some state legislatures and courts have limited the effect and applicability of such
provisions. For example, Colorado enacted an anti-indemnity statute that states that any provision
requiring a person to indemnify another for damages or injuries caused by the negligence or fault
of that party “is void as against public policy and unenforceable.”71 California, Georgia, Kentucky,
Montana, New Mexico, New York, and many other states have passed similar legislation.72
Contractors should be cautious when working outside of their home state because the enforceability
of indemnity provisions, in addition to the other provisions discussed earlier, will vary by state.
Contract provisions should be tailored to meet the standards established by the applicable laws and
judicial decisions of a given jurisdiction.
Many construction contracts contain “forum selection” or “venue selection” clauses that require
any disputes to be resolved in a court located in a particular state or county—often the home state
or home county of the party that authored the contract—which may be different than the loca-
tion of the project.73 The U.S. Supreme Court has made it clear that when parties agree to a valid
forum-selection clause, that clause will be given controlling weight by federal courts in all but the
most exceptional cases. 74 Thus, a federal court will ordinarily transfer the case to the forum specified
in the forum-selection clause. 75
Some states, such as Ohio, have statutes that make forum-selection clauses unenforceable on
projects in the state if the chosen forum has no substantial connection with the project.76 Some
federal courts, however, may decide to transfer a case to the forum specified in a forum-selection
clause in spite of a state statute of this kind. 77 When drafting forum-selection clauses, parties should
keep in mind these statutes, as well as the varying state and federal courts’ interpretations of them.
D. 	Effects of New Legislation
When preparing to work in a different state, contractors should consider the political climate of
that jurisdiction and any emerging trends that could affect their contract work. Public-interest
groups and media frequently champion issues of public concern to prompt lawmakers to enact new
legislation. The proposed or new legislation may directly target the construction industry, in which
case all players in the industry should carefully review and analyze such provisions to determine:
(1) the scope of any new rights and obligations; (2) the effect on pricing, schedule, or overall

VI. PRESERVATION OF LIEN/BOND RIGHTS 	107
attractiveness of a project; and (3) the effective date of the legislation. Knowing the impact of new
legislation on the front end may avoid potential and unnecessary problems during performance of
the contract.
Legislation that is not directly targeted at the construction industry may nonetheless ascribe
new obligations to the contractor. For example, in 2005 the Florida legislature enacted the “Jessica
Lunsford Act,” which is intended to protect children from sexual predators. The legislation mandates
stiff minimum sentences for child abusers and requires offenders to wear global positioning satellite
(GPS) monitors when released from prison. At first glance, this legislation seems inconsequential to
the work contractors perform in Florida.
But the law requires “contractual personnel” (defined as any vendor, individual, or entity under
contract with a school or the school board) who are permitted on school grounds when students
are present to undergo background screening and to provide a complete set of fingerprints. 78 Any
individual found to have been convicted of a crime of moral turpitude (terrorism, sexual miscon-
duct, murder, kidnapping, and so on) may not provide services on school grounds. Thus, this law
clearly has significant ramifications for a contractor performing construction work on school grounds
because the contractor now must undergo a background check and provide employees’ fingerprints.
This obligation applies to all contractors and subcontractors and to their employees. Many juris-
dictions have enacted legislation similar to the “Jessica Lunsford Act” and may impose additional
obligations on contractors under certain circumstances.
Likewise, a growing number of jurisdictions have enacted laws designed to crack down on unau-
thorized immigration. A common prominent aspect of such laws is a requirement that employers
verify a new employee’s citizenship status. In Arizona, for example, no employer may “intentional-
ly” or “knowingly” employ an unauthorized immigrant, 79 and unauthorized immigrants are explicitly
prohibited from employment on public works projects.80 Similarly, Colorado requires a contractor
to certify that it does not knowingly employ an unauthorized immigrant (or contract with a sub-
contractor that knowingly employs unauthorized immigrants) and that it has attempted to confirm
the residency status of new employees. 81 Pennsylvania, Vermont, New Hampshire, Georgia, and
Kansas have similar legislation prohibiting the knowing employment of unauthorized immigrants or
imposing an obligation to verify the residency status of its employees. 82 Contractors must be aware
of emerging trends in newly enacted laws and must devise a strategy to satisfy new obligations in
accordance with the applicable statutes.
VI. 	PRESERVATION OF LIEN/BOND RIGHTS
Lien laws are a creature of state law and vary significantly from state to state. Given the potential
importance of lien rights to a contractor’s ability to obtain payment, and the ways in which other
parties’ lien rights may affect the contractor (such as the need to obtain lien waivers from subcon-
tractors and suppliers in a form that will be effective in the state where the project is located), the lien
laws in foreign jurisdictions present significant challenges for contractors, subcontractors, suppliers,
and owners involved in construction projects outside their resident state. Lien law requirements are
often cumbersome and confusing, but a failure to meet these requirements precisely can be fatal to
a company’s legitimate lien rights.

108 	CHAPTER 6 WORKING IN A DIFFERENT STATE
A. 	Preconstruction Knowledge of Lien Law Peculiarities Is Essential
Typically, contractors and owners do not analyze and review the lien law requirements in a particular
jurisdiction until there is an immediate need to file a claim of lien or, from the owner’s perspective,
after the lien has been filed. This approach can be dangerous because many jurisdictions require
action from the contractor early in the project to preserve lien rights or, in the case of the owner, to
limit obligations to potential lien claimants. If these initial obligations are not satisfied, a contractor’s
lien rights may be lost forever, or the owner’s exposure may be increased considerably.
In some states, to avoid losing lien rights, affirmative action must be taken before the project
begins. In Alabama, for instance, a “full price” lien (as opposed to a lien on just the unpaid balance
of the owner/general contractor contract) is available only to those who have a direct contract with
the owner and materialmen who give notice to the owner before furnishing materials.83 An owner
receiving notice from a material supplier may avoid responsibility for the supplier’s materials by
issuing a “Predelivery Notice” to that supplier. The notice should convey to the supplier that the
owner will not be responsible for the price of the materials being furnished.84
In other jurisdictions, lien rights survive the start of construction but are in jeopardy if some
action is not taken very soon after project work begins. In Michigan, for example, if a “Notice of
Commencement” has been filed for a project, then, to preserve its lien rights, a subcontractor or
supplier must serve a “Notice of Furnishing” on the general contractor and on the owner’s designated
recipient within 20 days after first furnishing labor or materials to a construction project. 85 Any delay
in providing the owner with notice of the intended lien claim may result in a forfeiture of lien rights.
B. 	Lien Law Protections and Procedures Vary Greatly from State to State
A contractor must not assume that familiarity with its home state’s lien laws will equip the
company to protect its rights under the lien laws of another jurisdiction. As previously noted, lien
laws—perhaps more than any other statutory scheme affecting the construction industry—vary
widely from state to state. For example, in North Carolina, punch-list or warranty work typically
will not extend the time for filing a lien claim. In neighboring South Carolina, however, such
remedial or warranty work may qualify as a basis to extend the time for filing a claim of lien.86
C. 	“Almost Right” Is Almost Always Not Good Enough
In many areas of contract law, parties are not penalized when they are “almost right” or when they
have “substantially complied” with the contract or other legal requirements. For example, contractors
and subcontractors that fail to follow the precise notice requirements prescribed by a contract may
be excused by the owner’s actual knowledge of the circumstances requiring such contract notice or
by “substantial compliance” with the requirement.
In most states the lien laws are not so forgiving. The failure of a contractor, subcontractor, sup-
plier, or owner to precisely satisfy lien law requirements can be fatal to that party’s rights under the
lien statute. Even the slightest noncompliance can be costly. For example, the Maryland lien statute
provides that a “Notice of Intent to Claim a Lien” must be served within 120 days of the claimant’s
last work. This does not mean that the notice can be sent four months after the last work. There is
a difference between 120 days and four months, and the failure to recognize this difference can be
fatal to a company’s lien rights.87

VII. PROJECT RISK ASSESSMENT—“FOREIGN STATES” 	109
D. 	Valid Lien Claim Does Not Guarantee Payment
Even if a contractor successfully complies with the precise requirements of the lien laws in the “for-
eign” jurisdiction, the exercise of its mechanics’ lien rights may fall short of the payment guarantee
the contractor seeks. The inadequacy of lien rights as payment security may result from: (1) the lien
may be subordinate to other security interests that have a combined value greater than the value of
the property, such as the interests of the construction lender; or (2) the lien may not cover all of the
damages or costs to which the contractor is entitled.
From the contractor’s or supplier’s perspective, the limited scope of the damages covered by most
lien law statutes is a frequent problem. For example, delay damages, such as the extended job site
and home office overhead attributed to a project’s delay, are some of the consequences of a troubled
construction project that in some states cannot be included in a lien claim.
Lien rights are no substitute for proper financial management, which includes implementing and
following systems and procedures to prequalify those with whom the company intends to do busi-
ness. A contractor should obtain pre-project proof of adequate project financing from the owner and
should endeavor to avoid contracts that require the company to continue working and financing the
project during payment disputes.
E. 	Contractor Should Arm Itself Early with Accurate Lien Law Information
A contractor’s ability to exactly satisfy lien requirements—and to avoid the many pitfalls that await
it in the lien laws of foreign jurisdictions—begins with gathering reliable information on the lien
laws of each state in which the contractor is working. A number of sources for this information are
available to the construction industry. For example, mechanics’ lien filing services (as well as var-
ious contractor associations) have pamphlets, handouts, and other publications available that cover
basic—and even more sophisticated—lien law information. Preparing to exercise its lien rights may
also require the contractor to obtain an accurate legal description of the real property on which a
project is to be constructed before a need arises to file a lien against it.
Courts have often construed statutory language defining lien rights in ways that make a literal
reading of the underlying lien statute unreliable. Similarly, statutorily mandated lien forms may
be misleading to those who do not know how the lien statutes define the terms used in the lien
form. Investing time and resources in preparing to take full advantage of the lien laws and other
payment protections available to a contractor or subcontractor in the jurisdiction of any new project
is worthwhile.
VII. 	PROJECT RISK ASSESSMENT—“FOREIGN STATES”
Every project includes risks. The process of identifying construction project risks can be critical to
the company’s profit or loss. Pursuing an opportunity in a different (“foreign”) state increases the
potential for unfamiliar risks and pitfalls. Owners, design professionals, construction managers, con-
tractors, subcontractors, and suppliers cannot afford to wait until a problem arises to assess the risks
inherent in doing business in a different state for the first time. If a firm does not have a systematic
approach to risk identification, developing one should be a high priority. If a risk is not identified
and understood, it cannot be managed or mitigated.
A systematic risk-assessment process must start when considering a bid or proposal on the project.
The development and consistent use of project checklists can facilitate a systematic approach to
risk management. In addition, a checklist can assist in orienting a firm’s staff members, especially
if they are new to their positions. A methodology for risk assessment can adapt checklists and

-- 147 of 771 --

guidelines created by industry participants and associations to match the particular operational style
of that company. As with nearly every aspect of the construction process, documentation is crit-
ical. The contractor’s staff should be instructed to preserve the information gathered during the
risk-assessment process so that it can benefit the project management team.
The following list of topics and the sample checklist found in Appendix 6.1 can be used as a
starting point for an early and thorough review of the issues to be evaluated before bidding on and
performing work in a different (foreign) state. Once the basic list of topics is determined, many find
it useful to convert that information into a checklist containing a series of “Yes” or “No” questions.
In addition to identifying the project, project owner, or general contractor, the checklist should doc-
ument when it was prepared and who prepared or developed the answers. All responses (whether
yes or no) should be reviewed and, as necessary, approved by a senior member of the company’s
risk management team. If a question could not be answered, that uncertainty must be resolved by a
senior member of the risk management team.

For an overall review of a state’s or locality’s construction contracting requirements, the chapters of
the Associated General Contractors of America (AGC),88 the Associated Builders and Contractors
(ABC), 89 and other construction trade organizations can provide valuable information. For example,
the AGC publishes a Construction State Law Matrix that identifies some of the more significant
statutes that apply to construction in each of the 50 states, the District of Columbia, and Puerto
Rico. 90 Contacting these local organizations can also familiarize a contractor with each state’s unique
requirements.
Other construction industry trade associations (the Construction Financial Manager’s Asso-
ciation, for example) publish magazines, newsletters, and books with valuable information.
Construction-law seminars that focus specifically on the laws of a particular state can be found in
most or all states. Several publishing companies sell books that detail construction law issues for a
particular state or summarize how each of the 50 states handle a particular construction law issue.

➣ 	POINTS TO REMEMBER
• Construction work generally constitutes “doing business” in a state so a contractor preparing
to work in a different state for the first time usually must first obtain a certificate of authority
from the Secretary of State’s office.
• Many states require a bond from out-of-state contractors to ensure prompt and full payment of
taxes that become due as a function of performing construction work in the state.
• Some states require that a contractor be licensed before bidding or offering to perform con-
struction work, and all states require that architects, engineers, and other design professionals
be licensed.
• State lien and bond statutes often impose early filing or notice requirements. Identify those
requirements before starting work on a new project.
• The manner in which public construction projects are awarded varies by state and should be
understood and followed to ensure consideration of the bid.
• State and local regulations regarding such things as general contractor relationships with sub-
contractors, contract award preferences, and the enforceability of contract terms vary greatly
from one jurisdiction to another. Do not assume that the laws in a foreign jurisdiction will be
identical, or even similar, to those in one’s home jurisdiction.
• Perform a comprehensive risk assessment before bidding on a construction project and preserve
and revisit that assessment throughout the project to minimize potential problems.

COMPETING FOR THE
CONTRACT
I. 	INTRODUCTION: THE RATIONALE FOR COMPETITION
Government purchases of goods and services have not always been required to be procured on the
open market or by competition. In the early days of the United States, the chief officers of the
Departments of War and the Navy purchased goods and services through private contract, without
restriction. 1 In 1809, Congress passed legislation requiring that such procurements be made either
through “open purchase” in case of exigency, or by “previously advertising for proposals.” 2 One
rationale for the 1809 act was to prevent favoritism by restricting the discretion of those purchasing
government goods. The other was that competition was advantageous to the government and would
“give to the United States the benefit of competition between those who were disposed to render the
services or furnish the supplies which the government might require.”3
By the end of the nineteenth century, many jurisdictions had enacted laws requiring most public
construction projects to be awarded using a competitive bidding process (“sealed bids”) in accor-
dance with the applicable statutes, ordinances, and implementing regulations. This design-bid-build
procurement method has been prevalent for the past hundred years. In recent decades, new legis-
lation has given many public agencies the flexibility to award contracts using either the traditional
sealed bid process or a competitive negotiation process on the basis of the “best value” to the owner.
While there are some differences in the implementation of the public competitive negotiation pro-
cess from agency to agency, the basic goals are to provide the public owner the opportunity to select
the contractor offering the “best value” to the government while retaining the controls needed to
assure the overall integrity of the competitive award process. Competitive bidding requirements are
essentially designed for the protection of the public purse, providing a means by which goods or
services required by public authorities may be acquired at the lowest possible cost.4
1See generally 2 U.S. Op. Atty. Gen. 257, 259 (1829) (describing 1798 procurement act as directing that all purchases and

116 	CHAPTER 7 COMPETING FOR THE CONTRACT
Private owners are rarely, if ever, “required” to use competitive bidding procedures. Although
less prevalent in the private sector, a private owner may elect to use a competitive bidding process
as a means of obtaining an advantageous price while maintaining some control over the quality of
the successful awardee. However, for those private owners that do choose to solicit competitive bids,
both the owner and potential bidders should pay attention to general principles of public bidding,
because many of the same considerations are present, whether the project is public or private.
Because both the traditional competitive bid process and the negotiated best-value process remain
viable options for the award of contracts, this chapter will review the general principles for both,
beginning with a general overview of the competitive bidding process followed by a review of the
best-value award process. Although the general principles affecting the selection of a contractor for
any public project are similar, there are differences based upon the controlling federal, state, or local
law. Consequently, a contractor needs to be aware of these differences, especially when competing
for a project in a new state. 5
II. 	KEY CONCEPTS IN TRADITIONAL PUBLIC COMPETITIVE
BIDS—RESPONSIVENESS AND RESPONSIBILITY
Under the competitive (sealed) bid process, the essential tests for the award of public contracts at all
levels of government are similar. Public contracts are generally awarded to the contractor (bidder or
offeror) submitting the “lowest responsive and responsible” bid or the “lowest and best offer.” To
meet that requirement, the bid or offer must be “responsive” to the terms, conditions, and specifica-
tions provided by the public owner or contracting agency and be submitted by a “responsible” bidder.
Responsiveness differs from responsibility. The next sections discuss in greater detail responsiveness
and responsibility of the typical successful bid or offer.6
A. 	The Responsive Bidder
A bid for a public contract will usually not be accepted unless the bid is “responsive”—that is, the bid
must comply with all material requirements of the solicitation. Responsiveness focuses on whether
the submitted bid is an offer to perform the exact tasks spelled out in the bid invitation and whether
acceptance will bind the contractor to perform in strict conformance with the invitation.7 In most
public procurements, responsiveness will be determined as a preliminary matter in bid evaluation,
with the standards for such determination varying among different public entities.
A contractor’s failure to carefully comply with the requirements for competitive bidding may
result in the bid being declared “nonresponsive” or, if an award has been made, may render the
contract voidable or prevent the contractor from recovering full compensation for work performed.
In determining the responsiveness of a bid, the bidder’s intent must be clearly ascertainable from
the face of the bid.8 The contractor’s bid must be an offer to perform the requested work, be in
accordance with the conditions and restrictions of the invitation, provide a certain price, and bind
5 The Construction State Law Matrix (SLM) published annually by the AGC of America provides a summary of the
public-bidding statutes in each of the fifty states, the District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico.
6 Many of the principles (responsiveness, responsibility) related to competitive bidding have developed in the context of
federal government contracting. Therefore, reference is made to the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) and to so-called
bid-protest decisions by either the Government Accountability Office (GAO) or the United States Court of Federal Claims and
its predecessor courts. Collectively, these federal government procurements decisions help define the concepts and illustrate
their application.
7Johnson v. United States, 15 Cl. Ct. 169 (1988).
8Jarke Corp., Comp. Gen. B-231858, 88–2 CPD ¶ 82.

the bidder to perform as requested in the bid invitation.9 But responsiveness does not always require
exactitude. To rise to the level of nonresponsiveness and rejection of a bid, the deviation by the bidder
must be considered material.10
Deviation from the solicitation is considered material if it gives one bidder a substantial compet-
itive advantage that prevents other bidders from competing on an equal basis. A deviation is also
material if it goes to the substance of the bid or prejudices other bidders by affecting the price, quan-
tity, quality, or delivery of the items offered. 11 Generally, a contractor bidding on public work must
take the contract as presented. Thus, any qualification of a bid that limits or changes one or more
terms of the proposed contract subjects the contractor to the risk of its bid being deemed nonrespon-
sive. For example, in Fire-Trol Holdings, LLC,12 a contractor’s bid was found to be nonresponsive
where it offered to provide fire retardants that were not on the solicitation’s approved products list.13
Such a qualification, if accepted by the owner, could have given the contractor an unfair price advan-
tage over other bidders.14
The contractor’s inclusion of reservations or conditions in its bid generally renders the bid non-
responsive. According to the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR), a bid is nonresponsive if it
includes conditions such as the following:
• Protecting against future changes in conditions, such as increased costs, if total possible costs
to the government cannot be determined.
• Failing to state a price and indicating that price shall be “price in effect at time of delivery.”
• Stating a price, but qualifying it as being subject to “price in effect at time of delivery.”
• Conditioning or qualifying a bid by stipulating that it is to be considered only if, before date of
award, the bidder receives (or does not receive) award under a separate solicitation when that
is not authorized by the invitation.
• Requiring the government to determine that the bidder’s product meets the applicable govern-
ment specifications.
• Limiting the rights of the government under any contract clause. 15
Most rules concerning bid responsiveness are aimed at preventing a contractor from having “two
bites at the apple.” In other words, the concept of bid responsiveness is used to guard against a low
bidder having the opportunity, after bids are opened and all prices are revealed, to accept or reject
an award based on some contingency that the bidder created, and that applies only to, and works to
the advantage of, that bidder. 16
The prohibition against a bidder having “two bites at the apple” applies most often when a defect
in the bid or an ambiguity in a solicitation subjects the intended bid to differing interpretations.

included in its bid certain descriptive literature on which the word “optional” was written. The Gen-
eral Accounting Office (GAO) found that the inclusion of this term created two interpretations of
the bid, one of which rendered the bid nonresponsive. The GAO, therefore, upheld the government’s
rejection of the bid.
A bid will also be considered nonresponsive if the bidder attempts to make the bid contingent
upon some act or event. 18 In Hewlett-Packard, Co.,19 the bidder sent a transmittal letter stating that
the bid was contingent on the removal of a contract clause. The GAO found that the contingency
rendered the bid nonresponsive because the bidder sought to change the terms of the contract to the
bidder’s sole advantage.
A bid will also be considered nonresponsive where the bidder deviates from the bidding require-
ments by failing to acknowledge addenda (that is, changes to the bid documents issued before the
bids become due), particularly where the addenda contain a statutorily required provision.20 Also, a
bidder’s oral, rather than written, acknowledgment of an amendment is unacceptable.21
According to the GAO, a bid is also nonresponsive if it fails to acknowledge an amendment that
would impose a new legal obligation (even if it would not affect price)22 or fails to certify that a
federally mandated small business concern will be used.23
The failure to respond to the solicitation within the format required by the solicitation may also
be considered a material deviation. In Herman Construction Group, Inc.,24 the solicitation required
submission of a detailed price proposal in XLS spreadsheet format using, at a minimum, Microsoft
Excel 2003. The bidder submitted its price proposal as a portable document format file (PDF). The
proposal was rejected as nonresponsive, and the GAO denied the bidder’s protest because the bidder
failed to show it had submitted its proposal in the format required by the solicitation.
An offer may be found nonresponsive if the offeror fails to obtain certain required permissions to
perform the work set forth in the solicitation. The Court of Federal Claims has found a bid nonre-
sponsive where the software that ran certain required equipment was unique and exclusively owned
by another entity other than the offeror and the offeror did not obtain required permissions. In Chant
Engineering Co., Inc., the government issued a competitive solicitation for three general-purpose
hydraulic test systems (test stands), one hydraulic power supply, and the software necessary for inter-
facing with the existing equipment and computer networks. 25 Chant submitted the lowest-priced bid;
however, the government determined that the bid was deficient because Chant could not show how
it would use existing software and support equipment containing proprietary information owned by
a competitor. Chant protested. On review, the Court of Federal Claims agreed the government prop-
erly found Chant’s bid nonresponsive for failing to explain how its product would interact with the
proprietary software.
A materially unbalanced bid may also be deemed nonresponsive.26 In M. C. General, Inc., the
GAO upheld a determination that a bid was nonresponsive because it was materially unbalanced.27
The bidder contended the “unbalancing” resulted from its internal allocation of technical evaluation
and preproduction costs to first articles. The GAO concluded that where costs necessary to produce

Rejection of a bid as nonresponsive may also be proper when the principal on the bid bond sub-
mitted by the bidder is not the same legal entity as the offeror on the bid form. A surety can be
obligated on a bid bond only if the principal named in the bond fails to execute the contract after
award to that bidder. The refusal of another entity to contract with the awarding authority does not
result in a forfeiture of the bid bond. A defective bid bond constitutes a substantial deviation that
ordinarily requires rejection of the bid as nonresponsive, because such a bond does not protect the
public body and enables a bidder to avoid a contract with impunity. 29
Although many deviations may be considered “material” and these concepts are often strictly
applied, there is also a well-established policy that the awarding authority may waive minor irregu-
larities in a bid. 30 Permitting the waiver of minor irregularities or informalities preserves the focus
of competitive bidding on obtaining the lowest price, and discourages questions over matters not
affecting the substance of the bid. 31
The basic rule with minor irregularities is that the defect or variation in the bid must have triv-
ial or negligible significance when contrasted with the total cost or scope of the invitation for bids.
Deviations affecting price, quantity, quality, delivery, or date of completion are generally considered
material and merit especially stringent standards to protect against any bidder obtaining a competi-
tive advantage. 32 For a bid irregularity to be waived, it must be so inconsequential or immaterial that
the bidder does not gain a competitive advantage after all bids have been exposed. Thus, a minor
irregularity may be found where the bidder fails to initial a price change in its bid before bid open-
ing; 33 fails to mark its bid envelope with the solicitation number, date, and time of bid opening;34 or
fails to provide incidental information requested by the invitation.35 Furnishing a bid bond from a
surety with a less than specified quality rating did not render a bid nonresponsive and the irregularity
could be waived by the agency. 36
Determining what constitutes a minor informality is generally left to the discretion of the con-
tracting agency37 and courts often recognize the contracting agency’s broad discretion to determine
what constitutes a minor irregularity. For example, a Maryland court held that a bidder’s failure to
furnish a bid bond was not a material irregularity necessitating bid rejection. 38 Specifically, the court
characterized the governing considerations as follows:

cations. On the other hand, it is the duty of an administrative agency to secure the most

Another far-reaching example of a procuring agency’s exercise of discretion to award to the low-

on the bid price49

II. KEY CONCEPTS IN TRADITIONAL PUBLIC COMPETITIVE BIDS—RESPONSIVENESS AND RESPONSIBILITY 	121
important as the word “lowest.” Responsibility determinations focus on whether the contractor has
the necessary technical, managerial, and financial capabilities, and the integrity to perform the work.
A “responsible” bidder is a contractor capable of satisfactorily undertaking and completing the work.
Public contracting authorities will consider a number of factors in determining whether a contractor
is responsible. These factors, falling into two general categories, are also relevant to a private owner’s
evaluation of prospective contractors.
First, a contractor must be able to perform the work required by the solicitation. In determining the
contractor’s ability to perform, public contracting authorities will consider the contractor’s financial
resources, facilities and equipment, and experience, as well as licenses and permits. Second, a con-
tractor must be reliable and demonstrate desirable prior performance. In this category, procurement
officials will consider the ethical integrity of the contractor and the contractor’s ability to perform
and complete previous (and typically similar) projects.
In federal procurement, FAR § 9.104–1 specifies that a contractor must demonstrate the following
qualifications to be considered responsible:
1. Have adequate financial resources to perform the contract, or the ability to obtain them
2. Be able to comply with the required or proposed delivery or performance schedule, considering
all existing commercial and governmental business commitments
3. Have a satisfactory performance record
4. Have a satisfactory record of integrity and business ethics
5. Have the necessary organization, experience, accounting and operational controls, and tech-
nical skills, or the ability to obtain them
6. Have the necessary production, construction, and technical equipment and facilities, or be able
to obtain them
7. Be otherwise qualified and eligible for award under applicable laws and regulations
In general, under the principles governing federal contracting, the determination of respon-
sibility is based on the contractor’s demonstrated ability to perform the specified work when
such work is to commence, not at the time of bidding. 51 Consequently, a bidder will be deemed
responsible if the bidder can demonstrate, at the time when the responsibility determination is
made, that it has or can obtain the apparent ability to perform the work as of the date work is
to begin. 52
The responsibility of a low bidder may be challenged. If the question arises of whether a con-
tractor is responsible, it should be resolved through consideration of all available facts, whether or
not submitted with the bid. Since a public official is making a quasi-judicial decision when deter-
mining whether a bidder is “responsible” within the meaning of the governing statute, the bidder
is entitled to due process. Therefore, a public body’s finding that a bidder is not responsible should
be supported by a record establishing: (1) the facts on which the decision was based; (2) details of
the investigation that disclosed these facts; and (3) the opportunity that was offered to the bidder to
present its qualifications.
Generally, the contractor will be entitled to an informal hearing on the matter, although a formal
hearing may be prescribed by statute. Normally, the contractor is entitled to present evidence on
its behalf. Once a decision is made, however, the courts generally will not reverse the agency’s

In the federal procurement setting, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) has limited
challenges to responsibility determinations to those involving serious concerns that the contracting
officer failed to consider available relevant information or otherwise violated a statute or regulation.54
As a result, agency determinations are accepted in the vast majority of cases.55 However, where an
agency’s determination of nonresponsibility is so unreasonable as to be arbitrary and capricious, the
affected bidder will be permitted to recover its bid preparation costs.56
III. 	THE “LOWEST AND BEST” BIDDER
Some who engage in competitive bidding assume that an owner must award the construction con-
tract to the lowest bidder. This belief, however, is only partially accurate in public contracting and
is generally not correct at all in private contracting. A contractor’s bid, in a legal sense, is simply
an offer to perform work. Until the owner accepts that offer, no enforceable obligation arises.57
Highlighting that the bid itself is only an offer to perform, the owner’s invitation for bids usually
contains a provision to the effect that “the owner reserves the right to reject any or all bids.” This
provision puts contractors on notice in the bidding documents that the owner may choose not to
accept any of the offers (bids). 58 The public owner has broad discretion in deciding to reject all bids,
and this discretion generally will not be disturbed absent a showing of an abuse of discretion, collu-
sion, corruption, or subversion of the competitive process.59 Although the federal government must
consider factors other than price in the evaluation process, the relative pricing of bids is of great
importance in federal procurement. Federal agencies must accept the bid that is the most financially
advantageous to the federal government, so long as that bid is responsive to the terms of the solicita-
tion and the bidder is a responsible contractor. According to one federal statute, agency heads must
award contracts “to the responsible bidder whose bid conforms to the solicitation and is most advan-
tageous to the United States, considering only price and the other price-related factors included in

III. THE “LOWEST AND BEST” BIDDER 	123
the solicitation” (emphasis added).60 Even when the federal government elects to award construction
contracts using the “best-value” negotiated procurement process, it is still required to make cost or
price one of the evaluation criteria. 61
The federal concern for securing the most financially advantageous bid is well illustrated by the
evaluation of bids responding to solicitations with multiple items. In general, bids presented on this
type of solicitation must be evaluated based both on the unit price offered by a bidder, as well as the
total price. In S. J. Groves & Sons Co.,62 the GAO stated that “where awards on a combination of
schedules is contemplated the award made must result in the lowest cost to the government to carry
out the mandate of 10 U.S.C. § 2305(c).”63 As a result, a federal agency may actually be required to
make multiple awards if different bidders offer the lowest unit price on different specific items or if
the value of prices of individual items is lower than the total price offered by another bidder.
Even though the relative prices offered by bidders are of great importance to federal procurement
officials, a contractor submitting the low bid generally has no vested interest in the award of that
contract. 64 Nevertheless, that contractor cannot be denied the contract unless the denial would be in
the public’s best interest. A further qualification to the importance of price is that even if the bidder on
a federal contract does not present the lowest bid, the bid is entitled to fair consideration. 65 Where a
federal agency fails to consider adequately a bidder’s proposal, the bidder may be entitled to recover
bid-preparation costs. 66
Most state and local governments must also award their contracts to the lowest and best bidder.
Most states and many localities have enacted statutes or ordinances mandating award to the lowest
bidder whose bid meets the solicitation’s technical requirements and complies with applicable state
or local laws, such as domestic preference statutes.67 Some courts addressing state and local public

create a protected property interest in favor of the lowest responsible, responsive bidder in the expec-
tation of award, if the solicitation is subject to competitive bidding requirements protected by federal
or state law. 68 Other courts interpreting state or local competitive bidding requirements have found
that the lowest responsible, responsive bidder does not have a protected property interest in the award
of the contract. 69 Determining whether a protected property interest exists turns on the nature of the
state or local law, regulation, or ordinance governing the procurement at issue. 70

IV. 	NEGOTIATED “BEST VALUE” SELECTION PROCESS
Historically, the preferred method of contracting for construction in the federal government system
was through sealed bidding with the government issuing an invitation for bids (IFB). Bids were
received on the date specified in the invitation, and award was made to the lowest-dollar bid from
a responsive, responsible bidder. Negotiated procurement was another method of contracting but
was used only under specific circumstances set forth in statute and regulations. Under negotiated
procurement procedures, the federal government issued a request for proposals (RFP). Generally,
once proposals were received, the government and the offerors entered into negotiations under the
terms of the solicitation, with award being made to the offeror that ultimately submitted the lowest
negotiated price.
The negotiated “best value” procurement process is authorized under 10 U.S.C. § 2304 and the
FAR71 and is now used by federal agencies on a large majority of procurements for construction
projects. Under this procedure, the government is not required to award to the lowest-priced offeror.
Rather, through a trade-off evaluation process specified in the RFP, the government makes an award
to the offeror whose proposal provides the “best value” to the government. In this regard, FAR §
15.101–1 provides the following:
(a) A tradeoff process is appropriate when it may be in the best interest of the government to
consider award to other than the lowest priced offeror or other than the highest technically rated
offeror.
(b) When using a tradeoff process, the following apply:
(1) All evaluation factors and significant subfactors that will affect contract award and their
relative importance shall be clearly stated in the solicitation; and
(2) The solicitation shall state whether all evaluation factors other than cost or price, when
combined, are significantly more important than, approximately equal to, or significantly less
important than cost or price.
(c) This process permits tradeoffs among cost or price and non-cost factors and allows the gov-
ernment to accept other than the lowest priced proposal. The perceived benefits of the higher priced
proposal shall merit the additional cost, and the rationale for tradeoffs must be documented in the
file in accordance with [FAR §] 15.406.
The negotiated best-value procurement process has been the subject of numerous protests to the
GAO as well as actions in the United States Court of Federal Claims and the United States Court
of Appeals for the Federal Circuit. The GAO and federal courts will give substantial deference to
the government’s exercise of discretion in determining which offer is the most advantageous to the
government. For example, in Park Tower Mgmt., Ltd. v. United States,72 the agency selected a mainte-
nance services contractor after an extended negotiated procurement process. The disappointed bidder
filed a protest claiming that the agency’s best-value determination was unreasonable because, in part,
the award went to a contractor with a lower technical evaluation score. The Park Tower court upheld
the agency’s decision, noting that the best-value approach gives the agency substantial discretion.
71See FAR Part 15.
72 67 Fed. Cl. 548 (2005).

-- 162 of 771 --

IV. NEGOTIATED “BEST VALUE” SELECTION PROCESS 	125
The protestor’s burden when seeking to overturn an agency’s decision becomes heavier as the
agency’s level of discretion increases. In addition, evaluation scores are merely guidelines to be
used by the agency, which must exercise judgment in determining how differences in technical eval-
uation scores will affect overall performance on the contract. The ultimate standard or test applied
by both the GAO and the federal courts is: (1) whether the agency complied with the FAR require-
ments for negotiated best-value procurements; and (2) whether the agency followed the selection
and evaluation procedures set forth in the RFP.73
The negotiated best-value method is also widely used in state and local government procurement
and is sometimes referred to as competitive selection and negotiation.74 Even when state statutes
mandate the use of sealed bidding, some states permit the use of best value when a project’s overall
costs can be reduced while still maintaining public policy objectives or when sealed bidding is not
feasible or practical. 75 For example, when substantial cost savings could be achieved without encour-
aging favoritism and without substantially diminishing competition for public contracts, an Oregon
court upheld an agency’s decision to forgo the use of competitive sealed bidding.76 Sealed bidding
may not be feasible or practical in cases of insufficient competition, lack of detailed specifications,
or under emergency situations.
Although many states have permitted their procuring agencies to use the best-value approach,
particularly for design-build projects, there is little similarity between the details of various state
methods for doing so. The major differences lie primarily in the evaluation criteria used to determine
best value and the process by which the winning proposal is selected.
The process used to select the best value may involve specific requirements for creating the solic-
itation, scoring and ranking the submitted proposals, making an initial determination of the most
qualified bidders, or rules regulating negotiations with bidders. In general, however, the process may
be reduced to a two-step procedure consisting of a qualification stage and a best-value evaluation
stage. In the first stage, the procuring agency receives proposals and creates a short list of the best
candidates meeting a specified qualification threshold, based on appropriate selection criteria. The
most qualified candidates receive an invitation to negotiate or submit a priced proposal. For example,
Florida agencies seeking architectural or engineering services narrow the list of bidders to no fewer
than three candidates, based on the ability to furnish the required services.77 In the second stage, the
procuring agency typically conducts an in-depth evaluation of the qualified proposals and selects the
offeror that presents the best value to the project.
States following the best-value method have also created different guidelines and evaluation crite-
ria to award contracts. In some states, statutes enumerate evaluation factors that the procuring agency
must use.78 Colorado’s integrated project delivery statute, for instance, requires the use of price, tech-
nical approach, past performance, and project management and craft labor capabilities as factors.79
In other states, the procuring agency itself decides what factors determine best value. For example, a
California school district may independently determine appropriate best-value selection criteria for
design-build projects.80 Regardless of the guidelines used to create best-value criteria, state procure-
ment regulations are subject to the same types of challenges as seen in the federal arena. That is,
73Microdyne Outsourcing, Inc. v. United States, 72 Fed. Cl. 694 (2006); Widnall v. B3H Corp., 75 F.3d 1577 (Fed. Cir. 1996).

V. 	ELECTRONIC BIDS
Electronic commerce has been implemented in virtually all of the states and the federal government,
but there is no predominant pattern among the states. Many states have passed enabling legislation
allowing state officials to establish procurement programs for electronic commerce, while others pro-
vide only electronic solicitation notices. Some states allow online bidding as an alternative method,
and still others will accept electronic bids for selected agencies.
In accordance with FAR Subpart 4.5, “Electronic Commerce in Contracting,” the federal govern-
ment uses electronic procurement practices. While there is no provision in the FAR that specially
addresses the use of online actions, the GAO has consistently ruled that the use of an online pro-
curement process is consistent with FAR Part 13. 82 Still prohibited, however, is conduct that “favors
one offeror over another,” “reveals an offeror’s technical solution,” or “knowingly furnishes source
selection information” contrary to regulatory or statutory requirements. 83
Four decisions from the GAO illustrate problems that e-bidding for federal contracts may present.
In PMTech, Inc.,84 a contractor bidding online attempted to take the necessary steps to timely submit
its bid, but failed to submit anything other than the cover sheet for its proposal by the time responses
to the solicitation were due. PMTech provided the information missing from its original submittal one
day after solicitations were due; however, the bid was still rejected as untimely. PMTech protested
to the GAO. The GAO rejected PMTech’s arguments and stated in its decision: “We view it as an
offeror’s responsibility, when transmitting its proposal electronically, to insure the proposal’s timely
delivery by transmitting the proposal sufficiently in advance of the time set for receipt of proposals
to allow for timely receipt by the agency.”85 In a decision similar to those involving late delivery of
bids or late delivery of faxes, the GAO concluded that PMTech assumed the risk of submitting an
incomplete bid when it waited until only 13 minutes before the deadline for receipt of proposals to
begin to transmit its proposal.
Similarly, in Sea Box, Inc.,86 the GAO held that although the bid was received by the federal gov-
ernment’s email system before the deadline, it was untimely because it failed to reach the specified
email box by the stated deadline. In the Sea Box decision, the GAO pointed out that the protestor
sent its bid, consisting of seven emails, approximately 11 minutes before the stated deadline. The
seven emails reached the agency’s initial point of entry for email before the deadline, were held for
a period of time, then were sent to a virus-scanning server and subsequently arrived 7 to 24 minutes
late at the specified email box for receipt of bids. The agency rejected the bid as late and the GAO
agreed.
Under FAR § 14.304(b)(1)(ii), a bid that would otherwise be treated as a “late” bid may be
considered for award if it was under the government’s control before the deadline for receipt of

applied the Government Control exception and ordered the COE to consider the proposal as timely.
The Government Control exception has applied to the government’s rejection of an offer due to
the size of the email transmitting it. In Fed. Acquisition Services Team, LLC,90 the agency required
proposals to be emailed to a particular email address and warned that emails with files larger than
20 megabytes (MB) in size would be rejected. Federal Acquisition Services Team, LLC (FAST)
emailed its proposal to the required address and it was received by the government server more than
four hours prior to the deadline. A few minutes later a second server rejected the email due to size,
preventing its delivery to the destination mailbox. The agency declined to accept the bid.
FAST protested, arguing it timely submitted its email and it was incorrectly bounced back as
“undeliverable” because when the email left FAST’s server, it measured less than the 20 MB limit.
The GAO rejected the protest; however, the Court of Federal Claims reversed. At least four proposals
below the 20 MB limit were improperly rejected by the agency, and the court noted that no test had
been conducted by the agency prior to the issuance of the solicitation to determine the server’s size
limitation. This “misled offerors into believing that files totaling up to 20 megabytes in size could
be sent on one email,” when the actual limit was much lower. The court held that the agency acted
arbitrarily and capriciously in not applying the Government Control exception to accept FAST’s
proposal. In Tishman Construction Corp.,91 the prospective contractor submitted identical bids elec-
tronically and on paper as was required by the RFP for construction management services. The paper
version of the bid was received by the contracting entity approximately 73 minutes after the stated
deadline. The electronic version of the bid was received approximately 50 minutes before the bid
deadline. The agency rejected the bid as untimely. The GAO disagreed and sustained Tishman’s
protest, relying on a prior decision in which a bidder submitted its bid at two separate locations, as
required by the solicitation, but only one was timely. 92 In that earlier decision, the GAO found that
the agency had received a complete copy of the bid in a timely manner and no competitive advantage

sufficient time to protest the amended terms of the solicitation, the GAO concluded that it was the

cause of the insufficient time and denied the protest.
Firms submitting bids electronically should adhere to the strict and longstanding rules regarding
timeliness for the submission of bids or proposals in proper format.
VI. 	REVERSE AUCTIONS
The advancement of technology has also given rise to the use of online “reverse auctions.” A reverse
auction is a live, Internet-based auction in which prospective contractors bid down the price to pro-
vide the products or services sought by the purchaser. A typical reverse auction starts with the owner
selecting a list of prequalified bidders. Specifications and drawings are provided to the bidders before
the auction with sufficient lead time to prepare bids. Once the auction starts, the contractors bid
simultaneously and can evaluate their relative standing, although they do not know the identity of
the other bidders and may not have a competitor’s specific quote or bid. Bids are made in multiple
rounds and the duration of each round is relatively short. The auction ends at a predetermined time
and the lowest bidder is selected.
Reverse auctions may offer many potential benefits to owners. When the products being sought
are commodities or when owners can clearly define the scope, specifications, and conditions of the
desired products and services, a reverse auction may help to get to the bottom-line price. This is
especially true when there are many qualified bidders. The speed of a reverse auction may also
decrease procurement time because there is less need for negotiations between the owner and poten-
tial contractors. Finally, reverse auctions leverage technology, and owners may easily outsource their
auctions to third-party providers. This may lower the transactional costs of procurement and may
ensure that a detached and neutral party administers the process.
The use and efficacy of reverse auctions, however, is hotly contested in the construction industry.95
One of the chief complaints lodged by contractors and suppliers is that a reverse auction is heavily
focused on price to the exclusion of other relevant factors. Since construction products and services
can seldom be characterized as commodities, the focus on price may lead owners to ignore the
inherent variability found in construction projects. That is, the winning bidder’s price may simply be
a bare-bones bid that does not fully consider the numerous unknown issues likely to be encountered.
This may lead to disagreements over the necessity of change orders and the subsequent pricing of
such changes. Also, important qualitative factors, such as schedule, quality, and performance, are
likely to be discounted by the reverse-auction process. When these factors are deemphasized, the
resulting true cost of the project is likely to be higher than anticipated.
93ABT Associates, Inc., Comp. Gen. B-226063, 87–1 CPD ¶ 513.
94 Comp. Gen. B-291488, 2002 CPD ¶ 205.
95See, e.g., Associated General Contractors of America, White Paper on Reverse Auctions for Procurement of Construction
(2003).

VII. GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS WHEN COMPETING ON PRIVATE CONTRACTS 	129
Reverse auctions may also lead to bid gaming, in which the owner fails to obtain the lowest bid
that otherwise would have been offered. Because contractors understand that they may simply offer
a lower bid during a later stage of the reverse auction, there is little motivation to put forth the truly
lowest bid early on. Instead, contractors hold back their lowest bids and monitor the progress of the
other bidding. As a consequence, the winning bidder may win the auction with a bid that exceeds
the price it otherwise would have been prepared to offer. By contrast, in sealed bidding, there is
no opportunity to view the other bids and contractors have but one opportunity to offer the lowest
bid. Sealed bidders are, therefore, motivated to provide the lowest acceptable bid when initially
submitting their bid.
As noted above, the GAO has ruled that reverse auctions may be conducted by federal government
agencies under the authority of FAR Part 13 when the agency is procuring “commercial items.”96
State laws related to the use of reverse auctions for construction are in a state of flux. Many states
have not specifically addressed the use of the process for public projects. However, some others
have prohibited the use of the reverse-auction process to award public construction contracts, while
others expressly authorize its use. 97 Private owners are free to adopt the process and several large
commercial owners routinely use reverse-bid auctions.
VII. 	GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS WHEN COMPETING ON PRIVATE CONTRACTS
Few rules exist in private contract bidding that obligate the owner to award to a particular con-
tractor. Although a private owner is not bound by statute to operate under the “lowest responsible,
responsive bidder” approach, the private owner will likely consider many of the same factors when
reviewing bids. The private owner may select a contractor based on any criteria it deems appro-
priate and is generally under no obligation to award to the lowest bidder. A private owner might
even attempt to negotiate a lower price once the low bid has been determined. Moreover, private
owners are generally under no duty to disclose the bases for their decisions. Private owners may
open bids outside the presence of all bidders. Private owners may require the bidders to provide a
wide variety of information concerning the contractor’s ability to perform the project. In addition,
private owners may or may not require the contractor to provide a bid bond to guarantee its bid or
proposal, or payment and performance bonds or other security, to guarantee performance once the
work starts.
As with public bidding, the contractor should present itself as a responsible business responsive
to the owner’s needs and prepared to perform at a reasonable price. Although there is generally
no need to demonstrate “responsibility” in the context of private contract bidding, in many
jurisdictions, contractors offering bids, even on private projects, must be appropriately licensed. 98
The contractor should also take care to determine whether the owner can meet payment obligations
and provide promised logistical support. For the most part, a private owner presents a much
greater financial risk than a public body with its tax base. Additionally, the contractor should
carefully review all specifications and plans presented by the private owner. A private owner may
not have the resources to provide the review necessary to find and eliminate potential, and costly,
design problems.

97See Construction State Law Matrix published by the AGC of America for a state-by-state summary of the laws affecting
the use of reverse auctions in public contracting.
98See, e.g., Fla. Stat. Ann. § 489.115(1) (prohibiting person from engaging in contracting without being certified or registered

VIII. 	EFFECT OF PAST PERFORMANCE EVALUATIONS ON AWARD PROCESS
In federal contracting, a contractor’s past performance has long been a factor in determining if that
firm is deemed to be responsible. 99 In the context of a sealed bid competition, a responsibility deter-
mination is essentially a “pass-fail” type of evaluation as there is no process for federal agencies to
compare firms’ relative records of past performance. However, in the best-value negotiated selection
process, past performance is a mandatory evaluation factor in most source selections.100 Once the
federal agencies were authorized to consider and compare the offerors’ relative past performance
records, there was a need to implement a process to obtain and retain information on a firm’s past
performance record in a relatively consistent format, which could be reviewed by any federal agency.
While state and local governments are not subject to the laws and regulations controlling the award
of contracts by the federal government, the adoption of the negotiated best-value selection process,
especially in the context of design-build projects, is likely to increase the importance of the con-
tractors’ past performance records. Reflecting this trend, the Federal Highway Administration has
adopted a “Performance Contracting for Construction” guide, based on a pilot project conducted by
the Michigan Department of Transportation. 101 Other state government entities use a contractor’s
past performance as part of the prequalification process that predetermines a contractor’s eligibility
to submit bids to perform work for certain state agencies.102 Given this trend, any contractor seeking
to compete for public contracts (federal, state, or local) should recognize that the practices and poli-
cies underlying the federal government’s approach to the collection and use of a contractor’s past
performance data may be carefully examined by other public agencies and, to some extent, may be
used as templates and guides by these agencies.
In 1994, Congress passed the Federal Acquisitions Streamlining Act (FASA).103 In so doing,
Congress adopted a policy that a contractor’s past performance should be evaluated during a current
acquisition process to determine whether that contractor should receive future work. Section 1091
of FASA provides that “past contract performance of an offeror is one of the relevant factors that a
contracting official of an executive agency should consider in awarding a contract.” Under FASA,
all federal departments and agencies must have procedures to record contractor performance con-
temporaneous with that performance on all contracts over $100,000 and to use the contractor’s past
performance during future acquisition processes. The federal government believes that the use of
past performance evaluations will sufficiently motivate contractors to perform at the highest stan-
dards or, to the extent they are not, to improve their performance before they are rated again by an
agency or department. Past performance evaluations are a significant factor in the agencies’ determi-
nations of a best-value selection. Procuring agencies can better predict the quality of the contractor’s
performance and, therefore, the associated customer’s satisfaction.
The primary rationale supporting the evaluation of contractor performance and its use in future
procurements is twofold. First, Congress believes that an active dialogue between the contractor
and the government during performance will result in better current performance by the contractor.
Second, because contractors are made aware that their performance evaluations will be used by
other procuring agencies on future procurements, procuring agencies will be better able to select
high-quality contractors for new contracts. Some state and local public agencies have adopted this
rationale and consider past performance evaluations.

100 FAR § 15.304(c)(3)(i).

102See, e.g. Fla. Admin. Code R. 14-22.003 (using, among other things, contractor past-performance ratings from prior FDOT
