E. 	Revocation of Acceptance in Whole or in Part
The buyer may revoke its acceptance of a lot or commercial unit whose nonconformity substan-
tially impairs its value to the buyer if:58 (1) the buyer accepted on the reasonable assumption that
the nonconformity would be cured, but the nonconformity was not seasonably cured; or (2) the non-
conformity was not discovered and the buyer’s acceptance was “reasonably induced either by the
difficulty of discovery before acceptance or by the seller’s assurances.”59 A buyer’s revocation of
acceptance “must occur within a reasonable time after the buyer discovers or should have discovered
the ground for it and before any substantial change in the condition of the goods.” 60 For revocation
of acceptance to be valid, a change in the condition of the goods must be a result of only the goods’
own defects. In addition, revocation of acceptance is not effective until the buyer notifies the seller
of such revocation. 61
Several remedies are available to a buyer after proper revocation of acceptance.62 A buyer can
cancel the order and, regardless of whether the buyer chooses to cancel, it can recoup as much of the
purchase price as has been paid. 63 A buyer may purchase replacement goods (“cover”) and recover
the difference between the cost of the substituted goods and the contract price. 64 If a buyer does not
cover, then, in addition to the purchase price paid, the buyer may recover the difference between
the market price and the contract price. 65 Provable incidental and consequential damages are also
recoverable. 66
VII. 	WARRANTIES UNDER THE U.C.C.
The U.C.C. identifies the following four types of warranties to protect buyers of goods:
1. The warranty of title and against infringement warrants that the title to goods conveyed is
good and their transfer is rightful. The seller also warrants that the goods “shall be delivered
free from any security interest or other lien or encumbrance of which the buyer at the time of
contracting has no knowledge.”67
2. An express warranty made by the seller. An express warranty is created by “[a]ny affirmation
of fact or promise made by the seller to the buyer which relates to the goods and becomes part

The seller is not required to use the word “warranty” or “guarantee” to create an express
warranty. 69
3. The implied warranty of merchantability is the warranty that the goods will be fit for ordinary

A. 	Warranty Disclaimers
The U.C.C. includes rules governing a seller’s attempt to limit or disclaim warranty coverage. 75
Generally, a seller’s disclaimer language must conform to the wording suggested by the U.C.C. For
example, the U.C.C. states that “[l]anguage to exclude all implied warranties of fitness is sufficient
if it states, for example, that ‘There are no warranties which extend beyond the description on the
face hereof.’” 76 Nonetheless, the U.C.C. allows all implied warranties to be excluded by expressions
such as “as is,” “with all faults,” or other language that would commonly put the buyer on notice
to warranties being excluded and plainly shows that no implied warranty exists.77 Case law has
also upheld warranty disclaimers that stated “there is no implied warranty of merchantability or
any other implied warranty that extends beyond the express warranty included in this contract.” 78
The law addressing this subject has developed to the point that sellers have little trouble including
enforceable disclaimer provisions in their contracts. 79

B. 	Limitations on Remedies
Since warranties are easily disclaimed, contractual limitations on remedies for breaches, such as
delivery delays or delivery of nonconforming goods and materials, are frequently more important
to buyers.80 Sellers often seek to limit their exposure to buyers by limiting the buyers’ damages
or substituting an alternative remedy. For example, a seller may seek to limit the buyer’s remedy
to a return of the goods and repayment of the purchase price, or to repair and replacement of the
defective goods.81 To be effective in barring consequential damages—that is, business losses other
than those incurred to obtain conforming goods—the seller must provide that the alternative remedy
is exclusive of all other remedies. If the alternative remedy is not expressly exclusive, the stated
remedy will merely be one of many forms of relief.82 A U.C.C. disclaimer may not be effective to
eliminate tort liability—such as for negligence or strict liability in tort—although a seller may obtain
a waiver of tort claims through a properly drafted contract provision.
Lastly, the buyer generally has recourse to other U.C.C. remedies when the exclusive, limited
remedy fails of its essential purpose. 83 In other words, the buyer is not restricted to an exclusive,
limited remedy that fails to work. The most common limited remedy is repair or replacement of
the defective goods. Courts have found that if the defect cannot be repaired or replaced within a
reasonable time, that remedy may fail of its essential purpose and the buyer may be able to sue for
damages. 84 The majority of courts have upheld contractual limitations or exclusions of consequential
damages unless doing so would be unconscionable, regardless of whether the limited remedy clause
fails of its essential purpose. 85

VIII. STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS AND COMMENCEMENT OF THE WARRANTY PERIOD 	163
implies that the “seller has offered to deliver what he incorrectly believes to be conforming goods.” 87
Tender of delivery generally triggers the start of the warranty period for the goods and gives rise to a
cause of action or right to sue for delivery of defective goods. The statute of limitations begins to run
when the cause of action arises.88 In most states, the statute of limitations under the U.C.C. is four
years from tender of delivery. 89 Contractors and subcontractors need to recognize that the duration of
the U.C.C. statute of limitations may differ greatly from the limitation period applicable to a breach
of the construction contract/subcontract and may begin to run well before the construction project
is completed. This difference in the commencement of the warranty period can create a significant
“warranty gap” for the unwary buyer (contractor or subcontractor).
Several exceptions to these general principles exist. The most important exception permits
the parties to alter, by agreement, the timing of both the commencement of the warranty period
and the running of the statute of limitations. For example, the parties can agree to make both
events contingent upon acceptance of the goods by the buyer after a reasonable period for
inspection.
A second exception arises when the seller attempts to repair a defective good but is unsuc-
cessful. Sometimes such repair attempts are considered to “toll,” or suspend, the running of the
statute of limitations. The rules governing this exception vary significantly from state to state. Some
states hold that repair efforts do not suspend the running of the limitation period. 90 Other states
hold that the limitation period does not run during the seller’s repair efforts.91 A key factor in
determining whether a seller’s repair efforts toll the running of the statute is often whether the
seller made any promise or assurance to the buyer that the defects could be repaired. 92 A court
will usually examine such promise or assurance to see if they caused the buyer to refrain from
filing suit.93
A third exception arises where the seller makes a warranty of future performance. Some parties,
seeking to avoid the running of the limitation period, have argued that this exception applies merely
because they could not discover the defect until some point after tender of delivery. Courts usually
reject this argument unless the warranty required more in the way of future performance than merely
meeting the contract specifications. 94 One example of a construction warranty that extends to future
performance is the typical 10-year or 20-year roofing warranty where express language, such as
“bonded for up to 20 years,” may provide a warranty of future performance. 95 In contrast, a statement

or provisions of a warranty. This indemnity obligation may establish a separate basis for a claim
by the buyer. The statute of limitations on an indemnity-based claim generally does not begin to
run on a breach of an indemnification agreement until the seller refuses to honor it, even though
delivery of the goods occurred much earlier.97 For example, a breach claim may arise where the
purchase agreement provides that the seller will indemnify and hold the buyer harmless from claims
and losses arising from the sale of, or the buyer’s use of, defective goods, and the seller fails to
honor the indemnity provision. Contractors and subcontractors need to appreciate the distinction
between a warranty obligation and an indemnity obligation and ensure that the latter is addressed in
any lower-tier subcontracts and purchase orders.
IX. 	PERFORMANCE ISSUES
A. 	Anticipatory Repudiation/Adequate Assurance of Performance
When one party to a contract has reasonable grounds for insecurity about the other party’s ability or
desire to fully perform in the future, the aggrieved party has a right to require that the other party pro-
vide adequate assurance of full performance. 98 The reasonableness for insecurity and the adequacy
of any assurance are measured by commercial standards. 99 The parties may agree to define commer-
cial standards and the notion of insecurity in order to avoid many of the problems of interpretation
inherent in this concept.
The aggrieved party may make a demand on the other party, who then has the duty to provide ade-
quate assurance of performance within a reasonable time but not exceeding 30 days.100 The failure to
provide adequate assurances within a reasonable time is a repudiation of the contract. 101 When repu-
diation occurs, the aggrieved party is entitled to take certain actions to mitigate its damages.102 The
aggrieved party may: (1) “for a commercially reasonable time await performance by the repudiating

however, when the seller is demanding that payment be made on time. 106 Examples of adequate
assurances by a buyer would include presentation of statements from its banker, submission of a
letter of credit, establishment of an escrow account for future payments, or even offering a mortgage
on other property.
B. 	Dealing with the Other Party’s Insolvency
Under the U.C.C., a party is insolvent if it has ceased to pay its debts in the ordinary course of busi-
ness, cannot pay its debts as they become due, or is deemed insolvent under federal bankruptcy laws.
Upon discovering the buyer’s insolvency, the seller may:
1. Stop delivery if the goods are still in transit;
2. Refuse delivery unless the buyer pays cash for the delivered goods and all prior deliveries; or
3. Reclaim the goods:
(a) within 10 days, if the buyer received the goods on credit while insolvent; or
(b) at any time, if the buyer misrepresented its solvency in writing to the seller within three
months prior to delivery. 107
The seller’s right to reclaim the goods is an important right under the U.C.C., but it has certain
limitations. 108 The original seller’s right to reclaim is lost if the original buyer has resold the goods
to a good-faith purchaser.109 For example, in the construction context, a supplier may not recover
goods from an insolvent subcontractor, even if the goods have not yet been incorporated into the
project, if the prime contractor or owner has already paid the subcontractor for the goods. A prime
contractor or owner should, however, be cautious about attempting to use this exception to defeat a
supplier’s right to reclaim goods.
Payment to an insolvent subcontractor is generally unwise unless the subcontractor has already
performed the work for which it is entitled to be paid, as opposed to merely purchasing supplies that
it will later incorporate into the project. As this exception requires good faith by the prime contrac-
tor or owner, it may not apply if the subcontractor’s insolvency is obvious. Unless the subcontract
requires prompt payment and the contractor has made prior prompt payments for materials, a sudden
hasty payment to a subcontractor may show that the prime contractor knew of the subcontractor’s

and title to the goods.
The U.C.C. also addresses the opposite situation in which a buyer is faced with an insolvent seller.
A buyer may take possession of goods for which it has contracted, if:
1. The goods were bought for “personal, family, or household purposes, the seller repudiates or
fails to deliver as required by the contract”; or
2. “[T]he seller becomes insolvent within ten days after receipt of the first installment on the
price.”110
Absent these special circumstances, the buyer may not obtain possession, but may acquire a secu-
rity interest in the goods under Article 9 of the U.C.C.
C. 	Excuse of Performance by Failure of Presupposed Conditions
Purchase orders and sale-of-goods agreements usually include a force majeure clause. A force
majeure clause typically excuses nonperformance by either the buyer or the seller that is caused by
an act of God, war, strike by a common carrier, or other cause beyond the parties’ control. Under
the U.C.C., a force majeure clause is lawful and enforceable.
Where the contract does not include a force majeure clause, the U.C.C. provides that a delay in
delivery or non-delivery will be excused if the seller’s performance has been made commercially
impracticable by: (1) the occurrence of a contingency; (2) the contingency making performance
impracticable; and (3) the nonoccurrence of which was a basic assumption of the contract. 111 In
addition, delay in delivery or non-delivery may not be a breach if due to good-faith compliance
with a domestic or foreign governmental regulation, even if it later proves to be invalid. 112 Where
the seller remains capable of partial performance, the seller must allocate production and deliveries
among its customers.113 In addition, the seller must notify the buyer of delay or non-delivery and the
amount of any allocation of available deliveries. 114 If the agreed-upon manner of delivery becomes
commercially impracticable and a commercially reasonable substitute is available, the buyer must
accept the reasonable substitute.115
Commercial impracticability is a more lenient standard for excusing performance than is avail-
able under the common law that applies to most construction contracts. Consequently, contractors
should consider the ramifications of this section when purchasing goods, and should contract for
a greater obligation on the seller than the U.C.C. imposes.116 Otherwise, the contractor may be
required to perform while its suppliers—which are providing goods and, therefore, are governed by
the U.C.C.—will be excused from performance. 117
110Id. at § 2-502(1).

must be satisfied in order to excuse seller’s performance under a commercial contract as commercially impracticable); see
Burlington N. & Santa Fe Ry. Co. v. Kansas City S. Ry. Co., 45 F. Supp. 2d 847, 852 (D. Kan. 1999) (citation omitted)

Increased costs do not constitute commercial impracticability unless they result from an unfore-
seen contingency. 118 Mere unexpected difficulties and expenses do not excuse performance unless
they are so extreme that they are outside the contemplation of the parties.119 Some examples of
circumstances where commercial impracticability may be invoked include “a severe shortage of raw
materials or of supplies due to a contingency such as war, embargo, local crop failure, unforeseen
shutdown of major sources of supply or the like, which either causes a marked increase in cost or
altogether prevents the seller from securing supplies necessary to his performance.”120
D. 	Buyer’s Remedies
If the seller delivers nonconforming goods or fails to make delivery, the buyer may either purchase
replacement goods (“cover”) or, in appropriate circumstances, obtain specific performance by forc-
ing the seller to make delivery of conforming goods. 121
The measure of damages in the event of cover is the difference between the contract price and
the amount actually paid for the substitute goods, plus incidental and consequential damages.122
An alternate measure of damages for the buyer is “hypothetical cover.” Hypothetical cover is the
“difference between the market price at the time when the buyer learned of the breach and contract
price.”123 Hypothetical cover may be used to establish that the buyer’s actual cover price was unrea-
sonably high or low. Where the two measures of damages differ only marginally, however, the party
seeking damages may recover by using the more favorable amount.
A buyer may obtain specific performance where the goods are otherwise unavailable or the price
of replacement goods has increased so dramatically that it would be a poor business practice to
cover. 124 Specific performance is an extraordinary remedy that may be available from a court on
an expedited basis. The buyer must provide the seller with prompt notice of rejection or revocation
of acceptance. Failure to provide prompt notice will almost always constitute wrongful rejection or
revocation by the buyer.125 Prompt notice is important because the seller has the right to cure the
defects and tender the repaired goods as conforming to the contract if the time for performance has
not yet expired. 126 Although the seller’s right to cure does not extend to major repairs, the definition
of “major” in the construction context will vary, depending on the cost and nature of the goods.
E. 	Seller’s Remedies
Where the buyer wrongfully rejects goods, wrongfully revokes acceptance of goods, fails to make
payment, or repudiates the contract, the seller may: (1) stop or withhold delivery of the goods;
(2) resell the goods and sue for losses from the resale; (3) recover damages for nonacceptance; or

➣ 	POINTS TO REMEMBER
• Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code (U.C.C.) applies, to some extent, to virtually every
construction project.
• Article 2 of the U.C.C. applies to a contract that is predominantly for the sale of goods but not
to a contract that is predominantly for construction services. The U.C.C. defines “goods” as
“all things . . . which are movable at the time of identification to the contract for sale.” These
concepts typically apply to purchase orders for materials, equipment, or systems incorporated
into a construction project.
• Where a contract involves the sale of both goods and services, most courts will look to the
predominant purpose of the contract to determine whether the U.C.C. applies.
• Each state that has adopted the U.C.C. has done so through its state statutes. There may be
slight variances in these statutes. The state’s version of the U.C.C. that governs a particular
contract or project should be reviewed in analyzing U.C.C. questions, not the version of the
U.C.C. adopted by the National Conference of Commissioners on Uniform State Laws.
• Most of the terms imposed by the U.C.C. can be modified by agreement of the parties.
• Some of the traditional common-law rules governing contract formation do not apply under
the U.C.C. It is easier to establish the existence of an enforceable contract under the U.C.C.
than under the common law.
• The U.C.C. provides for four kinds of warranties for the protection of buyers of goods: warranty
of title, express warranties, the implied warranty of merchantability, and the implied warranty
of fitness for the goods’ intended purpose.
• Parties may disclaim or limit express or implied warranties, but the U.C.C. imposes limitations
on the warranties that can be disclaimed and may require specific language.
• The U.C.C. grants certain rights to the seller in the event that the buyer is insolvent.
• The U.C.C. contains a comprehensive scheme for allocating the risk of loss between the con-
tracting parties.
• Other issues expressly addressed by the U.C.C. include the buyer’s right to inspect the goods;
the circumstances under which a buyer may reject the goods; the buyer’s obligations and rights
upon acceptance of the goods; the requirements governing notice of a breach; and a party’s
rights upon learning that the other party is not likely to perform, which is known as anticipatory
repudiation.
• Most purchase orders and sale-of-goods agreements contain a force majeure clause. In the
absence of such a clause, the U.C.C. provides that late delivery or non-delivery will be excused
if: (1) the seller’s performance has been made impracticable by the occurrence of a contingency
that was a basic assumption of the contract, or (2) by good-faith compliance with a govern-
mental regulation.
• The U.C.C. sets forth the remedies that are available to a buyer or seller should the other party
breach the agreement.
127 U.C.C. § 2-703.
128Id. at § 2-710.

9
THE DESIGN PROFESSIONAL’S
AUTHORITY AND
RESPONSIBILITY
I. 	OVERVIEW
The design stage is an integral part of the construction process, in which an owner’s architectural
vision and programmatic requirements are translated into the drawings and specifications used to
build a physical structure. Because of the inherent complexity of the many tasks undertaken during
the design stage, many construction disputes have their genesis in real or perceived design problems.
The project architect or engineer, each of whom is often generically referred to simply as the
“design professional,”1 is generally responsible for a wide array of tasks ranging from designing the
project to administering the construction contract. The design professional’s responsibilities are often
related to the work performed by many other project participants, such as the owner, the contractor,
and subcontractors, and the design professional’s actions can affect virtually everyone involved in a
construction project. Accordingly, proper recognition of the design professional’s rights and respon-
sibilities is essential to understanding the parties’ legal relationships on such projects, and the proper
allocation of responsibilities and liabilities among those parties.
This chapter covers the design professional’s standard of care, professional responsibility and
liability, authority, supervisory and administrative functions, and other duties, as well as the design
professional’s liability to the contractor and third parties, statutes of repose, effects of contractual
limitations on design-professional liability, the contractor’s assumption of design liability, shared
responsibility and risk, and the design professional’s copyright for design documents.
II. 	STANDARD OF CARE, PROFESSIONAL RESPONSIBILITY, AND LIABILITY
A design professional owes a duty to comply with a “standard of care” when performing professional
services and can be liable for providing services below the required standard. This section discusses
the standard of care, the design professional’s professional duty, professional responsibility and lia-
bility, and the legal distinction between an architect and an engineer.
1 For the purposes of this chapter, the two professionals (architects and engineers) will be considered interchangeable (or
collectively as “design professionals”), as the principles discussed are in most cases applicable to both. See Redies v. Attorneys
Liab. Prot. Soc’y, 150 P.3d 930 (Mont. 2007) (defining A/E as design professional); Cramer Hill Residents Ass’n, Inc. v.
Primas, 928 A.2d 61 (N.J. Super. Ct. App. Div. 2007). Unless otherwise noted, the term “design professional” will be used
in this chapter to refer to licensed architects and engineers.
169

170 	CHAPTER 9 THE DESIGN PROFESSIONAL’S AUTHORITY AND RESPONSIBILITY
A. 	Standard of Care
The scope of the design professional’s authority and responsibility on a project is often defined in the
contract between the design professional and the owner. 2 The contract creates a direct relationship
between the design professional and the owner, which is known as “contractual privity.” 3 Contractual
privity allows the owner to sue the design professional directly for damages attributable to a breach
of contract, and similarly allows the design professional to sue the owner if the owner breaches the
contract.
Generally, the standard of care with which a design professional must comply is set forth in its
contract or is defined under common law,4 depending on whether the suit is based in contract or
tort. One example of a standard of care provision is “[o]ne who undertakes to render professional
services is under a duty to the person for whom the service is to be performed to exercise such care,
skill, and diligence as men in that profession ordinarily exercise under like circumstances.”5
If the design professional’s contract does not include an explicit statement or definition of the
standard of care applicable to the services to be provided, the professional nonetheless owes a duty
to comport with the common law standard of care. The common law standard of care is typically
defined as the performance of services with the level of skill and expertise “commensurate with that
provided by other professionals providing the same services in the same community.”6
Under this traditional standard-of-care definition, the design professional “is not required to per-
form perfect or error-free service.” 7 The design professional is not liable for the occasional inconse-
quential error in judgment, and for a plaintiff to recover on a professional liability claim, the error or
omission typically must rise to the level of a failure on the part of the design professional to exercise

(D. Minn. 2006).

II. STANDARD OF CARE, PROFESSIONAL RESPONSIBILITY, AND LIABILITY 	171
reasonable care and professional skill. If the design professional represents to the owner that it
possesses specialization and experience in a particular area, that design professional may be held
to a higher standard of care that incorporates that specialized expertise. 8 In addition, the description
of the design professional’s tasks or objectives may be sufficiently specific as to the final performance
of the completed project that those representations can amount to performance guarantees. Such a
circumstance arguably creates an express “warranty” of the design and its ability to achieve those
stated goals or objectives (with the resulting contractual liability applied), in lieu of or in addition to
a professional negligence standard. 9
A design professional that contracts to provide construction documents to a client may assume
a legal duty to third parties if it is foreseeable that the third parties will rely on the documents.
Accordingly, many courts have found that based on its contract with the owner, the design profes-
sional owes a common-law duty of care to third parties such as the contractor or subcontractor. 10
The design professional’s contract and scope of the contract “often determine whether a duty exists
to a third person.” The design professionals owe the public the standard of care as required under
common law, regardless of any provisions in the design professional’s contract.
It is important for the design professional and the owner to clearly identify the scope and extent
of the professional’s duty to avoid unintended consequences. The scope of the duty and the standard
of care required to meet that duty can and should be specifically determined by contract, but is also
subject to the standard set by the community of design professionals. Experts in the industry are
usually required to testify regarding what a given standard of care is, how that standard was or was
not followed in a given situation, and how standards of care are generally applied by professionals in
similar situations. Notwithstanding the need for expert testimony in any claim concerning a design
professional’s compliance with the standard of care, the standard of care is generally understood to
be that level of care demonstrated under similar circumstances by the average practitioner within the
particular discipline in question.
A design professional can contract to render services with a standard of care that is higher than
the typical or common law standard. Owners sometimes seek to secure a greater level of service or
performance from the design professionals with whom they contract by requiring the professional to
provide services in accordance with the “highest” standard of care, and far too many design profes-
sionals have unwisely exposed themselves to unnecessary liability by agreeing to such an elevated
standard. Design professionals should also avoid language such as meeting the “highest standard of
the profession” because it is ambiguous and courts can construe the language to mean error-free. 11
However, as a practical matter, this language may be difficult to enforce because the industry has not
set performance levels for these standards, and there is little or no guidance for identifying the per-
formance that constitutes compliance with the “highest” or “higher” standards, or for distinguishing
between them and a “normal” standard of care. As a result, a claim alleging a breach of a contractual
requirement for failure to perform in accordance with such a standard may be difficult to prove.
Design professionals typically seek to avoid agreeing to meet an owner’s objective standard of
care in the performance of services, such as specific performance criteria or a production rate for
a particular building system or component, or the completed facility, because this could create an
obligation that supplants or increases the traditional standard of care and creates a higher standard
for the design professional. 12 While uncommon, a design professional may also contract to provide
services in accordance with a lower standard of care, but that standard must not be less than what

is required under pertinent building codes. Furthermore, assuming a lesser obligation pursuant to a
contractual duty will not act to lower the standard of care required of the design professional under
the common law.
The standard of care generally arises in an action alleging negligence by the design professional,
which can be asserted in the context of contract and tort claims. For example, one court found that an
architectural and engineering contractor was not negligent when it designed a pre-engineered steel
building that the government alleged included overly restrictive deflection criteria that caused the
building to not be buildable. 13 The court found that the designer did not breach its standard of care
because there was a great difference of opinion about the appropriate deflection criteria to implement
when constructing a metal building, and the standard of care did not mandate that a design must be
easy to implement. 14 In another case, the court found that an architectural firm was negligent and
did not meet its standard of care where it failed to design an underground piping system that would
withstand the greatest amount of potential soil heave that was identified in the soils report.15 In a
different case, in which construction workers were injured while installing prefabricated trusses, the
court found that the architect was not liable, and had not breached the standard of care, because the
architect’s superior knowledge about trusses did not create or give rise to a duty for the architect to
provide instructions for installing the trusses. Furthermore, the architect was allowed to rely on the
adequacy of the performance and services provided by the engineer who designed the trusses.16
Even if the design contract is between the owner and a design corporation, individual design pro-
fessionals can be personally liable to the owner, where their actions are negligent and the professional
reasonably knew or should have known that a client would be injured by the negligent performance
of the design professional’s services. 17 This is particularly true where the individual in question was
the architect or engineer who affixed his or her professional seal to the construction documents. As
a general rule, all construction-related contracts contain an implied obligation and a duty to perform
the contract with the ordinary skill, care, and diligence commensurate with that of members of the
profession. 18 Unless the agreement states otherwise, the design professional must meet that duty
even if it is not specifically stated in the contract.19
In the traditional design-bid-build project delivery system, contractual privity (a relationship
between two parties that exists solely by virtue of the contract between them) is usually absent
between the contractor and the design professional. While design professionals do owe a duty to
persons other than their clients or others with whom they contract, a contractor generally cannot sue
for breach of contract a design professional engaged directly by the owner. A contractor or other
third party seeking to recover directly against a design professional must resort instead to lawsuits
based on legal theories such as negligence, third-party beneficiary, and breach of implied warranty,
which are discussed later in this chapter. In a design-build delivery system, the design professional
and the contractor are more likely in privity of contract. In that arrangement, a breach of contract
action by the contractor against the design professional is an available remedy. 20

II. STANDARD OF CARE, PROFESSIONAL RESPONSIBILITY, AND LIABILITY 	173
B. 	A Design Professional’s Professional Duty
Architects and engineers performing professional design services have a duty to parties that is
separate and distinct from their contractual duty, which is derived from their professional obligations
and is based in tort principles. 21 An architect must abide by a standard of care when performing its
duties. The standard of care required by an architect is generally the same as for all professionals,
which is “to exercise the skill and knowledge normally possessed by members of that profession
or trade, in good standing in similar communities, unless the professional represents that he or she
has greater or less skill or knowledge relative thereto.”22 Courts have recognized that an architect
has a general duty to use “due care in the design, construction, and inspection of the project,”
and this duty can be extended to people “foreseeably subjected to a risk of injury by a latent and
unreasonably dangerous condition attributable to the architect’s negligence.” 23
This professional duty has been found to extend to third parties with whom the design professional
does not have a contractual relationship. 24 In determining whether a duty of care exists between the
architect and a third-party plaintiff, courts have considered elements such as whether the architect’s
services or the contract were intended to benefit or have an effect on the plaintiff, whether harm to
the plaintiff was foreseeable, whether the architect’s performance was the cause of the plaintiff’s
injuries or harm, the architect’s culpability, and the public policy to impose sanctions or punishment
to prevent future harm. 25
Similarly, engineers have a duty to “perform their professional services in accordance with gen-
erally accepted engineering practices, and in relation to the practices of similar professionals dealing
with similar engineering problems, projects, and principles.” 26 The law requires that engineers “use
all care that is reasonable and appropriate in light of their superior learning and experience, and in
light of any skills, knowledge, or training that they may personally possess that is over and above
what is normally possessed by persons in that field of endeavor.”27 An engineer is liable for neg-
ligence if they breach the profession’s standard of care. Unless a statute dictates a more stringent
standard of care, an engineer has a duty to “exercise the degree of knowledge, skill, and care that is
usually possessed and exercised by other members of the profession, acting under similar circum-
stances.”28
C. 	Professional Responsibility and Liability
A design professional can render services throughout the design and construction process, including
the phases of planning, design, construction, project completion, and management of the completed
facilities. Under a standard professional services agreement, the services that a design professional
provides typically include:
• Preparing construction documents
• Estimating potential construction costs
• Observing the onsite work performed by the contractor

The services that a design professional provides to an owner are generally set forth in the contract

D. 	Legal Distinction Between an Architect and Engineer

and design of buildings and the preparation of drawings and specifications.” 43 To protect health,
safety, and welfare, for example, statutes generally do not allow a person to practice architecture
“unless he or she has the qualification and competency” required under the statute.44 In contrast,

professional services that require the professional license of the other profession.

typically the purview of the other profession if the provision of the services in question is “inciden-

is trying to avoid paying the architect or engineer because the architect or engineer was not licensed
to practice the specific services rendered. 50 An allegation of practicing without a license is another
situation where this issue can and does arise, usually where there is some dispute over payment.51
III. 	THE DESIGN PROFESSIONAL’S AUTHORITY
The design professional normally assumes one or more of three distinct roles on the construction
project delivery team: (1) independent contractor; (2) an agent of the owner; or (3) an interpreter
of documents and arbiter of disputes. How much control and authority the design professional has
over a particular project will determine its role, as well as the breadth of its influence and potential
liability. 52

III. THE DESIGN PROFESSIONAL’S AUTHORITY 	177
or the methods by which the design development work is carried out and achieved.53 As an indepen-
dent contractor, the design professional may not be deemed to be an agent of the owner and may not
have the power to bind the owner with regard to third parties. Moreover, given the nature of services
a design professional performs during the design-development stages of a project, the opportunity
or occasion to bind an owner (intentionally or inadvertently) may arise very infrequently. Once the
design is completed, a design professional may deliver ownership of all documentation to the project
owner or maintain ownership in the copyright of the design. This detail is one of many aspects of the
parties’ relationship that are best addressed in the contract between them. If the design professional
maintains ownership of its instruments of service, it must then grant a license to the contractor and
subcontractors to allow the further use of the design documents.54
When the design professional undertakes or assumes contract-administration services during
construction, including inspection and supervisory responsibilities, as often happens, that person
becomes a “special” agent of the owner with limited authority to act on behalf of the owner.55 The
scope, nature, and extent of this agency relationship are additional details that should be addressed
and determined in the parties’ contract. The parties may, by their conduct during the course of a
project, depart from the written terms of their contract, with the result being a modification of the
parties’ respective authority or responsibilities. In such circumstances, the limits of the design pro-
fessional’s job-site supervisory authority may be governed by application of the common law agency
principles of actual, implied, or apparent authority.
A. 	Actual Authority
Actual authority refers to the authority that an owner (i.e., the principal) expressly confers on its agent
(commonly the design professional) and that the agent accepts. As a “special agent,” the design
professional’s actual authority is usually outlined in its contract with the owner and is limited to
specific functions. For example, on a typical construction project, the design professional does not
have the authority to make or modify contracts on behalf of the owner/principal 56 or to materially
change the scope of the work, the contract price, or the contract time.57 The owner can, however,
grant to the design professional the actual authority to take these actions by so providing in the
applicable contracts. The design professional’s authority may also be established in documents to
which the design professional is not a party.
For example, it is common for the contract between the owner and the contractor to specify the
extent of the design professional’s authority to act as agent for the owner, so that the contractor
(not a party to the agreement between the owner and architect) can understand and predict when the
architect may properly exercise that authority. In addition, many standard form contracts, such as the
American Institute of Architects (AIA) Document A201 – 2017 General Conditions of the Contract
for Construction and AIA Document B101 – 2017 Standard Form of Agreement Between Owner
and Architect, describe the architect’s authority to act on the owner’s behalf.58

It is very important to include this information within the contractor’s agreement because the
limits set forth in the owner-design professional agreement typically do not bind the contractor.
Furthermore, during pre-contract negotiations, the parties often modify these standard forms. If the
various contracts and incorporated documents are not coordinated, disputes may arise due to the
imposition of inconsistent obligations on the parties.
Language pertaining to a design professional’s authority can often be found in the general condi-
tions, specifications, and even on the plans. Many disputes arise because one or more of the parties
failed to understand the limits of that authority. The design professional must, therefore, know the
extent of its authority to act on behalf of the owner. Every participant in the construction process
should be familiar with the design professional’s actual authority as expressed in its contract with
the owner and in the contract documents. The parties should resolve any inconsistencies before
disputes arise.
B. 	Implied Authority
The doctrine of implied authority allows the design professional to act in ways that are consid-
ered reasonable and necessary for the exercise of the design professional’s actual authority. The
design professional acting under implied authority may bind the owner to those acts even though
the authority to perform such acts is not expressly set forth in the contract. For example, in Cullum
Mech. Constr., Inc. v. S.C. Baptist Hosp., the contract made the design professional responsible for
the review and approval of pay requests and, therefore, by implication, the design professional was
also authorized to reject pay requests.59 In another case, the designer’s contract expressly granted the
design professional the actual authority to decide whether to require the contractor to post payment
and performance bonds. At least one court has found that the design professional had the implied
authority to represent to a potential subcontractor that a payment bond would be required.60
C. 	Apparent Authority
Apparent authority may arise when an owner acts in a way that leads a contractor or other third party
to reasonably believe that the design professional has authority beyond the actual authority expressed
in the contract, potentially causing the owner to be bound by the design professional’s subsequent
actions. Thus, by their conduct, parties may unwittingly expand the design professional’s authority
to act on the owner’s behalf.
Disputes frequently arise in connection with a design professional’s oral orders for extra work
or changes when the contract requires a written change order. Generally, the owner is not bound by
such oral authorizations unless the owner waives the written change order requirement. 61
AIA A201 limits the design professional’s authority to issue changes without the owner’s signa-
ture, with the exception of minor changes in the work that do not involve adjustment of the contract
sum or the contract time. 62 AIA A201 provides that the design professional is now responsible for

to ensure payments to subcontractors, but special conditions in the contract may give rise to a special relationship with
subcontractors and therefore a duty of care arises).

61See C.B.I. Na-Con, Inc. v. Macon-Bibb Water & Sewerage Auth., 421 S.E.2d 111 (Ga. Ct. App. 1992).

A design professional that issues orders or directives without authority risks exposure to potential
liability for the consequences of its actions. Some courts have demonstrated an increased willingness
to hold design professionals responsible for their actions and not allow them to shield themselves
behind concepts of agency, especially when a contractor has acted reasonably in relying on the design
professional. 66
D. 	Ratification of the Design Professional’s Authority
Contractual limits on a design professional’s authority to act on an owner’s behalf may afford some
protection to owners where an agent acts outside the limits of its authority. Still, a party (for example,
an owner or contractor) may undermine such protection by conduct or representations indicating a
ratification of the agent’s acts or the owner’s acceptance of the benefits related to them. For example,
in one case, the court found that a general contractor ratified an indemnification provision located on
the back of the concrete supplier’s delivery tickets by routinely paying the invoices without objection,
even though the general contractor’s superintendent who signed the delivery tickets had no authority
to agree on behalf of the contractor to indemnify the supplier. 67
IV. 	THE DESIGN PROFESSIONAL’S ADMINISTRATIVE FUNCTIONS
Responsibility for the administration of various aspects of the construction process is sometimes
retained by the owner or placed with an independent construction manager, particularly when the
federal government is involved. Many contracts, however, still require the design professional to
perform administrative functions during the construction phase.
A design professional’s responsibilities during the contract-administration phase generally
include overseeing the construction and inspecting for defects. Designers prefer to include terms
in the contract-administration section of the contract such as “review” or “observe,” rather than
“construction oversight” or “inspect,” because the design professional does not want to guarantee
the contractor’s work and wants to limit its own liability. A design professional may seek to include
in its contract language that explicitly states that it is not the “guarantor of performance of the
contractor” and it is “not responsible for construction means, methods, or sequencing.” However, a
design professional may be responsible for supervisory duties if they are specified in its contract, but
generally may not be liable for supervision if not explicitly required by the terms of the contract.68
During the contract-administration phase, the design professional may be reasonably expected to
do the following:

• Interpret ambiguities in and respond to inquiries about the construction documents
• Review and process shop drawings and submittals in a timely fashion so as to not cause
any delays
• Draft change orders and change directives, and advise the owner on the appropriate cost for

• Determine when substantial and final completion have been reached and provide certifications

• Work with the owner, contractor, and subcontractors by being an initial decision maker when

• Draft a punch list and then review the contractor’s work to decide whether the punch list work

In addition, the designer will frequently agree to periodically visit the work site to observe the
work and inform the owner and contractor about any inconsistencies observed, but this does not
require the designer to actively inspect the work.70
Five frequently occurring aspects of the design professional’s contract administration role include
the following:
1. Interpretation of the plans and specifications
2. Review and approval of shop drawings and submittals
3. Inspections and testing
4. Issuance of certificates of progress or completion in connection with the contractor’s applica-
tions for payment
5. Resolution of disputes between the owner and the contractor
A. 	Interpretation of the Plans and Specifications
The plans and specifications commonly generate questions during construction. Minor issues often
arise because a specific element of work is inadequately detailed or specified in the contract doc-
uments. It is virtually impossible for a design professional to depict every detail of the work to be
expressly set forth in the plans and specifications, and even if possible, the cost of doing so would
be prohibitively high. Thus, parties are often required to interpret the contract requirements based
on their prior dealings, industry practice, code requirements, and the parties’ conduct leading up to
the point of dispute. Simple contract interpretation is often inadequate to resolve disputes resulting
from inadequately detailed, ambiguous, or defective plans and specifications or oral change direc-
tives. Fortunately, most construction industry participants employ reasonable judgment and open
69Id.; see Del. Code Ann. tit. 24 § 303(c)(1)(b); Ga. Code Ann. § 43-4-1(2).
70Id.; see AIA Document B101 – 2017 § 3.6.2.1 (“The Architect shall visit the site at intervals appropriate to the stage of
construction, or as otherwise required in Section 4.2.3, to become generally familiar with the progress and quality of the
portion of the Work completed, and to determine, in general, if the Work observed is being performed in a manner indicating
that the Work, when fully completed, will be in accordance with the Contract Documents. However, the Architect shall not
be required to make exhaustive or continuous on-site inspections to check the quality or quantity of the Work.”).

communication to informally resolve the great majority of interpretation issues and other disputes,
relying on dispute review boards, arbitrators, or the courts only when necessary to resolve intractable
problems related to insufficiently detailed or defective design documents.
Under most standard form contracts and under many project-specific contracts, the design pro-
fessional has the authority to interpret the plans and specifications during the course of construction.
This authority gives the design professional some degree of control over the work as it progresses.
The responsibility that accompanies this authority, however, exposes design professionals to liability
to owners for negligent interpretation of the plans and specifications. This may be true even when
an owner uses the design of a separate design consultant. In general, however, a design professional
that seals drawings is assuming design responsibility for those plans. 71
The design professional’s authority to interpret the contract requirements does not include the
authority to place additional burdens or liabilities on the owner or the contractor by modifying the
contract terms. For example, in one case the court refused to allow a design professional to require
a contractor to provide additional fill material where the plans and specifications did not contain the
requirement.72
In addition to the literal wording of the contract documents, the design professional’s discretion
in interpreting the plans and specifications may be limited by construction industry general practices
and trade customs. For example, a court held that a subcontractor was entitled to additional compen-
sation for performing certain painting work beyond normal custom, despite the architect’s contrary
interpretation of the subcontract. The court stated that although the architect had the authority to
make final decisions regarding the meaning of plans and specifications, the contract implied that
the architect would render a reasonable decision that was consistent with industry custom or trade
usage. 73
Owners and contractors must also be careful to avoid giving the design professional’s opinion
more weight than the contract or law allows. For example, one court held that the Colorado Depart-
ment of Transportation’s contract did not give the engineer the power to make a binding decision
about a deadline for judicial review that could be admitted in a legal proceeding.74 Similarly, in
NCS Contractors, Inc. v. Borders,75 the Court of Appeals of Maryland ruled that while the con-
tract made the architect’s decision “relating to artistic effect” final and binding on the parties, the
architect’s subsequent refusal to certify the contractor’s final payment based upon its determination
of the damages due the owner to correct the artistic defect was not a final decision binding on the
parties.
B. 	Review and Approval of Shop Drawings and Submittals
The design professional generally reviews data submitted by the contractor, such as samples, shop
drawings, submittals, product data, and schedules. The primary purpose of shop drawings and sub-
mittals is for the owner and the design professional to understand how the contractor intends to
perform certain aspects of the work.76 These submittals also inform the design professional and

the owner of the processes, materials, and methods the contractor will use, which communicate the
contractor’s understanding of the contract requirements.
The design professional’s review of submittals does have legal consequences. Generally, the
design professional’s approval of the processes and methods included in submittals does not relieve
the contractor of its responsibility to comply with the specifications.77 In one case, the court found
that a subcontractor could not prevail on a claim against the design professional hired by the contrac-
tor for the purpose of approving the subcontractor’s shop drawings, which contained errors.78 The
court held in favor of the design professional, stating that the design professional owed no duty to the
subcontractor, that the subcontractor was responsible for meeting all of the requirements of its sub-
contract, and that the subcontractor had no right to rely on the design professional’s approval of its
shop drawings because the design professional was hired to provide services only to the contractor,
not to subcontractors.79
When a design professional’s review function goes beyond mere review and comment regard-
ing conformance with the contract documents, and the design professional attempts to change the
contractor’s scope of work, courts will be more likely to deem such an attempt beyond the scope of
the design professional’s authority, and the owner may not be bound by such approval. 80 AIA A201
contains language that relieves the contractor of responsibility for deviations from the contract docu-
ments contained in submittals, if and only if “the Contractor has specifically informed the Architect
of such deviation at the time of submittal” and the architect has given written approval to the specific
deviation, or a change order or construction change directive is issued.81 In addition, AIA A201
requires the contractor to specifically direct the architect’s attention, in writing or on resubmitted
submittals, to revisions in submittals, or else the architect’s approval of resubmitted submittals does
not apply to the revision. 82 ConsensusDocs 200 states that the “Constructor shall be responsible for
the accuracy and conformity of its submittals to the Contract Documents.”83 In addition, Consensus-
Docs 200 requires the contractor’s (constructor’s) written identification of deviations, substitutions,
or changes and express written approval from the owner authorizing the deviation, substitution, or
change.84 One difference in the two industry forms is that the ConsensusDocs form initially reserves
to the owner, not the design professional, the right to make such decisions or approvals.
Absent unusual circumstances, the design professional’s review is not to ascertain whether the
data is accurate, but whether the processes, means, and methods in question are in conformance
with the contract-document requirements. However, courts can and do impose liability on design
professionals for approving shop drawings that deviate from the contract documents. One notable
example is the case that arose out of the 1981 Kansas City Hyatt Regency disaster, in which a
multistory interior hotel bridge collapsed, killing 114 people and injuring 186. The cause of the col-
lapse was determined to be a faulty structural steel detail that was introduced in a shop drawing.85

The court discounted the engineer’s attempt to avoid liability for negligence by asserting a defense
that industry “custom and practice” allowed engineers to rely on fabricators “to design certain struc-
tural steel connections.” 86 The court noted that, by affixing his professional stamp to the documents,
the certifying engineer assumed responsibility for the entire engineering project and that his profes-
sional duties were nondelegable.87
The design professional generally has an obligation to review and act on a shop drawing or
submittal within a reasonable time. To the extent the contractor is delayed or hindered by the design
professional’s failure to timely approve or reject a submittal, the owner, and perhaps even the
design professional, may be liable to the contractor.88 AIA A201 attempts to limit an owner’s,
and design professional’s, liability for submittal review delays by requiring the contractor to
prepare a submittal schedule promptly after award of the contract and to submit the schedule for the
architect’s approval.89 The submittal schedule must be coordinated with the construction schedule
and allow the architect “reasonable time” to review submittals. If the contractor fails to submit the
submittal schedule, AIA A201provides that the contractor will not be entitled to any increase in
contract sum or an extension of time based on the time required for the review of submittals by the
design professional. 90
The trend toward the use of building information modeling (BIM), which provides a means for
members of the project delivery team to collaboratively share project design and construction data,
could present significant risks in the context of a design professional’s review and approval of shop
drawings and submittals. Because BIM is collaborative, multiple parties provide input into, and may
exercise control over, the review processes. A design professional involved in BIM should ensure
that responsibility for review and approval of such submittals is well-defined and that there is a clear
record of each party’s role and actions in the BIM process.
C. 	Inspections and Testing
An owner frequently engages a design professional to inspect or observe work to ensure conformity
with contract requirements. The design professional acts as the owner’s agent when performing
these duties. Under these circumstances, the design professional typically has the implied authority
to reject defective work (that is, work not in compliance with the contract documents). Disputes
often arise when the design professional rejects work that the contractor believes complies with the
contract. Factual disputes in this area cover every aspect of construction and generally turn on issues
of contract interpretation, workmanship, and sufficiency of materials.
The Engineers Joint Contract Documents Committee (EJCDC) form contract can afford an engi-
neer great discretion in determining substitution procedures for products incorporated into a con-
struction project. In one case, the parties used a standard EJCDC contract that contained a provision
granting the engineer sole discretion to determine if a particular product was an appropriate substi-
tution or conformed to the contract’s “or equal” clause. 91 The court held that the owner was justified
in relying on the engineer’s recommendations because the contractor agreed to the contract’s “or
equal” clause. Finding no evidence of fraud, bad faith, or failure to exercise honest judgment by the

engineer in rejecting the contractor’s submittals, the court concluded that the engineer acted within

Improper rejection of work generally will not expose the design professional to liability to the con-
tractor because the design professional is usually acting on the owner’s behalf.93 But the design pro-
fessional may be liable for incorrect or negligent observations or inspections that result in improper
rejection of the work or cause the owner to be liable to the contractor for damages. Additionally,
problems may arise when a design professional fails to observe work as required or fails to timely
detect nonconforming work as the work proceeds, which can allow a contractor to cover up or build
on nonconforming work or make corrections or remedial work more difficult.
The scope of a design professional’s potential liability for job site accidents caused by unsafe
working conditions continues to trouble many courts. Generally, the design professional’s obligation
to monitor the quality of the work is weighed against the contractor’s responsibility to control the
means and methods of its performance. The courts usually resolve this issue by closely examining
the language of both the design professional’s contract and the construction contract. 94 Generally, the
contractor retains the primary responsibility for contract compliance and for control of construction
means, methods, and techniques.95 Section 3.1.2 of ConsensusDocs 200 and Section 3.3.1 of AIA
A201 exemplify standard form means and methods clauses.
In addition, the design professional is not deemed to be responsible for supervision or inspection
of construction if it is not required by the contract. 96 For example, in an Indiana case, an owner
claimed its architect was liable for a defective floor because it did not sufficiently supervise the
contractor to confirm that the contractor complied with the plans and specifications. 97 The architect
was found not liable because the contract provided that the architect was not responsible for the
contractor’s failure to perform the work in accordance with the contract documents.98
However, a means and methods clause does not always absolve the design professional of liability.
In a Texas case, the court held an architect liable for failing to adequately inspect a project despite
exculpatory contract language stating that the architect would “not be responsible for the Contractor’s
failure to carry out the work in accordance with the contract documents.”99 The court reasoned that
an architect that is paid to protect the owner from construction defects should be held responsible
for failing to detect defective work. 100

In another case, a court considered whether a design professional could be held liable for a fire
that was apparently caused by the contractor’s improper placement of insulation around light fix-
tures, which the design professional had not detected. 101 The design professional had entered into a
standard AIA design contract with the owner that provided:
The Architect shall visit the site at intervals appropriate to the stage of construction … to
become generally familiar with the progress and quality of the Work and to determine in
general if the Work is proceeding in accordance with the Contract Documents. However,
the Architect shall not be required to make exhaustive or continuous on-site inspections to
check the quality or quantity of the Work. On the basis of such on-site observations as an
architect, the Architect shall keep the Owner informed of the progress and quality of the Work,
and shall endeavor to guard the Owner against defects and deficiencies in the Work of the
Contractor.
Despite the language in the AIA contract, the court denied summary judgment to the design
professional, reasoning that the design professional had a duty to be generally knowledgeable of
the quality and quantity of work to evaluate payment applications. The design professional was not
relieved from liability to the owner simply because the contractor had failed to perform its work
correctly. While the design professional was not a guarantor of the contractor’s performance, it still
had the responsibility to keep abreast of the quality of work.102
The design professional can be held liable to the owner for inspection and approval of a con-
tractor’s faulty or nonconforming work. The design professional is obligated to take action when
it discovers or should have discovered the contractor’s defective workmanship. For instance, an
architect who observed and approved inadequate waterproofing was found to have breached its
duty to guard the owner against defects and deficiencies in the work, and was liable to the owner
for the cost of repairing the interior wall coverings that were damaged when the waterproofing
failed. 103
A design professional’s periodic inspection of construction work and failure to object to non-
conforming materials and workmanship may, under certain circumstances, establish a constructive
acceptance of the work and preclude an owner from refusing to pay the contractor. The contractor is
more likely to prevail in these situations if it can show either a reasonable reliance on the design pro-
fessional to detect nonconforming work or other fault on the part of the design professional or owner
that contributed to or prevented the contractor from correcting the defective work. For example, one
court held that an architect’s failure to inspect the remedial work that the architect directed the sub-
contractor to perform meant the architect could not claim the repairs were unsatisfactory as a defense
to the subcontractor’s breach of contract suit. 104
However, a different court found that periodic inspections of work on a highway construction
project, and the approval of periodic payments to the contractor during earlier stages of the project,
did not amount to acceptance or certification that the inspected parts of the work were completed
in compliance with the specifications.105 As in that case, arguably exculpatory circumstances aris-
ing from the design professional’s observation duties are unlikely to relieve the contractor from
its responsibility for defective work. This is due to the fact that owners are becoming increasingly
sophisticated about the need to contractually limit their responsibility for construction defects that
are not reasonably discernible based on periodic site observation visits.

D. 	Issuance of Certificates of Progress or Completion and Certificates
for Payment
Most construction projects are performed over an extended time. Because of this, construction con-
tracts frequently contemplate interim, or progress, payments to the contractor at specified intervals
throughout the project. Extended construction projects also contemplate a final payment upon final
completion and acceptance of the work. Often the owner engages the design professional to issue
certificates of progress or completion, which generally are related to the owner’s duty to pay the
contractor for work performed.
Form contracts provide reasons to withhold approval of a certificate for payment or to reject
a payment request. AIA A201 provides the following seven grounds for the architect to withhold
approval on a certificate for payment:
1. Defective work that is not remedied
2. Third-party claims or reasonably suspected third-party claims
3. The contractor’s failure to properly pay subcontractors
4. Reasonable evidence that the work will not be completed for the remaining balance of the
contract
5. Damage to the owner or a contractor
6. Reasonable basis to believe the work will not be completed by the contract time and the remain-
ing balance will not cover actual or liquidated damages for the delay
7. Work repeatedly not being performed in accordance with the contract 106
ConsensusDocs 200 provides that the owner, rather than the architect, has the authority to adjust
pay requests and sets forth the grounds, similar to those in AIA A201, entitling the owner to adjust
or reject a contractor’s pay request. 107
Although form contract language may provide the design professional with reasons to withhold a
payment certification, a design professional can be liable for improperly failing to approve progress
payments. Failing to approve progress payments may be improper if it occurs after the design pro-
fessional accepts work or approves earlier pay requests for the same work. As with issues relating
to inspection of the work, the analysis of liability for refusing progress payments is almost always
fact and contract specific.
A design professional has a duty to use the care of one skilled in that profession when issuing
payment certificates and can be held liable for damages resulting from a failure to act accord-
ingly. For example, in one California case the owner asserted that the architect was negligent in
issuing certificates of payment without first determining whether the contractor had fully paid its
subcontractors and materialmen. 108 The court held that the architect was contractually required to
protect the owner by making certain that all bills were paid or by insisting on lien waivers from
suppliers. 109
Wrongfully withholding a payment certificate can also result in a design professional’s liability
to the contractor or subcontractor. 110 For example, a Mississippi court found that an engineer that
reduced a contractor’s pay request contrary to an audit of the contractor’s work, without consulting
the contractor and without adequately checking the extent of the work, was directly liable to the
106 AIA Document A201 – 2017 § 9.5.1.
107 ConsensusDocs 200 § 9.3 (© 2011, Revised 2017).
108Palmer v. Brown, 273 P.2d 306 (Cal. Ct. App. 1954).
109Id.
110See Lyndon Prop. Ins. Co. v. Duke Levy & Assocs., LLC, 475 F.3d 268, 273 (5th Cir. 2007).

contractor and was liable for bad-faith damages to the contractor. 111 Similarly, a Missouri court
held that an engineer’s failure to properly interpret the contract requirements, which resulted in
withholding payment from the contractor, entitled the contractor to release of the contract balance. 112
In a different case, a subcontractor on a public project was allowed to sue the architect on the theory
that the architect negligently allowed the disbursal of funds to the contractor without first verifying
that the contractor provided a payment bond. 113
The design professional’s negligence in approving pay requests and issuing progress certificates
may also expose it to liability to third parties with a financial interest in the project, such as banks or
sureties. For example, a West Virginia court found that a project engineer has a “special relationship”
with the surety, which provides the surety the right to sue the engineer for financial losses due to the
engineer’s negligent certification of progress payments to the contractor. 114
In National Surety Corp. v. Malvaney,115 an architect was found liable to the contractor’s surety
for the negligent issuance of a substantial completion certificate. Under the contract, the architect
could require the contractor to present evidence that payroll and material bills had been paid before
releasing retained funds. The architect, however, failed to enforce this requirement. Consequently,
the contractor collected its retainage and then defaulted, leaving the burden of completing the work
and satisfying claims to the surety.
The court rejected the architect’s argument that its lack of privity of contract with the surety
insulated it from liability to the surety. The court relied on a negligence theory, ruling that the design
professional owed a duty to determine whether the contractor had paid the bills to both the owner
and the surety for whose mutual benefit and protection contractor funds were retained. The surety’s
failure to take steps to ascertain whether outstanding bills were being paid by the contractor was not
held to constitute contributory negligence, because the surety had a right to assume that the retainage
would not be released until the contract was fully performed. Furthermore, in Peerless Insurance Co.
v. Cerny & Associates, Inc.,116 the court determined that a surety was subrogated to any claim that the
owner would have against the architect for negligent certification of progress payments.117 Similarly,
in Westerhold v. Carroll,118 the court confirmed that an architect can be held liable to the indemnitor
of a contractor’s surety for certifying payments in excess of the value of work performed.
Although the contractor is generally entitled to receive periodic payment as work progresses, this
right must be balanced against the owner’s right to verify that the contractor is performing the work
in accordance with the contract documents. To address this, construction contracts usually state that
periodic payment to the contractor does not constitute acceptance of the work and does not waive
the owner’s right to demand contract compliance. Industry form contracts also typically state that
the architect’s approval of the contractor’s payment applications does not mean that the contractor
has performed in accordance with the contract documents. For example, AIA A201 provides that

Architect’s knowledge, information and belief, the Work has progressed to the point indicated and
that the quality of the Work is in accordance with the Contract Documents … [and] that the Contrac-

However, the design professional’s certification of progress or completion may still benefit the

an effective defense to the owner’s claim against the contractor for noncompliance with the plans

payment for its work can be evidence that the subcontractor’s work was satisfactory. 121
The requirement that the design professional issue a certificate before payment is made to the
contractor may be excused or waived by the parties. In one case, the court found that neither the

receiving progress payments for completed excavation work. Consequently, the contract provision
requiring a certificate before final payment was deemed waived so that neither party could insist on
strict compliance with the contract requirement.122
Furthermore, an architect cannot delegate its responsibility for certifying progress payments to
another architect and thereby escape liability for a defective building. In Sheetz, Aiken & Aiken, Inc.
v. Spann, Hall, Ritchie, Inc.,123 the Alabama Supreme Court ruled that the project architect’s duty
as inspecting architect was to verify that the contractor had performed the work in accordance with
the plans and specifications, while the duty of the architect hired to certify progress was merely to
determine the amount due the contractor for direct construction costs and not to ensure a defect-free
building.
E. 	Evaluation of Claims and Resolution of Disputes between the Owner
and the Contractor
Another important function that the design professional may perform is evaluating claims and resolv-
ing disputes between the owner and contractor. Many of the older standard construction documents
designated the “Architect” as the initial arbiter of disputes and evaluator of claims between the
owner and contractor. 124 AIA A201 (2017 ed.) provides that claims, with a few exceptions, “shall
be referred to the Initial Decision Maker for initial decision” and that the “Architect will serve as the
Initial Decision Maker, unless otherwise indicated in the Agreement.”125 AIA A201 also requires
an initial decision prior to mediation of any claim that arises before final payment is due, unless
a decision has not been rendered within 30 days of the claim being referred to the initial decision
maker. 126
ConsensusDocs 200 goes further in removing the design professional from the dispute resolution
process by requiring the owner’s and contractor’s representatives to initially conduct direct discus-
sions in good faith and, if those fail, to have the senior executives of the parties meet to try to resolve

does not resolve the dispute, the parties can then proceed to mediation and, if necessary, ultimately
to arbitration or litigation. 128 Absent designation by the owner as the owner’s representative, there
is no decision-making role for the design professional in the ConsensusDocs 200 dispute procedure.
Even where a contract states that the design professional is the initial decision maker, courts are
reluctant to recognize that a design professional has final and binding power to resolve disputes
unless the contract clearly and unambiguously assigns that power. 129 This reluctance may be based
on the idea that a design professional may be partial to the owner, or because such recognition would
result in the waiver of a party’s right to its day in court or arbitration.
More difficult issues can arise with contracts that require claims to be submitted to the design pro-
fessional for decision before a party commences litigation. How long must a contractor or the owner
wait for a decision from the design professional before commencing with arbitration or litigation?
What if the design professional repeatedly asks for additional documentation to support the claim,
thus delaying a decision? What if the design professional is unable to reach a conclusive determina-
tion? Courts typically will not consider initial referral of a claim to the design professional to be a
condition precedent to arbitration or litigation unless the contract clearly states the requirement.130
If the contract requires the design professional to render a decision within a certain period of time,
the commencement of arbitration or litigation would be appropriate after the time for a decision has
elapsed. 131 If no time is specified, “a reasonable time” is often assumed. Some courts have held
that the design professional’s role as arbitrator of disputes between owner and contractor ends once
the design professional is no longer responsible for observing the contractor’s performance of the
work. 132
When a design professional assumes the role of an impartial decision maker and the contract
deems its decision to be final, some design professionals have enjoyed limited immunity from arbi-
tration or litigation brought by owners and contractors resulting from the professional’s decision
because of the performance of a quasi-judicial function. 133 Such immunity is limited to those acts
performed in a judicial capacity. The crucial factor in such situations is whether the challenged
act was within the scope of the design professional’s decision-making duties.134 Distinguishing the
design professional’s protected functions from other duties can be difficult. The deliberate or negli-
gent misuse of the design professional’s powers as arbiter may excuse a party’s disregard of a design
professional’s decision. 135
