VI. 	THE DESIGN PROFESSIONAL’S LIABILITY TO THE CONTRACTOR
AND THIRD PARTIES
Under certain circumstances, the design professional may be liable to the owner for damages based
on the design professional’s failure to properly perform its administrative responsibilities. These
same acts or omissions may also justify an action by the contractor or other third parties either
against the owner or directly against the design professional. Design professionals are increasingly
being held directly liable to contractors under various legal theories, with the most prevalent being
the design professional’s negligent breach of a duty owed to the owner or to the contractor. This
section discusses negligence and the economic loss rule, intentional torts, the third-party beneficiary
theory, professional liability coverage, and liability to third parties.
A. 	Negligence and the Economic Loss Rule
The negligent breach of a duty by one person often injures another person. Such harm may include
bodily injury, injury to property, or injury to a financial or business interest of some type. The latter
is often referred to as an “economic loss.” It has long been established that a person may sue in
negligence for personal injuries and property damage even where the person has no contractual
relationship with the defendant.136 Historically, courts have been reluctant to allow parties to recover
in negligence for purely economic loss where there is no contractual privity between the parties. This
limitation on negligence actions is called the “economic loss rule.”137
The economic loss rule is still recognized in many states 138 and was unanimously upheld by
the United States Supreme Court in an admiralty case.139 The economic loss rule is not applied
136MacPherson v. Buick Motor Co., 111 N.E. 1050 (N.Y. 1916).
137See Indianapolis-Marion Cnty. Pub. Library v. Charlier Clark & Linard, P.C., 929 N.E.2d 722, 736 (Ind. 2010) (holding
that the economic loss rule generally precludes a plaintiff’s recovery in tort for purely economic loss, and applies to negligence
claims brought against design professionals, even if the plaintiff is not in contractual privity with the design professional);
see BRW, Inc. v. Dufficy & Sons, Inc., 99 P.3d 66, 74 (Colo. 2004) (holding that the economic loss rule applies to interrelated
contracts and barred the subcontractor’s negligence claim against the engineering firm and inspector on a public works project,
even when the subcontractor did not contract directly with the firm); Flagstaff Affordable Hous. Ltd. P’ship v. Design Alliance,
Inc., 223 P.3d 664, 665 (Ariz. 2010) (holding that the economic loss doctrine limits a property owner to its contractual remedies
when an architect’s negligent design causes economic loss but no physical injury to persons or other property).

of duties 141 such as intentional and negligent preparation of defective plans and specifications, 142
and negligent evaluation of soil permeability. 143 In one case, the court found the economic loss
rule did not bar the contractor’s negligent misrepresentation claims against the engineer based on
the engineer’s evaluation that the city’s water slide was defective and needed to be immediately
replaced. 144
Some courts recognize that the design professional owes a duty to the contractor based on the
design professional’s inherent power over the contractor. For example, in one case, the court found
that the economic loss rule did not prevent the contractor’s claim because the amount of author-
ity that the design firm exercises on a project, sometimes in a manner that directs the contractor’s
performance, necessarily requires a duty of care on the part of the design professional even though
privity did not exist. 145 In a different case, the court held that both the architect and the engineer
were liable to the contractor for negligently issuing incorrect instructions to the contractor and for
failing to revise and coordinate modified corrective plans and specifications that they subsequently
issued to the contractor. 146 The court allowed the contractor to recover damages for delay directly
from the architect partly because of the architect’s significant control over the contractor, which was
“tantamount to a power of economic life or death over the contractor.”147
If a design professional has agreed to perform supervisory tasks on a construction project, the
contractor on the project may have a right to rely on the competence of that supervision. 148 In one
case, the contractor claimed that the architect failed to properly design an erosion plan, failed to
grant an extension for time due to weather delays, and improperly nullified valid pay requests. 149
The court stated that an architect with general supervisory power that determines final compliance
with a contract between the owner and contractor, and that negligently performs a contractual duty,
may be liable to the contractor. 150 The court recognized that each participant in a construction project
must be able to rely on the others’ performance, thus obligating each to perform its duties with
due care.

administrative. The court concluded that the use of the word “supervision” in the jury instructions
did not connote a higher or lower standard of duty than the use of the word “inspection.” The court
further held that the basic question was whether the design professional had exercised reasonable
care in making the observations and inspections at the project. 152
Even in jurisdictions rejecting the economic loss rule, design professionals have successfully
defended against claims for economic damages by asserting that they do not owe a duty to the
contractor. For instance, in one case, the court found that the economic loss rule did not bar the
contractor’s professional negligence claim against the engineers and engineering firm based on their
evaluations to the city that a water slide constructed by the contractor was defective and needed to
be immediately removed. 153 However, the court nonetheless found that (1) the engineers and engi-
neering firm owed a duty to only the city that hired them to provide advice on the water slide project;
(2) the engineer did not have the “power of economic life or death” over the contractor; and (3) the
engineer did not have a “sufficiently close nexus” to the contractor to owe the contractor a duty
of care. 154
Some courts may not allow a contractor to sue the design professional if the contractor cannot
prove its claim against the owner. For example, in a case where a contractor sued an owner for
delay damages allegedly caused by the design professional’s negligence, the court stated that the
no-damages-for-delay clause in the contractor’s contract with the owner caused the contractor to
bear responsibility for its own actions absent any interference by the owner or the owner’s represen-
tative. 155 The contractor was unable to prove interference by the design professional acting as the
owner’s representative, and thus could not prevail on its claim against the owner.156
In jurisdictions recognizing a contractor’s right to sue the design professional in negligence for
purely economic loss, contractors have a difficult burden to establish that the design professional is
liable. In general, it is much easier to establish owner liability for defective design under contract
and warranty theories than it is to prove professional negligence on the part of the design profes-
sional. Negligence is determined by evaluating the alleged wrongdoer’s acts or omissions under the
applicable standard of care.
B. 	Intentional Torts
A design professional can also be liable for an intentional tort.157 However, actions for intentional
tort are less common than those for negligence. One example of an intentional tort is the tortious
interference with an existing contract, which in the context of a construction project typically means a
contractor’s contract with the owner or its subcontractors. Such a claim can include allegations that an
architect willfully and intentionally interfered with a subcontractor’s submittal of a deductive change
order. 158 Another example of an intentional tort is fraud, which can include claims that an architect
fraudulently induced a party to enter into a contract with the architect to design a building.159
A design professional will not be held liable for tortious interference with contractual relations
where the design professional has a bona fide interest in the project.160 In one case, the court stated

C. 	Third-Party Beneficiary Theory
A contractor might also argue that it is a third-party beneficiary of the contract between the owner
and the design professional. A “third-party beneficiary” is a third party who may bring an action to
enforce the provisions of the contract between the original contracting parties.163 To do so, the third
party must have been an intended beneficiary of the contracting parties’ contract. In other words, the
parties to a contract must intend to confer a direct or immediate benefit on the third party that claims
to be a beneficiary.164
Courts require a clear expression of intent to recognize a third-party beneficiary, which can be
difficult to prove in the absence of writing.165 When a third party benefits by an agreement, but that
benefit is not the specific object of the intended contractual obligation, the third party is referred
to as an incidental beneficiary. Incidental beneficiaries do not have a legal right to bring an action
to enforce the provisions of the contract.166 Due in large part to the requirement of a clear, written
expression of the contracting parties’ intent to confer beneficiary status on a third party, a contractor
is more likely to succeed in a tort action than through a third-party beneficiary theory.167 Courts
typically determine whether a contractor is a third-party beneficiary by examining the apparent intent
of the contracting parties.168
If the parties intended to make a third party a beneficiary, they should ensure that their contracts
specifically state this. However, there may be circumstances in which the design professional
assumes extra responsibilities to the contractor by its conduct. An example is where the archi-
tect conducts extensive and thorough on-site inspections, despite the absence of a contractual
duty to do so. 169 Accordingly, in some cases a contractor may recover as a third-party benefi-
ciary for damages that result from the design professional’s improper performance of assumed
duties.
Courts have found that a party may assert a claim against a party that it lacks privity with, if the
relationship between the two parties was so close as to approach the existence of privity.170 In one
case, the court found that an owner could assert a claim against two engineering consultants who
had been retained by the architect even though there was no direct contractual relationship between
the engineers and the owner, because the relationship between the engineers and the owner was so

A design professional can reduce or avoid third-party beneficiary claims by carefully drafting
the contract to explicitly state that neither the contract documents nor the design professional’s
preparation of them act to create any kind of contractual relationship with any other parties. For
example, AIA A201 provides that “the Contract Documents shall not be construed to create a
contractual relationship of any kind” between the contractor or owner and the architect or the
architect’s consultants, between the owner and any subcontractor or sub-subcontractor, or between
any person or entity other than the contractor and owner. 175 EJCDC C-700 includes a similar
provision, which provides that neither the engineer’s authority or responsibility, nor any decision
by the engineer, “shall create, impose, or give rise to any duty in contract, tort, or otherwise owed
by Engineer to Contractor, any Subcontractor, any Supplier, any other individual or entity, or to
any surety for or employee or agent of any of them.”176 In addition, ConsensusDocs 200 provides
that the parties’ agreement is for the “exclusive benefit of the Parties, and not for the benefit of
any third party” and that their agreement “represents the entire and integrated agreement between
the Parties, and supersedes all prior negotiations, representations, or agreements, either written
or oral.”177
Usually, such clauses are judicially enforced.178 A court might be persuaded by a third-party
beneficiary argument where the argument is needed to salvage a cause of action. In most cases,
however, the same act that would constitute the basis for a third-party beneficiary action would also
constitute a negligence action, which is a more likely basis for relief. 179

D. 	Professional Liability Coverage
Often design firms are of relatively smaller size or have less financial strength than the owners and
contractors with whom they work. Consequently, contractors and third parties with large claims often
obtain a more substantive recovery by suing the owner rather than the design professional. However,
professional liability insurance available to architects and engineers increases a party’s prospects for
recovery against a design professional while at the same time reducing the potential impact on the
design professional of a large judgment in a negligence action.
Every professional liability insurance policy contains language that limits or defines the scope of
coverage. Professional liability insurance policies are very specific as to the negligent acts that are
covered. Design professionals risk being exposed to an uninsured claim if they perform services out-
side of their covered range of services and those uncovered services are the subject of a negligence
claim. 180 Some design professional liability policies expressly exclude from coverage certain acts
that are not considered “insurable risks” because they involve conscious and deliberate conduct on
the part of the professional. 181 Such exclusions commonly include a design professional’s failure to
complete drawings or specifications on time or when a professional commits an intentional tort. Oth-
ers include exclusions for claims alleging a breach of contract or other cause of action not grounded
in the insured’s professional negligence or malpractice. Professional liability insurance coverage is
very limited and often excludes coverage of claims for a design professional’s general negligence in
the performance of its duties, as opposed to professional negligence. 182
E. 	Liability to Third Parties
A design professional may be liable to third parties for negligently performing certain administrative
tasks, including certifying payments or releases. In one case, the court found that an architectural
firm was liable to unpaid subcontractors who could have recovered from the general contractor’s pay-
ment bond, when the architect breached its duty to confirm that the contractor obtained the required
payment bond before the architect certified payments to the contractor.183 In a different case, the
court stated that an architect may be liable to a surety for negligently approving the release of the
owner’s retainage to the contractor, which resulted in a loss to the surety.184
A design professional may be liable for negligence to third parties injured on the construction
site. 185 Some standard form contracts have been modified to help architects and engineers limit their
liability for workers injured on the site, but this may not extinguish a designer’s potential liability.
For example, in one case a court determined that an architect was liable to a hospital employee who
slipped and fell on the emergency room floor.186 The court ruled that the architect was liable because

VII. 	STATUTES OF REPOSE
Injury and resulting liability relating to construction projects often do not surface until many years
after the work has been completed and accepted. With the increased scope of liability for design
professionals and the prospect of perpetual liability, many state legislatures have enacted statutes of
limitations and statutes of repose to bar claims for damages against design professionals, contractors,
and other participants in a construction project after a set period of time.
State statutes of limitations generally provide that a suit must be filed within a specific period of
time following substantial completion or the discovery of the act or omission giving rise to the claim.
A failure to file suit within the applicable statute of limitations would result in the claim being “time
barred” and subject to dismissal if filed. Some states allow claims to be brought within a certain
period of time following the discovery of a defect, injury, or damage, which typically extends the
time within which claims may be successfully asserted, particularly if the defect is not discovered
for a few years after substantial completion. Conversely, statutes of repose establish an outer time
limit beyond which a party such as the design professional or contractor cannot be held liable for
design and construction defects, regardless of when the defect was discovered.192
A party that discovers its claim after the expiration period provided in the statute of repose is
barred from asserting that claim. The language of statutes of repose varies from state to state. Often
these statutes are broadly written, so as to bar claims against “any person performing or furnishing
the design, planning, supervision, or observation of construction or the construction or repair of
the improvement” that are brought after the specified time. Therefore, a contractor suing a design

the building was not liable for the death of an individual due to smoke inhalation without showing that the placement of the

complies with the applicable statute of repose. Most, if not all, statutes of repose apply to tort
claims, such as those brought under negligence or intentional tort theories. Many of the statutes
also apply to and can be relied on to defeat breach of contract claims. Thus, a party suing a design
professional on a third-party beneficiary theory must pay close attention to the applicable statutes

Statutes of repose usually take one of two forms. Most set a maximum time after completion of
the construction, beyond which no claims may be brought relating to the project’s design or construc-
tion. 193 The second type also sets a maximum time after project completion for bringing a claim,
but, in addition, may also specify a shorter time period to file an action after the cause of action
accrues (e.g., a ten-year statute of repose may include a provision that allows a claim that accrues
in the tenth year to be asserted up to two more years after the expiration of the otherwise ten-year
limitation). 194 Statutes of repose will specify when the statute begins to run. Depending on the juris-
diction, the statute may begin to run upon completion of the project, substantial completion of the
project, termination of the design of the improvement, or termination of the construction services.195
Furthermore, a few statutes can be triggered by other events, such as the date of actual possession
by the owner of the improvement, the date of the issuance of a certificate of occupancy, or the date
of completion or termination of the contract between the design professional, or the contractor, and
the owner. 196
One court determined that an engineering firm was liable for claims in response to a bridge col-
lapse, even though the claim was barred by the applicable statute of repose. 197 In that case, the state
of Minnesota sued the engineer and the maintenance contractor for negligence, breach of contract,
and the resultant damage based on the I-35 bridge collapse in 2007, which caused 13 deaths and
145 injuries. 198 The bridge was substantially complete in 1967 and the Minnesota statute of repose
barred claims after 1982. 199 However, the victim’s compensation fund statute provided that the state
could recover from third parties that caused the bridge collapse. 200 The Minnesota Supreme Court
held that the victim’s compensation fund statute allowed the state to recover from third parties that
were responsible and that the statute could revive claims that were previously extinguished.201 The
decision essentially eliminated the defendant’s statute of repose defense. While the persuasive effect
of this decision outside the state of Minnesota is unclear, it illustrates the risks to all parties following
an event with tragic consequences. Therefore, all participants in the construction process, including
design professionals, contractors, and so on, should be wary of the efficacy of the statute of repose
in other states.

VIII. 	EFFECTS OF CONTRACTUAL LIMITATIONS ON DESIGN
PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY
A design professional may be able to limit its liability through explicit contractual limitations
on liability. A contractual limitation on liability is typically called a limitation-of-liability
clause.
A. 	Limitation-of-Liability Clauses
Limitation-of-liability clauses are used by design professionals in an effort to place a limit on the
damages recoverable from the professional in a lawsuit. The party including the clause seeks to
limit its damages to a specific cap, such as the insurance coverage amount or a dollar amount.202
Capping the recoverable damages at the amount of the designer’s fee is a common provision.
Limitation-of-liability clauses are generally not favored, but may be upheld in a contract between
private parties who have roughly equal bargaining power.203 A court is also less likely to strike
down a limitation-of-liability clause when the parties specifically negotiate for the clause and the
clause includes a dollar limit that has a rational relationship to the design professional’s risk in the
contract.
The decision by the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit in SANS Hotel Group,
LLC v. Environs, Inc., 204 provides a good example of the latter rationale, which many courts use when
considering such clauses. In that case, the owner contracted with an architect to design a six-story
hotel, and the contract executed by the parties included a clause that limited the architect’s “to-
tal liability” to the owner to the amount of its fee, or $70,000. The completed building had to be
demolished, without ever opening for business, due to the existence of irreparable structural defects,
resulting in damages of over $4 million for the owner. The owner filed suit in an attempt to circum-
vent the limitation-of-liability clause, asserting claims in negligence and breach of contract. The trial
court held that under applicable Indiana law, the negligence claims were barred by the economic loss
rule. The court further ruled that the architect had indeed breached the contract by failing to design
the project in accordance with the contractual requirements, but that the limitation of liability was
enforceable and limited the owner’s recovery to the amount of the architect’s fee. In affirming the trial
court’s ruling that the owner’s recovery was limited by the application of the limitation-of-liability
clause, the appellate court pointed to the parties’ contract, which it characterized as a “sophisti-
cated commercial contract.”205 The court’s opinion indicates that it was influenced by the context
presented—a commercial agreement executed by knowledgeable, sophisticated parties who had pre-
viously contracted with a similar limitation-of-liability clause and who had negotiated the allocation
of risk between them at arm’s length.
State courts are divided on whether to enforce limitation-of-liability clauses. Some states, such as
Pennsylvania, Florida, and New Jersey, tend to uphold the clauses, whereas other states, such as Ore-
gon and Wisconsin, have a tendency to find them invalid.206 A few states, such as California, have
enacted legislation that allows for a limitation-of-liability clause under certain circumstances. 207
202See AIA Document B503 – 2017 Guide for Amendments for AIA Owner-Architect Agreements § C-6.
203Georgetown Steel Corp. v. Union Carbide Corp., 806 F. Supp. 74, 77 (D.S.C. 1992), aff’d in part, rev’d in part, remanded,
Georgetown Steel Corp. v. Law Eng’g Testing Co., 7 F.3d 223 (4th Cir. 1993).

VIII. EFFECTS OF CONTRACTUAL LIMITATIONS ON DESIGN PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY 	199
Notwithstanding the existence of a state statute concerning the validity of limitation-of-liability
clauses, California courts have not uniformly enforced the clauses. In a case interpreting Penn-
sylvania law, the court upheld a limitation-of-liability clause where the developer claimed that the
architect breached the contract and negligently determined that a property was not burdened by a
height restriction. 208 The court ruled that:
1. The limitation-of-liability clause in the architect’s proposals was part of the contract with the
developer, even though the developer did not sign the contract.
2. Pennsylvania law does not disfavor limitation-of-liability clauses, especially when they are in
contracts between informed parties who negotiated at arm’s length.
3. The $50,000 cap on liability was not a nominal value in violation of public policy when the
architect’s fee was $7,000.
4. The disputed clauses did not violate public policy in Pennsylvania or run afoul of the Penn-
sylvania indemnification statute.
5. The developer suffered a loss due to the architect’s negligence, but the developer could not
escape the contract by trying to limit the provision to the negligence claim instead of the
breach-of-contract claim. 209
However, in a Georgia case, a court held that an engineering firm’s limitation-of-liability clause
in its contract for the design of a storm-water drainage system violated public policy under a Georgia
statute, because the clause arguably limited the firm’s liability to its contracted fee on any third-party
negligence claims. 210 The court determined that the Georgia indemnification statute deemed void
and unenforceable any provision in an agreement where a contractor alleges to “waive liability for
property damages allegedly resulting from the sole negligence of the contractor’s agents or employ-
ees.”211 First, the court ruled that while the clause did not exculpate the engineering firm from all
liability, the clause was an indemnity provision as defined under Georgia law. 212 Specifically, the
clause was held to be an indemnity provision because it applied to any and all claims by third par-
ties, and allowed the engineering firm to limit its liability for third-party injuries even where it was
solely negligent in causing those injuries. 213 Second, while third parties would still be allowed to
sue the engineering firm, the firm’s liability was limited to its contracted fee of $80,514.00 and
the firm could recover payment from the developer for liability beyond or above that amount. 214
Third, the court found that the liability cap of $80,514.00 had already been reached because the
developer had expended over $250,000.00 to repair the drainage system.215 The court stated that

An indemnification clause is another provision that can be used to limit a design professional’s
liability. Indemnification clauses shift a class of risk from one party to another party and often cover
liability from third-party bodily injury or property damage. Many states have statutes that prevent
parties from indemnifying themselves against all loss, 217 and broad indemnification clauses may be
struck down by the courts based on not being clear and unequivocal. If a state has enacted legisla-
tion barring broad-form indemnity clauses in contracts relating to construction, that legislation may
provide a basis to challenge a broadly worded limitation-of-liability clause. For example, Georgia’s
anti-indemnity statute provides:
A covenant, promise, agreement, or understanding in or in connection with or collateral to a
contract or agreement relative to the construction, alteration, repair, or maintenance of a build-
ing structure, appurtenances, and appliances, including moving, demolition, and excavating
connected therewith, purporting to indemnify or hold harmless the promisee against liability
for damages arising out of bodily injury to persons or damage to property caused by or result-
ing from the sole negligence of the promisee, his agents or employees, or indemnitee is against
public policy and is void and unenforceable, provided that this subsection shall not affect the
validity of an insurance contract, workers’ compensation, or agreement issued by an admitted
insurer. 218
An exculpatory clause can also be used to limit a design professional’s liability. Exculpatory
clauses can be very broad, such as a provision relieving a party from all liability upon substantial
completion, or narrow, such as a waiver of subrogation provision. Broad exculpatory clauses, like
broad form indemnification clauses, are generally not favored by the courts.219 One common excul-
patory clause is the waiver of consequential damages clause, which includes indirect damages such
as a party’s expected or anticipated profit.
New York state courts do not enforce exculpatory clauses where the party attempts to enforce
that clause in its favor in response to its gross negligence.220 These courts have stated that when
a party invokes gross negligence as a basis for not upholding the limitation-of-liability clause, the
gross negligence must “smack of intentional wrongdoing” and constitute “conduct that evinces a
reckless indifference to the rights of others.”221 That can be a rather difficult requirement to meet
in the context of a design professional’s negligence. For example, in one case an architect failed to
follow its contractual obligation to use the flood elevation provided by the owner and to consult with
the local FEMA coordinator when designing a home. 222 The court found the architect’s actions did

B. 	Limitation of Liability in Standard Form Contracts
Some standard-form contracts include terms that attempt to limit the design professional’s liability.
For example, AIA Document B503 suggests two options for limiting liability; one option is to limit
liability to the amount of the architect’s contract compensation, the second option is to limit liability
to the amount of available insurance. 225 The liability limitations do not apply to acts amounting to
willful or intentional wrongs. 226 Courts are divided on whether to accept such limitations on the
design professional’s liability.227
IX. 	ASSUMPTION OF DESIGN LIABILITY BY THE CONTRACTOR
Traditionally, the design professional or owner is responsible for defects and other problems associ-
ated with the project design. There are several ways, however, that a contractor may assume design
liability. When this happens, a contractor may be required to bear not only the costs it incurred
because of the defect, but also those extra costs incurred by the owner or other parties related to the
defect.
As discussed in Chapter 3, a very common situation where a contractor assumes the risks of
design defects is on design-build projects. A design-build contractor performs tasks ordinarily
assigned to the design professional in addition to its construction duties. 228 Some owners are
attracted to design-build contracts because they seek to create a single source of responsibility.
Design-build contracts also relieve the owner from being caught between its design professional
and its contractor during design disputes. In addition to assuming the risks of defects in design,
the design-build contractor also assumes the risk that construction will cost more and take longer
than originally anticipated. As long as the performance criteria provided by the owner are not
impracticable, a design-build contractor may bear the extra cost of its performance and added
expense due to the extended construction time.
Owners are not completely immunized from design liability by entering into a design-build con-
tract. An owner may be subject to liability for design defects depending on the level of the owner’s
technical expertise, the owner’s active direction of the design process, or the design-related infor-
mation provided by the owner at the project’s outset. Owners, contractors, and design professionals
must scrutinize their contract language carefully because the design-build project delivery regime
deviates from the traditional allocation of design risks and alters the traditional relationships between
the parties.

into an agreement.”).

A contractor performing under the traditional design-bid-build delivery scheme may assume a
degree of design liability by the owner’s use of performance specifications and criteria or if it elects
to make an “or equal” substitution. Although performance specifications dictate the results to be
achieved by the contractor, they do not tell the contractor how to accomplish the desired results.
Consequently, the contractor is responsible for the costs associated with achieving the end result
specified. AIA A201 also provides for the design professional to allocate design responsibility to the
contractor. 229 However, a design professional must recognize that an attempt to shift professional
responsibilities to a non-professional can violate state professional licensing and registration laws.
Standard form contract documents allow for delegating design responsibility. Thus, a contractor
must take great care to: (1) competently perform any design tasks assumed; (2) account for the added
costs and exposure related to assumption and performance of professional duties; and (3) make sure
that the risks represented by such exposure are insured or otherwise managed.
Conflicts may exist between design and performance specifications. 230 A contractor must notify
the owner and the design professional to avoid potential liability if the contractor recognizes, or
should recognize, such a conflict between the design and performance specifications.
The owner’s use of a “brand name or equal” specification may also create contractor design liabil-
ity. Using the specified brand-name product does not necessarily relieve the contractor of liability for
noncompliance with applicable performance criteria and does not necessarily fall within the owner’s
implied warranty of the adequacy of the specifications. If the contractor has a choice of products,
the contractor may bear the burden of compliance. 231
As discussed above, one of the common duties of a design professional is to review and approve
contractor submittals, which includes shop drawings.232 If shop drawings prepared by the contrac-
tor require a change to the original design, the contractor may be responsible for how that change
adversely affects the overall construction even though the change was approved by the design pro-
fessional. Where the contract requires the contractor to determine field conditions, the contractor
may be liable for submittals or shop drawings that fail to comply with the actual field conditions
even if the submittals are approved by the owner or architect. For example, in one case the court
found the contractor was still liable for shop drawings that would not work with the actual field
conditions, despite the fact that the owner had approved the shop drawings. 233 The court reasoned
that the contract required the contractor to determine the field elevations for the shop drawings, the
drawings contained no representations regarding the elevations, and the contractor’s failure to obtain
the proper field elevations meant the contractor was responsible for deficiencies in the shop drawings
despite the owner’s approval.234 A contractor may be able to reduce its risk for this type of design lia-
bility by immediately notifying the owner or design professional of any shop drawing-related design
modifications.
Statutes may limit risk-shifting related to product or material substitutions so that an architect’s
approval of the contractor’s suggested substitution may not relieve the contractor of some warranty
obligations. In one case, the architect and engineer approved the contractor’s substitution of a par-
ticular air-conditioning unit on a condominium project, but many of them later failed. 235 Several

condominium unit owners filed a class-action lawsuit against the developer, which, in turn, sought
indemnity from the contractor in a third-party action. The court held that while developers are subject
to statutory warranties of merchantability or fitness for the purposes or uses intended, the contrac-
tor’s statutory warranty is only to provide work and materials that “conform to the generally accepted
standards of workmanship and performance of similar work.” 236 In short, although the contractor
had a duty to provide acceptable materials (a duty that was not affected by the design professional’s
approval of the substitution), it did not have a duty to evaluate broader issues of suitability of those
materials for the purpose intended. Presumably, such duty would fall to the developer and the devel-
oper’s architect or engineer.
Finally, contractors should be wary of standard contract clauses that expose the contractor to
potential liability for design gaps or omissions. Many contracts contain clauses that, for example,
could require the contractor to supply any and all labor and materials that can be reasonably inferred
from the plans and specifications as being necessary to achieve a complete project. If the contractor
fails to include such labor or materials in its proposal or bid, the contractor may be required to fill
the “gap” and furnish the missing scope of work with no increase in the contract price.
X. 	SHARED RESPONSIBILITY AND RISK
Alternative project delivery systems have caused the design professional, owner, and contractor to
share more responsibility and risk during the construction process. The shared risk and responsi-
bility have been reflected in standard form contracts, and all parties to the construction process
should recognize the ramifications of the shared risk and responsibility before entering into such
an agreement.
A. 	Shared Risk and Alternative Project Delivery Systems
Many states have enacted legislation to provide for alternative project delivery systems. 237 For
example, Kansas has enacted alternative project delivery statutes that allow state agencies to use
alternative project delivery methods, such as design-build and construction management at risk. 238
Prior to engaging in an alternative project delivery system, design professionals should review state
statutes on such systems to determine whether additional requirements or obligations exist.
Because alternative project delivery methods are being used more frequently, design profession-
als are providing more services and, therefore, assuming more nontraditional risks.239 To be prudent,
design professionals may want to consider taking on additional insurance coverage to protect them-
selves against liabilities because their core coverage may not cover these nontraditional risks.240
Many different alternative project delivery systems exist. Integrated Project Delivery (IPD) pro-
vides for the owner, architect or engineer, and contractor to all enter into a single contract to work
as a collaborative team.241 With IPD, the parties design and build the project together, as well as

share the risks and rewards.242 The shared risks and rewards, which are achieved by making part of

goals, are meant to create an incentive for all parties to finish the project as effectively, efficiently, and
quickly as possible.243 The shared risks and rewards based on the project outcome discourage self-
ish actions, increase project commitment, and align participants to the desired project outcome. 244
Designer-led design-build is another example of an alternative project delivery system where, in
its simplest form, the owner hires a design professional for a design-build project and the designer
contracts with all the different trades to build the project as the design requires.245 In designer-led
design-build, the designer and contractor also share risks and rewards which create incentives for
the parties to collaborate to avoid losses.246
B. 	Recent Standard Form Contract Efforts Regarding Shared Responsibility
and Risk
The tension regarding the responsibilities of the design professional, the owner, and the contractor
for project design and contract administration has led some industry groups to propose standard form
multi-party agreements to encourage collaboration and minimize risks and disputes. For example,
ConsensusDocs 300 Standard Multi-Party Integrated Project Delivery (IPD) Agreement includes the
concept of a collaborative relationship among the project design team, the owner, and the contractor,
all party to one contract. It states, “Each IPD Team member accepts the relationship of mutual trust,
good faith, and fair dealings established by this Agreement, and agrees to cooperate and to exercise
its skill and judgment to further the interests of the Project . . . .The IPD team will promote harmony
and collaboration on the Project.” 247
ConsensusDocs 300 outlines the designer’s responsibilities in the collaborative agreement by
stating that: “[c]onsistent with the collaborative approach set forth in this Agreement, Design Pro-
fessional shall draw upon the assistance of Constructor and other IPD Team members in developing
the Project design, but Design Professional shall retain overall responsibility for all design decisions
as required by Laws. Cost and schedule are design criteria and Design Professional, in collaboration
with the IPD Team, shall create Design Documents that fully consider cost and schedule implica-
tions.”248 However, ConsensusDocs 300 also states that “Design Professional’s duties, responsibili-
ties, and limitations of authority shall not be restricted, modified, or extended without written consent
of the Core Group.” 249
ConsensusDocs 300 further attempts to assign risk in line with the goal of collaboration. Article
12 addresses risk identification, management, and allocation. And Section 12.6 addresses limitations
of liability.
The collaborative process emphasized and encouraged by ConsensusDocs 300 has been success-
ful on multiple projects. The growth of standard form multi-party contracts may encourage a trend
toward collaboration among all contracting parties, which could minimize risks and liabilities for
design professionals, contractors, and owners.

XI. THE DESIGN PROFESSIONAL’S COPYRIGHT FOR DESIGN DOCUMENTS 	205
XI. 	THE DESIGN PROFESSIONAL’S COPYRIGHT FOR DESIGN DOCUMENTS
Design professionals are increasingly taking legal action to protect their proprietary designs from
unauthorized use. Recognizing this reality, industry standard forms seek to address the parties’
respective rights and to provide guidance regarding circumstances in which intellectual property
rights might not remain with the design professional by virtue of the parties’ agreement. For example,
ConsensusDocs 240 states, “Owner shall receive ownership of the property rights, except for copy-
rights, of all documents, drawings, specifications, electronic data and information (‘Documents’)
prepared, provided, or procured by Design Professional.” 250 However, ConsensusDocs 240 also pro-
vides the parties the option to decide whether the owner shall “obtain ownership of the copyright of
all Documents” for an agreed-upon price, but “[i]f the Parties have not made a selection to transfer
copyright interests in the Documents, the copyright shall remain with the Design Professional.”251
ConsensusDocs 240 also transfers certain rights to the owner, even if copyright interest was not
transferred to the owner, by stating that “[a]fter completion of the Project, the owner may reuse,
reproduce, or make derivative works from the Documents solely for the purpose of maintaining,
renovating, remodeling, or expanding the Project at the Worksite.” 252
In contrast, other standard form contracts provide that all copyrights remain with the design pro-
fessional. EJCDC E-505 specifically grants the design professional ownership and property interest
in all of the documents related to a particular project, regardless of whether the project is com-
pleted. 253 AIA A201 more specifically provides that the architect retains control of the copyrights
for its design documents, stating that “[t]he Architect and the Architect’s consultants shall be deemed
the authors and owners of their respective Instruments of Service, including the Drawings and Spec-
ifications, and retain all common law, statutory, and other reserved rights, including copyrights.”254
AIA A201 adds, “The Contractor, Subcontractors, Sub-subcontractors, and suppliers are authorized
to use and reproduce the Instruments of Service provided to them … solely and exclusively for exe-
cution of the Work.”255 AIA B101 Standard Form of Agreement Between Owner and Architect
contains similar but more detailed provisions, which set forth the rights and responsibilities of the
owner and architect with respect to the use and ownership of the plans, specifications, and other
intellectual property of the architect and its consultants.
Under federal copyright laws, 256 design professionals’ copyrights can apply to drawings,
specifications, and even the buildings themselves. The damages available for infringements of
such copyrights can be substantial and can include an award of all the infringer’s profits. Gener-
ally, under federal law, the design professional is required to show only the accused infringer’s
gross revenues. The burden then shifts to the accused infringer to prove costs unrelated to the
infringement. 257
Furthermore, damages can be assessed at many times the gross fees or revenues realized by a par-
ticular infringer. In one case, the contractor gave the original drawings it obtained from the architect
of record to a replacement architect, who used those plans despite not having the copyright or license

from the original architect. 258 The original architect was awarded damages of over $107,000 against
the replacement architect and the contractor who copied the original architect’s drawings even though
the original architect charged only approximately $16,000 for the original house design. 259
A design professional may also have a claim against another party that creates a design substan-
tially similar to the design professional’s original work. In Shine v. Childs,260 a federal court in New
York found that the architect and his firm that had designed the “Freedom Tower” on the site of the
World Trade Center may be liable to a former architecture student, Shine, for infringement. While a
student, Shine had prepared two similar designs, one of which was called the “Olympic Tower,” for a
Yale University class on skyscrapers in 1999. Shine’s final review jury at Yale included Childs, a con-
sulting partner at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill. When the “Freedom Tower” design was unveiled in
2003, Shine believed there were similarities in the unique design features of his “Olympic Tower.”
Shine registered his designs in 2004 with the U.S. Copyright Office and, shortly thereafter, sued
Childs for copyright infringement. The court would not dismiss the lawsuit, finding that, to succeed,
Shine needed to show ownership of a valid copyright and copying of the original components of
Shine’s work. The court found the registration of the copyright was strong evidence of a valid intel-
lectual property right. The court then found that to prove copying, Shine had to show that Childs
had access to Shine’s design and that there were substantial similarities between the two designs.
Childs had acknowledged that he had seen Shine’s design, so the only issue remaining was whether
the designs were substantially similar.261
Determining ownership of intellectual property rights in a design can be extremely complicated
when the design includes materials (drawings and specifications) that were prepared by engineering
subconsultants to the architect. Even if the architect agrees to transfer the copyright for its draw-
ings or to grant a license to its design to an owner, that transfer or license may not be effective with
respect to the copyrights of the consulting engineers who prepared specific drawings or specifica-
tions. For example, in Guillot-Vogt Associates, Inc. v. Holly & Smith,262 the contract between the
State of Louisiana (State) and its architect mirrored a State statute and provided that the architect
conveyed to the State copyrights related to contract documents for the project. The issue was whether
that contract and statute were effective to transfer the consulting engineer’s copyrights to the doc-
uments it prepared for the project pursuant to an oral subconsultant agreement with the architect.
Notwithstanding the contract between the State and the architect and statute, the court determined
these did not operate to negate the rights provided to the subconsultant under federal copyright law
(17 U.S.C. § 201(e)) as the subconsultant was not bound by the terms of the contract between the
State and project architect.
In some circumstances, copyrighted architectural works may be used or reused without the copy-
right owner’s explicit permission. 263 Some states have enacted statutes allowing public agencies to
reuse the plans they purchase for one project on later projects. 264 Copyright law recognizes a “fair
use” exception regarding copyrighted materials. Under this doctrine, copyrighted materials may be
reproduced and distributed for limited purposes, such as news reporting, teaching, scholarship, or
research. 265 Factors for determining whether the fair use exception applies include: (1) whether the

➣ 	POINTS TO REMEMBER
• Parties can avoid many construction contract disputes by understanding the project design pro-
fessional’s authority, responsibility, and duties.
• Owners, design professionals, and contractors need to carefully review their contract docu-
ments to ensure that the design professional’s authority, responsibilities, and standard of care
of are clearly stated.
• A design professional owes a duty to abide by the applicable standard of care when rendering
professional services and can be liable for providing services below the required standard.
The standard of care applicable to a design professional is often, but not always, stated in its
contract, but architects and engineers also have a common-law duty to provide their services
in accordance with the required standard that arises from their professional licensure.
• In any given case, a design professional may have authority to do certain things on the job site
based on actual authority, implied authority, or apparent authority. Actual authority means the
authority is expressly stated in the contract documents; implied authority means the authority
is incidental or necessary to the exercise of the design professional’s actual authority; and
apparent authority means the owner’s acts would lead a reasonable person to believe the design
professional had such authority.
• During construction, the project design professional is generally responsible for initially inter-
preting the plans and specifications, reviewing and approving shop drawings and other sub-
mittals for conformance with the design concept and compliance with the contract documents,
observing the work, reviewing the contractor’s pay requests and certifying progress and com-
pletion, and arbitrating certain disputes between the owner and the contractor.
• On most jobs, the design professional does not have authority to make changes to the work,
direct the contractor’s operations, or deviate from the contract requirements.
• Some contracts, such as the AIA standard form contract documents, may emphasize the design
professional’s role as administrative and seek to insulate the design professional from poten-
tial liability to the contractor or owner for negligently or improperly interpreting, reviewing,
inspecting, approving, and performing other functions set out in the contract documents.
• In some states, the design professional may be liable to the contractor for economic losses suf-
fered due to negligent performance of the design professional’s duties and responsibilities, even
though there is no contract between the design professional and the contractor. The applicable
law on this issue must be reviewed in each case to determine if a cause of action is available
and, if so, what damages are recoverable.
• The design professional may be able to limit its liability through explicit contractual limitations
on liability. While limitation-of-liability clauses are not favored in some jurisdictions, they may
266Monge v. Maya Magazines, Inc., 688 F.3d 1164, 1171 (9th Cir. 2012).
267See, e.g., ConsensusDocs 240 § 10.1.1 (© 2011, Revised 2017).

be upheld when the parties specifically negotiate for the clause and the clause includes a dollar
limit that has a rational relationship to the design professional’s risk in the project.
• A contractor may assume design liability in certain situations such as a design-build project.
However, a contractor may also take on certain design-related liabilities even in a traditional
design-bid-build project. To avoid such liability, the contractor should always notify the owner
and the design professional about inconsistencies between the design and the performance
specifications, as well as any changes to the design resulting from the contractor’s shop draw-
ings and submittals.
• The design professional generally will control the copyright to its design work, particularly the
unique components of its design, and anyone who wants to use that design will need to obtain
the design professional’s authorization to use the copyright or a license, or secure ownership
of the copyright from the design professional. Otherwise, the user may find itself liable to the
design professional for substantial damages for copyright infringement.

10
SUBCONTRACT
ADMINISTRATION AND
DISPUTE AVOIDANCE
Successful project performance depends on the legal and business relationship among the prime
contractor and the subcontractors and suppliers because although the prime contractor is responsible
for the satisfactory and timely completion of the project, subcontractors and suppliers perform much
of the work.
A subcontractor’s unsatisfactory performance often generates disputes among the prime
contractor, the subcontractor, the owner, and possibly other subcontractors. Disputes also arise
between the prime contractor and the subcontractor from problems for which the owner may be
responsible. Similarly, whenever the prime contractor fails to perform, everyone involved with the
project is affected. These disputes spawn lawsuits or arbitrations. Unfortunately, formal dispute
resolution—such as litigation or arbitration—is costly, time consuming, uncertain, and often does
not solve the problem when it arises.
This chapter focuses on dispute avoidance and contract administration among the prime contrac-
tor, subcontractors, and suppliers. To help parties identify and prevent problems from the outset, this
chapter also concentrates on areas where prime contractor and subcontractor disputes often originate.
I. 	DISPUTE AVOIDANCE BEGINS AT THE BIDDING STAGE
A. 	The Importance of Price
Price is one important consideration in selecting a subcontractor. Yet the lowest-cost subcontract
may turn out to be the most expensive one if the subcontractor is unwilling or unable to do the work.
A prospective subcontractor should consider the prime contractor’s overall pricing strategy.
Unfortunately, a subcontractor may never be completely sure how the prime contractor is pricing
the project during the bid or proposal stage. History, however, may provide a workable indication
about whether the prime contractor is likely to underprice the contract with the expectation of
negotiating lower subcontract prices after the award or of making up deficiencies on extras.
B. 	Know the Other Parties
Avoiding problems begins at the bidding or proposal stage, when both prime contractors and subcon-
tractors identify potential contractors with whom they will bid and enter into contracts for the work.
209

-- 247 of 771 --

210 	CHAPTER 10 SUBCONTRACT ADMINISTRATION AND DISPUTE AVOIDANCE
Dealing with irresponsible or unscrupulous contractors very likely will result in disputes. Thus, all
contractors should consider the five following factors before deciding whether to contract with a
particular company:
1. Identity
2. Reputation
3. Financial resources
4. Experience and qualifications
5. Union versus nonunion status
1. 	Identity
A critical step in avoiding disputes is taking the time to confirm the corporate identity of the firm
with which a prime contractor or subcontractor seeks to do business. Perhaps too obvious, it is easy
to overlook such a concern. Make sure to accurately identify the correct business entity in quotations,
proposals, and contracts. Consider, for example, a prime contractor operating as a joint-venture lim-
ited liability company. Anxious to submit its proposal, a subcontractor may mistakenly address one
member of the joint venture rather than the joint venture itself. Neither party may catch this mis-
take until after it has been perpetuated through bonding and contracting, creating the potential for a
proper-party dispute down the road. Having to argue about the proper parties to a claim before turn-
ing to the merits of the claim significantly increases the cost of dispute resolution. For these reasons,
a prudent contractor should ask itself: “With whom, exactly, am I entering into a contract?”
2. 	Reputation
A company can avoid numerous headaches and possible losses simply by investigating the past
performance record of a potential prime contractor or subcontractor. To avoid unreliable contractors,
deal with reputable individuals with a proven ability to perform, run credit checks, and ask other
owners and contractors about their experiences with that company.
Even a cursory investigation may yield clues to potential problems. For example, engaging a sub-
contractor with a reputation for shoddy or defective work may force the prime contractor to remedy
an unsatisfactory work product at its own expense. A subcontractor may find that a prime contractor
has a history of slow performance at the start of a project, forcing the subcontractors to encounter
extended schedules, frequent payment delays, or end-of-project acceleration. A particularly litigious
contractor may, in the event of a disagreement, refuse to negotiate a settlement, thereby disrupting
the project schedule by refusing to work and possibly forcing arbitration or a court battle, along with
the associated extra expense.
3. 	Financial Resources
A contractor that lacks adequate working capital brings myriad problems to a project, even without
a default. For example, suppliers concerned about the contractor’s ability to pay may hold deliveries
until they receive payment. Laborers may refuse to work because they are not paid on time. These
problems can affect the project.
For most subcontractors, the prime contractor’s financial resources are the ultimate concern
because the prime contractor often must finance part of the performance. For instance, the contractor
may be forced to finance corrective work for defects caused by other subcontractors or to continue
performance in the face of differing site conditions or changes in the work while negotiations or

-- 248 of 771 --

I. DISPUTE AVOIDANCE BEGINS AT THE BIDDING STAGE 	211
litigation resolves ultimate entitlement to payment. If the prime contractor lacks sufficient financial
resources to continue performance and pay its subcontractors and suppliers in the face of delayed
payments from the owner, the potential of a prime contractor failure arises, affecting everyone
involved with the project. That prospect warrants considerable attention to the reputation and
resources of the prime contractors with whom subcontractors and suppliers do business.
Similarly, a subcontractor with insufficient working capital may be encouraged to front-end load
pay requests so that payment may be made for more than the work actually performed is worth or
for work not yet performed. If an overpaid subcontractor defaults, the cost to complete the work,
combined with the sum already paid to the defaulting subcontractor, may be substantially greater
than the amount originally allocated by the prime contractor for the work. The difference, of course,
may come out of the prime contractor’s pocket.
4. 	Experience and Qualifications
State and local laws may require licensing of general contractors and certain subcontractor trades.
(See Chapter 6.) Such licensing requirements may provide some assurance of the contractor’s com-
petence, but the investigation should not stop there.
Inquire into the contractor’s or subcontractor’s experience on projects of similar type and size to
the one being bid or proposed. The best residential electrical subcontractor in the county may not be
the best subcontractor for a high-rise hotel project. That subcontractor’s reputation may be built on
its personal integrity and quality of its employees’ work, which are laudable achievements, but they
do not necessarily assure that the subcontractor has the experience to manage the work of 15 other
electricians and coordinate with multiple other trades—likely requirements for a subcontractor’s
work on a high-rise hotel project.
The subcontractor may learn from other subcontractors and suppliers that a prime contractor
has considerable experience with one type of project, but that this experience is different from the
requirements of the prospective project. The subcontractor may also learn that the prime contractor
is overcommitted on existing contracts, which may affect the prime contractor’s performance on a
new project.
Similarly, a prime contractor must explore the subcontractor’s experience in light of special
performance requirements for the particular project. For example, if the specifications give only per-
formance criteria, the subcontractor must be able to produce engineering and design details to timely
meet the criteria. If a subcontractor proposes to sub-subcontract out the engineering or design work,
it should investigate the proposed design professional’s credentials and experience.
Some building product and component suppliers condition the warranty of their products on
installation or application by an approved (certified) subcontractor. In some cases, such requirements
are not necessary and may serve to inflate the cost of the work. However, the applicable warranty
and the legal basis to enforce that warranty must be reviewed before dismissing a supplier’s or man-
ufacturer’s requirements. The prime contractor may find that its subcontractor is insolvent and that
the supplier has no warranty obligation for failure of a roof or wall system because an unautho-
rized subcontractor installed its product. By contrast, if an approved installer performs the work, the
prime contractor may be protected by both the supplier’s periodic inspections and the product and
installation warranties.
5. 	Union versus Nonunion Status
A prime contractor’s choice of a union or nonunion subcontractor generally depends on its own
union status. If a union subcontractor and a nonunion prime contractor contract for a project, the
subcontract should contain provisions dealing with labor relations on the work site and give the prime

-- 249 of 771 --

212 	CHAPTER 10 SUBCONTRACT ADMINISTRATION AND DISPUTE AVOIDANCE
contractor the right to terminate the subcontractor if labor problems delay or impede the progress of
the work.
A subcontractor should carefully consider its contractual right to time extensions in the event
the prime contractor or another subcontractor has labor problems that affect its work. One option
available to contractors is to operate “double-breasted.”1 In general, a double-breasted contractor is
a union contractor that forms a second, separate company that operates as an “open shop,” in essence
creating two employers: one union and one nonunion. To establish a legally correct, double-breasted
operation, the contractor must establish conclusively that both entities (for example, the union oper-
ation as well as the open-shop operation) are distinct and separate business concerns and not merely
convenient distortions, or alter egos, of each other. This form gives the contractor the choice of being
able to operate without a union where this is feasible while at the same time continuing operation of
the union company where the use of union labor sources is desirable or required.
Of course, double-breasted operations do not guarantee freedom from labor problems, and
some organizations may find that the cost of maintaining two separate companies is prohibitive.
Importantly, using a double-breasted operation also requires careful adherence to very specific and
technical labor law requirements. For example, the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) has
enumerated four criteria used to determine whether the two operations are truly independent in every
conceivable aspect of their operation: (1) common management and supervision of operations;
(2) common control of personnel policies and labor relations; (3) interrelation of operations; and
(4) common ownership or financial control.2 Of these, the NLRB has held the most important factor
to be the control that one party maintains over the other party’s labor relations. 3
Double-breasted operations can be an effective alternative for a contractor that wants to compete
with open-shop contractors in some areas while maintaining good relations with the union where
union labor predominates. Contractors should seek the advice of a labor attorney before attempting
to establish a double-breasted operation to ensure compliance with the requirements of applicable
laws and regulations.
C. 	Subcontract Bids—Potential Issues
When is there an enforceable agreement between a prime contractor and subcontractor? The simple
answer is only after both parties have signed the subcontract agreement. But this simple answer may
also be wrong.
For example, a prime contractor that has relied on a subcontractor’s telephone bid may be entitled
to enforce that bid even though the parties have not signed an agreement. A letter of intent or a
bid made by telephone may create binding obligations such that a refusal to execute a subcontract
agreement may itself constitute a breach.
Oral agreements can be binding, although they may not be enforceable in certain transactions.
When a transaction involves primarily the sale of goods, the Uniform Commercial Code (U.C.C.)
generally governs the creation of a binding contract. The U.C.C. requires that the parties agree to

1. 	Enforcement of Subcontractor Bids
Practically every contractor has had a subcontractor or supplier revoke its bid or proposal after the
contractor has entered into a contract with a third party in reliance on the subcontractor’s bid. This
issue has generated substantial litigation between prime contractors and subcontractors, especially
when severe inflation affects the construction industry.
Many early cases held that the subcontractor was not bound to the prime contractor or, similarly,
that the supplier was not bound to the subcontractor, unless the parties had actually signed a contract. 5
Therefore, bids and proposals could be withdrawn up until the point where the parties executed
formal documents.
In recent years, many courts (but not all) have held that a subcontractor is bound to the prime
contractor when notified within a reasonable time after award that the prime contractor relied on
the subcontractor’s bid in obtaining the prime contract award and intends to use the subcontrac-
tor for the project. 6 What constitutes a reasonable time for acceptance of an offer depends on the
circumstances.7
The trend toward binding subcontractors to the prime contractor based on the bidder’s
proposal—even without a contract document—is a response to the hardship a contractor faces when
it is awarded a contract based on the subcontractor’s proposal, and then the subcontractor is not
obligated to proceed with performance. Many contractors seek to avoid this problem by requiring
that bidders also agree that their proposal will not be revoked for the same period of time allowed
for award of the prime contract in the owner’s bid documents.
When a contractor is forced to hire a replacement subcontractor to perform the work following the
original subcontractor’s repudiation of its bid or proposal to the contractor, the damages can be sig-
nificant.8 Over the past five decades, courts have generally applied the same measure of damages in
such instances.9 Typically, a contractor may recover the difference between the original subcontrac-
tor’s bid and the amount paid to the replacement subcontractor. This measure of damages, sometimes

called “expectation damages,” places the contractor in the same position that it would have occupied
if the original subcontractor had performed as promised.
2. 	Subcontractor Rights Against the Prime Contractor
Although subcontractors may be responsible to prime contractors that rely on their bid, prime con-
tractors are less frequently bound to the subcontractors whose bids were relied on by the prime
contractor. 10 The fact that the prime contractor used the subcontract bidder’s proposal in its bid to
the owner does not ordinarily provide the subcontractor with rights equivalent to those that the prime
contractor may have to bind the subcontractor to a contract. Each set of circumstances must be judged
on its own merits.
An argument can be made that if the prime contractor sends the subcontractor a letter of
intent or a clear statement that it intends to have the subcontractor perform the proposed work
for a mutually acceptable price, and the subcontractor begins performance based on the prime
contractor’s request, there is a basis to find that the parties have entered into a contract, even
though it is not completely reduced to writing. 11 Under such circumstances, a subcontractor may
be entitled to recover damages for breach of contract if the prime contractor later withdraws its
commitment. 12
The fact that the parties have not executed a formal contract is not necessarily controlling. If the
circumstances indicate that a subcontractor intends to perform a specifically identified scope of work
on mutually agreeable basic terms of price and time, and if the subcontractor begins performance
pursuant to such terms with no objection from the prime contractor, there is support for a finding that
the parties are bound to each other. Thus, the subcontractor may be entitled to a remedy for breach
when it is later not allowed to complete the work.

At the outset, a company should decide whether to draft its own subcontract or use a standard sub-
contract form. Form subcontracts developed by industry trade organizations, such as the American
Institute of Architects (AIA), ConsensusDocs, and the Engineers Joint Contract Documents Com-

relatively inexpensive and fairly widely accepted.

a series or family of relatively coordinated documents that address a variety of needs and reflect
“buy-in” from multiple segments of the construction industry. For example, the ConsensusDocs

parties using the AIA form subcontract must confirm that they reference the correct version of AIA

Care should be taken when using industry forms for the contractor-subcontractor relationship
that are designed for the owner-prime contractor relationship. The contracting parties should
carefully review the standard forms, as they may not address the contracting parties’ specific items
of concern or may contain terms unnecessary for the particular project or contractual relationship.
For that reason, some contractors may choose to develop their own forms; however, parties can
use the modern, standard forms’ software to modify the forms to address particular concerns
or needs.
Regardless of whether you use an industry-standard or a custom-drafted document, an adequate
subcontract form should, at a minimum, accomplish the following:
1. Define the exact undertakings of the subcontractor so that there can be no dispute about the
scope of work the subcontractor is to perform, including standard of quality and performance
time.
2. Detail the terms and conditions of payment, including the method of computing progress pay-
ments, terms of payment for stored material, due dates for pay requests, handling of interim
retainage, and final payment.
3. Anticipate areas of trouble or dispute and define the consequences if work is not properly or
timely performed.
4. Specify the relief that the nonbreaching party is entitled to receive.
5. Avoid favoring one party to such an extent that the other party will decline to sign the proffered
form or refuse to perform under its terms—a subcontract should be tailored to fit the needs of
a particular project.
A collection of uncoordinated provisions from various unrelated form contracts can result in a
monster that may create substantial unanticipated problems for both parties. Such monsters typ-
ically are created in one of two ways. The first is a “cut-and-paste” operation by which various
provisions are borrowed from different subcontracts and brought together in one document without
being reconciled or analyzed for consistency. The second is an “inclusion” operation, by which the
contractor includes (either expressly or by reference) in its subcontract the general and special con-
ditions of the prime contract, terms and conditions that it has prepared specially, and perhaps some
other standard-form document, such as the contractor’s project procedures. The justification for an
inclusion contract rests on the theory that more is better. The result is often a hodgepodge of contract
documents that lack consistency and coordination.
Instead, someone competent for the task should prepare and modify a subcontract form as needed
for the conditions of each project. Also, it should be reviewed periodically in light of lessons learned
through experience and changes in the law. Unlike terms of many public contracts, which are set
by law or regulation, there are no “standard” subcontract terms for private contracts. The following
points should be considered in drafting the terms of a subcontract.

A. 	“Flow-Down” Obligations
A flow-down clause, which contractually ties, for instance, the subcontractor to the prime contractor
in the same manner as the prime contractor is bound to the owner, is imperative. 15 One example
of a basic, yet enforceable, flow-down clause reads: “[C]ontractor shall have the same rights and
privileges as against the Sub-contractor . . . as the Owner in the General Contract has against the
Contractor.”16 Since subcontractors at every level are bound together on the project by a series of
contracts, all subcontracts should contain flow-down clauses. The absence of a flow-down clause can
leave the contractor exposed to liability but unable to demand of the subcontractor the performance
that the contractor is required to undertake.
In return for this protection, the prime contractor will generally provide the subcontractor with the
same rights that the prime has against the owner, including making claims, protesting, and providing
notices to the owner. In other words, the rights and duties flow both ways: upward to the prime
contractor, as well as downward to the subcontractors at each level. This tends to keep the parties
on an even basis, despite there being no privity of contract (that is, direct contractual relationship)
between the owner and the subcontractors.
B. 	Scope of Work
Every subcontract must have a clearly defined scope of work. From a practical standpoint, it is
very difficult to define all of a subcontractor’s work in a subcontract’s scope-of-work description.
Therefore, the subcontract form should refer to all of the applicable contract documents between the
owner and prime contractor in defining the subcontract scope of work.17
The general contract bid items are often too general to incorporate by reference into the subcon-
tract as the definition of the scope of work and parties should avoid this practice. Instead, the work
description must explicitly define responsibilities for the scope of work and the responsibilities each
contractor assumes for its own activities.
The scope of work for a project is not simply the items of performance that are subcontracted out
for a particular project. A scope-of-work provision also includes the responsibilities for the facilities
and for contract administration. Therefore, a detailed description of the actual work the subcontractor
is to perform on a project—including incorporation of the owner’s description of the work from
the general contract—must be supplemented with provisions that address other requirements and
contingencies.
