13
SCHEDULES, DELAYS,
AND ACCELERATION
Contractors, subcontractors, and owners all recognize the importance of time on construction
projects. As a general rule, these parties will incur additional costs or lose income if a project is
late. Because delays can cost money, contracts typically define and limit the time to complete the
work by establishing a specific number of days for performance of the work or by identifying a
contractually required completion date. Owners often insert detailed scheduling requirements into
their construction contracts to emphasize the importance of timely completion, as well as to assist
the owner in managing the project. Liquidated damages and early completion bonus provisions can
be included to provide direct economic incentives to the contractor to meet or beat the contract
performance time.
Construction delays are a significant risk on any project. A properly drafted construction contract
will therefore address identified risks of delay and allocate those risks between the parties. Owners
often include provisions that protect them in the event of delays caused by the contractor. Such
provisions include liquidated damages, default, and termination.
Contractors and subcontractors are typically given some protection in the event of delays that
are not their fault. Contract clauses that excuse the contractor (and its subcontractor(s)) from certain
delays include a force majeure clause, a scheduling clause, the time extension clause, the changes
clause, the differing site conditions clause, and the claims clause.
Construction scheduling is a common tool in day-to-day construction management. Scheduling
has become more sophisticated and complicated with the use of computers and specialized software.
Critical Path Method (CPM) scheduling is a detailed mathematical model of the construction plan
that generally requires the use of computers to manage and implement. In simple terms, “critical”
work consists of work activities that must be completed at a certain point in time on a project, oth-
erwise the overall project completion date will be delayed.1 Thus, critical-path work is the longest
chain of work activities that run through a project from start to finish, so that if any of these activ-
ities is delayed, the project will be delayed. Project personnel use CPM scheduling as a means for
determining what work must be completed at any point in time to ensure the entire project remains
on track. Owners also use CPM schedules to measure the contractor’s performance while work is
under way.
1 AACE International Recommended Practices No. 29R-03, ¶ 1.5(A) (2011); K-Con Building Systems, Inc. v. United States,
131 Fed. Cl. 275, 327 (2017).
305

-- 343 of 771 --

306 	CHAPTER 13 SCHEDULES, DELAYS, AND ACCELERATION
Frequently, the most visible work to a casual observer may not be the most important activities
from a CPM scheduling standpoint. While some project personnel have a natural sense of which
work activities are critical from a scheduling perspective, many others need a tool to identify those
activities that are critical and to otherwise manage a complex job. A properly prepared and updated
computer-software-based schedule is that tool.
Schedules have also been used to compute progress payments or act as a payment tool. In these
situations, work activities detailed on the CPM are cost loaded for payment purposes. As the schedule
is updated to reflect actual progress, the value of the work completed to date can be computed. Thus,
on some jobs, the computer software not only tracks progress and projects a completion date, it also
computes the value of progress payments.2 Schedules can also be used to track and evaluate project
resources, such as labor.
In short, scheduling can affect every aspect of a construction project. Developing a schedule
before the bid often influences how much the final bid price will be. Scheduling helps the contractor
control how long a project will take. It can also affect crew size and makeup, influence the equipment
needed on the job, and identify when to order permanent equipment and long-lead materials.
This chapter addresses the legal issues pertaining to time on a construction project. Topics include
setting the contract performance time, scheduling the work, the different categories of delay, the risks
of delay, the right to contract time extensions, how to pursue and defend against delay claims, con-
tract limitations barring or limiting delay claims including “no damages for delay” clauses, and the
damages that often arise from project delay. Although the context of the discussion of the principles
in this chapter is generally the owner–prime contractor relationship, these basic principles also apply
to prime contractor–subcontractor relationships.
I. 	ALLOCATING THE RISK OF PERFORMANCE TIME IN THE CONTRACT
The parties’ contract is the first place to look to identify: (1) performance time and how time will
be measured; (2) scheduling requirements; (3) adjustments to the performance time; and (4) the
allocation between the parties of the financial risks associated with schedule changes, delays, sus-
pensions, and accelerations. A party entering into any construction contract must carefully read and
understand how the contract addresses these issues, because delays, suspensions, and acceleration
can significantly affect job costs.
While the express terms of the contract will typically address many of the issues involving time,
additional legal rights and duties can arise from obligations that the law will imply or read into every
contract. For example, there is an implied contract obligation that both parties will act in good faith
in the contract relationship and that neither party will delay, hinder, or interfere with the performance
of the other party. 3 A party that hinders or prevents performance by the other party, or that renders
performance impossible, may not benefit from its wrongdoing. 4 This rule of law prevents a party
from taking advantage of its own contract breach. These implied obligations provide a legal basis
for a breach of the contract and the recovery of damages arising from delays that are the fault or
responsibility of the breaching party.
2 Tying payments to the CPM schedule may produce unintended and adverse consequences. A requirement for cost-loaded
schedules often leads contractors to manipulate the schedule to maximize cash flow. While increasing cash flow is important,
contractors may sacrifice scheduling accuracy. When a schedule is designed for cash-flow purposes rather than as a realistic
planning and scheduling tool, it will create problems for a contractor when major delays occur and the existing schedule is
not capable of identifying the consequences of the delay.
3Metcalf Constr. Co., Inc. v. United States, 742 F.3d 984, 990 (Fed. Cir. 2014).
4See United States v. Killough, 848 F.2d 1523, 1531 (11th Cir. 1988) (discussing within the context of quantification of
damages the principle that a wrongdoer shall not profit by its wrongdoing at the expense of its victim).

-- 344 of 771 --

I. ALLOCATING THE RISK OF PERFORMANCE TIME IN THE CONTRACT 	307
Traditionally, the contractor’s obligation to complete the work within a certain period of time is
expressly set forth in the written contract. Contracts usually set the performance time either by a
specific completion date or by a defined performance time, such as a certain number of “work days”
or “calendar days” from issuance of the Notice to Proceed. A defined performance time is a material
term of the contract when the contract states that “time is of the essence.”
A. 	“Time Is of the Essence” Clause
Under the common law, 5 performance time is not a material term of a construction contract. Unless
the parties made time a material term of their agreement, the law will imply that the contractor
has a “reasonable time” to perform its work. As a result of this common law rule, parties usually
include a provision in their written contracts making “time of the essence.” Courts have long
construed this language as making time a material term of the contract. Once so designated, an
unexcused delay in completion would constitute a material breach. In an owner-prime contractor
relationship, the owner would be entitled to recover any damages arising from such a breach.
Failing to make “time of the essence” can create many practical and legal problems during
performance. 6
The party that drafts the contract may add language to the “time is of the essence” clause to
further reinforce the importance of time. For example, an owner might add a sentence to the clause
that states, “Any additional or unanticipated cost or expense required to maintain the schedule shall
be borne solely by the contractor.” Similarly, a subcontract that lists a specific completion date also
may include a clause that states, “The contractor shall have the right to decide the time, order, and
priority in which the subcontractor’s various work items shall be performed and all other matters
relative to the timely and orderly conduct of the subcontractor’s work.” This type of language not
only purports to make time a material term of the contract, but allocates specific risks or contract
rights to one of the parties; however, it should be drafted consistent with other provisions throughout
the contract regarding the time for performance. Evaluating a party’s rights or duties under a contract
requires consideration of all the contract’s language.
The next sections begin with the traditional clauses and progress to the more detailed contract
provisions that affect how delays, work suspensions, and work accelerations are handled.
B. 	Contract Commencement and Completion Dates
Most time-related questions arising on construction contracts begin with the contract start and com-
pletion dates. Construction contracts usually specify performance periods either by setting out start
and completion dates or by establishing that the work shall be completed within a specified number
of days after receipt of the Notice to Proceed or commencement of work. Performance days may be
specified in either calendar days or work days.
Contracts may include interim milestone dates, which identify the dates certain elements of the
work must be completed. Where time is declared to be of the essence, the unexcused failure to meet
defined milestone dates or performance times will provide bases for claims for actual or liquidated
damages, an acceleration directive, or may result in default and, possibly, termination.
5 Common law is a body of legal rules made by judges as they issue rulings in court cases.
6See Gunn v. Heggins, 964 So. 2d 586 (Miss. Ct. App. 2007). See also International Production Specialists, Inc. v. Schwing
America, Inc., 580 F.3d 587 (7th Cir. 2009) where the court had to consider whether time was a material term of the agreement
when the written contract did contain “time is of the essence” language. In RDP Royal Palm Hotel, L.P. v. Clark Construction
Group, Inc., 168 Fed. Appx. 348 (11th Cir. 2006), the court found that an owner could not recover liquidated damages from
the contractor because the owner had abandoned any right to rely on the “time is of the essence” clause in its contract by
issuing numerous change orders after substantial completion of the project.

-- 345 of 771 --

308 	CHAPTER 13 SCHEDULES, DELAYS, AND ACCELERATION
If a contract provides a specific date for the commencement of work, the owner is generally
deemed to have warranted that the work site will be ready for work to proceed on that date and that
any conditions precedent for which the owner is responsible (for example, permits, insurance, and
so on) have been satisfied. If the owner fails to have the work site prepared so that the contractor
can begin work on the date promised, the contractor would be entitled to an extension of the per-
formance time and the owner may be liable for any delay damages suffered by the contractor.7 To
avoid liability for such delays, owners often include a statement in the contract that the specified
commencement date is only a projection or an estimate. To avoid misunderstandings and disputes,
all parties should clearly define start dates, when performance time commences, interim completion
milestones, performance times, and substantial completion and final completion dates.
C. 	Substantial Completion and Final Completion
Courts developed the concept of “substantial completion” of a construction contract to protect con-
tractors from the otherwise harsh rules governing executory contracts. Under the common law, the
promisor was not generally entitled to be paid until it fully completed performance. That rule proved
impractical in construction when minor items of incomplete work (for example, punch-list work)
could substantially delay the contractor’s right to any payment.
The courts developed the concept of “substantial completion” or “substantial performance” to
give the contractor legal entitlement to payment even though some minor work remained uncom-
pleted. Under this legal principle, once the contractor achieved “substantial completion,” it was
entitled to the contract price less the value of the uncompleted work. This principle applies to all
construction contracts unless the express terms of the contract state otherwise.8
Many contracts will define “substantial completion.” For example, substantial completion may
be defined as “the stage in the progress of the Work when the Work or a designated portion thereof is
sufficiently complete … so the Owner can occupy or utilize the Work for its intended use.”9 Under
this definition, substantial completion can be achieved even though minor omissions or deficiencies
exist so long as the omissions do not affect the use of the project or designated portion thereof.
Most contracts allow the contractor to bill for its retainage once substantial completion has been
achieved, less an amount sufficient to protect the owner for the incomplete work. Generally, an owner
may not assess, and a contractor is not liable for, delay or liquidated damages after the project is
substantially complete.10 Thus, even when a contractor has not fully completed the work specified in
its contract, the owner may not recover actual delay damages or liquidated damages if the contractor
has achieved substantial completion.
Final completion is reached after the contractor has completed all work activities. Warranty work
(as opposed to punch-list work), however, does not affect final completion.
7See, e.g., Renda Marine Inc. v. United States, 66 Fed. Cl. 639, 718 (2005) (stating that the government would be in breach
of contract for interfering with a contractor’s access to a job site controlled by the government). Some parties have argued
that a delay in the start of work excuses the obligation to proceed. Those arguments have generally been rejected. While the
contractor (or subcontractor) may have a remedy for delays, it is not entitled to “walk off the job.” See Ross Group Constr.
Corp. v. Riggs Contracting, Inc., No. 12-cv-0246-CVE-FHM, 2012 WL 5511644, at *7 (N.D. Okla. Nov. 14, 2012) (holding
that subcontractor “did not have the option to refuse to perform merely due to a change in the schedule, especially because
[subcontractor] knew that the schedule was delayed at the time it signed the subcontract”).
8RAJ Partners, Ltd. v. Darco Constr. Corp., 217 S.W.3d 638, 643 (Tex. App.-Amarillo 2006, no pet.). Similarly, once sub-
stantial completion has been achieved, the project owner is no longer entitled to asses liquidated damages after that date. See
Fortec Constructors v. United States, 8 Cl.Ct. 490, 509 n.5 (1985), aff’d, 804 F.2d 141 (Fed. Cir. 1986); J.M. Beeson Co. v.
Sartori, 553 So.2d 180, 182 (Fla. 4th DCA 1989); All Seasons Constr., Inc. v. Mansfield Hous. Auth., 920 So.2d 413, 416
(La. App. 2d Cir. 2006). In federal government contracting, the assessment of liquidated damages should cease at “beneficial
occupancy.” See, e.g., Gaffney Corp., ASBCA Nos. 37639 et al., 94-1 BCA ¶ 26,522.
9See, e.g., AIA Document A201 – 2017 General Conditions of the Contract for Construction § 9.8.1.
10See U.S. Fid. & Guar. Co. v. W. Rock Dev. Corp., 50 F. Supp. 2d 127, 129 (D. Conn. 1999).

I. ALLOCATING THE RISK OF PERFORMANCE TIME IN THE CONTRACT 	309
Some owners will include a provision in their contracts providing for a separate liquidated-
damages amount for any delays in reaching final completion after substantial completion is achieved.
Such a provision can give the owner the right to specified damages if final completion of punch-list
work is not accomplished within a stipulated number of days following the date of substantial
completion.
Contractual warranty periods may commence upon substantial completion of the work, benefi-
cial occupancy of the project, or final completion of a project or phase of the project. On projects
with phased completion dates, the warranty commencement date(s) may not correspond to the dates
when systems or equipment are to be placed into operation. As many vendors’ warranties are often
tied to the initial date of operation, a contractor or subcontractor could face a significant warranty
gap. Therefore, during the bid or proposal stage, contractors and subcontractors should carefully
review the contract documents to identify all warranty requirements and commencement dates and
compare that information to the warranties offered by vendors or required by the contract documents.
D. 	Typical Contract Time and Scheduling Clauses
There is no uniformity in how construction contracts address scheduling, delays, and time extensions.
Each contract needs to be reviewed and understood without assumptions as to how these issues are
handled. Generally speaking, contract clauses addressing scheduling and time have become increas-
ingly detailed over the last 30 years. Parties must often consider multiple provisions in the contract
to understand the scheduling and time obligations, as well as the nature, size, and scope of changes
a party can make to the schedule before it must compensate the other party. They should also review
any incorporated contract documents that may further define performance obligations, such as the
project specifications.
A construction contract may contain provisions covering one or more of the following topics
pertaining to scheduling, performance durations, and delay:
• Provisions making time of the essence, setting the contract performance time, and defining
when contract time commences
• Provisions detailing the contractor’s obligations to prepare, update, revise, and use a construc-
tion schedule
• Provisions giving the owner the right to actual or liquidated damages in the event the contractor
is late
• Allowable time for weather delays during a given period
• A force majeure clause identifying those delays considered excusable and that, if encountered,
entitle the contractor to a time extension
• Time extension provisions providing instructions on how the contractor must apply for a time
extension when it believes an excusable delay has occurred
• A claims clause that provides instructions on how the contractor is to seek time extensions and,
in certain circumstances, delay damages for excusable delays; may include a requirement that
any time-extension request or request for delay-related costs be support by a specific type of
CPM schedule analysis
• A no-damages-for-delay clause limiting the contractor’s right to additional compensation for
delays that otherwise may be compensable
• A suspension of work clause allowing the owner to suspend the contractor’s performance and
identifying what relief the contractor may obtain for any such suspension
• Default and termination clauses giving the owner rights, including the right to terminate or
order acceleration, if the contractor falls behind schedule

-- 347 of 771 --

310 	CHAPTER 13 SCHEDULES, DELAYS, AND ACCELERATION
Parties should always identify and understand all contract provisions addressing scheduling, how
changes to the schedule are made, how delays are to be evaluated, the process for obtaining contract
time extensions, and which party bears the risks of any costs associated with different types of delay.
AIA A201 and ConsensusDocs 200 both address delays and time extensions. AIA A201 provides:
§ 8.3 DELAYS AND EXTENSIONS OF TIME
§ 8.3.1 If the Contractor is delayed at any time in the commencement or progress
of the Work by (1) an act or neglect of the Owner or Architect, of an employee of
either, or of a Separate Contractor; (2) by changes ordered in the Work; (3) by labor
disputes, fire, unusual delay in deliveries, unavoidable casualties, adverse weather
conditions documented in accordance with Section 15.1.6.1, or other causes beyond
the Contractor’s control; (4) by delay authorized by the Owner pending mediation
and binding dispute resolution; or (5) by other causes that the Contractor asserts, and
the Architect determines, justify delay, then the Contract Time shall be extended for
such reasonable time as the Architect may determine.
§ 8.3.2 Claims relating to time shall be made in accordance with applicable provisions
of Article 15.
§ 8.3.3 This Section 8.3 does not preclude recovery of damages for delay by either
party under other provisions of the Contract Documents. 11
ConsensusDocs 200 provides:

for the Owner’s and Architect’s information a Contractor’s construction schedule

In keeping the scheduling specification in the A201 document both general and brief, the AIA
decided to let the parties decide for each project whether further scheduling provisions were needed.
Typically, any additional provisions will be found in an addendum to the A201 General Conditions
or in Division 1 of the technical specifications.
Division 1 (General Requirements) of the technical specifications is easy to overlook and may
contain important provisions on how the project is to be scheduled and how delays are to be treated.
Scheduling provisions can run for pages14 and identify a host of scheduling activities the contrac-
tor must perform. For example, detailed clauses may require: (1) the contractor to prepare both a
preliminary schedule and an overall computerized CPM schedule meeting specified requirements;
(2) regular look-ahead schedules; (3) periodic updates to the CPM schedule to reflect actual progress
and changes in the logic of the overall construction plan, including changes in activity logic or the
use of float; and (4) details on how the schedules will be used to assess and quantify delay.
Scheduling clauses may require the contractor to submit at the contractor’s expense a recovery
schedule when the project falls behind schedule. Such a provision might read: “If the contractor’s
schedule is delayed on its critical path by fourteen (14) calendar days or longer, the contractor shall
be required to, at no additional cost to the owner, prepare and submit to the owner and architect
a supplementary recovery schedule to explain how those activities shall be rescheduled to regain
compliance with the contract schedule.” The contract may also obligate the contractor to accelerate
its performance so that the project completes on time. The contractor should be careful in labelling
schedule submissions as “recovery” or “acceleration,” so as not to inadvertently subject itself to
potential liability for the triggering delay event.
Subcontracts may include scheduling provisions that identify the subcontractor’s specific respon-
sibilities if it falls behind schedule. The following subcontract clause illustrates this point:
In the event subcontractor fails to meet any interim completion date provided for in the
subcontract for any reason, contractor shall be entitled to direct subcontractor to immediately
implement whatever means are necessary to bring the Project back on schedule, including
supplying additional manpower, working overtime at subcontractor’s sole expense, or by
re-sequencing and/or accelerating the Work, provided such re-sequencing and/or acceleration
is possible.
II. 	USE OF SCHEDULES IN PROJECT MANAGEMENT
Parties involved in construction should understand that there is no single best way to schedule a
project. Different contractors have different ideas on scheduling based on past experience and the
characteristics of the job in question. Of course, the contract may have mandatory requirements
13 AIA Document 201 – 2017 § 3.10.
14See, e.g., United States Army Corps of Engineers ER 1-1-11 Administration PROJECT SCHEDULES (18 September 17),
available at https://www.publications.usace.army.mil/USACE-Publications/Engineer-Regulations/.

-- 349 of 771 --

312 	CHAPTER 13 SCHEDULES, DELAYS, AND ACCELERATION
detailing how to develop and maintain the schedule and how to track progress via the schedule. Be
mindful that the schedule is one of the most easily manipulated project documents.
Most construction project schedules are created and managed using CPM computer-based
scheduling software, such as Primavera P6 Professional Project Management or Microsoft Project.
Since the mid-1990s, the Primavera products have used the Precedence Diagramming Method
(PDM) of CPM scheduling, which allows the user to define relationship activities (logic) in more
ways than “start to finish,” as did the older arrow-diagramming method. Relationships can be
defined in PDM as start to start (tying the start of one activity to the start of another) and finish to
finish (tying the finish of one activity to the finish of another). With “leads” or “lags,” a user can
define activities that lag behind or lead other activities by an identified number of days, thus giving
more scheduling flexibility than was available in earlier software.
One of the most useful aspects of computer scheduling is the ability to define the critical path of
activities through to the completion of the project. By definition a delay to a work activity on the
critical path will directly delay the completion of the project (based on the logic of the schedule).
Many activities are not on the critical path and delays to those activities would not affect the project
completion date until a delay lasted long enough to push the activity onto the critical path.
Noncritical activities have “float,” the amount of time an activity can be completed late without
affecting the overall project completion date. Under typical time-extension clauses, a contractor
would not be entitled to a contract extension for delays to a noncritical work activity until the delay
consumed all available float associated with the activity.
The wide availability of inexpensive scheduling software has created its own problems. For
example, someone with little experience in CPM scheduling can generate an impressive-looking
but potentially inaccurate schedule. Anyone preparing a schedule needs to have experience with
the software system, as well as an understanding of both the general construction process and the
specific work to be performed.
Schedulers can underestimate the time required for a particular task or deliberately build extra
time into a schedule to allow greater flexibility or to ensure avoidance of liquidated damages. These
schedules can create problems when preparing updates during performance. Some schedulers may
try to mask delay by changing or deleting logic, failing to report progress correctly, constraining
work activity dates, or adopting other assumptions in their updates even though the assumptions
cannot be supported by manpower, equipment availability, or subcontractor capacity. For example,
in attempting to recover the scheduled completion date, a scheduler may input simultaneous or stag-
gered additional crews where those resources did not previously exist in the schedule. In these
circumstances, the schedule is used to hide performance problems and can become a confusing,
inconsistent, and counterproductive tool.
Good schedulers try to anticipate and provide for all foreseeable events, including lead time
for material deliveries and expected weather, to name only two. While a good scheduler will con-
sider many potential variables, it is impossible to predict all factors that might affect performance
time. Thus, it must be understood that a construction schedule is only a documented plan that
is subject to change as time goes by and events unfold. The actual work may proceed faster or
slower than scheduled. Moreover, the critical path can shift numerous times during the course of
a project. 15
Under any scheduling format, there are several general principles to keep in mind when develop-
ing and updating a schedule, including the following:
• A schedule should be a management tool for planning, sequencing, and performing the work.
If it serves some other purpose or serves no purpose at all, it may create problems.
15See, e.g., George Sollitt Constr. Co. v. United States, 64 Fed Cl. 229, 240–241 (2005).

-- 350 of 771 --

II. USE OF SCHEDULES IN PROJECT MANAGEMENT 	313
• The schedule should reflect the contractor’s intended plan for doing the work. As construction
plans change during the course of the work, the schedule should also change.
• A well-developed and properly updated schedule is an extremely valuable tool for keeping the
owner both informed and happy.
• Delays in performance should be reflected in updates to the construction schedule. It is not
advisable to hide delays by manipulating the scheduling software. When that happens, the
altered schedule ceases to be a management tool and can create problems for the contractor.
• Subcontractors need to be aware of the overall plan for the work. Different schedules for dif-
ferent participants (for example, owner versus subcontractor) are usually seldom worth the
problems they create.
• Subcontractors’ entitlement to time extensions is determined by their written subcontracts.
A contractor can aggressively manage subcontractors but should not ignore a subcontractor’s
rights when the subcontractor is entitled to a time extension. A properly updated schedule helps
to manage subcontractors.
• Some delays will not affect the critical path and thus not affect the projected completion date.
Other delays may be critical and will generate schedule slippage. Either way, the parties are
better off knowing the status of the project based on a realistic schedule.
Contractors sometimes finish ahead of schedule, which allows them to save considerable sums of
money in overhead and time-sensitive expenses. Certainly, no court would penalize a contractor for
completing a project early, unless, of course, the contractor achieves early completion by violating
the contract or the implied duty of cooperation owed to the owner or another party involved with the
project.
With limited exceptions, a contractor has the right to schedule the job to finish early. A bidder
sometimes prices a job based on a performance time shorter than the time provided in the contract
to save general conditions costs and put itself in a more competitive position to win the work. A
contractor may publish a schedule showing an early completion date and then work to achieve that
schedule. Unless the contract states otherwise, the owner is obligated to cooperate and not impede
the contractor’s efforts to achieve early completion.
Problems can arise when a contractor falls behind an early completion schedule or suffers delay
that prevents the contractor from completing early, but still allows it to finish by the contract comple-
tion date. Whether a contractor is in violation of its contract when it falls behind an early completion
schedule may depend on the precise wording of the contract. For example, some default clauses pro-
vide that the contractor can be found in default if it fails to make sufficient progress to complete the
work by the contractually required completion date. Other contracts provide that the contractor is in
default if it falls behind the approved construction schedule. Under the second example, a contractor
falling behind an early completion schedule may be in technical violation of the contract even if it is
still on track to complete the work by the contract deadline. A contractor needs to understand how
the contract is drafted before announcing any intention to finish early.
A contractor suffers a “constructive penalty” when it is prevented from finishing a job early by
an uncooperative owner. If the delay does not extend performance beyond the originally scheduled
completion date, the owner may argue that because the contractor finished “on time,” either the
contractor was not delayed or it suffered no damage as a result of the delay. However, as a general
principle, a contractor can be damaged when it is precluded from finishing early. 16
Delay can occur to activities on the critical path or can consume some or all available float
on noncritical activities. Conceptually, loss of float time can reduce the contractor’s flexibility in
16See Weaver Bailey Contractors v. United States, 24 Cl. Ct. 576 (1991); Grow Constr. Co. v. State, 391 N.Y.S.2d 726 (N.Y.
App. Div. 1977); Metro. Paving Co. v. United States, 325 F.2d 241 (Ct. Cl. 1963).

sequencing its work and allocating resources and may increase the cost of performance even if there
is no overall project delay. To the extent that the contractor uses its own float time, it cannot com-
plain, but owner-caused delays that consume only float time could indirectly affect the critical path
or increase the contractor’s cost. While delays occurring to certain activities having float may have
no adverse consequences on the contractor (other than delaying that noncritical activity), delays to
other noncritical activities may create problems or result in added cost for the contractor.
Thus, there can be a difference between owners and contractors as to who “owns” float.17 Some
government agencies and private owners have begun to use clauses specifically dealing with own-
ership of float. Two possible solutions to this issue have been suggested. One position is that the
contractor owns float. In that context, the owner may use float without cost unless and until the con-
tractor can show it needed that same float for its own planning and performance purposes. Once the
contractor can show a need for the float that the owner has taken, the owner must compensate the
contractor for taking the float.
The alternative and much more common position is that float belongs to the party that first uses
it and no party can complain if the other consumes float for its own purposes.
III. 	ANALYSIS OF PROJECT DELAY
Delays on a project can occur for an infinite number of reasons. Some delays are caused by actions
or inactions that are within one of the parties’ control and some delays occur due to the intervention
or lack of cooperation by some third party. Still other delays occur due to circumstances beyond any
of the contracting parties’ control, such as adverse weather.
As previously discussed, delays may affect only noncritical activities that do not impact the com-
pletion of the job. Other delays, however, directly impact critical activities and, by definition, impact
the completion of the project. Some delays are not only critical but cause a complete suspension of
the project.
A legal evaluation of a construction delay considers the nature of the delay, the party or parties
responsible for the delay, the activity or activities that were delayed, and whether the delay affected
the overall project. In terms of the effect on the project, types of delay include the following:
• Critical Delay. A delay to a work activity on the critical path of a project. The delay to a critical
activity directly affects overall completion of the project. In CPM scheduling terms, a critical
activity is any activity that has zero float or the largest amount of negative float. Near-critical
(or subcritical) delays should also be considered in evaluating delay.18 Critical delay may be
excusable or nonexcusable depending on the cause of the delay.
• Noncritical Delay. A delay to one or more noncritical work activities on the project. A noncrit-
ical work activity is an activity that is not on the critical path and therefore any delays do not
affect the overall duration of the project. Noncritical activities have float time as compared to
the critical path. A delay to a noncritical activity typically does not entitle the contractor to any
extension of time since the delay should not affect the overall completion date of the project.
However, if the duration of a delay to a noncritical activity lasts long enough, the delayed
activity will become critical and further delays will impact project completion. 19
17 One of the more comprehensive treatments of float ownership issues is the paper by John C. Person, Who Owns the Float?
Construction Briefings No. 91–7 (Federal Publications, Inc. May 1991).
18 AACE International Recommended Practice 29R-03 Forensic Schedule Analysis (2011).
19 In certain cases, however, delay damages may be recoverable for work delays that are not on the critical path or do not delay
the overall project completion. See E.R. Mitchell Constr. Co. v. Danzig, 175 F.3d 1369, 1373 (Fed. Cir. 1999); Clark Constr.

III. ANALYSIS OF PROJECT DELAY 	315
Once a delay event to a contractor’s work is classified as either critical or noncritical, it then
becomes necessary to determine if that event is an excusable or nonexcusable delay. That determi-
nation generally controls the contractor’s entitlement to an extension of time and compensation for
that time.
A. 	Excusable Delays Versus Nonexcusable Delays
The occurrence of a delay raises the issue of which party should bear the responsibility for the delay.
In deciding this question, courts look to the causes of the delay and to the express and implied
obligations imposed by the contract.
Construction delays fall into two legal categories: excusable delays and nonexcusable delays.
An excusable delay provides a contractual basis for an extension of the contract performance time.
Excusable delays can also be further subdivided into either compensable delays, which permit the
contractor to recover both time and money, or noncompensable delays, which permit the contractor
to receive a time extension, but not money.
If the cause of delay stems from the actions or inactions of the owner, or if the cause of the delay
is beyond the contractor’s control, the contractor’s delay typically is excusable.20 Accordingly, the
owner cannot recover liquidated damages for these types of delays. 21 In addition, the contractor can
often recover delay damages due to owner-caused delays to the project.22
In contrast to an excusable delay, a nonexcusable delay is a delay for which the contractor must
accept responsibility. In that regard, the contractor must recover the lost time or be responsible for
the problems created by the delay. For example, the contractor may be liable to the owner for delay
damages or liquidated damages for delay.
The reasons for nonexcusable delays vary and can include lack of adequate manpower, slow
progress due to unqualified workers, poor planning, defective work, failure to forward submittals
in a timely manner, and so on. In such cases, the contractor will not receive additional compen-
sation or time to complete the work and may be liable for damages to the owner caused by such
delay.
B. 	Excusable Delays
Typically, the contract will define when a delay is excusable. Contracts often include force majeure
clauses that list some, if not all, excusable delays. Some contracts specifically enumerate the types
of excusable delays for which a time extension is due. 23 For example, as mentioned previously, AIA
A201 lists the following excusable delays:
§ 8.3.1 ordered in the Work; (3) by labor disputes, fire, unusual delay in deliveries, unavoidable
casualties, adverse weather conditions documented in accordance with Section 15.1.6.1, or
other causes beyond the Contractor’s control; (4) by delay authorized by the Owner pending
Group, Inc., GAOCAB No. 2003-1, 2004 WL 5462234 (“The primary circumstance for allowing the recovery of these type
of delay damages is that the claimed damages not be based upon an extended prime contract term (because then there is no
recovery unless it has been shown that the contract performance term was extended), but be for impact or disruption costs
caused by a particular action causing delay in an aspect of the contract that amounts to a constructive change or suspension
to the contract by the government.”)

Other causes of excusable delays to a contractor’s performance typically include differing
site conditions, design problems, changes in the law or governmental regulations, and adverse

Some contracts list examples of excusable delays and may or may not seek to limit the grant-

the subcontractors or suppliers.24
Each party to a construction contract must have a clear understanding of excusable delays when
requesting time extensions or analyzing time-extension requests.
IV. 	TYPICAL CAUSES OF COMPENSABLE DELAY
In most cases, faulty or negligent acts or omissions or other conduct by the owner in contravention
of the contractor’s rights will not only result in an excusable delay, but also entitle the contractor to
recover its increased costs or damages arising from the delay. The duty to compensate the contractor
for its costs associated with such a delay arises out of the owner’s obligations under the changes
clause (to issue a modification due to the change in the performance time), to fix or account for a
defective specification, or to compensate the contractor for a breach of the owner’s implied obligation
to cooperate.
24 FAR § 52.249–10.

-- 354 of 771 --

IV. TYPICAL CAUSES OF COMPENSABLE DELAY 	317
The owner’s obligation to compensate the contractor for certain delays can be altered by an
enforceable no-damages-for-delay clause in the contract or other risk-shifting clauses. No-damages-
for-delay clauses are discussed later in this chapter. Some examples of acts or failures to act that can
typically result in excusable and compensable delay are discussed in the sections that follow.
A. 	Defective Drawings or Specifications
Federal courts, as well as most states, have adopted the Spearin doctrine, which holds that an owner
generally impliedly warrants that the plans and specifications or other design criteria it provides to
the contractor are reasonably free from defects and errors.25 If such plans have errors or are otherwise
insufficient for the contractor to perform the work, the owner may owe the contractor time, as well as
money, to compensate the contractor for any resulting increased performance costs or time impacts.26
Under the Spearin doctrine, a contractor would be entitled to a change order to compensate it for
problems caused by defective plans or specifications. Under a typical changes clause, the change
order would include the additional direct costs the defective specification caused the contractor to
incur, as well as an extension of the contract performance time. The scope of the change order would
also include compensation for any costs arising from time-related impacts (for example, delays or
labor inefficiencies) caused by the defective specification.
The applicability of the Spearin doctrine in delay cases may be altered by a no-damages-for-delay
clause. For example, in one Ohio case, the court declined to apply the Spearin doctrine to delays
arising out of a defective specification because the contract in question contained an enforceable
no-damages-for-delay clause.27 The contract at issue in that case was executed in 1997—one year
before the Ohio General Assembly declared no-damages-for-delay clauses “void and unenforceable
as against public policy ‘when the cause [of delay] is a proximate result of the owner’s act or failure
to act.’”28 Because the contract was entered before passage of the statute, the no-damages-for-delay
clause was still enforceable under Ohio law.29
Because the no-damages-for-delay clause was, at that time, enforceable, the court explained, “In
order to hold in favor of [the contractor], we would need, first, to find that the state had implicitly
warranted that its plans were buildable, accurate, and complete, and second, to hold that the implied
warranty prevails over express contractual provisions. To do so would contravene established prece-
dent, which we will not do.”30
B. 	Failure to Provide Site Access or Improper Site Preparation
The owner is generally required to provide the contractor access to the work site in a timely and
properly sequenced fashion.31 At the time the Notice to Proceed (NTP) is issued, the contractor has
a right to commence the work without restriction (unless the NTP or contract provides otherwise)
and assumes all necessary conditions are in place. The contractor also has the right to receive a site

contract if it fails to provide access to the site in the condition promised in the contract and the
contractor would be entitled to recover the cost of any delays attributable to the owner’s failures.
Under the right facts, the contractor may have a delay claim for the owner’s delay in issuing
the Notice to Proceed (NTP). In one federal government contract case, the court found that the
contractor had stated a cause of action when the government delayed issuing the NTP beyond when
it represented that it would be issued.32
In an effort to limit its exposure, however, the owner may insert an exculpatory clause into the
construction contract providing that the contractor assumes the risk of access or site problems.33 By
inserting a sufficiently clear and express exculpatory clause into the contract, the owner may be able
to shift the risk of site-access delays to the contractor.
Generally, it is the owner’s duty to make available to the contractor a work site that is adequate
for the contractor to perform its work. 34 A common example of this situation is where the owner
retains a grading contractor to perform the earthwork at a site. If the follow-on building contractor
encounters problems and delays because the grading contractor’s work was late or deficient, the
building contractor would be entitled to a compensable time extension from the owner.
The contract may require the contractor to inspect the work site before beginning work. Should
the contractor fail to discover site-preparation problems that a reasonable inspection would have
revealed, or should it fail to raise any objections in a timely manner, the contractor may be precluded
from recovering its added costs, including any delay damages. 35
C. 	Delayed Delivery of Owner-Supplied Fixtures or Equipment
In many construction contracts, the owner is responsible for supplying certain fixtures, materials, or
equipment. The owner needs to provide these items within the timeframes promised in the contract or,
if no timeframe is specified, within a reasonable time consistent with project needs. This obligation
arises from the express terms of the contract or from the owner’s implied duty to cooperate with
the contractor. Should the owner breach this duty by failing to provide such items on a timely basis,
the owner may be liable for delay damages.36 Contractors would be wise to include such owner
obligations in the project schedule.
D. 	Failure to Timely Approve Shop Drawings/Process Submittals
Contractors are typically required to submit shop drawings, product technical data brochures,
material submittals, and cut sheets for review. The owner or its architect/engineer (design profes-
sional) then reviews these submittals for compliance with the contract technical requirements. For

contractors, the submittal and review process can become a source of delay if the contractor cannot

Contracts sometimes spell out the amount of time the owner or its representative has to take action

The owner’s liability to respond timely to Requests for Information (RFIs) is similar to that for

E. 	Failure to Coordinate Prime Contractors
When an owner elects to execute a project with multiple prime contractors, many jurisdictions recog-
nize a duty on the owner’s part to coordinate the work activities of the separate prime contractors.41
Thus, the owner may be responsible to one prime contractor for delays caused by another. Even where
the owner attempts to shift this duty to coordinate to one of the prime contractors, the owner may
still be liable for delays if the lead contractor is not also given the power to enforce its coordination
responsibilities. 42
Some states, however, will enforce exculpatory contract provisions requiring that separate con-
tractors coordinate with each other and stating that the owner will not be responsible for any conflicts
arising between the two contractors. 43 If a contractor is considering a multi-prime project in any
jurisdiction, a key question to be addressed, prior to submitting a bid or proposal, is the effectiveness
of such an exculpatory clause under the applicable law.

F. 	Failure to Give Timely Orders for Work
If the owner fails to issue the Notice to Proceed (NTP), or other commencement-triggering docu-
mentation, within the time provided in the contract, or within a reasonable time if the contract does
not indicate a specific time, the owner generally will be liable for any time-related costs arising
from the owner’s actions. Although contract time does not commence before the NTP is issued,
unexpected delays in the NTP can sometimes impact performance. If a delay to the NTP pushes
performance into a cold or rainy season, the contractor may have a claim for the delay in issuing
the NTP.
It has been held that where the contract is silent as to time of issuance of the NTP, the owner
or its designated representative must issue the NTP within a reasonable time after contract award.
An unreasonable delay in issuing the NTP may amount to a breach of contract or a constructive
suspension of work.44
In determining what constitutes a reasonable period within which to issue the NTP, the federal
government boards of contract appeals and the United States Court of Federal Claims will consider
the time required to resolve any pending bid protest.45 If the contractor wants the NTP to be issued
expeditiously, it should make a specific request.46
The owner’s obligation to take timely action can also apply to delays in authorizing changes or
responding to RFIs. 47 The owner’s legal duty arises either from express provisions in the contract or
from the owner’s implied obligation to cooperate with the contractor.
G. 	Failure to Make Timely Payments to Contractors
Should the owner fail to make timely payment, the contractor generally has the right to suspend
performance. Some contracts also allow the contractor to terminate the contract or to continue with
the contract work and seek damages. Generally, the contractor can recover any damages arising
from the owner’s breach of its payment responsibilities, including compensation for any delays
arising therefrom, interest on the late payments, and, in some jurisdictions, consequential damages
suffered due to late payment. 48
H. 	Failure to Inspect
Under the typical contract, an owner has the right or duty to inspect the contractor’s work as it
progresses. (See Chapter 14.) The owner may be liable to the contractor for delays caused by the
late, improper, or excessive inspections performed by the owner or its representatives.49
I. 	Suspensions
A suspension is a form of delay that usually results from the owner’s purposeful interruption of the
work. Suspensions can occur on any type of contract and most contracts give the owner the right to

order a suspension of the work for various reasons. For example, the standard Suspension of Work
clause in the Federal Acquisition Regulation provides, in part:
SUSPENSION OF WORK (APR 1984)
(a) The Contracting Officer may order the Contractor in writing to suspend, delay, or interrupt
all or any part of the work of this contract for the period of time that the Contracting Officer
determines appropriate for the convenience of the Government. 50
This clause provides the owner the right to halt construction temporarily if, for example, the
owner experiences funding problems or needs to restrict access on a temporary basis. The clause also
provides equitable compensation for any resulting additional costs and extended performance time.
Express suspensions arise from the owner’s express directives to stop the work. “Constructive”
suspensions arise indirectly from events and actions that force the contractor to stop performance. If
the events were under the owner’s control, the end result is still a suspension, even if the owner did
not expressly order it. 51
Suspension clauses may expressly address indirect or constructive suspensions. For example, the
federal Suspension of Work clause becomes operative wherever there is an act or omission by the
contracting officer resulting in suspension or delay to the contractor:
(b) If the performance of all or any part of the work is, for an unreasonable period of time, sus-
pended, delayed, or interrupted (1) by an act of the Contracting Officer in the administration
of this contract, or (2) by the Contracting Officer’s failure to act within the time specified in
this contract (or within a reasonable time if not specified), an adjustment shall be made for any
increase in the cost of performance of this contract (excluding profit), necessarily caused by the
unreasonable suspension, delay, or interruption, and the contract modified in writing accord-
ingly. However, no adjustment shall be made under this clause for any suspension, delay, or
interruption to the extent that performance would have been so suspended, delayed, or inter-
rupted by any other cause, including the fault or negligence of the Contractor, or for which
an equitable adjustment is provided for or excluded under any other term or condition of this
contract. 52
Contractors performing under contracts with such provisions have been allowed to recover for
several types of delays including: (1) delays in making the site available; (2) delays in issuing change
orders; and (3) delays caused by defective plans and specifications. The clauses, however, may pro-
vide specific information as to how compensation is calculated.
J. 	Excessive Change Orders
When the owner orders an excessive or unreasonable amount of changed or extra work, the contrac-
tor may be allowed to recover delay damages for the cumulative impact of all the changes. 53 The
contractor needs to show that the large number of changes was not contemplated and that it adversely
impacted the performance of unchanged work. Damages arising from excessive changes on a project
are commonly referred to as “impact costs.”

Claims for impact costs arising from a large number of changes are often difficult to establish.

V. 	CONCURRENT DELAY
Concurrent delay, in addition to excusable delay and nonexcusable delay, is another category within
the analytical framework for identifying and evaluating construction delays. The term “concurrent
delay” refers to when an excusable delay and a nonexcusable delay occur to one or more critical
activities during the same time period. One example of a concurrent delay is when a contractor
cannot commence work on the second phase of a project because the owner has failed to obtain a
necessary right-of-way (an excusable delay) and, simultaneously, the contractor finds itself unable
to commence the second phase by its own failure to timely mobilize equipment needed for the work
(a nonexcusable delay).
Concurrent delay can create complex legal issues regarding assessing responsibility for overall
project delay. The analysis of concurrent delays may be further complicated if: (1) the delay periods
are different lengths; (2) the delay periods are not entirely concurrent; (3) the delay periods have
different impacts on the number and types of work activities they affect; (4) the severity of the
impact on the affected work activities is different for each of the delays; and (5) there are numerous
causes for the delay.
A. 	Traditional View: No Recovery by Either Party
Traditionally, when project performance was concurrently delayed, neither party was allowed a mon-
etary recovery from the other. The courts took the view that when each party proximately contributed
to the delay, the law would not provide for the apportionment of monetary damages between the par-
ties.55 Rather, a concurrent delay is excusable and therefore the contractor would be entitled to a time
extension only, and the owner would not be entitled to assess liquidated damages.
In J.A. Jones Constr. Co. v. Greenbriar Shopping Ctr.,56 the prime contractor caused delay through
the failure of its subcontractors and materialmen to timely perform, and the owner caused delay by
changing the design and by the late issuance of drawings. The court held that neither party was
entitled to any affirmative recovery, meaning the owner and contractor each bore its own costs even
though one may have been responsible for more delay than the other.
B. 	Emerging Trend: Apportionment of Delay Damages
In contrast to the analysis of concurrent delays in the J.A. Jones case, the trend in concurrent delay
analysis is to separate the delays and apportion them between the delaying parties. This approach has
become more feasible due in part to the use of CPM techniques for evaluating construction delay.
CPM computer software makes it possible to segregate and quantify the separate impacts of separate
delays that otherwise may be considered concurrent.
Logically, if the impact of one delay exceeds that of the other, the party responsible for the shorter
impact should be allowed to recover damages for the extended delay for which it has no responsi-
bility. Apportionment analysis, at least on its face, would seem to allow for more equitable results
than a no-apportionment analysis.
54Centex-Bateson Constr. Co, Inc., VABCA No. 4613, 5162-5165, 99-1 BCA ¶ 30,153.
55United Constructors, LLC v. United States, 95 Fed. Cl. (2010); Malta Constr. Co. v. Henninston, Durham & Richardson,
Inc., 694 F. Supp. 902 (N.D. Ga. 1988).
56J.A. Jones Constr. Co. v. Greenbriar Shopping Ctr., 332 F. Supp. 1336 (N.D. Ga. 1971), aff’d, 461 F.2d 1269 (5th Cir. 1972).

VI. EXCUSABLE BUT NONCOMPENSABLE DELAYS 	323
If the effects of concurrent delay cannot be accurately segregated and quantified, the court will
likely revert to a no-apportionment type review and no damages will be awarded. 57
An example of the approach to parse what is otherwise a concurrent delay is found in the Federal
Circuit Court of Appeals’ decision in Essex Electro Engrs., Inc. v. Danzig. 58 In that case, the court
of appeals found that each party’s delay could be apportioned and, thus, responsibility should
have been divided between each responsible party. In arriving at its decision, the Federal Circuit
noted that:
The contractor generally cannot recover for concurrent delays for the simple reason that no
causal link can be shown: A government act that delays part of the contract performance does
not delay “the general progress of the work” when the “prosecution of the work as a whole”
would have been delayed regardless of the government’s act. 59
However, the court held that, “if there is in the proof a clear apportionment of the delay and the
expense attributable to each party, then the government will be liable for its delays.”60
VI. 	EXCUSABLE BUT NONCOMPENSABLE DELAYS
Generally, excusable delays are those that are not the contractor’s fault or responsibility. For such
excusable delays, the contractor would be entitled to a time extension upon giving timely notice and
properly seeking a time extension under the appropriate contract provisions.
Excusable delays may or may not entitle the contractor to additional monetary compensation.
Typically, whether a delay is compensable depends on what caused the delay. Excusable delays that
arise for reasons independent (beyond the control) of the owner or its agents are not compensable,
absent contract language to the contrary. The law will not penalize the owner by requiring it to pay
the contractor for project delay if the owner was not responsible for the delay. In that situation, the
contractor will be limited to a contract time extension.
A. 	Weather
Under many contracts, unusually severe weather conditions can give rise to an excusable, but non-
compensable, delay. 61 For example, the force majeure clause found in ConsensusDocs 200 Section
6.3.1 lists “adverse weather conditions not reasonably anticipated” as a justification for an excusable
delay. 62
Unusually severe weather is weather that is unusual for the time of year and the location. Unusu-
ally severe weather may be shown by comparing weather averages with the actual weather experi-
enced during performance. The mere fact that the weather is harsh or destructive is not sufficient
if the contractor should reasonably have anticipated that type of weather at the time and place it
occurred. Some bad weather is always to be expected and the contractor should anticipate normal

weather delays. By way of example, if the contract period is for 600 days, the contractor obviously
does not have the right to expect 600 dry, sunny days with its crews and subcontractors working at
full force.
Questions often come up about excusable delay arising from an unusual weather event when the
impacts from the event last substantially longer than the event itself. For example, some soils may
require several days to dry out from a one-day rain event. Assuming that the rain event was an excus-
able delay (for example, not reasonably anticipated under the ConsensusDocs language above), is the
excusable delay for one day or more? This may turn on the precise wording of the contract. However,
once the contractor can show that the weather event was unusual and therefore excusable, the length
of the time extension should be computed based on the actual delay to the contractor. This situa-
tion may also arise where delays push weather-sensitive activities into periods of adverse weather.
For example, where concrete operations are planned to occur during summer months, but a design
delay pushes those activities into winter months, the contractor may be able to recover increased
time or costs for the new period of performance.
Some contracts spell out the number of inclement weather days the contractor should anticipate
during each month of performance. If inclement-weather days for any one month exceed the num-
ber set forth in the contract, the contractor is automatically entitled to an extension for the excess
bad-weather days. Owners like this approach because it takes much of the subjectivity out of any
weather-delay analysis. However, this approach still has its problems, the biggest of which is how
to define an inclement-weather day.
While the general rule of recovery for adverse weather is “time but no money,” a contractor
may receive both time and money if the weather delay affected the contractor as a consequence of
prior compensable owner-caused delay. 63 In other words, if an owner delay unexpectedly pushes
the contractor’s performance into the rainy season, this may result in compensable delay for the
contractor. 64
B. 	Other Acts of God
The Comptroller General of the United States has defined an act of God as “some inevitable accident
which cannot be prevented by human care, skill, or foresight, but results from natural causes such
as lightning, tempest, floods and inundations.”65 Examples of acts of God are tornadoes, hurricanes,
floods, earthquakes, and other natural disasters.
Unless the contract specifically provides otherwise, acts of natural forces are treated much like
unusual weather and will entitle the contractor to an extension of contract performance time, but not
to a contract price adjustment. On this basis, a highway contractor was granted a time extension, but
denied a contract price increase, for delays encountered when the government reasonably refused to
alleviate flooding on the work site caused by heavy rains. 66
Hurricane Andrew hit Florida in August 1992. It caused delays to essentially every active con-
struction project in South Florida. While contractors uniformly received time extensions, there was
significant argument over how long any extension should be. Was the excusable delay the three days
covering the actual days of bad weather or a substantially longer time period that took into con-
sideration the practical impacts the storm had on job access, subcontractors, manpower, deliveries,

C. 	Labor Problems
Delays resulting from most, but not all, strikes and labor disturbances are considered excusable.67
Most strikes occur for reasons independent of the specific project and delays from such strikes are
generally excusable.
If, on the other hand, the strike arises from actions by the contractor or one of its subcontractors,
the delay is likely not excusable. For example, when a strike is provoked by an unfair labor practice on
the contractor’s part, the delay might not be considered to be due to a “cause beyond the contractor’s
control.”
If a strike is in effect or anticipated at the time of contracting, a court may find that the labor prob-
lems were foreseeable, and the contractor should have anticipated and planned for them. Finally, with
few exceptions, delays that result from labor shortages, as opposed to labor disputes, are generally
a risk borne by the contractor.
VII. 	ACCELERATION
When the owner forces its contractor to complete the work by a date earlier than a properly adjusted
contract completion date, “acceleration” of the work occurs. In determining whether the contractor’s
work has been accelerated, the contract completion date should reflect any time extensions due the
contractor for excusable delays to its work. An acceleration may or may not be the basis to claim
additional compensation depending on the reasons why the acceleration occurred. If an acceleration
order is issued to direct the contractor to make up for time it has lost due to nonexcusable delays, the
acceleration would generally not be compensable. A project is considered accelerated once the con-
tractor makes efforts to finish earlier than the contract requires, even if the contractor is unsuccessful
in its efforts.
Acceleration of the contractor’s work can occur under two different circumstances: (1) actual (or
directed) acceleration or (2) constructive acceleration. Actual acceleration occurs when the owner
expressly directs the contractor to complete the project earlier than what the contract requires.
Constructive acceleration occurs when the contractor is entitled to a time extension and properly
requests an extension, but the owner fails or refuses to grant the time extension and demands that
the contractor achieve an earlier completion of the project or milestone. Because of the contractual
risks of late performance, the contractor strives to achieve the owner’s demanded completion date,
which is earlier than the properly extended contract completion date.
Acceleration damages include any costs the contractor incurred in an effort to maintain the com-
pletion date directed by the owner or to overcome owner-caused delays. Typical acceleration costs
include premium time pay for overtime work, shift work, added crews or increased crew sizes, addi-
tional tools and equipment required for added crews, additional supervision and job-site overhead,
and labor inefficiency that may occur due to longer hours or increased crew sizes.
67See Murdock & Sons Constr., Inc. v. Goheen Gen. Constr., Inc., 461 F.3d 837 (7th Cir. 2006) (finding that an organized
slowdown by laborers did not constitute a labor dispute although laborers were laying only 50 blocks per day as opposed to
150 as anticipated); McNamara Constr. of Manitoba, Ltd. v. United States, 509 F.2d 1166 (Ct. Cl. 1975).

A. 	Directed Acceleration
In federal government contracts, the Changes clause for fixed-priced construction contracts found at
FAR § 52.243–4 specifically allows the contracting officer to direct acceleration in the performance
of the work:
CHANGES (AUG 1987)
a. The Contracting Officer may, at any time, without notice to the sureties, if any, by written order
designated or indicated to be a change order, make changes in the work within the general scope
of the contract, including changes—
1. In the specifications (including drawings and designs);
2. In the method or manner of performance of the work;
3. In the Government-furnished facilities, equipment, materials, services or site; or
4. Directing acceleration in the performance of the work. 68
Thus, the government’s order to a contractor to accelerate the modification to an air-conditioning
system in a medical facility to speed completion of operating rooms was a compensable change
because the government was aware that excess costs for overtime would be incurred. 69
A directed acceleration is effectively a change order when the contractor is ordered to finish the
work, or a designated portion thereof, earlier than the contract requires. The compensation due the
contractor in this instance would be determined under the changes clause. To satisfy the requirements
of most changes clauses, contractors should always demand an acceleration order be issued in writing
by the owner representative having the authority to issue such directives.

compliance with a given schedule expressly without regard to the existence of any excus-
able delay,

government;
3. Failure or refusal by the government to grant the requested extension within a reasonable time;
and
4. A government order, either express or implied, to (a) take steps to overcome the excusable
delay, or (b) complete the work at the earliest possible date, or (c) complete the work by a

VIII. 	CONTRACTUAL LIMITATIONS TO RECOVERY FOR DELAYS
A contractor is generally entitled to extra time for any excusable delay that occurs during the exe-
cution of the work. The contractor, however, should be aware of its obligations to give notice and to
seek a time extension under the time-extension provisions of the contract.
The contractor must also be aware of any clauses in its contract that purport to bar time exten-
sions for certain delays or preclude recovery of monetary damages for delays that otherwise might
normally be compensable.
A. 	Requirement for Written Notice
Most construction contracts require the contractor to submit written notice of delay to the owner or
its designated representative within a defined period of time after the delay-causing event and before
submitting any claim for additional compensation or time. Such notice requirements are imposed to
protect the interest of the owner, who may be unaware of the causes of a particular delay and thereby
precluded from taking immediate measures to rectify the situation and mitigate its cost. Failure to
give prompt notice may result in a waiver of the contractor’s rights or result in a time-consuming
litigation effort, which may ultimately prove unsuccessful.73 In a 2013 Connecticut case, a contractor
lost its right to pursue a delay claim for its failure to give the contractually required notice. 74
Formal notice may be unnecessary when the owner has actual or constructive knowledge of the
problem, or when the lack of notice does not prejudice a legitimate owner interest. The contractor,
however, should never knowingly forgo written notice on the assumption that one of those conditions
is present. Some courts view notice as a condition precedent to recovery.75 The contractor that gives
the owner prompt written notice of delays and disruptions increases its opportunity to recover the
costs generated by those problems.
B. 	Submission of a Delay Claim
In addition to requiring contractors to give written notice of a delay, contracts will typically provide
instructions on how the contractor must present its request for a time extension and, if applicable,
its request for time-related compensation. These instructions may be found in the contract changes

clause, in the delay and time extension clause, in a claims clause, or in a technical specification.
These clauses may place a time limit on the submission of the claim and may identify the minimum
information that must be submitted to support a claim. In that regard, contract provisions might
require some or all of the following information:
• A narrative explaining the nature of the delay and its impact on the work
• Copies of documentation and correspondence relating to the delay
• An updated CPM schedule, with delay impacts shown to the affected activities, and showing
how the delay affects the completion date of the contract or designated portion thereof
• A statement on the contractor’s efforts to mitigate the delay
• Cost documentation supporting any delay costs the contractor is seeking to recover
• Cost information on any extended field overhead the contractor is seeking to recover
• Detailed cost proposals from subcontractors seeking to recover damages for the delays
Owners will sometimes seek to deny delay claims on the basis that the contractor’s claim sub-
mission did not satisfy the requirements of the applicable contract provisions. Before signing the
contract, contractors need to fully understand their obligations to give notice and how to submit
proper claims. Understanding notice and claim procedures before a claim arises goes a long way in
preventing the contractor from making crucial mistakes once a claim arises.
If a contractor can prove a compensable delay on a project, it generally has the right to recover all
damages arising from the delay. Typically, a contractor’s delay damages include extended job-site
overhead (sometimes referred to as “general conditions costs”) and extended home-office overhead.
Extended overhead and general conditions costs are time-sensitive costs that increase as the duration
of the project increases.
Other types of damages a contractor may incur as a result of delays include extended equipment
costs, idle-equipment costs, escalation of material and/or labor costs, constructive acceleration, loss
of labor productivity, mobilization costs, and other indirect costs.
Extended job-site overhead is often computed on a per-day basis. An average daily rate can be
computed by adding all job-site overhead costs for the duration of the project and dividing by the
number of calendar days. Contractors are well served to have a cost accounting system that tracks
general conditions or job-site overhead costs for specific jobs. Most owners, once they recognize
that a delay is both excusable and compensable, will not have significant problems in granting
extended job-site overhead if the contractor can prove its time-sensitive costs and establish them as
reasonable.
Contract language can narrow or eliminate the contractor’s rights to recover its delay dam-
ages. For example, clauses waiving recovery of consequential damages are common. Also,
clauses may restrict the contractor’s rights to recover extended job-site overhead or home-office
overhead.
C. 	No-Damages-for-Delay Clauses
Despite the widely recognized right of a contractor to recover damages stemming from delayed or
out-of-sequence work caused by the owner, the owner (or the prime contractor if the claimant is a
subcontractor) may succeed in asserting one of several possible defenses to a delay claim. The most
notable potential defense is when there is an enforceable no-damages-for-delay clause in the contract
or subcontract.
A no-damages-for-delay clause typically states that the owner (contractor) will not be liable for
monetary damages resulting from any types of delay or for certain specified delays. Most clauses

-- 366 of 771 --

VIII. CONTRACTUAL LIMITATIONS TO RECOVERY FOR DELAYS 	329
of this kind provide that the contractor’s (subcontractor’s) sole remedy for such delays is a time
extension.
In many jurisdictions, if the language of the no-damages-for-delay clause is clear and unambigu-
ous, it will be enforced as written.76 However, given the harsh effect of these clauses, many courts will
strictly construe them. In addition, various jurisdictions have developed exceptions to the enforce-
ability of no-damages-for-delay clauses to account for situations where the strict enforcement of the
clause was punitive or unreasonable.77 Some states consider the clauses to be “exculpatory clauses”
and apply special narrow rules on how they should be interpreted.
A common approach to the analysis and enforcement of a no-damages-for-delay clause is
reflected in the court’s opinion in Corinno Civetta Constr. Corp. v. City of New York:
A clause which exculpates a contractee from liability to a contractor for damages resulting
from delay in the performance in the latter’s work is valid and enforceable and is not contrary
to public policy if the clause and the contract of which it is a part satisfy the requirements for
the validity of contracts generally. The rule is not without its exceptions, however, and even
exculpatory language which purports to preclude damages from all delays resulting from any
cause whatsoever are not read literally. Generally, even with such a clause, damages may be
recovered for:
1. Delays caused by the contractee’s bad faith or its willful, malicious or grossly negligent
conduct,
2. Uncontemplated delays,
3. Delays so unreasonable that they constitute an intentional abandonment of the contract by
the contractee, and
4. Delays resulting from the contractee’s breach of a fundamental obligation of the contract. 78
Some state legislatures have determined that no-damages-for-delay clauses should not be
enforced and have passed statutory restrictions on these clauses. Statutes invalidating the enforce-
ment of certain no-damages-for-delay clauses in public contracts have a relatively long history,79
but some states have only recently passed legislation that bars enforcement of no-damages-for-delay
clauses in private construction.
Washington was one of the first states to enact a statute providing that a clause in any construction
contract that “purports to waive, release, or extinguish the rights of a contractor, subcontractor or
supplier to damages or an equitable adjustment arising out of unreasonable delay in performance
which delay is caused by the acts or omissions of the contractee or persons acting for the contractee
is against public policy and is void and unenforceable.”80 Louisiana also refuses to enforce these
provisions on the basis that they violate public policy.81
Ohio has enacted a statute that declares any provision in a construction contract or subcontract
unenforceable as a matter of public policy if the provision waives liability for delay when the delay
