450 	CHAPTER 16 PAYMENT BONDS
• Payment bond coverage can vary significantly among federal, state and local, and private
projects. The federal Miller Act applies only to first-tier and second-tier subcontractors and
suppliers. The scope of public payment bond coverage for state and local contracts varies from
state to state; some cover all project subcontractors and suppliers, while others do not extend
beyond second-tier subcontractors and suppliers (that is, subcontractors to subcontractors and
suppliers to subcontractors). Under the federal Miller Act and many Little Miller Acts, cover-
age does not extend to suppliers to suppliers. For private projects, the scope of bond coverage
generally depends on the terms of the bond.
• Payment bonds, whether statutory or private, involve various notice and timing requirements
relating to claims and litigation. Such requirements must be identified and followed. Failure to
comply may bar otherwise valid claims.

17
PERFORMANCE BONDS
AND TERMINATIONS
Most construction projects end with the satisfactory completion of the contracting parties’ respec-
tive obligations. There is, however, some risk on any project that the construction contract might not
be completed to one or more parties’ satisfaction. Project owners or developers can face significant
financial disruption and harm when a general contractor fails to perform its contractual obligations.
General contractors face similar risks when a subcontractor fails to perform its subcontract satis-
factorily. These risks can be mitigated by including express terms in the written contract that allow
for termination of the construction contract in the event of such a failure by the contractor, and by
obtaining a third-party surety’s guaranty to arrange for completion of the contract if the contractor
fails to do so. A general contractor may also benefit from the inclusion of express contract terms
permitting termination of the construction contract where the owner becomes unable or unwilling
to perform as agreed. Terminating a construction contract before completion of the work is a drastic
step that should not be considered lightly. Even so, most construction contracts and subcontracts
anticipate that the contract can be terminated for nonperformance.
This chapter analyzes two distinct but related topics concerning management of the risk of
nonperformance under a construction contract. First, it discusses surety performance bonds,
contractual instruments by which a third party gives assurances that a construction contract will
be completed, even if the contractor runs into trouble performing. Second, this chapter discusses
contract-termination provisions, which typically set out steps that will be followed if the owner or
the contractor terminates the construction contract.
I. 	SURETY PERFORMANCE BONDS
A. 	Fundamentals of Suretyship Law
The typical surety relationship involves three parties: (1) the principal that is primarily responsible
for performing the underlying bonded contract; (2) the party to whom the principal is obligated to
perform the contract, known often as the obligee; and (3) the surety, known also as the obligor,
that provides a bond pledging financial support to complete the underlying contract, if that becomes
necessary.
A claim is usually made on a performance bond upon the occurrence of a contractual default
or alleged default by the bond principal, the contractor, or the subcontractor who furnished the
451

-- 489 of 771 --

452 	CHAPTER 17 PERFORMANCE BONDS AND TERMINATIONS
performance bond. The claim is directed to the bond surety, calling on the surety to perform as
it pledged to do under the bond. A basic explanation of the legal principles applicable to the default
aspects of the performance bond is set out in the next several sections.
Using a surety to ensure or guarantee that one party to a contract will perform as promised is
an ancient practice, mentioned as long ago as biblical times. The surety provides a second con-
tract, usually referred to as the surety’s “bond.” Under the bond, the surety gives its additional
promise to guarantee the performance of the contract agreed to by the contractor. If the contrac-
tor does not perform the contract, the surety is contractually obligated to ensure that the princi-
pal’s obligations are performed. Historically, the surety was often a relative, business associate, or
friend of the contractor, who gave the additional pledge that the surety would use its own wealth
or resources, if necessary, to support the contractor’s promise to perform the contract. In mod-
ern times, the surety is typically an insurance company that is also in the business of providing
bonds, pledging the surety’s credit and financial resources to ensure completion of a contract as
promised by the party who agreed to complete it, in exchange for the payment of a bond premium by
that party.
The surety for a construction contractor often also writes a separate bond, known as a payment
bond, which ensures that the bond principal/contractor will pay its subcontractors and suppliers
on the project. This chapter, however, discusses only surety performance bonds assuring that the
contractor will perform the work agreed to with the obligee or owner. Chapter 16 addresses payment
bonds.
This chapter frequently refers to the bond obligee as the owner of the project. The use of this
terminology is not intended to imply that only owners are bond obligees. Performance bonds may
also be posted by a surety to ensure the completion of a subcontractor’s subcontract with a general
contractor. In this case, the general contractor is the obligee and the subcontractor is the bond prin-
cipal. 1 This three-party bonding relationship can exist at any tier of the contractual chain. Thus, a
surety can also post a bond to assure the completion of a sub-subcontractor’s work to a subcontractor,
and so on. Bonding a lower-tier subcontractor’s work is more common on larger projects, where the
subcontract value would justify the effort and expense of such a bond. Nevertheless, this situation
could, in theory, arise on any size construction project.
Although the form of the performance bond as a three-party contract is well-defined, because
bond terms vary widely, sureties, contractors, and owners regularly struggle over the rights and lia-
bilities each has under the specific terms of their particular bond. 2 Contract terminations, and the
performance bond obligations that often follow the termination, may be encountered less frequently
than other construction law issues discussed in this book, but extraordinary risks are often involved
for those affected by a contract termination and any resulting demands on the performance bond.
Therefore, every construction industry participant should have a basic understanding of the rights
and potential liabilities associated with performance bonds.
Performance bonds also indirectly affect the selection of contractors on private construction and
government building or public works projects. For example, performance bonds ensuring completion
of a contractor’s duties have long been required by law on public works projects, and standard form
contracts used for private construction projects may require performance bonds as well.3 Thus, many
projects require performance bonds. Of course, sureties do not want to write bonds for projects on
which there is an unusual (that is, heightened) risk of default. Therefore, sureties tend to decline
1 In such a case, the owner might also be named as a co-obligee on the subcontractor’s performance bond.
2See Section I.F of this chapter for a discussion of industry performance bond forms.
3See 40 U.S.C. § 3131 (requiring performance bonds on federal projects); ConsensusDocs 200 Standard Agreement and
General Conditions Between Owner and Constructor (Lump Sum) § 10.7 (© 2011, Revised 2017) (making performance
bond optional); AIA Document A201 – 2017 General Conditions of the Contract for Construction § 11.1.2 (owner may
require performance bond).

bonds for contractors on projects for which the contractors lack expertise or adequate financing.
A contractor that cannot get a performance bond may be unqualified to bid for a given contract. An
inability to qualify for bonding will be, at the least, a fact the owner or prime contractor may take
into consideration in selecting their contractor/subcontractor and it may automatically disqualify a
contractor from bidding on public projects.
1. 	Performance Bonds Are Not Insurance Policies
Under the law, a surety bond is not treated as an insurance policy, despite the apparent similarities
between the two.4 Insurance has been defined as “a contract whereby one undertakes to indemnify
another against loss, damage or liability arising from an unknown or contingent event; whereas a
contract of suretyship is one to answer for the debt, default or miscarriage of another.” 5 The two
parties to an insurance contract (the insurer and the insured) agree on terms for protecting the insured
from the occurrence of a future, unknown accident (“coverable risk”).
A performance bond involves three parties: the “principal,” the “obligee,” and the “surety,” who
are not protecting against an unknown future accident that is largely beyond the control of any party,
but are guarding against the possible failure of the contractor or subcontractor (principal) to perform
its existing obligations under the bonded contract. In this tripartite relationship, the surety does not
agree to indemnify any of the parties, but rather to protect the owner (contractor) from loss or damage
resulting from the failure or default of the contractor (subcontractor) to perform.6 In other words,
the surety must perform under the performance bond only when the principal fails to perform as
promised. This differs from insurance, where the covered risk is an accident over which the insured
has little or no control. Because the surety must perform under the performance bond only when the
principal fails to perform its promise, the surety may recover its losses on the bond from the principal
responsible for the default under an indemnification agreement between the principal and surety, or
in the absence of an enforceable indemnification agreement, under common-law indemnity. This
is a basic difference from insurance, where the insurer typically cannot recover its losses from the
insured. Further, different legal duties and standards apply to the relationship between an insurer
and its insured, where a fiduciary standard applies, and a surety and its principal, where a fiduciary
standard is not applicable.7
Most bond forms require that the principal be “in default” to trigger the surety’s obligations under
the bond. Because the performance bond surety must act when the principal is in default of its con-
tract obligations, the obligee must give a clear declaration of default. A surety has no duty to act in
the face of mere obligee complaints or threats to declare the principal in default. 8 Further, the default
must constitute a “material breach” of the contract. Under typical bond forms that require a default
to trigger a surety’s obligations, a surety is not liable to the obligee for partial or minor breaches

2. 	Indemnification—The Bottom Line
Because the surety promises to perform the obligations for which the principal is liable, the law
implies a promise by the principal to repay the surety the amount the surety had to pay as a
result of the principal’s failure to perform. The law gives the surety a right to sue its principal
for such repayment.11 This legally implied promise by the principal to indemnify its surety may
be expressly stated and strengthened in a written indemnification agreement, commonly called a
“general agreement of indemnity” or “agreement of indemnity.” A surety regularly will require its
principal to execute an agreement of indemnity before the surety will write a bond for the principal.
The surety often requires that the contractor’s individual owners, shareholders, or officers (and
often their spouses) add their respective indemnity promises by personally signing such indemnity
agreements as well.
Surety indemnity agreements typically include many provisions to protect the surety if it incurs
a liability or loss under the performance bond (or payment bond; see Chapter 16). A few such
provisions are: (1) a promise to assign to the surety, in the event the principal defaults, all tools,
materials, and equipment on the job site and the principal’s interest in future contract payments;
(2) a promise to indemnify and legally protect the surety from any loss, expense, or claims under
the bond; and (3) a promise to deposit funds with the surety, as additional security, if the surety so
demands, or if it receives or becomes liable for a bond claim.
Although indemnity agreements are drafted for the purpose of making indemnitors broadly
responsible to the surety for any loss incurred under the bond, an indemnitor is not without
defenses against its surety. The surety’s obligation comes into play only if the principal is properly
terminated. 12 Under most common bond forms, if the principal is not properly defaulted, the surety
has no duty to perform. 13 A surety may have no right to recover costs from its principal if they were
incurred as a result of complying with an owner’s demands that the surety does not in good faith
believe to be proper. 14 Conversely, if the surety unreasonably or in bad faith rejects a favorable
settlement offer that would have reduced the indemnitors’ losses, the indemnitors may be able to
claim a discharge from liability to the extent that the surety’s damages exceeded the amount for
which it could have settled. 15
Although indemnitors may defend themselves if the surety acts unreasonably, indemnity agree-
ments typically give the surety the right to settle bond claims, and that right is generally enforce-
able. 16 The surety must deal in good faith and fairly with all parties interested in the bond, including
the principal, the obligee, and the indemnitor, but the surety will likely be able to enforce its indem-
nity agreement, unless it has violated its duty of good faith and fair dealing in taking the actions

3. 	“Common Law” versus “Statutory” Bonds
Performance bonds are often required by statutes in connection with public construction projects
at the federal, state, and municipal levels. For example, with certain limited exceptions, the fed-
eral Miller Act 21 requires performance bonds on federal government construction and public works
projects. The statutes requiring performance bonds frequently list specific terms and provisions that
the bonds must contain. Generally, courts read such a bond in light of the purpose of the statute
requiring it, and some standard bond forms expressly provide that the parties intend the bond to be
read in that way. 22 This may result in reading statutory provisions into a bond, even if the bond does
not expressly state those requirements, or reading provisions out of the bond that are contrary to the
applicable statute. 23 If the bond exceeds the statute’s requirements, thus creating more rights than
the statute requires, however, the bond may be interpreted as giving the claimant all the statutory
rights and additional rights under the provisions that exceed the statutory bond requirements.24
Statutory provisions may be critical in determining whether a bond claim is allowed, and the fine
points of the type of bond given in a case (that is, statutory, nonstatutory, or a “statutory plus” com-
mon law bond) can be both decisive and difficult to determine. The primary test involves examining
the bond, concentrating on the obligations imposed on the principal and its surety, and comparing
the language contained within the bond with the minimal requirements enunciated in any applicable
statute. 25 If the surety’s obligations have not been extended beyond the statutory minimum require-
ments, the bond is statutory. 26 Even a bond furnished incident to a public works project, however,
may not necessarily be construed as a statutory bond. 27 Furthermore, a bond that fails to reference

4. 	Surety’s Obligations
The nature of the surety’s obligation is financial, but the terms of the bond itself are the bedrock of
that obligation and must be analyzed on a case-by-case basis. The performance bond surety generally
binds itself with its principal to pay to the obligee a sum up to the contract amount (the penal sum of
the bond). Performance of the bond obligation becomes due if the principal wrongfully and without
legal justification defaults on the primary obligation (the bonded contract), and only to the extent of
the loss covered by the bond. Generally, the surety’s liability to perform is strictly limited by both
the terms of the bond and the terms of the underlying contract, which are typically incorporated into
and made a part of the bond.29
Because the bond is intended to secure the performance of the underlying contract, a performance
bond and the bonded contract are read together. 30 As a result, the surety’s obligations are usually
defined by the scope of the work set out in the incorporated contract documents.31 Since the surety
guarantees only the principal’s promise to perform the underlying contract, the surety can assert all
contractual defenses that the principal would have been able to assert. 32
B. 	Extension of Performance Bond Surety’s Liability to Third Parties
Although a single obligee is typically named in a performance bond, sureties have occasionally
been held liable to other project participants on a “third-party beneficiary” theory. Under this theory,
a claimant that has a claim against the contractor, although not named in the performance bond
(such as a subcontractor or supplier), is nonetheless deemed as intended to have the right to assert
a claim against the surety. For example, a federal court has held that the federal Miller Act’s dual
requirement of performance and payment bonds would allow suppliers whose payment bond had
been exhausted by claims exceeding the penal sum to claim against the performance bond.33 In
reaching such results, courts reason that unless language exists in the bond limiting who can be
claimants, if the contractor had a duty under the construction contract guaranteed by the performance
bond to pay for subcontractors’ or suppliers’ work and materials, those subcontractors or suppliers
may make their claims for payment directly under the contractor’s performance bond.34
In addition, where there are several primes working together on a multiprime (or parallel prime)
construction project, some of them may attempt to assert claims against the performance bond of
the other parallel primes. Performance bond sureties have attempted to defend against claims by
other prime contractors on the basis that the applicable performance bond gives rights only to the

In other instances, the performance bond surety has been held liable to a parallel prime contractor
under a third-party beneficiary theory. Usually the surety’s liability depends on the degree to which
the principal’s duty to coordinate and cooperate with other prime contractors is incorporated into, or
referred to, by the bonded contract and the terms of the bond itself. In some jurisdictions, a surety may
be held liable for damages sustained by the principal’s failure to perform a contractually assumed
duty to a co-prime contractor. 36 Mere status as a co-prime contractor, however, may be insufficient
to sustain a third-party beneficiary claim in the absence of a specific contractual provision accepting
liability for harm caused to another co-prime contractor.37
C. 	Surety’s Liability Exceeding the Penal Sum of the Performance Bond
A surety’s obligation is limited to the terms stated in its bond. Therefore, courts historically have
declined to hold a surety liable for an amount greater than the limit, known as the penalty or penal
sum, which is usually stated in each bond.38 A surety may waive the penal sum of the bond if the
surety agrees to perform all remaining work itself, thereby consenting to pay whatever costs are
necessary to perform that promise.
Performance bond sureties may face claims and damages beyond the express penal sum of the
bond. Courts have found that liability may exceed the penal sum when a surety steps into the contrac-
tor’s shoes and takes over completion of the contract; however, liability may not exceed the penal sum
when the surety simply pays off its obligation under the bond.39 Continental Realty Corp. v. Andrew
J. Crevolin Co. 40 was an important early case holding that a surety could be liable in an amount
beyond the bond penal sum for breaching its duty—independent of the principal’s default—to com-
plete the surety’s duties in a timely manner or pay the cost of completion. In Crevolin, the obligee
recovered its actual damages, which exceeded the penal sum of the bond. In essence, the surety was
held liable in the Crevolin case for costs that the surety could have avoided had it performed promptly
and properly. For instance, water damage occurred after the contractor abandoned the project, which
the surety could have avoided by performing its performance bond obligations timely.
Statutes and regulations increasingly provide independent claims against a surety for reasonable
attorney’s fees and other damages, in addition to the surety’s liability stated under its bond. For
example, in Boland v. Trans Coastal Roofing, 41 the Florida Supreme Court held that a Florida statute
required a surety to pay the attorney’s fees of a prevailing claimant, even where those fees exceeded
the penal sum and the surety had not engaged in any independent misconduct. 42 Similarly, in Town
of Clarkstown v. North River Insurance Co.,43 a federal court awarded interest in excess of the penal
sum under a New York statute permitting the award of interest to put a claimant in the same financial
position that it would have been in had the surety paid promptly.44

Performance bond sureties may be liable for attorney’s fees or expenses (such as interest) even
in the absence of an express bond provision or a specific statutory right. If the bond incorporates a
construction contract that provides for recovery of attorney’s fees, the surety may be required to pay
those fees. 45
Although punitive damages are generally not allowed in breach of contract actions,46 some
statutes and regulations permit claimants to recover penalties, punitive damages, or both, against
sureties as a remedy for wrongful conduct. 47 For example, in Colorado Structures, Inc. v. Insurance
Co. of the West,48 a general contractor recovered attorney’s fees in addition to its contract damages
for a subcontractor’s performance bond surety’s wrongful denial of payment.
Improper conduct by a surety may also give rise to complaints of bad faith and, in some jurisdic-
tions, claims for negligence and punitive damages. 49 As discussed in Section I.A.2 of this chapter, a
surety’s acts of bad faith may breach the implied obligation that the parties to a contract exercise good
faith and engage in fair dealing with one another. When surety misconduct allegedly results from bad
faith, such as actual malice, fraud, or willful and wanton disregard for the obligee’s rights, the surety
may have committed a wrong independent of its bond obligations, for which punitive damages may
be recovered. 50 For example, a Colorado court, in finding that a performance bond surety breached
its duty of good faith and fair dealing by unreasonably refusing to settle a claim,51 concluded that
the surety should be held liable for punitive damages in order to discourage such conduct when it
was motivated by a desire to save interest by deferring payment or to force compromise claim set-
tlements under duress. A Delaware court allowed punitive damages because of a bad-faith breach of
a surety contract based on: (1) the Delaware legislature’s intent; (2) the purpose of a performance
bond, which is to protect an obligee from a calamity if the principal defaults and, therefore, allowing
the surety to purposefully delay or intentionally manipulate payment for the surety’s benefit would
undermine the purpose of the bond; (3) the fact that the surety has more control than the obligee
over whether and when to pay; and (4) the “special relationship” between the surety and obligee.52
As previously noted, however, the burden of proving bad faith can be significant. 53
In summary, sureties may be held liable for improper conduct in handling claims. This may give
the obligee or principal some remedy for such conduct by sureties. Further, because the liability arises
from the surety’s wrongful act, the surety may be denied a claim to recover from its indemnitors the
consequent loss it incurs.54 Some states, however, are reluctant to recognize bad-faith claims against
performance bond sureties. In these states, courts are likely to focus on the differences between
insurance contracts and contracts of suretyship, and to conclude that the state can deter bad-faith
acts by sureties through exercise of regulatory powers. 55

D. 	Surety’s Defenses to Performance Bond Liability
The foregoing discussion of the surety’s liability for failure to properly perform its obligations in
no way diminishes the many defenses on which sureties may rely to deny bond claims. A surety
generally may have a number of independent defenses arising out of the language of the performance
bond itself (also known as technical defenses) or out of the nature of the surety relationship. As stated
earlier in Section I.A of this chapter, a surety’s liability for the bonded obligations cannot be greater
than the principal’s liability. 56 Conversely, a defense normally available to the principal, but that the
principal is barred from asserting, is likewise unavailable to the surety.57
A surety may waive its defenses if it fails to raise them in the time and manner required by its
bond. For example, courts have held that a surety that fails to respond to a claim within the time
required by its bond waives the right to dispute that claim.58
A surety generally may defend based on the language of the performance bond requiring the
obligee to comply with conditions precedent under a performance bond.59 If the obligee fails to
perform a necessary condition for making a claim under the bond, the surety may be discharged
from a liability it would otherwise have had under the bond. For example, the standard form AIA
A312 – 2010 Performance Bond contains several conditions the obligee must observe to make a
valid bond claim.60 These conditions include: (1) notifying the contractor and surety that the owner
may declare a contractor default; (2) trying to meet and discuss with the surety how to perform the
remaining contract; (3) properly declaring the contractor in default and terminating the contractor’s
right to complete the contract; 61 and (4) agreeing to pay the remaining contract funds to the surety, or
to the surety’s designee, for completing the contract, in accordance with the terms of the construction
contract. 62 If the surety fails to perform its duties under the AIA A312 – 2010 Performance Bond,
the owner must give additional notice to the surety demanding that it perform and then wait seven
days before the owner can deem the surety to be in default of its duty to perform.63 Some courts
have held that the surety is entitled to insist on the obligee’s strict compliance with these conditions
of notice, declaration of default, termination of the contractor, and right to investigate and cure the
default. 64 Other courts have reached the opposite results, however, by carefully reading the bond
language, including language from the bonded contract incorporated into the bond, or by finding
that the failure to promptly declare a default was a nonmaterial breach of the owner’s duties under
the bond. 65
56See generally P. Alces, The Law of Suretyship & Guaranty § 1:1 (2003). See also Cal. Civ. Code § 2809; State Athletic

460 	CHAPTER 17 PERFORMANCE BONDS AND TERMINATIONS
Not all standard bond forms contain conditions on the obligee’s right to make a claim on the
bond. For example, the Miller Act performance bond form66 does not contain conditions like those
found in the AIA form. Similarly, the ConsensusDocs Performance Bond form67 does not impose
conditions on the obligee comparable to the AIA form. Owners and contractors should carefully
review a proposed bond form to determine if that form contains conditions on a right to assert a claim
on the bond. In determining the extent of any waiver, discharge, or conditions precedent to liability
under the bond, parties must review the terms of the bond, the terms of the principal’s construction
contract, and any applicable statutory provisions. For example, statutory performance bonds may
incorporate conditions precedent from the governing statutes, thus creating another set of conditions
that may discharge the surety. 68
An additional defense, arising in part from the contract, may be available where the surety is not
notified of, and does not consent to, a material change to the contract it has bonded. The surety may
be discharged either in whole or to the extent of injury caused by such a material alteration. 69 In
recognition of this rule, many standard performance bond forms provide that the surety consents in
advance to permit the owner and the principal to modify the work scope in the normal course of the
construction contract without further consent of the surety. 70 Further, a surety must normally show
it suffered some injury before it can claim a discharge from the work scope alteration.71
The surety has another defense based in part on the bond language when the owner makes unau-
thorized or premature payments or fails to withhold contractually required retainage.72 For example,
in Federal Ins. Co. v. Turner Constr. Co.,73 a subcontract modification provided that the subcontrac-
tor would perform up to eight million dollars’ worth of work, without payment unless or until a third
party submitted the subcontract for registration with the New York City mayor’s office, was found
to materially increase the risk to the subcontractor’s performance bond surety of having to complete
its principal’s work, releasing the surety of its performance bond obligations.
The rationale for this rule is that a surety relies on provisions of the bonded contract in executing
the bond. Contract terms, such as payment according to a set schedule and retainage requirements,
benefit the surety by controlling the expenditure of contract funds. Overpayment by the owner to
the contractor may discharge the surety’s obligations because such voluntary action by the owner in
violation of the contract terms reduces the contract balance the surety would expect to have available
for completion of the project in the event of a default. 74 Thus, if the owner substantially overpays
the surety’s principal, the surety may defend based on overpayment. 75

Overpayment may not discharge the surety, however, if the obligee makes payments in good
faith. 76 Unauthorized prepayments made by an owner/obligee may not discharge a compensated
surety so long as the funds were used in actual construction of the project and the surety was not
prejudiced by the prepayments. 77 When an architect has negligently certified progress payments to
a contractor, thereby damaging the surety by reducing the contract balance available to the surety
upon completion of the work, however, the surety may have a cause of action against the architect
for the resulting damage. 78
The principal’s fraud in obtaining a bond from the surety will not alone discharge the surety,
although the surety may have a claim against the principal for its fraud79 because such a discharge
would injure the obligee without its having done any wrong. If the obligee has perpetrated a fraud
on the surety, or even participated in the principal’s fraud, the surety may be discharged from its
obligation.80 A related issue arises when the obligee has practiced no active fraud, but has knowledge
of facts that might affect the surety’s willingness to provide a bond. 81 In such a situation, the duty
of the obligee to disclose those facts may depend on whether the obligee: (1) had reason to believe
that the facts materially increase the risk beyond that which the surety intended to assume; (2) had
reason to believe such facts were unknown to the surety; and (3) had a reasonable opportunity to
reveal such facts to the surety.82 Given these considerations, the nature and extent of the dealings
between the obligee and the surety may become relevant if, for example, the obligee knows from
past dealings that the surety relies on the obligee for certain types of information. The law will not
favor an unseeing surety, however, that fails to exercise reasonable diligence to learn relevant facts
for itself. 83
E. 	Surety Entitlement to Contract Funds
In addition to its defenses, the surety has the important right upon a default termination of the
contractor-principal to receive the contract funds due to the principal and to receive all remaining
contract funds as they become due. 84 The surety “earns” the right to receive these funds by perform-
ing its bond obligation. These contract funds must be applied to reduce or satisfy the loss incurred
by the surety in performing its bond obligations toward the defaulted principal’s contract.85

The surety’s right to these funds is solid to the extent that the funds are needed to pay losses
incurred under the performance bond, being superior to a claim by a financial institution with a
security interest in those funds86 and even to a bankruptcy trustee’s rights when the principal has
filed for bankruptcy. 87 In some cases, a performance bond surety has been given priority to the
contract funds before permitting setoffs by the obligee. 88 To guard against the owner’s potential
setoff right, a surety will often require the owner to agree, in exchange for the surety’s performing
its obligations, that the owner will pay remaining contract balances to the surety as the project is
completed. There are limits, however, to a surety’s right to the contract proceeds. For example,
a surety that had entered into a completion agreement to perform its defaulted principal’s work,
in exchange for the contract balance, could not claim entitlement to the contract balance as a
priority over a claim by a state’s Department of Labor for unpaid back wages or by the Internal
Revenue Service for taxes. In that case, a state law deemed the contract balance to be funds held in
trust and, therefore, the surety’s claim to funds did not take priority to the extent such funds were
needed to pay wages or satisfy taxes owing for work done on a public works project. 89 Finally, a
surety may be able to claim only the funds from the specific project that it bonded and completed
performance on.90
F. 	Industry Performance Bond Forms: A Comparison
A widely used industry form for performance bonds is the AIA A312 – 2010 Performance Bond.
Other leading industry professional organizations have also developed performance bond forms.
These include four bond forms issued as part of the ConsensusDocs series of contract documents. 91
The ConsensusDocs forms may be more advantageous to obligees, depending on the type of project
or project delivery method and the relative lack of conditions that must be satisfied to trigger a
surety’s obligation under the bond.
The EJCDC Form C-610 Performance Bond mirrors the AIA form and is the only performance
bond form issued as part of the EJCDC’s construction documents. Like the AIA form, this form
requires, and imposes time limits for, a pre-default meeting among owner, surety, and contractor,
as well as time constraints on how long the owner must wait before it can terminate the contract.92

ConsensusDocs offers four different performance bond forms for different sets of parties or

used with a variety of contracts. 94 ConsensusDocs 470 is a performance bond form for use on a
design-build project (one party responsible to owner for both project design and construction), where

These standard industry performance bond forms reflect similarities despite employing different
terminology. For example, ConsensusDocs 260 refers to the maximum liability under the bond as the
“Bond Sum,” while AIA A312 and EJCDC C-670 use the term “Bond Amount.” Yet these forms do
contain distinct differences touching on such important issues as when the surety’s bond obligation is
triggered, the surety’s options for performing when a contractor is at default, and when the limitation
of action for bringing an action against the surety starts to run. An important difference in AIA A312
is that it does not specifically address a surety’s potential design liability if that bond form were to be
issued to a design-build contractor. Liability for performing design services differs significantly from
liability for construction services and the unwary surety, owner, or contractor might face exposure
to unintended risks if the performance bond form does not adequately address the liability and risk
where the contractor takes on design responsibility.
G. 	Effect on the Surety of Arbitration of Construction Disputes
Arbitration is a common method of dispute resolution in the construction industry and is espe-
cially popular in the private sector. Many standard construction contract forms provide that disputes
between the owner and contractor may or will be resolved by arbitration. 98 Typically, no specific
reference to the surety is made in the construction contract’s arbitration provisions, and the basic
rule is that arbitration can be enforced only when there is an agreement between the parties to arbi-
trate. Thus, the mere fact that the principal has entered into an arbitration agreement may not be a
basis to compel the surety to arbitrate any disputes involving the performance bond.99 If the obligee
has no agreement to arbitrate with the performance bond surety, a potential problem is created in
that the obligee might be forced to pursue relief in two separate forums: in court against the surety
93Id.

95See ConsensusDocs 470 Design-Build Performance Bond (Where the Surety Is Liable for the Design Costs of the Work)
(© 2007, Revised 2011).

464 	CHAPTER 17 PERFORMANCE BONDS AND TERMINATIONS
and through arbitration against the principal. Such a piecemeal dispute resolution process creates
additional expense and the risk of inconsistent results. As a partial solution to this problem, and in
an effort to avoid multiple proceedings in different forums, the standard construction contract forms
have become more lenient toward allowing the contractor and the owner to join related parties (for
example, sureties) in an arbitration. 100
A more effective solution to the multiple-proceedings problem has been built on the fact that
performance bonds regularly refer to and incorporate the underlying construction contract. Currently,
a strong federal policy and federal statutes favor arbitration. Recognizing this policy and law, courts
have held that a surety that has not directly signed an arbitration agreement may nonetheless be
held to have agreed to arbitrate claims, if the surety’s bond incorporates a bonded contract requiring
arbitration. For example, one court found that a surety on a general contractor’s payment bond was in
privity with the contractor and therefore could compel arbitration between a lower-tier subcontractor,
subcontractor, and the surety even if the surety did not sign the subcontract. 101
Rules governing which parties may be forced to arbitrate in a given case are complex, and
outcomes may be hard to predict because they may require the simultaneous interpretation of
multiple contracts. This poses a problem because a party may suffer serious consequences if it fails
to participate in the correct proceeding. For example, if a surety has notice of and an opportunity
to defend its principal in a lawsuit for breach of a bonded contract, a surety may be bound by
the determination in that lawsuit regardless of whether the surety participated.102 Accordingly, a
surety should participate in an arbitration on behalf of its principal if the surety has notice and
an opportunity to defend. In such an arbitration, the surety should have a right to plead any of
its own defenses, such as material alteration of the obligation or failures of conditions precedent
under the bond. The surety likewise could raise the defense that the arbitration included matters
outside of the liability of the surety or matters not covered by the performance bond and, in
some jurisdictions, the surety may raise defenses that could have been raised by the principal but
were not.103

II. TERMINATION 	465
bonds.105 Subcontractor default policies are designed for use by general contractors on large projects
involving multiple subcontractors. Although the product is available to owners, its primary users have
been large general contractors. The use of subcontractor-default insurance does not negate statutory
requirements to provide performance and payment bonds under the Miller Act.
There are several significant advantages to the use of subcontractor-default insurance. First, it
allows the general contractor direct control over evaluating the financial stability of its selected sub-
contractors. Further, upon a subcontractor’s failure to perform, the subcontractor-default insurance
is more flexible than a bond in allowing the general contractor to fashion an appropriate remedy.
This insurance policy allows the general contractor to control insurance and financial concerns at all
levels of subcontractors on the project through one master policy issued to the general contractor, as
opposed to dealing, potentially, with multiple surety bonds and multiple surety companies. Use of
a subcontractor-default policy allows (and usually requires) the general contractor to prequalify its
subcontractors, thereby avoiding subcontractors that cannot provide a bond after being awarded a
subcontract for part of the work. Finally, subcontractor-default insurance may allow for a negotiated
contract of insurance in which the terms can be modified, added, or deleted to customize the policy
for a specific project.
The subcontractor-default insurer may require the general contractor to first qualify itself and
the project under the policy requirements before a subcontractor insurance policy is issued. At that
point, the insurer will assist the general contractor in establishing a subcontractor-control program
by which each eligible subcontractor must also qualify for the policy.
Subcontractor-default insurance is a useful tool in some circumstances, but it is not appropri-
ate in all cases. Like surety bonds, the cost of coverage varies with the type of project, the parties
involved, and the risks covered. The subcontractor insurance policy typically requires the insured
general contractor to fund any default and make a claim only after the covered loss has occurred.
Further, unlike the surety bond, subcontractor-default insurance policies may include a significant
deductible per event, which ranges from $500,000 to much higher, depending on the value and type
of project, and may include an aggregate deductible often in excess of $2 million before recovery on
the policy is realized. Thus, the general contractor takes on a significant financial risk in relying on
a subcontractor-default insurance policy.
Like many other insurance policies, a subcontractor-default policy may be canceled for nonpay-
ment, material change, or post-issuance violation of policy terms or applicable qualifications. This
represents another disadvantage when compared to a surety bond, which is generally not cancelable
absent fraud or misrepresentation of the obligee. Further, the subcontractor insurance policy may not
satisfy any statutory payment and performance surety bond requirements on public projects. Thus, in
many jurisdictions the subcontractor insurance policy may have to be modified to meet the statutory
bond requirements.
II. 	TERMINATION
A. 	Overview
The performance bond surety’s involvement on a project is generally the result of the owner’s (or
general contractor’s) termination or threatened termination of the bonded contract due to the con-
tractor’s (or subcontractor’s) default. Virtually all construction contracts expressly recognize the
right to terminate the contract for the default of a breaching party in certain circumstances. Such
provisions usually afford the nonbreaching party a right to recover damages resulting from the
termination.
105See, e.g., SMI-Owen Steel Co., Inc. v. St. Paul Fire & Marine Ins. Co., 199 F.R.D. 209 (S.D. Tex. 2001).

-- 503 of 771 --

466 	CHAPTER 17 PERFORMANCE BONDS AND TERMINATIONS
Even in the absence of a contractual termination provision, the right to terminate a contract is gen-
erally implied against a party that has materially breached the contract. Many public contracts, and
an increasing number of private construction contracts, also contain “termination for convenience”
clauses authorizing the owner (or prime contractor) to terminate the prime contractor (or subcon-
tractors) even without cause. Practically, a termination for convenience clause acts as a very specific
changes clause in a contract—the change being that the owner no longer wants to proceed with the
work through no fault of the contractor. When the termination is for convenience, payments to the
terminated contractor are usually limited to actual costs incurred by that contractor, and may not
include overhead or other standard breach of contract damages or lost profits.106
B. 	Termination for Default
The right to terminate a construction contract for default generally arises only when a material or
substantial provision of the contract has been breached or a party has failed to perform a material
obligation. The parties’ rights and liabilities in such a termination are determined by the common law
(made up of prior court decisions applying the law in similar situations), by regulations or statutes
applicable to the contract, and by the contractual terms governing the termination. Under the com-
mon law, minor deviations in performance or failures to meet nonmaterial provisions of the contract
have not been viewed as grounds to terminate for default.107 Although such deviations or failures in
performance may give the nonbreaching party a right to recover damages caused by the failure, they
are not viewed as the basis for a complete termination of the contract. The common law has mea-
sured the materiality of a breach by the importance of the event or act to the purpose of the contract
as a whole, or to the stated basis of the agreement set out in the contract between the parties. By the
terms set out in their contract, therefore, the parties can expand, limit, or redefine the grounds for
termination for default, compared to the grounds that would otherwise exist under the common law.
They can also provide for the payment of damages and for the imposition of other obligations after
the contract is terminated for default.
C. 	Standard-Form Contracts: Grounds for Default Termination
Federal government construction contracts provide an example of how rights and duties can be
allocated by the parties’ contract when there is a default. The default clause used by the federal gov-
ernment in fixed-price construction contracts is set forth at Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR)
§ 52.249–10. This standard federal government construction contract termination clause affords the
government several remedies in addition to the relief generally available at common law. If a con-
tractor fails to perform by the date specified, produces defective or nonconforming work, or refuses
or fails to prosecute the work to ensure its timely completion, the government may pursue its admin-
istrative remedy under the terms of the default clause. 108 Under that clause, the government may
terminate the contract, take over the work, and complete the work at the contractor’s expense. The
clause makes the contractor liable for any liquidated or actual damages caused by unexcused delays
in the completion of the work.
At the same time, FAR § 52.249–10(b) gives the contractor the right to contest a default termi-
nation based on excusable delays that extend the time for the contractor’s performance duty. Under
FAR § 52.249–10(c), however, if the contractor successfully challenges a wrongful termination for
106But see AIA Document A201 – 2017 § 14.4.3 (allowing a termination fee, if in the contract).
107See L&A Contracting Co. v. S. Concrete Servs., Inc., 17 F.3d 106, 110 (5th Cir. 1994); Colorado Structures, Inc. v. Ins.
Co. of the W., 167 P.3d 1125, 1132 (Wash. 2007).
108See FAR § 52.249–10(a).

default, the termination for default is converted automatically into a termination for the government’s
convenience, thereby limiting the terminated contractor’s remedies. The remedy available under a
termination for convenience is less than what a terminated contractor could seek in a suit for wrongful
contract termination under common law.
Like the federal default termination clause, industry contract forms address, and supplement,
common-law remedies for the owner in the event of a default termination. AIA A201, for example,
describes the instances in which an owner may terminate a contract for cause in addition to circum-
stances relating to the contractor’s financial situation:
§ 14.2.1 The owner may terminate the Contract if the Contractor:
1. repeatedly refuses or fails to supply enough properly skilled workers or proper mate-
rials;
2. fails to make payment to Subcontractors or suppliers in accordance with the respective
agreements between the Contractor and the Subcontractors or Suppliers;
3. repeatedly disregards applicable laws, statutes, ordinances, codes, rules and regula-
tions, or lawful orders of a public authority; or
4. is otherwise guilty of substantial breach of a provision of the Contract Documents.109
AIA A201 also requires that the architect certify that sufficient cause exists for the termination.110
The owner must also give notice to the contractor and its surety seven days before terminating the
contract.
ConsensusDocs 200 sets forth grounds for a default termination similar to the AIA A201 terms,
provided that the contractor fails to remedy the grounds for termination after receiving notices to
cure. 111 Unlike the AIA form, however, the ConsensusDocs form does not require an architect’s or
other third party’s certification that cause exists to justify a termination for default.
For the most part, the federal FAR termination clause and the ConsensusDocs and AIA termina-
tion clauses provide for termination based on facts that would likely be deemed to constitute material
breaches of contract at common law. Specific situations in which sufficient grounds for termination
of a construction contract have been found to exist are discussed next. Remember also that the par-
ties may define in their construction contracts those breaches of contract that they deem sufficiently
“material” to justify a default termination.
1. 	Refusal or Failure to Prosecute the Work
A typical default termination clause will include a provision stating, in substance, that, “If the con-
tractor refuses or fails to prosecute the work or any separable part, with the diligence that will
insure its completion within the time specified in this contract,” the contract may be terminated
for default. 112 To invoke this termination provision, the terminating party has the burden of showing
both that a significant lag in performance has occurred and that the contractor, at the time of the
termination, could not have completed performance on time. 113

The fact that the contractor’s progress lags during one stage of the work may not alone support
termination. For example, a termination for default has been overturned as premature where sufficient
time remained in the contract schedule for the contractor to complete performance. 114 Although
factual determinations vary from case to case, courts have interpreted the standard default clause to
require a showing that timely completion was clearly in jeopardy.115
2. 	Failure to Complete on Time
As a general rule, a construction contract stating that time is “of the essence” and containing fixed or
specific performance dates is interpreted to mean that the time for performance is a material element
of contract’s performance. In a federal government construction contract containing such a time
clause, if timely performance does not occur, the government can terminate immediately without
notice and without affording the contractor an opportunity to cure. 116 When time is not described as
being of the essence, however, late performance is only one of the factors to be considered in deter-
mining the adequacy of performance and the justification for a default termination. 117 For example,
a delay in final completion may not justify a default termination if the work is sufficiently complete
that it can be used for its intended purpose and the contract does not require full and final, timely
completion. 118
3. 	Repudiation by the Contractor
The termination of a contractor for repudiating or declaring it will not perform its contract generally
arises from the contractor’s refusal or complete failure to prosecute the work in a timely manner.
To terminate a contract on the basis of repudiation by the contractor, the owner must show that the
contractor manifestly cannot or will not perform the contract. The cases speak in terms of a “positive,
definite, unconditional and unequivocal manifestation of intent … on the part of a contractor” not to
perform. 119 However, current case law recognizes that anticipatory repudiation may apply where the
obligee has reasonable grounds to believe that “the obligor will breach the contract. In that setting,
the obligee ‘may demand adequate assurance of due performance’ and if the obligor does not give
such assurances, the obligee may treat the failure to do so as a repudiation of the contract.”120 It
must be apparent that the contractor is unable to, or will not, perform the contract. A failure to make
progress alone does not constitute anticipatory repudiation absent some objective manifestation of
an inability to, or intent not to, perform.

When a contractor repudiates the existence of the contract it has entered into, the contractor is
subject to default termination regardless of its rate of progress in performance.121 For example, courts
recognize that a contractor can be terminated for default for failing to continue performance while
the resolution of a dispute is pending. 122 In addition, a court found that a contractor repudiated a
contract when the contractor stopped work, withdrew from the project, and provided no indication
that it would return to work.123 In another case, a concrete supplier’s breach of contract claim was
rejected on the grounds the supplier had anticipatorily repudiated the contract when the supplier
threatened to “begin immediately shutting our New York operation down for the winter” unless
the contractor provided written acceptance of a proposed pour schedule within a few hours of the
supplier’s demand. 124 Similarly, another court found that the government’s default termination was
proper when a contractor abandoned a project because its subcontractor stopped performing after
the contractor refused to pay the subcontractor. 125
The Disputes clause in federal government contracts expressly obligates a contractor to continue
performance pending a resolution of a dispute. 126 A refusal to proceed as directed by the contracting
officer has been treated as a repudiation of the contract by the contractor and justification for a default
termination. 127 Private contracts may obligate the contractor to continue the work during a contract
dispute. 128 In some circumstances, however, a contractor’s refusal to perform may be justified and
will not be regarded as an anticipatory breach or repudiation of the contract. For example, when
the contract specifications are impossible to perform, the contractor has a right to stop work on the
basis that no other practical alternative exists.129 Further, a contractor should not be terminated for
default where it is reasonably awaiting clarification from the government of drawings, specifications,
or other central requirements. If, for example, the contractor cannot proceed until it obtains guidance
from the government, the delay in work is justified. 130 However, a contractor cannot condition its
performance that is required under the contract on the other party’s acceptance of the additional or
different terms. 131

4. 	Failure to Comply with Other Material Provisions of the Contract
A contractor’s failure to comply with other terms of the contract may be a material breach for which
the owner can terminate the contract for default, but the owner will have to prove that the contract
provision not complied with is material to the contract and that the failure to perform is a material
breach of the contract. For example, many courts have found that a contractor’s failure to furnish
sufficient bonding as required by the contract is a material breach that warrants termination for
default. 137 Similarly, a subcontractor’s failure to maintain contractually required liability insurance
has been found to be a material breach justifying termination. 138
D. 	Defenses of the Contractor
1. 	Excusable Delay
Virtually all construction contracts excuse certain types of delays from counting against the time
allowed for performance. As an example, paragraph (b) of the default clause typically used by the
federal government excuses delays and, therefore, will not allow such delays to be used as a cause
for default termination where a contractor’s work is delayed by “unforeseeable causes beyond the
control and without the fault or negligence of the contractor.”139 Although the contract may excuse
certain kinds of delays, it generally will do so only if the contractor follows the procedure set forth in
the contract for obtaining a time extension (for example, by giving notice of the excusable delay, sub-
mitting a time-extension request within a short period of time after the delay occurs, and documenting
the effect of the delay on the project schedule).140
2. 	Waiver by the Owner
A contractor may defend against a default termination by showing that the owner waived strict com-
pliance with the contract completion date or other contract performance provisions, and thereby gave
up its right to terminate for that reason. 141 Even if the contract specifically states that its terms may be

A waiver can be effective without an exchange of value or a new contract agreement. 142 There will

While the right to terminate a contract for default may be waived if not timely exercised, it can
also be expressly reserved. 144 Reserving termination rights makes it more difficult for the oppos-
ing party to show that the right has been waived. 145 In Indemnity Insurance Co. of North America
v. United States,146 the government expressly reserved its right to terminate a takeover surety for
default by informing the surety that the owner was continuing to assess liquidated damages and

to terminate the contract immediately after expiration of the completion date did not constitute a
waiver under those circumstances. However, in federal government contracts, the waiver defense
has been viable “only … when exceptional or rare circumstances are presented in a construction
contract case.”147
An owner declaring default termination based on a specific cause does not mean the owner
has waived other potential causes for default termination.148 For example, in one case where the
contractor violated the Davis-Bacon Act 149 and Buy American Act, the court upheld the finding
that the termination for default based on the Davis-Bacon Act was justified, even though the
violations were not discovered until after the termination.150 In Joseph Morton Co. v. United
States, 151 the government’s decision to terminate for default was upheld based on the con-
tractor’s fraud, even though the government was unaware of the fraud when it terminated the
contract.
3. 	Contractor Response to Threat of Termination
When faced with a termination or the threat of a termination, the contractor (subcontractor) should
first seek advice of counsel familiar with construction contracts and termination issues. Decisions
must be made quickly and competently to protect the contractor’s position. In addition, the follow-
ing checklist suggests some general considerations for a contractor (subcontractor) to formulate an
action plan when faced with a threatened default termination.

✔ 	CONTRACTOR ACTION CHECKLIST
• Assess and document the factual accuracy of the notice. If the complaints are inaccurate, doc-
ument their inaccuracy in writing and, if possible, using photographs or video, and any other
appropriate means. Rebut, in writing, any inaccuracies in the termination threat.
• Assess the legal adequacy of the termination threat. Check contract documents to determine
whether the termination notice meets the contract requirements and was issued when and as
the contract requires. Does the contract provide a right of termination for the contract breach
set out in the notice? Does the termination notice follow the procedural requirements (adequate
notice, right to cure, given at the correct time, and to the correct parties, and so on) specified
in the contract?
• If the contract terms include a cure period, invoke the right to cure. If there is any legitimacy
to the complaints being made, address those complaints in a curative plan of action developed
and communicated in writing to the complaining party within the contractual cure period.
• If the contract provides no specific cure period, develop and communicate in writing a curative
plan as soon as possible.
• Implement a cure. Take action immediately to show an effort to implement the plan to cure any
legitimate complaints.
• If the termination notice is improper because it really seeks to accelerate work without paying
for acceleration, act accordingly by acknowledging the work will be accelerated. When the
termination threat is unwarranted, determine whether to treat the threat as an order to accelerate
under the contract change clause. If so, advise the complaining party of an intention to claim
a change based on acceleration.
• Document the status of the work at the time of the termination threat (for example, by mark-
ing up plans to show as-built conditions as well as through photographs and videos) and any
obstacles to performing the work.
• If the contract gives the owner or surety a right to take possession of materials and equipment,
adequately inventory and record the materials and equipment on site.
• Assess the subcontractor’s and supplier’s termination rights. Review various subcontract and
purchase order provisions addressing such termination rights and liabilities. Consider notice
obligations to the subcontractors and their entitlement to termination costs under their subcon-
tracts.
• Consider the possible loss of project staff. Termination of a construction contract is frequently
accompanied by the loss of valuable members of a contractor’s project staff. Memorialize the
knowledge and advice of project staff about issues likely to arise in a dispute over the ter-
mination decision. Memories will fade and employees will leave or lose interest in a former
employer’s project problems. Consult with counsel as to whether sworn declarations or affi-
davits should be taken from project staff to preserve and “lock in” their testimony.
• Ensure the protection of project records. After termination, the terminating party may request
project records to assist in the completion of the contractor’s work. Protect confidential or
sensitive information.
• Reassure the performance bond surety. A threat to terminate a contract will likely draw the
scrutiny of a contractor’s performance bond surety. Assure your surety of a proper response to
the threat.
• Anticipate potential subcontractor and supplier claims. Assess and document the status of work
by subcontractors and suppliers in anticipation of potential termination claims.

E. 	Remedies of the Owner
When a contractor is terminated for default, the owner typically may: (1) complete the contract
work itself; (2) contract with another contractor to complete the work; or (3) allow the defaulted
contractor’s surety (if it is a bonded contract) to complete, or arrange to complete, the contract. 152
Usually an owner will not complete the work with its own employees or forces unless the project
is substantially complete and little work remains. Otherwise, the owner will commonly enter into
another contract or will rely on the surety to complete, assuming the project is bonded and the surety
agrees.
An owner completing a contract, either on its own or through a completion contractor, must take
reasonable steps to minimize its completion costs. This duty to mitigate damages limits the recovery
the owner can obtain, due to breach of contract, to the cost of reasonable efforts to complete the
contract economically and efficiently.153 The reasonableness of these actions will be determined in
light of the facts and circumstances of each case.
AIA Document A312 Performance Bond obligates the defaulting contractor’s surety to cover
the cost of completion up to the amount of the bond. 154 Although the surety may not be obligated
to complete the contract work, at least where the default is not contested by the contractor, most
sureties will cooperate with the owner in arranging for completion of the contract. In most cases, the
surety will be allowed to take over the work unless there is reason to believe that the party proposed
by the surety to complete the work is incompetent or unqualified to such an extent that the owner’s
interests would be substantially prejudiced by such efforts. 155
Where the surety tenders another contractor to complete the work, the bonds of the surety under
the original contract remain effective. 156 In addition, the owner may often receive the benefit of
additional surety bonds provided by the completion contractor.
Where a surety elects to have the work completed by another firm without either a valid assign-
ment or a takeover agreement, it may seek to assert the defaulted contractor’s claims against the
owner. The surety’s ability to do this may be affected by other laws. For example, on federal gov-
ernment contracts, a surety cannot prosecute a claim against the federal government under the con-
tract “disputes” clause in the surety’s own name.157 Under such circumstances, the surety must be
assigned the right to advance the defaulted contractor’s claim, and thus submit the claim as a repre-
sentative of the contractor. 158 On federal government contracts, it is generally prohibited to transfer
a claim from a contractor to the surety, unless the government consents to transfer the claim.159
1. 	Reprocurement Costs
The terms of the contract’s default clause often provide the basis for computing the contractor’s
damages liability upon a default. For example, under the default clause at FAR § 52.249–10, the
federal government can recover its “increased costs”—those additional costs in excess of the original
contract price that are necessarily incurred in completion of the work including its administrative
procurement costs. 160

recover from the defaulted contractor only those costs attributable to the work in the original con-

provided by law or under this contract.”
2. 	Delay Damages
Similar to the liquidated damages clause in many construction contracts, the federal government
construction liquidated damages clause, FAR § 52.211–12, provides that regardless of whether the
contractor is terminated for default, the contractor is liable for damages resulting from the contrac-
tor’s refusal or failure to complete the work within the specified time. Absent a liquidated damages
provision, the owner is entitled to actual damages caused by the contractor’s delay. Actual damages
under the FAR include, for example, the cost of keeping a government inspector on the job after the
specified completion date.164
When the contract contains a liquidated damages provision, the federal government is entitled to
damages for the period from the specified contract completion date to the actual date of completion,
whether the contract is completed by the contractor, the surety, or a reprocurement contractor. The
default clause provisions attempt to secure for the federal government the same measure of recovery
it could obtain under common law, that is, to put it in as good a position as it would have enjoyed
had the delay not occurred.

institutions arising out of failed projects. Lender liability claims have been asserted when a project

liability. If, however, the lender becomes directly involved with the contractor, makes direct repre-

be held liable to the contractor if the project owner breaches the construction contract by failing to
make payment.
While a construction lender traditionally has very little risk to a project’s contractor, that risk
increases when a lender makes direct representations to the contractor regarding forthcoming pay-
ments or the financing for the project. Following a project owner’s bankruptcy in North Carolina, a
bankruptcy court allowed the contractor’s claim for breach of fiduciary duty to proceed against the
project’s lender; the lender’s repeated written representations to the contractor that the project was
“fully funded” and payment would be forthcoming were sufficient to support a finding of a fiduciary
relationship between the contractor and the lender under North Carolina law. 165 In an Idaho case, a
contractor’s third-party beneficiary claim against a construction lender survived the lender’s motion
to dismiss because the contractor alleged the loan agreement specifically recognized the contractor
as an intended beneficiary of the construction loan.166
The majority of lender-liability claims raised by contractors fail due to the lack of a sufficient
relationship or direct communications between the lender and contractor. A contractor working with
a financially distressed owner should attempt to create a direct line of communication with the project
lender and seek assurance in writing regarding funding of the construction financing and future
payments to the contractor.
G. 	Termination for Convenience
The parties to a construction contract may include a clause allowing one party (usually the owner)
the right to terminate another party without cause—that is, for convenience. Although the federal
government’s right to terminate a contract for convenience is generally deemed to be implied as
a matter of law, 167 the FAR includes a specific clause, incorporated into most federal government
construction contracts, that expressly provides for this right. 168 Likewise, state or local governments
often include express contract provisions affording the government entity the right to terminate for
convenience.169
1. 	Standard Industry Forms—Private Contracts
In order for one party to a private commercial contract to terminate for convenience, an express
provision in the contract must give it the right to do so. If one party terminates another for conve-
nience, the terminated party’s right to compensation upon such termination may be set out in, and
limited by, the contract’s terms. The private owner’s right to terminate for convenience is as varied
as the specific convenience-termination provisions that parties choose to include in their contracts.

2. 	“Bad-Faith” Convenience Terminations: Theory and Reality

many jurisdictions, the question is not resolved. 175 At least one court has held that there are circum-

may not be exercised in bad faith. 176 Other courts have hesitated to hold that there is a good-faith
requirement in terminating for convenience. A federal court applying New York law found “on the
basis of existing precedents, that such a [good-faith] restriction would probably not be imposed by
New York courts.”177

In the federal procurement context, the government’s right to terminate for convenience, although
extremely broad, cannot be exercised in bad faith. Termination is permitted “if the Contracting Offi-
cer determines that a termination is in the Government’s interest.”178 That provision expresses a right
that has long been recognized, even in the absence of a termination for convenience clause in the con-
tract. 179 Courts have held that a contracting officer may not terminate a contractor for convenience in
bad faith. 180 To prove bad faith in a termination for convenience, however, the contractor must show
clear and convincing evidence (a heightened evidentiary standard) that the government acted with
malice and the specific intent to harm the contractor. 181 While the government has broad discretion
to terminate for its convenience, it may not do so in bad faith or without a change in circumstance
warranting the action. 182
H. 	Convenience Termination Costs
In federal procurement law, the contractor whose contract is wholly or partially terminated for
convenience must be made financially whole by compensation for the direct consequences of the
government’s termination. Negotiated termination settlements are limited only by the requirements
of reasonableness of cost and the contract price. Individual cost items need not be negotiated. Costs
incurred may even be recovered where the contract is terminated for convenience before any actual
work was performed. 183
In addition, a federal contractor is entitled to a “fair and reasonable” profit on the work it per-
formed, unless it can be demonstrated that the contractor would have lost money on the contract. 184

Expected or anticipated profits on future work are not recoverable in the absence of a wrongful
termination. Profit is allowable only on the work performed. 185 If it can be shown that the contractor
would have incurred a loss in completing the contract, the contractor is not entitled to any profit
markup, and the termination costs may be reduced by the anticipated loss the contractor would have
suffered.
The standard federal termination for convenience clause under FAR § 52.249–2 entitles the con-
tracting officer to terminate all or part of a contract. Where only a portion of the contract is terminated
for convenience, the contractor’s measure of cost recovery is governed by the same principles appli-
cable to termination of the entire contract. The contractor may recover costs incurred until the date of
the termination, including a fair and reasonable profit, and the cost of settlement with subcontractors,
suppliers, and the government. The partial termination settlement proposal must be submitted within
90 days after the effective date of the partial termination. In addition, the contractor is entitled to an
equitable adjustment in the price of the work that is not terminated, if it is shown that eliminating a
portion of the work caused an increase in the cost of the remaining work.

➣ 	POINTS TO REMEMBER
• Performance bonds are not insurance. Sureties may not react to claims in the same way that an
insurance company might respond to, for example, a general liability insurance policy claim.
• The language of the bond is critical; read it carefully. It may contain claim requirements or
refer to a statute that contains such requirements.
• Determine if the bond is a statutory or common law bond; this distinction may affect claim
requirements.
• The penal sum of the bond is usually, but not always, the surety’s limit of liability.
• A surety has all of the defenses of its principal plus additional technical (strictly bond-related)
defenses.
• A surety may be bound by arbitration requirements in the bonded contract. Obligees should
insist that surety bonds specifically incorporate by reference the principal’s contract documents.
• Subcontractor performance (or “subcontractor default”) insurance is available and should be
considered as an alternative to performance bonds for each subcontractor, although these pro-
grams may be most suitable on large, complex construction projects.
• Termination for default is a remedy of last resort. Consult with counsel to carefully consider
your rights, duties, obligations, and options if this situation arises on your project.
• Any attempt to terminate usually requires an opportunity to cure performance deficiencies,
even if the contract does not specifically provide a cure period. Some courts, however, may not
find an implied right to cure if the breach of contract at issue is addressed by the contract terms
as an absolute ground for termination.
• The primary defenses to termination are excusable delay and the failure to pay for work as
required by the contract.
• Converting a termination for default into a termination for convenience generally limits the
contractor to recovery of the costs of performance on the work completed, plus reasonable
profit thereon, as well as reasonable termination costs.
• A contract clause that provides for the automatic conversion of a wrongful termination for
default to a termination for convenience may reduce substantially the risks associated with a
contract termination decision.

189 EJCDC C-700 Standard General Conditions of the Construction Contract § 16.03A (2018 ed.).
