19
AN OVERVIEW OF
ENVIRONMENTAL AND SAFETY
CONCERNS ON THE
CONSTRUCTION SITE
A maze of evolving federal, state, and local environmental and safety obligations apply to construc-
tion projects in ways that, if not planned for, can cause delays and increase risks and costs. The
time to begin planning for potential environmental and safety issues is while developing the initial
proposal. At this early stage in the process, contract terms and insurance coverage should also be
carefully reviewed to ascertain the obligations that must be met to satisfy environmental standards
in light of the possibility that hazardous materials may be encountered or created or that a worker
will be injured on the job. This chapter provides an overview of potential environmental and safety
issues that affect a construction project.
I. 	SOURCES OF ENVIRONMENTAL REGULATION AND LIABILITY
The federal government’s regulation of hazardous materials and its ability to impose liability for
environmental cleanup is well established and far reaching. Although the Comprehensive Environ-
mental Response, Compensation and Liability Act of 19801 (CERCLA), commonly referred to as
“Superfund,” is perhaps the most well-known of such federal environmental laws, it is not the only
federal environmental statute that may apply to a construction project.
Additionally, some federal environmental laws, such as the Clean Water Act, 2 may be imple-
mented by state agencies that have enacted their own federally approved programs. Other aspects
of environmental law may be subject to state and local laws that are unique to each jurisdiction.
Regardless of the existence of any specific federal or state environmental statutes, a contractor may
also face liability under traditional common law causes of action. The consequences of running afoul
of this web of environmental liability are not limited to job delays and civil liability payable by a
company but can involve fines and criminal penalties assessed by the federal or state governments
against individuals. This section focuses on the civil liability aspects of CERCLA and other key
federal environmental statutes, which, despite their importance, are not the only legal requirements
that may apply to a construction project.
1 42 U.S.C. §§ 9601–75 (2000).
2 33 U.S.C. § 1251.
509

-- 547 of 771 --

510 	CHAPTER 19 AN OVERVIEW OF ENVIRONMENTAL AND SAFETY CONCERNS
A. 	Encountering Hazardous Materials on a Construction Site—CERCLA Liability
Under CERCLA, the government is authorized to take remedial actions to clean up hazardous-waste
spills and seek reimbursement from parties it deems responsible. Broadly speaking, CERCLA
imposes liability for cleanup costs on those parties responsible for the contamination at the
listed site. 3 The parties subject to CERCLA liability are referred to as “potentially responsible
parties,”4 or “PRPs.” A “potentially responsible party letter” (PRP letter) is a letter issued by the
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) notifying the recipient that the EPA considers it to be a
potentially responsible party for contamination at a given site.5 Additionally, where an imminent
and substantial endangerment to the public health exists, the government may take legal action to
compel potentially liable parties to undertake their own cleanup actions. 6
The breadth of CERCLA liability, combined with the low level of involvement that can trigger
liability, makes CERCLA a serious concern for many construction projects. In addition, the recovery
costs under CERCLA are not left exclusively to the government; private individuals who incur
cleanup costs can look to other PRPs from which to recover their costs.
1. 	Strict Liability under CERCLA
If a party meets the statutory definition of a PRP, it is liable. 7 CERCLA imposes “strict liability,”
which means automatic liability without regard to fault or negligence. Only a few, very limited
defenses are allowed because CERCLA was created to address environmental damage from haz-
ardous wastes. The tough measures were deemed necessary to fulfill the statute’s important reme-
dial purpose.
2. 	PRPs
CERCLA identifies the following four categories of PRPs that face strict liability:
(1) The owner and operator of a vessel or a facility;
(2) Any person who at the time of disposal of any hazardous substance owned or operated any
facility at which such hazardous substances were disposed of;
(3) Any person who by contract, agreement, or otherwise arranged for disposal or treatment, or
arranged with a transporter for transport for disposal or treatment, of hazardous substances
owned or possessed by such person, by any other party or entity, at any facility or incin-
eration vessel owned or operated by another party or entity and containing such hazardous
substances; and
(4) Any person who accepts or accepted any hazardous substances for transport to disposal or
treatment facilities, incineration vessels or sites selected by such person, from which there is a
release, or a threatened release which causes the incurrence of response costs, of a hazardous
substance. 8
3See Niagara Mohawk Power Corp. v. Chevron U.S.A., Inc., 596 F.3d 112 (2d Cir. 2010) (plaintiff owner was entitled to seek
contribution, but not reimbursement for costs).

I. SOURCES OF ENVIRONMENTAL REGULATION AND LIABILITY 	511
On their face, the categories are broad and, over time, courts have interpreted them even more
broadly. For example, the contractor that unwittingly stumbles on and innocently transports or
disturbs hazardous materials resulting in contamination of a site can be just as liable for cleanup
costs under CERCLA as the party that knowingly handles and purposely disposes of hazardous
materials in an illegal fashion. That may sound like a theoretical worst-case scenario with no
relevance in the real world, but it is not. Consider the contractor’s treatment in Kaiser Aluminum &
Chemical Corp. v. Catellus Development Corp. 9
In Kaiser, the court held that a contractor could be liable under CERCLA simply by cutting and
filling soil on a site that, unknown to the contractor, had been contaminated by hazardous materials
decades earlier. The property owner engaged the contractor to grade and prepare the site for a housing
development. This work required the contractor to “excavate” and “disperse” some of the soils on
site. The contractor did not remove soil from or import fill material onto the site. After the contractor
started work, it was discovered that, decades earlier, the site and some of the soil handled by the
contractor had been contaminated by hazardous chemicals.
Once hazardous material contamination was discovered, the owner had to clean up and restore the
site per CERCLA and the United States Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) corresponding
regulations. The owner then sued the developer, which had sold the property, to recover the site
cleanup costs and restoration. The developer responded by also suing the grading contractor under
CERCLA, claiming that the contractor had worsened the situation by excavating contaminated soil
and then spreading it onto uncontaminated areas at the site. The claim against the contractor was
initially dismissed, but that decision was reversed by the court of appeals’ determination that the
contractor could be an “operator” of the property and also a “transporter” of hazardous materials
and therefore liable for the cleanup costs under CERCLA.
a. 	Liability as an Operator 	In Kaiser, the court ruled that whether a party is an “operator”
of a facility turns on the degree of control the party exerts over the activity causing the contami-
nation when the contamination occurs. In Kaiser, although site contamination originally occurred
in the 1940s, decades before the contractor ever moved a shovel of dirt, the court found that the
activity producing the contamination was site excavation and grading, which occurred during con-
struction and while the site was under the contractor’s control.10 Thus, the court concluded that the
excavating contractor had sufficient control over this phase of the development to be an “operator”
under CERCLA.
In reaching this conclusion, the court relied on CERCLA’s definition of “disposal,” which includes
“the discharge, deposit, injection, dumping, spilling, or placing of any … hazardous waste into or on
the land,” which can be read broadly to include subsequent movement, dispersal, or release of haz-
ardous materials during landfill excavations and fillings. In the court’s view, to limit liability for
“disposal” to the initial contamination would result in “a crabbed interpretation [that] would subvert
Congress’ goal that parties who are responsible for contaminating property be held accountable for
the costs of cleaning it up.”
9 976 F.2d 1338 (9th Cir. 1992).
10Kaiser Aluminum & Chem. Corp. v. Catellus Dev. Corp., 976 F.2d 1338 (9th Cir. 1992) (“Excavator that spread some
displaced contaminated soil from property over other parts of property was ‘operator’ of facility so as to be liable under
CERCLA to contribute to cost of removing contaminated soil from property; allegations of excavator’s operations on
property tended to show that excavator had sufficient control over that phase of development of property to be ‘opera-
tor’”); but see United States v. Quest Corp., 353 F.Supp.2d 1048 (D. Minn. 2005) (holding that CERCLA operator lia-

b. 	Liability as a Transporter CERCLA defines “transportation” as “the movement of a haz-
ardous substance by any mode,” and in the court’s view, the contractor’s movement of contaminated
soil by excavation and grading was well within that definition. The court noted that although trans-
portation as defined by CERCLA applied to “sites selected by” the contractor, the transportation of
hazardous materials to an uncontaminated area of the same site was no different than transporting
them to another site.
c. 	Exceptions to Strict Liability An exception to strict liability under CERCLA exists for con-
tractors specifically engaged to clean up hazardous materials, called a “response action contractor”
(RAC).11 RACs are provided insulation from strict liability because it would be impossible to get
any responsible contractor to perform cleanup work without this limitation. Even RACs, however,
are not totally relieved from CERCLA liability and remain liable for negligence, gross negligence,
and intentional wrongdoing in performing cleanup work. The CERCLA exception to strict liability
for RACs applies only to federal statutes and does not in any way limit the RAC’s potential liability,
including strict liability that may be imposed under state law.
3. 	Joint and Several Liability
In addition to strict liability, CERCLA imposes joint and several liability on PRPs, 12 meaning that
if a party is liable for any part of the contamination (for example, 20 percent of the contamina-
tion), it may be liable for 100 percent of the cleanup costs. Thus, the party seeking to recoup the
cleanup costs at a Superfund site, whether the federal government or a private party, can pursue any
responsible party for the entire cost, regardless of the respective contributions of the various respon-
sible parties to the contamination. Not surprisingly, this joint and several liability provision makes
solvent companies with deep pockets especially attractive targets for the government and private
litigants alike.
4. 	Defenses to Liability under CERCLA
The three potential defenses to liability under CERCLA are: (1) innocent landowners; (2) bona fide
prospective purchasers; and (3) contiguous property owners.13 Any individual who seeks to establish
one of these defenses to liability must conduct investigations, including all appropriate inquiries
necessary to identify the releases or threatened releases of hazardous substances.
On December 30, 2013, the EPA released ASTM International’s E1527-13 “Standard Practice for
Environmental Site Assessments: Phase I Environmental Site Assessment Process” as the standard
for conducting “appropriate inquiries” necessary to qualify for the regulatory defenses to liability
to CERCLA. 14 This standard amended 40 C.F.R. Part 312 without removing reference to the 2005
ASTM standard. Contractors have the option of using this 2013 standard for conducting “all appro-
priate inquiries.”
5. 	Contribution
The impact of joint and several liability on a responsible party under CERCLA can potentially
be mitigated by the ability of one responsible party to seek contribution for cleanup costs from

other responsible parties. 15 Congress added the contribution provision to CERCLA by enacting the
Superfund Amendments and Reauthorization Act of 1986 (SARA).16
As noted, “contribution” means that if just one responsible party is sued, it can bring a separate
action against another responsible party that it contends is partially or completely responsible for
CERCLA cleanup costs actually assessed.17
Frequently, initial PRPs will assert claims against other PRPs, who in turn can directly assert
contribution claims against the other in the same lawsuit. Sometimes, an entirely separate contri-
bution action may be initiated by one PRP against another. Notably, where a responsible party has
previously resolved its liability for cleanup costs with the federal or state government (usually by
executing a written settlement agreement commonly referred to as a consent order), it is protected
from contribution claims by other responsible parties.18 The costs and burdens of CERCLA litigation
are so great that they alone can provide an incentive for a named PRP to bring certainty and closure
to the process by contributing to a settlement with the federal or state government. Consequently,
the claimant and each PRP often try to promptly involve most, if not all, other responsible parties
in the litigation. However, if the other PRPs no longer exist or lack financial resources to contribute
meaningfully to a settlement or judgment, a deep-pocket PRP can be left to pay all of the costs,
regardless of its relative fault.
B. 	Water Quality
Congress’s policy is to recognize, preserve, and protect the primary responsibilities and rights of
States to prevent, reduce, and eliminate pollution, 19 to plan the development and use (including
restoration, preservation, and enhancement) of land and water resources, and to consult with the
Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in the exercise of their authority under
the law. 20 In furtherance of this policy, Congress enacted the Federal Clean Water Act.
The federal Clean Water Act (CWA)21 makes it unlawful for any person to discharge any pol-
lutant, including “dredged spoil” and “rock, sand, [and] cellar dirt,” 22 into the nation’s “navigable
waters”23 unless a permit for such a discharge is issued under the act. This applies to discharge of

C. 	Air Quality
The federal Clean Air Act 30 enables the EPA to establish outdoor air-quality standards. The EPA has
set standards for the concentrations of a number of air pollutants, including sulfur oxides, hydro-
carbons, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, lead, ozone, and total suspended particulate matter.
Regulation of air pollutants at both the federal and state levels can affect a construction project. More-
over, as concerns about climate change, and increased carbon footprints continue to grow, air-quality
regulations will continue to affect construction, and industry professionals will increasingly be called
on to take steps to refine construction processes to mitigate such threats.
1. 	Greenhouse Gas Emissions
In 2007, the United States Supreme Court held that the EPA must regulate so-called greenhouse gas
emissions (GHGs) from motor vehicle emissions. 31 The chemical compounds that make up GHGs
consist predominantly of carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, and hydrofluorocarbons. GHGs are
considered to be a significant contributor to the relatively recent global warming or climate change
phenomenon. In the construction industry, emission reductions must be quantified and documented
on a case-by-case basis.
Historically, the EPA has had a difficult time quantifying and documenting the construction
industry’s GHGs because of the large number of construction companies and construction sites,
the prevalence of small businesses, and the lack of data. To address these challenges, in 2007, the
EPA recommended that the following factors be used for measuring performance: 1) energy use;
2) greenhouse gas emissions; 3) diesel air emissions; 4) storm water compliance; 5) construction
and demolition debris management; and 6) green building practices. Since 2007, the EPA’s use of
these factors has indicated the following trends:
• Construction-related energy use is outpacing growth in the construction industry;
• Construction companies are reducing air pollution by retrofitting older diesel equipment;
• The percentage of recycled construction/demolition materials varies widely by state; and
• More contractors are making a conscious effort to go “green.”32
To help the construction industry understand which environmental regulations apply to them and
the ways that they can lower their GHGs, the EPA’s Office of Compliance has published Manag-
ing Your Environmental Responsibilities: A Planning Guide for Construction and Development (the
MYER Guide), which can be used during different phases of a construction project. 33 Hard copies of
the MYER Guide are available at no cost from the National Service Center for Environmental Publi-
cations (NSCEP) at (800) 490-9198. Requesters must specify document number EPA305-B-04-003.

2. 	Asbestos and Lead
Renovation and demolition projects, particularly projects involving buildings constructed before
1980, 34 can present significant risks of exposure to airborne asbestos and lead, as well as special risks
to workers. To address these risks, the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
has promulgated regulations specifying safety and health measures to be followed on construction
projects involving asbestos, lead,35 and silica. Most of these procedures and requirements are similar
for these airborne substances, but there are important differences that cannot be overlooked. State
and local regulations may also apply.
Regulations covering asbestos, lead, and silica apply to all construction work, including
demolition or salvage, renovation, remodeling, repair, installation of products containing these
materials, transportation, disposal, and emergency cleanup situations. Each regulation contains
an “action level” that represents the maximum concentration of the substance allowable over
a specified time period before the contractor must comply with most aspects of the regulation.
These regulations also list a “permissible exposure limit” (PEL), which is the maximum level of
exposure to the substance that the contractor’s employees can endure without respiratory protection.
(See Table 19.1.)
Each contractor must initially determine if any employee on the job site may be exposed to one of
the substances at or above the action level. This initial determination can be waived, however, when
the contractor can prove through objective data that its employees cannot be exposed to concentra-
tions of the substance above the action level even in worst-case scenarios, or when the contractor has
monitored for substance exposures within the last 12 months during work operations conducted
under workplace conditions closely resembling the current operation.
When the initial determination shows the possibility of substance exposure at or above the action
level, the contractor must conduct monitoring that is representative of the exposure for each employee
in the workplace who is exposed to the substance at least every six months and must notify affected
employees of the monitoring results. If exposure is above the PEL, periodic monitoring must be
performed every three months. If the initial monitoring shows no possibility of substance exposure
above the action level, no further monitoring is necessary. Regardless of previous measurements,
however, the contractor must repeat the initial monitoring process whenever there has been a change
in process, control equipment, personnel, or work practices that may result in new or additional
exposures above the action level limit.

The contractor must employ engineering controls and work practices to reduce and maintain
employee exposure to the substances below the PEL to the extent such controls are feasible.
Wherever the feasible engineering controls and work practices are not sufficient to reduce the
substance concentration below the PEL, the contractor must supplement its controls with respiratory
protective devices, protective clothing, changing and shower facilities, special signage, and training
programs, among other measures. The contractor is also required to institute a rigorous medical
surveillance program of exposed employees, including blood tests and physical examinations.
a. 	Inadvertent Asbestos Abatement 	A construction or renovation project may be transformed
quickly into an asbestos abatement project if the contractor unknowingly demolishes or disturbs
asbestos-containing building materials. Under the EPA’s National Emission Standards for Haz-
ardous Air Pollutants (NESHAP) for asbestos-containing materials,36 demolition and renovation
work become an asbestos-abatement project whenever regulated asbestos-containing materials in
quantities of greater than 260 linear feet on pipes, such as pipe insulation, or 160 square feet of
“other” facility components, are disturbed. The EPA’s asbestos NESHAP standards are also trig-
gered if the total asbestos-containing waste product generated from facility components exceeds
35 cubic feet. These quantities are all relatively small amounts of material. If a contractor disturbs
asbestos-containing materials exceeding these thresholds without notification, it is conducting an
illegal asbestos-abatement operation and is subject to penalties under each subsection of the asbestos
regulations it is violating.
Generally, to avoid possible violations, it is necessary to notify the regulators 10 working
days before beginning any asbestos-abatement project and update the notice if the quantity
of asbestos-containing materials changes by 20 percent or more. The only exceptions to this
notification requirement would be for emergency operations and unsafe buildings. Further, a
new notification is required if the commencement date of the asbestos abatement changes. If the
contractor inadvertently renovates or demolishes regulated asbestos-containing building materials,
then, in addition to being subject to citation for violation of the notification requirement, it also may
be fined for failing to properly control airborne asbestos emissions.
If a contractor unknowingly disturbs asbestos-containing materials, it could commit the following
violations:
• Failure to properly contain the work area
• Failure to provide workers with proper respiratory protection and protective clothing, hygiene
facilities, and training
• Failure to employ proper and necessary medical surveillance of workers
• Failure to adequately wet asbestos-containing building materials during demolition
• Failure to properly seal and label, transport, or dispose of asbestos waste
• Failure to maintain proper records of an asbestos-abatement project
In addition to fines or penalties levied on contractors by regulatory agencies, the contractor that
wrongly or unlawfully disturbs regulated asbestos-containing materials also faces liability to third
parties and potentially criminal charges. 37 Employees, building owners, tenants, and occupants

b. 	Inadvertent Lead-Based Paint Abatement 	Similarly, if lead is present in building materi-
als, typically in the form of lead-based paint, and the contractor accidentally disturbs it or does not
perform an initial exposure assessment, the contractor must assume exposure at a level of 10 times the
maximum permissible exposure level. With that assumption, the contractor must provide its work-
ers with respiratory protection and protective clothing, provide hygiene facilities, conduct medical
surveillance, conduct employee training, maintain extensive records, and post warning signs at all
entrances and exits to the work areas. Failure to comply with these requirements makes the contractor
liable for violating each subsection of the standard.
Under the standard, if lead is present, the contractor must presume that its construction activities
will cause airborne emissions of lead in excess of permissible exposure limits. Therefore, the con-
tractor should obtain all sampling and test data from the owner before commencing its demolition
and renovation activities. Further, the contractor should ask the owner to perform appropriate test-
ing in all areas that will be affected by the construction activities and should not start work until it
receives the requested test results.
c. 	Other Federal Statutes Other federal statutes, such as the Resource Conservation and Recov-
ery Act of 1976 (RCRA), 38 deal with the current handling, storage, treatment, and disposal of listed
hazardous materials. For all items and contracts over $10,000, RCRA requires federal agencies to
procure items with the “highest percentage recovered materials practicable”39 and to give preference
in procurement programs to items and practices that maximize the use of post-consumer recovered
materials. 40 Because contamination may occur during handling, storing, treating, or disposing of
hazardous materials, there can be considerable overlap between CERCLA and RCRA.

hazardous material work. As discussed in Chapter 12 and shown through the checklists included

1. 	Exclude Hazardous Materials from the Scope of Work
To minimize exposure on a private job that, according to the contract documents, contains no
work involving hazardous substances or materials, the generic hazardous materials specification
sections and related clauses should be stricken and the contractor’s proposal or bid submission
should expressly exclude the performance of any work involving hazardous materials. Upon award
of the contract, the contractor should confirm that the hazardous material condition (or exception)
in its bid or proposal has been expressly incorporated into the contract. On a similar public project,
however, such a qualification exception may render the bid nonresponsive. Accordingly, the public
works contractor must decide whether it wants to take the risk of being directed by the government
to perform hazardous material work.
2. 	Determine What Materials Will Be Encountered
Any renovation or demolition work on a project necessarily requires the contractor to address exist-
ing building materials. Before signing the contract, the contractor must know what materials it is
going to encounter or run the risk of environmental violations and lawsuits by workers or others
exposed to hazardous materials in the workplace. Therefore, the contractor should answer the fol-
lowing questions before submitting a bid or proposal for such work:
• Do the contract documents include any hazardous-material remediation or asbestos or
lead-based paint abatement?
• Do the contract documents refer to standards for performing hazardous-material remediation
or asbestos or lead-based paint abatement?
• Does any part of the work involve hazardous materials, asbestos, lead-based paint, silica, under-
ground storage tanks, wetlands, or protected natural resources?
• If the contract documents describe environmental remediation, is sufficient insurance coverage
in place?
• Does the contract allocate risk or responsibility for hazardous materials including asbestos,
silica, or lead-based paint? Is the contractor required to indemnify the owner or others for
losses associated with such materials?
• Is the owner aware of any hazardous materials including asbestos, silica, lead-based paint,
wastes, or contaminated soil or water that might affect the contractor’s scope of work?
• Have any environmental site assessments been conducted? If these assessments have not
been provided, make a specific request to the owner or agency. Are there any building
surveys or inspection reports on asbestos, lead-based paint, underground storage tanks,
soil or water quality, or other hazardous materials on the site? Has a written request for
disclosure of this information been submitted to the owner prior to submission of the bid or
proposal?
• Did the site visit and inspection indicate distressed vegetation, hydrocarbon or chemical con-
tamination, underground storage tanks, transformers, drums, suspect lead-based paint, or sus-
pect asbestos-containing materials?

-- 557 of 771 --

520 	CHAPTER 19 AN OVERVIEW OF ENVIRONMENTAL AND SAFETY CONCERNS
• Has the site ever been subject to any environmental permits, or has the site ever been the subject
of a regulatory enforcement action? Is there a closure report?
• Has the owner been required to fully disclose its knowledge as to all environmental issues on
the site?
• If unanticipated asbestos, silica, lead-based paint, tanks, drums, contaminated soil, polychlori-
nated biphenyls (PCBs), or other hazardous materials are encountered, what are the contractor’s
obligations to address these?
To obtain answers to some of these initial questions, a prudent contractor should submit a written
environmental prebid inquiry to the owner or others on the project delivery team.
Given the risk of unlimited liability, the prudent contractor should conduct a comprehensive
site visit before submitting its bid or proposal. Record what was observed and observable with
photographs, videos, and trip reports. Look for distressed vegetation, unusual depressions, storage
tanks, drums, wells (or pipes protruding from the ground), suspect lead-based paint, and suspect
asbestos-containing materials. Obtain and review all as-built drawings for additional information
about building components and materials. After the site visit, submit written questions to the owner
regarding conditions of concern and building materials that are suspected to contain asbestos or be
layered with lead-based paint. In addition to requesting copies of any environmental site assessments,
ask for copies of any bulk sample results and paint analyses.
This approach shifts at least some of the initial burden of identifying hazardous materials onto, and
forces disclosure by, the owner as to what it knows or should know about the building or property.
Although this is a good start, courts often assume that contractors are also fully knowledgeable
about building materials and conditions and will therefore not allow a contractor to escape liability
from environmental violations based on blind reliance on plans and specifications. Accordingly, the
contractor should not submit its proposal or bid until after it has assessed and, if necessary, allocated
or removed environmental risks and concerns from its scope of work.
B. 	Contract Provisions and Indemnification
The risk of unanticipated hazardous materials should be the subject of specific contract terms and
conditions appropriately and equitably allocating such risk among the parties. Absent such express
treatment in the contract, routine clauses imposing considerable risk on the contractor for the
unknown can apply to unanticipated hazardous materials. For example, a specific contract provision
requiring the contractor to examine the site and shifting responsibility for concealed or unexpected
conditions could be invoked to cover an unexpected condition, such as a concealed hazardous
material contamination rather than additional rock or muck removal. Likewise, broad indemnity
clauses in favor of the owner can generally be quite burdensome under routine situations and can
be devastating if applied to the discovery of unexpected hazardous materials. Although a standard
differing site conditions clause may afford the contractor some protection from the costs associated
with unanticipated hazardous material on construction sites, far greater specificity will help ensure
protection.
The need for specific contract provisions to address the possibility of contamination by haz-
ardous materials has been recognized, but not fully addressed nor universally applied. The American
Institute of Architects’ (AIA) Document A201 – 2017 General Conditions of the Contract for Con-
struction addresses the discovery of unanticipated hazardous materials. AIA A201, however, does
not protect the contractor from liability for all hazardous materials that may be encountered on the
construction project. Instead, the clause puts an affirmative obligation on the contractor to comply
“with any requirements included in the Contract Documents regarding hazardous materials.” This

means that the contractor must review all contract documents to determine whether there are any
hazardous material requirements. 41
AIA A201 also includes the following indemnification provision in favor of the owner:
§ 10.3.5 The Contractor shall reimburse the Owner for the cost and expense the Owner incurs
(1) for remediation of hazardous materials or substances the Contractor brings to the site and
negligently handles, or (2) where the Contractor fails to perform its obligations under Section
10.3.1, except to the extent that the cost and expense are due to the Owner’s fault or negli-

Under AIA A201 §10.3.1, a contractor must stop work in the affected area and notify the owner
and architect if: (1) it encounters a hazardous material or substances not addressed in the contract
documents; and (2) through reasonable precautions, the contractor cannot prevent foreseeable bodily
injury or death resulting from such unanticipated hazardous materials. Just what constitutes “unan-
ticipated” hazardous materials and “reasonable precautions” to prevent injury or death under AIA
A201 is unclear, however, so the prudent course for the contractor when encountering hazardous
materials is to stop work. Under AIA A201, work cannot resume until the owner and contractor
enter into a written agreement.
Under AIA A201 §10.3.4, the owner shall not be liable for hazardous materials or substances
that the contractor brings to the site unless such materials or substances are required by the contract
documents.
C-700 Standard General Conditions of the Construction Contract, published by the Engineers
Joint Contract Documents Committee (EJCDC), affords protection by expressly placing the respon-

C-700 sets forth specific procedures for the contractor to provide notice to the owner about the haz-

can be required to resume work in the affected area. 43

This is a thorough, comprehensive, and balanced contract provision dealing with the possibility
of unexpected hazardous materials and the associated risks and liabilities. 46
Regardless of whether a form contract or a custom-drafted contract is used, that contract must
specifically allocate the risk of unexpected hazardous materials. Definitive procedures should also
be set forth so that the parties know precisely how to respond and react to the situation if encountered.
Obtaining indemnification from the consequences of hazardous materials is critical, but by no
means foolproof. Many state laws limit the enforceability of indemnity clauses. These limitations
reflect a public policy against allowing anyone to obtain indemnification from its own negligent
acts. As liability under CERCLA is strict and without regard to negligence, this limitation may not
apply in many situations. Nonetheless, the prudent contractor should consider the law applicable to
its contract and the extent of the enforceability of any indemnity terms associated with hazardous
materials. 47
Many contractors assume tremendous potential liability by naively believing that they can
subcontract away the project’s environmental risk. Although it is true that specialty environmental

III. MANAGEMENT TECHNIQUES FOR ENVIRONMENTAL RISKS DURING CONTRACT PERFORMANCE 	523
remediation contractors are available, it is also true that a contractor is still exposed to regulatory
enforcement actions and personal injury actions despite favorable subcontract language and
indemnification clauses. Given the potential liability, the prudent contractor should subcontract
environmental remediation work to only the most experienced and financially healthy environmental
remediation subcontractors.
From the general contractor’s perspective, it is much better, if possible, to delete environmental
remediation work from the proposed work scope and rely on the owner to contract directly with
an environmental remediation contractor. By doing so, the owner maintains responsibility for the
adequacy and timing of the environmental remediation work, as well as for the proper disposal of
the resulting waste stream. This approach can significantly reduce the environmental risk for the
general construction contractor.
If the contractor begins work with no knowledge of the project’s environmental hazards and then
encounters such hazards during project performance, many owners will attempt to get the general
contractor to simply subcontract out the environmental remediation work. This approach is extremely
risky for the general construction contractor. It also likely places the contractor into an uninsured
position while possibly compromising any potential claim it might have for suspension of its work
due to the undisclosed environmental hazards.
C. 	Insurance
Once the magnitude of environmental liability in the construction industry was recognized, insur-
ance coverage rapidly receded. Now new forms of coverage are becoming available as the insurance
market readjusts. Still, coverage is far from complete and often comes at substantial cost. Gener-
ally, standard forms of insurance, such as commercial general liability (CGL) insurance, will not
afford protection from liability associated with hazardous materials because CGL policies contain
so-called pollution exclusion clauses. Therefore, specific pollution coverage must be procured. (See
Chapter 20.)
Complete insurance protection for unanticipated hazardous materials is either impossible or finan-
cially impractical to obtain. Evaluating specific environmental risk coverage is nonetheless an appro-
priate step. Insurance planning for construction projects, particularly as it relates to insuring against
environmental risks, is too complex and specialized to be left to the inexperienced layperson. Even
contractors that employ full-time insurance specialists or risk managers should rely on insurance
professionals to assist in procuring proper coverage at a competitive price. This is particularly true
in the environmental liability insurance market, which continues to experience rapid change and
evolution as new environmental hazards continue to surface.
Before the contractor decides to assume responsibility, for example, for asbestos abatement, it
is important to scrutinize the contractor’s own insurance to verify that there will be coverage or a
defense if any claims are made against the contractor. As previously mentioned, a standard CGL
policy contains a pollution exclusion that affords the contractor no coverage for any of the risks
inherent in dealing with asbestos. Unless a specialized policy is purchased, there is no insurance
coverage available, yet the potential liability is virtually unlimited even where the environmental
remediation work has been subcontracted.
III. 	MANAGEMENT TECHNIQUES FOR ENVIRONMENTAL RISKS DURING
CONTRACT PERFORMANCE
The increasing use and comprehensiveness of environmental site assessments by owners and lenders
can reduce, but not eliminate, the likelihood of encountering unexpected hazardous materials. To

-- 561 of 771 --

524 	CHAPTER 19 AN OVERVIEW OF ENVIRONMENTAL AND SAFETY CONCERNS
mitigate the risk of unanticipated hazardous materials, constant reassessment of this risk must be
performed at the management level on the job site.
A. 	Management Review of Environmental Risks
The prudent contractor should assign overall responsibility for environmental matters to a senior
company official who will be a resource for the entire company in the evaluation of and protection
against unanticipated hazardous materials on each project. This individual should be familiar with
applicable environmental laws and regulations affecting the company’s work and knowledgeable
about applicable contract provisions, the nature of the construction, the peculiarities of any given
job site, and the need for insurance. Given the importance of these issues, the company official
responsible for environmental matters must be authorized to address unacceptable environmental
risks directly or in conjunction with other company officials. The contractor should also have a
specific and mandatory written procedure to be implemented immediately upon encountering unex-
pected hazardous materials.
One individual, however, cannot completely manage all environmental risks that a contractor may
encounter in its ongoing operations. Therefore, all personnel, especially project management, must
also be aware of such risks and be prepared to respond or at least seek advice and direction as to a
response.
Finally, efforts to address environmental risks at the management level will be wasted if such
efforts do not extend to each job site and the individuals working in the field.
B. 	Have a Response Plan
When environmental risks are encountered, the appropriate response should be according to a writ-
ten and mandatory procedure reinforced through in-house training. Accordingly, before construction
starts, this standard procedure should be reviewed and supplemented with the areas of responsibility
for specific individuals for the new project. Contact information should be listed for all federal, state,
or local agencies requiring notification or from whom an emergency response may be required. The
procedure should also be coordinated with representatives of the owner, design professional, and con-
struction manager as well as subcontractors. Although the response will be the primary responsibility
of construction project management, the response cannot be triggered or properly implemented with-
out the aid of all project personnel, including subcontractors and their employees. Once the response
plan is developed, relevant aspects of the plan should be reviewed in project meetings, subcontractor
coordination meetings, and toolbox safety meetings to ensure that it is understood.
C. 	Immediately Stop Work in the Affected Area
Generally, unanticipated hazardous materials are not the contractor’s responsibility. If they are sim-
ply discovered but not disturbed, the hazardous materials certainly present a problem, but, from the
contractor’s perspective, a problem of limited scope. If, however, the contractor goes beyond merely
exposing the hazardous materials and disturbs them, the contractor may have unwittingly subjected
itself to liability under CERCLA and/or other statutory or common law causes of action. A prudent
contractor should avoid performing any further work in the affected area or any other areas where
the same condition might exist. Indeed, this is required in ConsensusDocs 200, 300, and 410; AIA
A201; and EJCDC C-700.
D. 	Provide Immediate Notice
Upon discovery of a suspected hazardous material, the contractor should immediately notify the
owner, the design professional, and any construction manager. Written confirmation of any oral

-- 562 of 771 --

IV. MOLD: DEVELOPING A PROGRAM TO LIMIT LIABILITY 	525
notice should be provided as soon as practical. The notice should make clear that the unanticipated
hazardous materials are the owner’s responsibility and that the contractor is awaiting direction from
the owner or the owner’s representative about how to proceed. The contractor should also expressly
reserve its rights to seek indemnification from all claims resulting from encountering hazardous
materials and to seek adjustments in contract time and price based on any work stoppage. In this
notice, the contractor should also consider addressing other concerns, such as providing notice to
regulatory agencies, insurance carriers, and other project delivery team members.
The owner or its representative certainly should report the release or spill of a hazardous material
or substance to the appropriate government officials. However, because the contractor may also be
deemed a “person in charge” of the site and therefore required to promptly report the release or spill,
a prudent contractor will also report the incident.
E. 	Do Not Resume Work without Proper Authorization
Once hazardous materials are uncovered, the contractor should not resume work in the affected
areas without written authorization from the owner and the appropriate government agency. All
such authorizations should be clear and in writing. If the owner orally directs the contractor to
clean up the hazardous material, the contractor should insist on specific written cleanup instruc-
tions and confirmation that such instructions have been approved by the appropriate government
agency. The contractor should also require that the owner specifically indemnify the contractor
from the risks of undertaking the cleanup. Even if the owner agrees to these points, the contrac-
tor should carefully consider whether it wants to undertake the additional risks of environmental
clean-up work. As a practical matter, the owner’s indemnification is only as good as its ability to pay
and does not insulate the contractor from third-party claims. Undertaking the cleanup of hazardous
materials can cause problems with the contractor’s insurance carrier and surety if environmental
cleanups are not within the contractor’s typical line of work on which its insurance and bonding
are based.
IV. 	MOLD: DEVELOPING A PROGRAM TO LIMIT LIABILITY
“Toxic mold” has become another in the modern lexicon of environmental risk terms. The fact that
the adverse health effects from exposure to mold are not fully known48 has not stopped a steady
procession of construction defect claims and multimillion-dollar lawsuits. The frequent occurrence
of mold during or as a result of the construction process, combined with the perceived health risks
and a heightened public awareness of such risks, has created a breeding ground for litigation and the
corresponding costs and uncertainty of such litigation.49
Specifically, OSHA has implemented the following regulations pertaining to mold:
• General Industry – 29 CFR §1910
• General Industry (Sanitation) – 29 CFR §1910.141
• Shipyard Employment – 29 CFR §1915
• Construction Industry – 29 CFR §1926
• Construction Industry (Sanitation) – 29 CFR §1926.51
48See, e.g., Fraser v. 301-52 Townhouse Corp., 831 N.Y. S.2d 347 (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 2006).
49 Individual states have begun developing their own mold-remediation requirements. For example, on August 18, 2017, the
Texas Commission of Licensing and Regulation (Commission) adopted its own set of rules for the Mold Assessors and
Remediators program, located at 16 TAC, Chapter 78. The Commission’s rules were effective November 1, 2017, (42 Tex.
Reg. 4619).

-- 563 of 771 --

526 	CHAPTER 19 AN OVERVIEW OF ENVIRONMENTAL AND SAFETY CONCERNS
Preventing the rampant growth and spread of mold requires controlling temperature, humidity,
and moisture in the construction environment. To prevent, limit, and control the presence of mois-
ture requires a cooperative and coordinated effort by the project delivery team, which includes: (1) a
good design; (2) consideration of mold risks in the selection and specification of building materials
as well as construction means and methods; (3) a thorough construction quality assurance/quality
control program (including, but not limited to, documented inspections); and (4) proper project doc-
umentation.
One of the first questions a construction professional should ask in assessing and addressing the
risk of mold is, “Do I have insurance for this?” As is often the case, the answer may be unclear. The
standard CGL policy carried by most contractors contains a number of exclusions that may allow
the contractor’s insurance carrier to assert that the risk of mold is not covered. These include certain
“business risk” exclusions and the “pollution exclusion.” Courts that have addressed the issue have
reached conflicting conclusions as to whether mold-related claims are covered by a contractor’s CGL
policy or whether the insurance carrier is relieved of responsibility for such claims under the standard
pollution exclusion.
The primary legal theory under which mold contamination litigation arises is the common law
doctrine of negligence. 50 In such cases, the design professional, contractor, subcontractor, or devel-
oper owes a duty of care to the plaintiff. To determine whether a party has breached its duty of care,
the plaintiff must determine the “duty” by examining relevant construction standards. By demon-
strating a specialist’s failure to abide by the practices of other similarly situated specialists, claims
of negligence involving a design professional are often accompanied by a professional malpractice
claim.
Fraud and misrepresentation claims arise from a false statement that is made by a defendant
if the defendant knew or reasonably should have known that the statement was false when made,
it intended the plaintiff to rely upon the statement, and the plaintiff relied on the statement to its
detriment. Under such cause of action, an owner may be liable for fraud and misrepresentation if the
owner represents that the structure was inspected and found to be “clean” when such an inspection
was never conducted, and mold was found to be present. If such a fraudulent statement or false
impression causes another party to enter into a contract in reliance on such a statement or impression,
the innocent individual may have a right to have the contract rescinded because of the fraudulent
inducement to enter into the contract.
V. 	ENVIRONMENTALLY FRIENDLY CONSTRUCTION: GREEN BUILDINGS
In addition to environmental risks in construction because of hazardous materials, water quality, and
air quality, industry professionals should understand the movement toward environmentally friendly
construction. The “green building” concept has become an industry trend, the purpose of which is
to promote design and construction using means, methods, and materials that present less risk to the
environment and less risk of exposure to environmental contaminants.
A. 	LEED Certification
The United States Green Building Council (USGBC)—a nonprofit organization comprised of own-
ers, developers, facility managers, design professionals, general contractors, subcontractors, suppli-
ers, and government agencies—has tasked itself with identifying green-building practices. This effort
50See Stanley Martin Cos., Inc. v. Universal Forest Prods. Shoffner LLC, 396 F.Supp.2d 606 (D. Md. 2005); Sabella v. Wisler,
377 P.2d 889 (Cal. 1963).

-- 564 of 771 --

V. ENVIRONMENTALLY FRIENDLY CONSTRUCTION: GREEN BUILDINGS 	527
resulted in the Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED) Green Building Rating
SystemTM . 51
LEED is shorthand for what makes a construction project green, environmentally friendly, or
energy efficient. LEED is actually a series of checklists targeted at specialized projects. Projects
accumulate points by meeting criteria and, based on those points, are designated LEED certified
(the baseline), LEED Silver, LEED Gold, or LEED Platinum.
Familiarity with the LEED certification system is required for government contractors and is rec-
ommended for contractors working in the private sector. Many public entities at the federal,52 state, 53
and local levels 54 now require that their public projects meet LEED certification standards and offer
incentives to private LEED projects. As time goes on, more and more government agencies may
add such requirements and current requirements, as noted above, may become more stringent. The
USGBC has created several different guides to assist contractors in obtaining LEED certification.55
B. 	Green Globes Certification
In 2012, because of concerns about the increasingly stringent LEED standards, 56 members of
Congress and the American High-Performance Buildings Coalition (AHPBC), a trade organiza-
tion that represents suppliers in the construction industry, asked the United States General Services
Administration (GSA) to consider an alternative to LEED Certification.56 The AHPBC suggested
“Green Globes,” a building assessment and certification program promoted and operated by the
Green Building Institute (GBI) in the United States. 57
The Green Globes program has three modules: Green Globes for New Construction, Green Globes
for Continual Improvement of Existing Buildings, and Green Globes CIEB for Healthcare. The
Green Globes rating system gives projects a rating of up to 1,000 points based on efficient use of
energy, water, and resources, as well as low emissions. Buildings that receive 35 percent or more of
the 1,000 points possible are eligible for certification. Projects may receive a certification for one
(35–54 percent), two (55–69 percent), three (70–84 percent), or four Green Globes (85–100 percent).
On October 25, 2013, the GSA sent a recommendation to the U.S. Department of Energy for the
use of green-building rating systems, stating that agencies may choose either LEED or Green Globes
certification. 58 The minimum goal for new buildings is LEED Certified or 1 Green Globe. After
GSA’s recommendation, agencies will accept Green Globes as an alternative program for assessing
building sustainability.59

C. 	Design and Construction Issues Affected by Green Building Construction
The earlier in the planning phase that the owner decides to seek LEED or Green Globes certification,
the lower the construction costs. As a rule, design costs for certified projects exceed design costs for
noncertified projects. Arguably, however, the increased emphasis on front-end design reduces con-
struction costs by potentially reducing the number of changes required. If an owner wants or requires
certification, the project participants need to understand the process when estimating, bidding, and
building the job. LEED touches many aspects of the construction project including, but not limited
to, site selection, selection of materials, handling of construction waste, storm water, MEP design,
and building finishes. Green Globes considers project management, site, selection of materials and
resources, reduction and efficient use of energy and water, emissions, and indoor environment.
When an owner decides to obtain a LEED or green-building certification for a project, the first
step is designating either a LEED Accredited Professional (AP)60 or Green Globes Professional to
oversee and shepherd the process. No matter who serves as the LEED or Green Globes Professional,
for a project to be cost effective, all project participants—not just the designers—need to understand
from the beginning the requirements for certification. Contractors may be surprised that they are
likely working in ways that would earn points for certification.
LEED projects accumulate points in the following six core areas:
1. Sustainable sites (for example, conforming to the required storm water permit requirements)
2. Water efficiency (for example, capturing rainwater, using native landscaping, and using inno-
vative water-efficient fixtures)
3. Energy and atmosphere (for example, conforming with the American Society of Heating,
Refrigeration, and Air Conditioning Engineers 61 standards reducing energy demand, using
HVAC and fire suppression systems without hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs) or Halons,
and using onsite renewable energy (for example, photovoltaics) or other green energy
4. Materials and resources (for example, storing and collecting recyclables, reusing shell and
non-shell components in renovations, diverting construction waste from the landfill, using
recycled or rapidly renewable materials, and using local or regional materials)
5. Pollutants and indoor environmental air quality (for example, choosing low or no-emitting
materials adhesives, sealants, paints, carpets, and composite wood products; flushing or filter-
ing out any pollutants)
6. Innovation in the design process
The LEED AP must submit documentation to support every point the project is claiming, so all
project participants involved with a particular point must document it.62
AIA B214 – 2012 Standard Form of Architect’s Services: LEED Certification specifically
addresses an architect’s duties and responsibilities when the owner seeks LEED certification. Under
AIA B214, an architect’s services include, among other things: (1) conducting a predesign workshop
where the LEED rating system will be reviewed and LEED points will be targeted; (2) preparing a
LEED Certification Plan; (3) monitoring the LEED Certification process; (4) providing LEED spec-
ifications for inclusion in the contract documents; and (5) preparing a LEED Certification Report

D. 	Bearing the Risk: Legal Issues Raised by LEED and Green Globes
Although LEED and Green Building certifications are an emerging trend, the common law has not
yet developed as to the nature or extent of liability related to such certification. Potential issues and
risks will likely include:
• Who warrants the content of materials for certification purposes?
• Does certification operate as an affirmative defense to building defect claims after construction?
• Is a contractor liable for moisture (or mold) issues related to mandated mechanical or
moisture-control systems?
• Who bears the risk of the project not meeting criteria?
• Is it enough that the project meets the applicable criteria or that it actually be certified by the
USGBC or USGBI?
• Who has the authority to decide whether a project meets LEED requirements if not the USGBC
or USGBI?
• Who bears the risk of a project not meeting the level of certification required by the owner?
What is the remedy?
As with all projects, the participants should evaluate the contract documents carefully to deter-
mine the potential risks associated with environmentally friendly green-building projects. The pru-
dent construction industry professional should pay close attention to any mention of LEED or Green
Globes and know its responsibilities, if any, with regard to the respective certification processes.
E. 	Post-Construction Obligations of Green Building Construction
Pursuant to Federal Acquisition Regulation § 36.104, after completion of a green-building construc-
tion project, agencies must exercise sustainable operation and management practices, implement
efficient renovation and repair practices, and prevent excessive pollution and waste. These agency
obligations directly affect contractors, as the long-term obligations of green building influence each

VI. 	CONSTRUCTION SAFETY
Despite both increasing safety standards and improving safety records, construction remains a dan-
gerous business. There were 971 fatal construction workplace injuries recorded in the U.S. in 2017.64
Safety is an integral concern in the construction industry and a field where questions frequently
arise regarding compliance with job-site safety requirements.
A. 	Sources of Safety Requirements: OSHA-Specific Project Procedures
In the United States, the predominant regulatory scheme governing job-site safety on construction
projects is the federal Occupational Safety and Health Act (OSHA)65 and the corresponding regula-
tions written and enforced by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration. 66
The Secretary of Labor is responsible for implementing OSHA standards by promulgating safety
regulations through formal rule-making proceedings. 67 OSHA compliance officers may enforce the
regulations by conducting unannounced, routine onsite inspections in accordance with OSHA’s Field
Operations Manual (FOM) 68 as well as investigations when violations of OSHA occur. 69
Violation of OSHA regulations may trigger a range of civil and criminal penalties. There are
four kinds of OSHA violations: willful, serious, repeated, and other-than-serious. Serious and
other-than-serious violations can result in fines up to $12,934 per violation, 70 whereas willful
or repeated violations can result in fines up to $129,336 per violation. 71 Willful violations that
result in death can result in six months of imprisonment. Further, although such violations do not
constitute negligence as a matter of law, or “negligence per se,” they are admissible as evidence of
the applicable standard of care in third-party civil suits.72
In addition to Department of Labor regulations, many federal agencies also publish their own
manuals or directives, establishing health and safety policies for construction projects managed

Such state-specific safety programs often pertain to higher-risk construction operations, such as

far too many preventable injuries and illnesses occur in the workplace. The following is a list of the
top 10 most frequently cited standards following inspections of worksites by federal OSHA.77

Of course, the best way to avoid liability for job-site personal injuries is to prevent accidents from
happening. Preventing accidents will: (1) reduce exposure to fines and liability under federal and state
safety laws, such as those enforced by OSHA; (2) reduce premiums for workers’ compensation and
liability insurance; (3) reduce the odds that the company may be liable for injuries not covered by
indemnification or insurance; and (4) help to ensure positive past performance evaluations for future
proposals. Four basic steps to preventing accidents are as follows:
1. Every company working a construction site should develop and implement a written safety
program, commonly referred to as a safety manual.80
2. Management and employees must be committed to safety and to complying with the com-
pany’s safety manual and must demonstrate that commitment to everyone working on the
project.
3. Companies should appoint a qualified person who ensures compliance with the safety pro-
gram by conducting inspections and employee training and keeping proper records that safety
measures are being maintained.
4. Job forepersons should continuously perform project-safety inspections and conduct necessary
safety training or toolbox safety meetings.
C. 	Who Is Responsible for Project Safety?
Because of the number of entities potentially involved in a construction project, as well as the range
of legal relationships that may exist between and among them, a simple answer to this question is
extremely difficult to provide. OSHA regulations often provide part of the answer. The contractual
relationships among owners, general contractors, subcontractors, suppliers, construction managers,
and other design professionals can shuffle, shift, and ultimately allocate primary responsibility for
many recurring safety issues and therefore help to further answer the question.
These legal principles notwithstanding, all employers are responsible for providing a safe work-
place and ensuring compliance with standards, rules, and regulations issued under OSHA. Employers
are also encouraged to examine their workplace to make sure that they conform with all state, local,
and federal requirements.
1. 	Contractors
A contractor, just like anyone else, may be liable for actions that do not comply with the law or were
performed without due care and, as a result, directly caused an injury. Although one contractor is
generally not responsible for acts of another independent contractor,81 there are many exceptions
to this traditional rule. For example, under certain circumstances, a general contractor can be held
liable for the injuries to a subcontractor’s employee even though the employee’s injuries were directly
caused by the subcontractor’s negligence.
Some jurisdictions impose responsibilities on contractors to prevent subcontractor employees
from being exposed to hazards not ordinarily found on a construction project. Liability can even
be imposed for “ordinary” hazards if the contractor knows, or should know, that the subcontractor

liability on contractors for injuries to subcontractor employees where the contractor retains

common when a contractor assumes some type of safety-related supervisory duty, such as providing
a safety supervisor, initiating a safety program, or ensuring compliance with safety rules and

Other courts have predicated liability on the general contractor’s safety responsibilities in

When permissible by state law, general contractors may elect to include indemnification provi-

2. 	Design Professionals
A design professional, such as an architect or engineer, can also be liable for the injuries of some-
one else’s employee even though the design professional did not directly cause the employee’s
injuries. Such liability can be based on either the contractual or voluntary assumption of certain
responsibilities.89
Although most construction contracts place primary responsibility for project safety on the gen-
eral contractor, they may also name the design professional as the owner’s representative during
construction and require the design professional to inspect or observe the work to ensure compliance
with plans and specifications. Often an injured worker will try to establish that the design profes-
sional failed to adequately fulfill these duties, resulting in an unsafe work condition that caused the
resultant injury.
In general, design professionals’ supervisory duties on a project are for the benefit of the owner
and are primarily intended to ensure that work is completed in accordance with the construction
documents.90 Thus, design professionals are often found to have no safety duties to injured workers
unless such duties are clearly written into their contracts.91 Some courts, however, have found a
design professional to have a duty to provide safety supervision even though a general contractor
may have contractually assumed primary responsibility for project safety. These courts hold that the
design professional has a duty to ensure that the general contractor complies with its contractual
duties.92 In response to such rulings, design professionals often place provisions in their contracts
clarifying their safety responsibilities on a project. 93
Moreover, even though a design professional may not be contractually responsible for project
safety, the design professional can still face potential liability for personal injuries on the job by
voluntarily assuming extracontractual responsibilities based on: (1) the scope of the design pro-
fessional’s actual supervision or control over the work; (2) the extent of the design professional’s
participation in the project; and (3) whether the design professional assumed responsibility for safety
precautions. 94 A design professional can also be held liable for failing to take appropriate action
where it actually knows of a safety violation even though it has not contractually or voluntarily
assumed safety responsibilities.95
AIA A201 – 2017 § 11.1.1 attempts to provide the architect with an additional measure of
protection—even where the architect might be liable for project safety—by requiring the general
contractor to name not only the owner but also the architect as an additional insured on the
contractor’s comprehensive general liability insurance policy. Thus, under the AIA contract, even
where the architect might incur liability for project safety, it would seek to transfer this risk to the
general contractor and the contractor’s insurance provider.

3. 	Construction Managers
Generally, a construction manager is responsible for reviewing safety programs developed by each
contractor and for coordinating a safety program for the entire project. A construction manager with
such responsibilities may be responsible for personal injuries on the job even though the construc-
tion manager did not directly cause the injuries. On at least one occasion, a construction manager
contractually obligated to supervise overall project safety was liable for an injury where one of the
construction manager’s employees negligently failed to observe or prevent a subcontractor laying an
unsecured plank that later caused an injury. The court found the construction manager liable even
though an indemnification clause was set forth in the construction manager’s contract. 96
4. 	Owners
An owner usually delegates responsibility for project safety to an independent contractor, such as a
general contractor, design professional, or construction manager. As a general rule, and absent some
form of control over an independent contractor’s method of operation, the construction project owner
is not liable for injuries to the contractor’s employees.97
Three recognized exceptions to this general rule are where: (1) the owner has undertaken a non-
delegable duty based on a contract; (2) the activity is “inherently or intrinsically dangerous”; and
(3) the owner negligently exercises or retains control over an independent contractor’s work. 98 For
this last exception to apply, the owner generally must retain some degree of control over the manner
in which the independent contractor performs its work. It is usually not enough merely to retain the
right to stop the work, to inspect the contractor’s progress, or to make suggestions or recommenda-
tions that need not be followed. Instead, the owner must retain supervision or control such that the
contractor is not entirely free to do its work as it sees fit. 99
D. 	Indemnification
One way to avoid exposure to job-site safety liability is to seek contractual indemnification for any
losses. Although it may not always be possible to obtain indemnification agreements as part of con-
tract negotiations, at a minimum, the parties to a construction contract should specifically state each
party’s responsibilities for project safety. While a contractor will be responsible for the safety of its
own employees in carrying out their assigned duties, the contract should clearly exclude responsi-
bility for the safety of others on the project.
In contrast, if a contractor agrees to be contractually responsible for project safety, this agreement
will likely include responsibility for injuries to all persons on the project even though the contractor
did not directly cause the injury. Where a contractor assumes such responsibilities, it may be possible
to obtain an indemnification agreement from other companies working on the project.
E. 	Workers’ Compensation Statutes
A common claim faced by a construction company is from an injured employee. Liability for such
a claim will likely be addressed through a state workers’ compensation statute, which at mini-
mum requires employers to obtain insurance, usually covering medical expenses, disability income,
and death benefits. Additionally, standard workers’ compensation insurance policies usually cover

third-party claims against the employer. For example, an employee may sue a jackhammer supplier
for their injuries, claiming that the injury was caused by a defect in the jackhammer. The jack-
hammer supplier may then try to bring the employer into the lawsuit, alleging that the employee’s
injuries were not caused by a defect in the jackhammer but by the employer’s failure to maintain the
jackhammer. Such a third-party claim may be covered by the workers’ compensation policy.
Workers’ compensation statutes typically hold the employer liable for its employee’s workplace
injuries regardless of the employer’s fault and, in return, limit the amount of compensation that the
employee may recover in an action to that provided under the workers’ compensation statute. The
employer can lose statutory immunity from civil suit under two circumstances: (1) the employer’s
immunity may be stripped if the employer fails to procure the required workers’ compensation insur-
ance; 100 and (2) an employer will generally not have any immunity for “willful” or “intentional”
conduct. What constitutes willful or intentional conduct varies from state to state. Courts in many
states have interpreted this exception as applying only if the employer specifically intended to cause
the employee’s injuries.101 Some courts and legislatures, however, have required less than inten-
tional harm, and apply this exception to situations where an employer is aware of a risk created by
the violation of a safety statute.102
Finally, as previously mentioned, workers’ compensation laws are intended to address payment
to employees injured, disabled, or killed in the performance of their job, without regard to liability
or fault of the employer. This strict liability scheme may not, however, insulate the construction pro-
fessional from liability for workplace injuries where the construction professional is in a contractual
relationship with the injured worker’s employer. Accordingly, reliance on workers’ compensation
laws should not be a substitute for negotiating contractual provisions limiting responsibility for
project safety and indemnifying the construction professional from liability for injuries to employees
of others on the worksite.
F. 	Hazardous Chemicals
The OSHA Hazard Communication Standard,103 governs the evaluation and communication of haz-
ards associated with chemicals on construction sites. This standard requires chemical manufacturers,
distributors, or importers of hazardous chemicals to provide safety data sheets (formerly known as
material safety data sheets) for each hazardous chemical they produce or import to communicate the
health concerns with exposure. Construction owners are required to have safety data sheets for their
exposed employees and must also provide training.
Previously, chemical manufactures and importers were permitted to convey the hazard infor-
mation in whatever format they chose. This modified standard provides a standardized format for
classifying chemicals and labeling the potential hazards.
Major changes to the Hazard Communication Standard include:
• Hazard classification: 29 CFR § 1910.1200 provides specific criteria to address health and
physical hazards as well as classification of chemical mixtures.
• Labels: Chemical manufacturers and importers are required to provide a label on all hazardous
chemicals that includes a signal word, pictogram, hazard statement, and precautionary state-
ment for each hazard class and category.

G. 	Occupational Exposure to Crystalline Silica
Crystalline silica—a common mineral found in construction materials, including sand, soil, abra-
sives, concrete, and filter aids—becomes hazardous when airborne (known as respirable crystalline
silica). Respirable crystalline silica is created when workers drill, chip, grind or mix minerals
containing crystalline silica, thus releasing tiny particles of silica into the air. In the construction
industry, the most severe exposure occurs during abrasive sand-blasting, jack-hammering, drilling,
saw-cutting, concrete/grout-mixing, and grinding materials.
On March 25, 2016, OSHA published new standards 104 regulating workplace exposure to crys-
talline silica. The new standards require employers to measure and record levels of respirable crys-
talline silica when employees will, or reasonably may, be exposed to silica at or above 25 μg/m3
(micrograms of silica per cubic meter of air), averaged over an eight-hour day. Crystalline silica lev-
els above the action level trigger regular monitoring until two consecutive measures, taken at least a
week apart, are below 25 μg/m3 .
Under the new standards, which were enforced starting September 23, 2017, employers are
responsible for the following:
• Limiting employee exposure to respirable crystalline silica. Under the new regulations, the
personal exposure limit (PEL) for crystalline silica is reduced from 250 .tg/m3 to 50 μg/ m3,
as an eight-hour time-weighted average (TWA). If the PEL exceeds 50 .tg/m3, then engineering
controls (detailed in the regulation)105 must be used.
• Monitoring exposure levels and providing medical monitoring to their employees if their levels
are anticipated to exceed an eight-hour TWA of 25 .tg/m3 for at least 30 days in one year (this
is classified as the action level).
• Offering chest X-rays and lung function tests every three years to workers exposed to respirable
crystalline silica at or above an eight-hour TWA of 25 .tg/m3 for at least 30 days in one year.
• Offering chest X-rays and lung function tests every three years to construction workers required
to wear a respirator for 30 or more days in a year.
• Training employees to limit their respirable crystalline silica exposure.
• Maintaining records of employee exposure to respirable crystalline silica and employer-
provided medical examinations.
The Construction Industry Safety Coalition (CISC), a group of national trade associations, includ-
ing the Associated Builders and Contractors, The Associated General Contractors, and American
Subcontractors Association, have called for the withdrawal of OSHA’s proposed rule. On December
22, 2017, the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia rejected all of the industry’s
challenges to the regulation. 106 At the forefront of the District of Columbia Court of Appeal’s opin-
ion, it outlines “the substantial evidence standard,” 107 under which OSHA needed only to provide

➣ 	POINTS TO REMEMBER
• Many overlapping federal and state laws create a complex web of rules relating to hazardous
materials and substances, water and air quality, environmental risk issues, and workplace safety
affecting construction. These laws impose broad liability as well as regulatory and reporting
requirements.
• Conduct a prebid environmental review of the contract documents. Assess potential safety or
environmental risks for each particular project before entering into a contract.
• Make an environmental prebid inquiry on every project.
• During contract negotiations, be wary of standardized contract clauses that may impose burden-
some responsibility and liability for workplace safety or environmental risks. Allocate the risk
of encountering unexpected hazardous materials in the contract through specifically drafted
clauses.
• Appoint a senior manager or risk assessment team to become thoroughly familiar with federal,
state, and local environmental and safety laws and to oversee compliance with these laws.
• Educate the job-site workforce regarding environmental and job-site safety laws and what must
be done to comply with them. Make everyone part of the environmental and safety risk man-
agement team.
• Develop a comprehensive safety plan and environmental response plan. Employees should be
safety conscious and sensitive to environmental risks.
• Evaluate insurance coverage with respect to environmental and job-site safety risks and
liabilities.
