damages. By displaying this information in an attractive, visual way, in combination with other
written and oral presentations, the claim can be advanced in a more compelling and persuasive man-
ner. However, the goal of the demonstrative presentation is lost unless it is clear (which usually means
summarized and simplified), understandable, and firmly supported by underlying foundational facts.
Discussions of the importance and usefulness of demonstrative evidence as a means of persuasion
are generally found in trial-advocacy materials. But there is no need to hold such a powerful and
effective tool in reserve until trial or arbitration. Demonstrative evidence should be developed and
used to simplify the claim and to persuade the other side as soon as possible during negotiations or
mediation.
IV. 	CONTEMPORANEOUS RECORDS
The importance of creating and maintaining contemporaneous project records cannot be overem-
phasized. The success of any claim presentation, whether formal or informal, depends largely on
the quality and comprehensiveness of reliable documentary and visual evidence. Contemporaneous
records engender integrity and trustworthiness essential to persuading the opposing party in a negoti-
ation or mediation, an arbitrator, or a judge and jury. Federal and state rules of evidence used in court
trials require contemporaneity in order to admit certain types of documents at trial. For example, the
“business records” exception to the hearsay rule is often the only avenue by which certain project
records are admissible in court. Under the Federal Rules of Evidence, a project document qualifies
as a “business record” (that is, “Records of a Regularly Conducted Activity”) when it: (1) contempo-
raneously records events or conditions; (2) is authored by a person with knowledge; (3) is routinely
kept in the regular course of the business; and (4) lacks any indication of untrustworthiness.4 Most
states adhere to the same or a similar evidentiary rule.
All projects need documentation systems in place that preserve a record of activities from the
time a project is offered for bids or proposals through physical completion of the work, acceptance
by the owner, and financial close-out. Documentation programs must be designed and implemented
in a manner that accurately and comprehensively records job progress and problems in “real time.”
Documentation programs can take many forms and can be in paper or electronic format, or both.
Common types of project records include RFIs, meeting minutes, prime and subcontractor daily
reports, payroll records, equipment usage and maintenance reports, materials delivery reports, sur-
vey data, correspondence and email, job-site diaries, progress schedules and updates, progress and
defective-work photographs and video, as-built drawings, and cost documentation. The documenta-
tion system should be designed to record project progress and events on a continual basis, as well
as to assure compliance with contractual notice provisions, circumstances giving rise to requests for
time extensions, extra work, changes, differing site conditions, and grounds for or against termina-
tion. The system must be designed so that all of these events are thoroughly documented as they
occur. The properly implemented documentation program, faithfully followed, enhances the like-
lihood of favorably resolving disputes without arbitration or litigation or of winning disputes that
cannot be amicably resolved.
V. 	COMPONENTS OF A WELL-PREPARED CLAIM DOCUMENT
Construction claims can be technically complex and factually intensive; therefore, simplicity to pro-
mote prompt understanding, while making the claim interesting and well supported, is the key to
4See Fed. R. Evid. 803(6).

-- 665 of 771 --

628 	CHAPTER 23 RESOLVING CONSTRUCTION DISPUTES
effective claim preparation and presentation. One way to synthesize the claim is to use a claim
document (letter or memorandum)—that is, a written synopsis of the claim that can be presented
to the opposition at the early stages of the dispute. As with essentially every other aspect of claim
preparation, the claim document serves two alternate purposes. First, its immediate and primary goal
is to bring about a prompt and satisfactory resolution of the claim. Failing that, the second purpose
of the claim document is to provide an outline or plan for further claim prosecution.
The claim document provides an opportunity for the claimant to explain the matter in a compre-
hensive chronological or other logical fashion. The process of preparing the claim document is an
important step in developing a claim strategy, because it requires the claimant to refine and synthesize
the underlying facts of the claim from beginning to end. The claim document should be viewed as
telling a story. It should have a clear and definite theme that can be easily communicated, understood,
and remembered. The theme should be the strongest argument supporting the claimant’s theory of
recovery.
The typical claim involves gathering a considerable quantity of facts. Presenting and arguing
each and every one of these facts will simply overwhelm and confuse the reader. When multiple and
unrelated claims are presented in one document, the document must be structured to emphasize the
strongest claim and to segregate other support for the claim.
The primary communicative component of the claim document is reference to pertinent con-
tractual requirements and a factual narrative. Although this narrative will certainly focus on the
claimant’s point of view, it should not be expressed in overly argumentative or combative terms.
Instead, to the extent possible, the facts should speak for themselves. The guiding principle must be
“facts not feelings,” leaving out most adjectives and adverbs. The writing style should be clear and
precise, stated in short, declarative sentences, but should not read like technical specifications. It is,
after all, a story, not simply a recital of a string of facts. The narrative should be comprehensive and
logically organized so it can be used as a resource throughout negotiations and further prosecution
of the claim. If the complexity of the matter makes the narrative exceedingly long, preface it with an
executive summary.
The factual narrative is often followed by a written discussion of the legal principles that support
and illustrate the theories on which the claim is based. Assistance from an attorney experienced
in construction claims is generally required to fashion the legal arguments and otherwise ensure
that the factual narrative is presented in a manner consistent with applicable legal principles. The
need for, or extent of, a legal discussion is generally geared to the expertise or experience of the
opposition’s ultimate decision-maker. For example, in federal construction contracts, certain theories
of entitlement are so firmly established and recognized on all levels that little or no legal discussion
is required. In other situations, the legal discussion may be a crucial element in causing the other
side to recognize its liability and exposure. A one-time owner may have no idea of what comprises
a differing site condition or why the contractor should be paid for the extra work the owner caused.
Claims against local governmental entities that contract regularly may be ruled on by elected officials
who also require an education in construction law before they can be expected to recognize the need
to settle a claim.
Pricing the claim and supporting such calculations is every bit as important as establishing lia-
bility for the claim and causation of damages (extra costs and profit). The claim document must
recognize the importance of damages and include a specific dollar figure and fairly detailed cost
analysis and breakdown showing added labor, equipment, and materials, plus applicable markups.
Supporting information and sources should be identified, summarized, and appended if they are not
too voluminous.
Finally, the claim document should be used to showcase and highlight the most persuasive doc-
umentary and demonstrative evidence. The most potent documents should be quoted or even repro-
duced in their entirety in the body of the narrative. Documents that do not merit incorporation into

-- 666 of 771 --

VI. CALCULATING AND PROVING DAMAGES 	629
the text, but that are referenced and support the claim, can be included in an indexed appendix of
cross-referenced exhibits. In this manner, the narrative can be reviewed without having to sift through
every bit of paper, but the reader will know that backup is readily available.
In addition to supporting documents, charts, spreadsheets, graphs, drawings, and photographs,
other demonstrative and visual evidence should be incorporated into the claim document to the extent
practicable. Similarly, consider including relevant reports by experts as exhibits attached to the claim
document and, within the narrative, incorporating appropriate references to, and quotes from, the
reports.
In certain situations, the nature of the claim or the opposition’s character or capacity may counsel
against submitting an extensive claim document. The opposition may lack the financial resources or
genuine interest in resolving the claim by negotiation, which is a primary goal of the claim docu-
ment. Instead, the opposition may seek a one-way flow of information, willing to receive a detailed
presentation of the claim, but unwilling to explain or document any response, defense, or counter-
claim until trial. The claimant must evaluate whether pursuing the race for disclosure by providing
a claim document will ultimately eliminate roadblocks to negotiation and settlement or simply bet-
ter equip the opposition to defend the claim, without a commensurate benefit on information from
the opposition. Generally, a sound, well-documented and prepared claim should withstand and be
improved by the opposition’s feedback. Moreover, even if the decision is made not to submit an
extensive claim document, that should not stop the claimant from preparing a claim document for
internal use to better synthesize the claim and to prepare for whatever proceeding may follow. Of
course, if the contract mandates formal claim submission, the claimant should follow such a require-
ment, although the extent of the submission may vary. In most instances, preparing and submitting
a detailed claim serves to shape the debate in the claimant’s favor.
VI. 	CALCULATING AND PROVING DAMAGES
The issue in construction disputes that typically receives the most attention is liability. Does a differ-
ing site condition exist? Who caused the delay and is it compensable? No less important however, are
the issues of causation—linking the liability for the compensable event to damages or costs flowing
from the events that give rise to liability, and the amount of those damages or time extension. Too
often, calculating and proving damages takes a backseat, with little precision or scrutiny applied
until the eve of the trial. That approach can result in an entirely misguided claim effort, missed
opportunities for settlement, and eventually loss at trial or in other dispute forums. An early analysis
of damages can help determine whether a claim really exists and the best means of preparing and
positioning the claim for affirmative recovery.
The problem of calculating and proving damages can be substantially reduced by maintaining
financial books and records in accordance with industry standards and initiating proper project cost
accounting at the project’s inception, including fully developed pre-award bid or proposal calcula-
tions. This may help provide an early indication of whether unanticipated work, delay, disruption,
or extra costs have been incurred upon encountering certain events. Once a claim is identified, these
cost-accounting procedures can be used to capture the extra or unanticipated costs—for example,
by separately cost-coding and accounting for extra work. Accounting measures can be established
to segregate and carefully maintain separate records flowing from an apparent compensable event.
If such a procedure is followed, proof of damages can be reduced to little more than the presenta-
tion of evidence of separate accounts. Unfortunately, this ideal situation seldom exists because the
problem is not recognized in time to set up separate accounting procedures, the maintenance of sep-
arate accounts is simply not possible because of an inability to isolate costs, or no attempt is made
to establish the requisite procedures. These circumstances necessitate developing some sufficiently

-- 667 of 771 --

630 	CHAPTER 23 RESOLVING CONSTRUCTION DISPUTES
reliable formula that establishes a valid, reliable, and convincing basis for negotiations or permits an
arbitrator or a court to allow its use as proof of damages. (See Chapter 18 for a detailed discussion
of the approaches to pricing a claim or a Request for an Equitable Adjustment [REA].)
The sections that follow offer specific approaches and alternatives for prosecuting frequently
encountered types of claims. Many of the principles and approaches are common to all construction
claims.
VII. 	PURSUING NEGOTIATION AND SETTLEMENT
Although claims and disputes are a part of the construction process, they need not and should not
dominate the process. When claims and disputes cannot be avoided, efforts should be redoubled
to resolve them as quickly as possible. The complexity, time, and cost of mediation, arbitration,
or litigation should cause the parties to favor negotiation and settlement. Formal dispute resolution
processes such as arbitration or litigation are not good business models because of the uncertainties
inherent in the process. In those instances, a claimant cedes control to a third party who will never
know, or care, as much about the claim as the claimant does. Therefore, a claims policy should
favor prompt resolution between the parties, maintaining control over the outcome by collaboration
rather than contest. Project and management personnel should be indoctrinated and trained along
those lines.
Although parties should comply with contract provisions regarding notice of claims and other
technical requirements, they should not overlook other lines of communication on the project as a
means of bringing a claim to quick settlement and avoiding the need for the dispute process to run its
full course. It is far easier and less expensive to resolve problems when and where they arise in the
field, rather than in the courtroom later. Even if early settlement is not achieved, negotiations force
the claimant to seriously examine the merits of its claim and to reveal its strengths and weaknesses
at an early stage.
Comprehensive and careful claim preparation greatly enhances the likelihood of early resolu-
tion and settlement. A party attempting to settle a claim should know its own case intimately and
should anticipate as many of the opposing party’s points as possible. Use of a well-prepared claim
document, as previously discussed, is helpful both as a starting point and as a reference during set-
tlement discussions. People with firsthand, detailed knowledge of the underlying facts and decision
makers with the authority to negotiate are an essential part of any negotiating effort. There is sim-
ply no substitute for involving the person who lived with the project’s problems on a daily basis.
Most important, successfully negotiating a claim to resolution often means compromise, including
the possibility of a bottom-line agreement based on risk analysis if certain factual disputes cannot
be resolved.
Alternatives to litigation, or alternative dispute resolution (ADR), are now well known in the con-
struction industry as a means of resolving disputes when negotiations break down. ADR includes
mediation (essentially, negotiations facilitated by a third-party mediator), a combination of mediation
and arbitration (Med-Arb), minitrials, dispute review boards, and several other methods of conflict
resolution that the parties may agree upon. To invoke one of these ADR processes on a private con-
struction project, the contracting parties need to include an agreed-upon process in their contract or
agree to the process when considering the claim. On public projects, such processes may be required
by statute, regulation, ordinance, or terms of the contract imposed by the governmental owner.
A. 	Mediation
When unassisted negotiations fail, mediation is a popular, if not the most popular, method for
attempting to resolve construction disputes. Although not a panacea for all project ills, mediation

-- 668 of 771 --

VII. PURSUING NEGOTIATION AND SETTLEMENT 	631
can provide an opportunity to resolve disputes while maintaining more control over the outcome and
without the higher costs and time requirements associated with arbitration and litigation. Mediation
is more a business process than a legal process.
Many standard-form contracts require or allow mediation as part of the formal process for dispute
resolution. For example, EJCDC C-700 allows mutual agreement by the owner and the contractor to
mediate and stay the claim process prior to arbitration or litigation. 5 ConsensusDocs 200 provides
for mediation after “direct discussions” (unassisted negotiations) have been unsuccessful and “no
dispute mitigation procedure has been selected” (a “Project Neutral” or “Dispute Review Board”),
but before “Binding Dispute Resolution” (a box may be checked for arbitration or for litigation).6
American Institute of Architects (AIA) Document A201 requires claims to go to mediation as a con-
dition precedent to binding dispute resolution, 7 except those claims waived relating to final payment 8
and consequential damages. 9
Mediation, unlike arbitration, is nonbinding. Rather than advocating the dispute before a judge
or judge-like arbitrator, mediation relies on negotiations facilitated by the mediator and collabo-
rative discussions by the parties to “find the deal” and end the dispute. The parties search for a
mutually acceptable resolution by compromising their respective positions. The mediator may make
observations and even suggestions but does not issue a decision. Mediation is much less costly than
arbitration or litigation and is a relatively quick process. Mediation is attractive to businesspeople
because it allows them to control the process and ends the uncertainty inherent in claims arbitration
and litigation.
Each mediation will likely be unique to the facts and circumstances of the underlying dispute. The
process is flexible, and an effective mediator will mold the process based on the parties’ dynamics
and the progress of the discussions. However, there are some typical characteristics common to the
mediation process.
1. 	Preparing for the Mediation
Frequently, once the mediator is selected, the parties will be required to sign a mediation-process
agreement. This document is intended to memorialize the parties’ intent to preserve the confiden-
tiality of the mediation process and sets out broad parameters and other expectations for the sessions
with the mediator. Mediation is usually conducted in conjunction with a more formal dispute reso-
lution process. That is, arbitration or litigation may already be filed and pending while the parties
attempt to settle via mediation. Effective mediation can happen only when both sides are willing to
compromise their positions, even though such positions could be damaging in the underlying dispute
resolution process. The mediation agreement, which establishes confidentiality, allows the parties to
compromise their positions without worrying that such positions would be used against them if the
mediation is unsuccessful and arbitration or litigation follows.
Before the mediation begins, the mediator may ask the parties to submit written position state-
ments. The parties should understand and agree ahead of time whether the statements will be confi-
dential or will be shared with the opposing party. These statements are intended primarily to help the
mediator understand the issues and the parties’ respective positions. A position statement is also a
useful tool to help the submitting party and mediator formulate a game plan for the mediation. Even
if the mediator does not request a written position statement, taking some time to map out positions,
5 EJCDC C-700 Standard General Conditions of the Construction Contract ¶ 12.01D (2018 ed.).
6 ConsensusDocs 200 Standard Agreement and General Conditions Between Owner and Constructor (Lump Sum) §§
12.4–12.5 (© 2011, Revised 2017).
7 AIA Document A201 – 2017 General Conditions of the Contract for Construction § 15.3.1.

9Id. at § 15.1.6.

632 	CHAPTER 23 RESOLVING CONSTRUCTION DISPUTES
frame the issues, and develop negotiating positions can only help to increase the likelihood of a
successful mediation.
A successful mediation will also depend significantly on who attends the mediation for the parties.
It is imperative that a representative for each party, with full authority to settle, attend the mediation
from the outset. Without such a person, the mediation is likely to fail. In addition to an authorized
decision maker, each party will want to have someone at the mediation with extensive knowledge of
the project, the disputed issues, and the claims being negotiated.
More and more, parties in mediation are represented by counsel because the mediation process has
become intertwined with arbitration or litigation. Although not required in the mediation, a qualified
construction attorney can assist a client in framing the issues for mediation, articulating the claim(s)
or defense against the claims, and coming up with the negotiation strategy.
In some mediations, particularly those involving multiple or complex claims or construction
issues—especially delay or specific technical issues such as soil conditions—a party may consider
bringing a technical expert or a claims consultant. These persons should attend the mediation only
if they can assist the mediator and other parties in better understanding the topic on which they are
speaking.
2. 	Understanding the Mediation Process
The actual mediation takes place in the form of a conference between the parties, with the mediator.
The mediation conference is usually scheduled for a set time period (typically one or two days). Most
often, the parties to the mediation attend the mediation in person, although lesser involved parties
may participate as needed by telephone or through video conferencing. The conference typically
convenes with all parties meeting in the same room for a preliminary session led by the mediator.
After introductory comments and ground rules, the claimant will be asked to summarize and to
briefly discuss its position. The party (or parties) to which the claim is being presented will then,
typically, respond. It is important to remember that the audience is the other party, not the mediator,
who has no decision-making authority. The claimant attempts to persuade the other party. After all
parties have expressed their positions, the mediator may allow further discussion or debate between
the parties. The mediator may also ask questions or seek clarification.
Once the preliminary session concludes, the parties typically adjourn to separate rooms and the
mediator begins caucusing with the individual parties, shuttling between them. This is when the
negotiations truly begin. Caucus sessions are fluid, and there are no set rules. In some cases, the
mediator will attempt to bring party representatives, usually decision makers, back together for
one-on-one negotiations. Whatever the process, an effective mediator’s ultimate goal is to facilitate
discussions that will lead to a settlement.
3. 	Timing of Mediation
Because mediation is nonbinding, the timing of the mediation is critical in successfully resolving the
claim. Some contracts require that mediation occur before, or as a condition precedent to, any formal
dispute resolution process like arbitration or litigation. Also, more and more courts are now either
mandating or strongly encouraging parties to engage in mediation before a dispute goes to trial.10
Although such a provision can dictate the timing for mediation, in general, to have a successful
mediation, the parties must agree that a compromise is in their respective best interests. This typically
means that they must appreciate the strengths and weaknesses of their and their opponents’ cases,
the legal costs of prosecuting or defending against the claim, and the costs of committing personnel
10See Section IX.F of this chapter.

-- 670 of 771 --

VIII. ARBITRATION 	633
to pursue arbitration or litigation. A competent mediator will assist each party in recognizing the
relative strengths and weaknesses of its position and the risks of going onto arbitration or litigation.
In some cases, the parties may understand these factors early in a dispute. In other cases, however,
it may require one or both of the parties to proceed with arbitration or litigation, until they reach a
point where they appreciate the facts and issues more fully. Forcing mediation before the parties are
ready may be a waste of time and money.
B. 	Dispute Review Boards
In disputes involving state and local public projects, many state and local government authorities
require that disputes between the government authority and the contractor first be heard by a dispute
review board (DRB) before litigation can commence. The goal is to create a mechanism whereby
disputes that occur throughout the project are addressed without waiting until the end of the project
and without interrupting the work’s progress. The process is somewhat similar to presenting claims
before the various boards of contract appeals on federal government projects, except that the parties
participating in the DRB process have more control over the process. Unless a panel is preselected,
the parties may have some control over selection of panel members for a particular case.
Typically, and similar to an arbitration panel, the DRB is composed of three panel members. The
government authority selects one, the contractor selects another, and these two panel members in turn
select a third member. The parties present their case to the panel similar to how they would present
their case in arbitration, and the panel then renders a decision. The difference between the DRB and
arbitration is that the DRB’s decision is subject to a full appeal, unlike an arbitration decision, which
may be overturned only under very limited circumstances.
C. 	Minitrials and Summary Jury Trials
A minitrial or a summary jury trial is a less-formal hybrid process based on arbitration and litigation
procedures. In a minitrial, each party presents its case before a mediator and senior representa-
tives from each party, who are generally unfamiliar with the dispute—usually corporate executives
or higher-level government officials. After hearing the presentation, the corporate representatives
attempt to negotiate the dispute with the assistance of the mediator. The benefit of this process is
that representatives from the disputing parties themselves are serving as judge, jury, and negotia-
tors. The goal is for the representatives to hear the evidence and, with the help of the mediator,
reach a settlement based on the evidence presented, weighing the strengths and weaknesses of each
side’s case.
In a summary jury trial, the parties engage in an abbreviated trial before a “judge” and a mock
jury. The entire trial typically lasts no more than a day. The jury then renders an advisory opinion,
which is nonbinding on the parties. Again, the purpose of the procedure is to allow the parties,
having observed the mock trial and hearing the mock jury decision, to understand the strengths and
weaknesses of their respective cases and to negotiate a resolution without the time and expense
associate with a protracted trial and trial preparation.
VIII. 	ARBITRATION
Arbitration is a binding dispute resolution process that offers a (usually) private alternative to a
lawsuit. One of the contracting parties will commence (or demand) arbitration when the parties
cannot resolve the claim amicably between themselves. The availability of arbitration, like any ADR
procedure, must be planned and provided for at the outset of the project, preferably in the contract

-- 671 of 771 --

634 	CHAPTER 23 RESOLVING CONSTRUCTION DISPUTES
itself. Although the parties are free to agree to arbitrate after a dispute has arisen, without mutual
agreement, the parties must look to the courts. No particular form or special words are necessary to
establish an agreement to arbitrate a dispute between the parties. There must, however, be a clear
indication from the contract language that the parties intended the disputed issue to be subject to
arbitration.
To avoid any dispute about the scope of the agreement to arbitrate, it is best to state expressly
that all disputes arising from the contract will be arbitrated. The arbitration clause contained in AIA
Document A201 provides a simple and clear directive if the parties choose arbitration as the ultimate
forum for resolving disputes, along with the process rules to be followed, and while also referencing
the required mediation:
§ 15.4.1 If the parties have selected arbitration as the method for binding resolution in the
Agreement, any Claim subject to, but not resolved by, mediation shall be subject to arbitration
which, unless the parties mutually agree otherwise, shall be administered by the American
Arbitration Association in accordance with its Construction Industry Arbitration Rules in
effect on the date of the Agreement.11
Under this standard contract provision, the parties can opt for arbitration by checking a box on
the signature page. The default for the AIA documents is litigation as opposed to arbitration. The
same is true under EJCDC C-700. 12
ConsensusDocs 200, likewise allows the contracting parties to decide, by checking a box, between
arbitration and litigation for resolution of contract disputes. 13 Unlike the AIA documents, however,
ConsensusDocs does not expressly specify that litigation is the “default” process if the parties do not
check the box for arbitration. Ideally, the parties using a contract document that allows an option for
arbitration should state this affirmatively in the contract. That is, they should check the box. If they
do not, it could be argued that the parties’ failure to check the box for arbitration would indicate that
the parties did not elect arbitration as a means of dispute resolution.14
The parties may agree (and should agree to avoid later disputes about procedure) on the location
(venue or forum) for arbitration proceedings. Parties typically agree on the forum considered most
advantageous in the context of other give-and-take in the contract. Such agreements will be upheld
unless there are extraordinary circumstances. The United States Supreme Court has determined that a
location later determined by one party to be inconvenient for that party or its witnesses typically will
not meet the heavy burden of showing public-interest factors needed to defeat the venue selection
provision of a contract. Note that public-interest factors are general in nature, such as a state statute
applicable to contracting within that state and are not focused on a single contractor or contract. 15
Arbitration is not new to the construction industry; contract clauses providing for arbitration of
disputes have been commonplace in the construction industry for many years. Although arbitration is
perceived as a way to avoid the delays and problems associated with litigation, time has demonstrated
the drawbacks, as well as the advantages, of relying on arbitration to formally resolve construction
claims. In general, there may be little or no cost savings when compared with litigation. Arbitration

may reach a conclusion more rapidly than litigation. Arbitration is usually less process oriented and
bureaucratic than litigation; however, discovery disputes and motions filed by one party or the other
can lengthen and complicate arbitration. The outcome in arbitration can be more predictable since
the arbitrators are usually more specialized and knowledgeable about engineering and construction
practices than most judges in state and federal courts. Many of the issues discussed below with
respect to arbitration may also be applicable to other forms of ADR.
A. 	Time and Costs of Arbitration
On balance, and particularly for smaller claims, arbitration does provide a faster resolution. However,
given the right (or perhaps wrong) set of circumstances (or arbitrators), arbitration can be as excru-
ciatingly time consuming and expensive as litigation. A dispute over the existence, scope, or validity
of an arbitration agreement itself can engender a protracted court proceeding and appeal before there
is even a determination of whether and to what extent the parties should proceed with arbitration. In
addition, arbitration of larger claims involving multiple parties can match the delays and complexity
of the most arcane court proceeding.
Although dependent on the parties involved and the issues’ scope and complexity, arbitration
may cost less than a comparable court proceeding. A shortened period for resolution will keep
costs down, but there are certain costs that may be incurred in arbitration just as in litigation.
These costs include discovery, examination, and analysis of documents; legal research; the use
of experts; the development of demonstrative evidence; and other limited discovery (typically
depositions).
Costs that can be avoided in arbitration usually involve trade-offs. For example, unless provided
for by agreement (including a specific set of rules) or statute, discovery may be either unavailable
or significantly limited. The costs of discovery, which can be substantial, can thus be avoided or at
least diminished. The lack of discovery, however, means less preparation for, and knowledge and
understanding of, the opposition’s case. It can also lead to a less-focused hearing, particularly as
rules of evidence are not strictly applied, which may then require more time and money. In addition,
certain costs are unique to arbitration, such as arbitrators’ fees, as well as administrative fees and the
cost of meeting rooms, all of which can be substantial.
Arbitration involves some costs not typically incurred (at least on the same order of magnitude)
in litigation. First, if the arbitration is administered by an outside organization, as it frequently will
be, that organization charges a fee for such service. These filing or administrative fees are typically
based on a percentage of the claim (and counterclaim). 16 The initial cost or fee for filing a lawsuit
is usually much less than an arbitration filing fee.
Second, the arbitrator (or arbitration panel) will most likely charge the parties a fee for their
services. This is typically in the form of an hourly rate for preparation and study time, participating
in hearings, deliberations, and award (decision) preparation. The latter can be particularly high if
the parties opt for a written “reasoned” decision, that is, specific findings of fact, a recitation of
applicable law, and application of that law to the facts to reach a conclusion. Arbitrators’ fees can
roughly triple if a three-member arbitration panel is required to resolve the dispute. Judges and
juries, while compensated for their time, are paid from public funds, not directly by the parties,
for their services. Although there may be a benefit to incurring these additional costs, such as a
more expeditious resolution of the dispute by more knowledgeable persons, the prudent construction
professional should understand and acknowledge the magnitude of these costs before agreeing to
arbitration.
16 The American Arbitration Association (AAA), for example, has a sliding scale for filing fees. See, e.g., AAA Construction
Arbitration Rules & Mediation Procedures (Rules Amended July 1, 2015; Fee Schedule Amended Oct. 1, 2017) at 11, 54.

B. 	Selection of Arbitrators
An arbitrator’s qualifications and fairness are essential to arbitration’s viability as a means of resolv-
ing disputes. The selection of arbitrators, like the selection of jurors, can be a major factor in the
success or failure of a claim. Some considerations must be addressed well in advance of any dispute
at the contract-drafting phase of the project, when the terms of the arbitration clause are determined.
Some basic but strategic considerations are the number of arbitrators and the manner in which they
are selected.
Arbitrators need not be lawyers but may be. An important consideration is whether the issues to
be decided are more “legal” or more “technical.” A party to arbitration should consult closely with
counsel for information better known to the party or counsel concerning proposed arbitrators who
are, respectively, non-lawyers or lawyers.
Arbitrators of construction disputes typically have more expertise in the construction industry
compared to a judge or jury. This is cited as one of the major advantages of arbitration. Of course, as
with a juror, an arbitrator’s experience and background can predispose the arbitrator for or against a
particular argument or party. For example, an owner in a dispute with an architect might fear choosing
an architect as an arbitrator or placing an architect or engineer on the panel. An owner with a strong
claim against an architect, however, actually might benefit from the heightened scrutiny another
architect might apply to a fellow architect. Another scenario might bring an arbitrator to the panel
considered to be a preeminent authority in a field applicable to the dispute. If the arbitrator rejects
the testimony of one’s expert, it is possible he or she will prevail in convincing fellow arbitrators
to do the same. The “preeminent authority” might substitute his or her opinion for those of other
experts. Many—and often subjective—factors bear on the selection process.
In terms of numbers, the basic choice is between a single arbitrator and a three-member panel.
A single arbitrator costs less and will probably simplify scheduling hearings or conferences to con-
sider preliminary matters, such as discovery or motions (if allowed). A three-member panel would
probably be more balanced since the arbitrators discuss and debate among themselves to reach con-
sensus. The three-member panel generally decides by majority vote—that is, two of the three panel
members can render a decision over the objection or dissent of the third member.
Parties in arbitration are free to agree on their own procedures for selecting an arbitrator. The
procedure is often set forth in the contract’s arbitration clause. Provided both sides agree, the
procedures can also be established or changed when the claim is submitted to arbitration. The
most widely employed method for selecting arbitrators is set forth in the American Arbitration
Association (AAA) Construction Industry Arbitration Rules (Construction Rules). The AAA’s
Construction Rules provide for selection of one or three neutral arbitrators, usually from a list
provided by the AAA, either by the parties’ mutual agreement or by administrative appointment if
no agreement can be reached. Another procedure that is sometimes used to select a three-member
panel allows each party to appoint one arbitrator, with the two party-appointed arbitrators jointly
selecting a third “neutral” arbitrator. As a practical matter, this process often makes the neutral
arbitrator the swing vote. Many arbitrators decline to serve as neutrals on such panels; the
prospect of having the parties’ respective positions reargued by one’s fellow arbitrators during
deliberations does not appeal to everyone, and may not best accomplish the goal of a truly neutral
arbitration panel.
C. 	Informality and Limited Appeals in Arbitration
The emphasis on arbitrators’ technical expertise usually involves a substantial de-emphasis of legal
principles and evidentiary rules and procedures, including the right of appeal. This aspect of arbitra-
tion is often cited as a positive, but the contrary can be argued as well.

-- 674 of 771 --

VIII. ARBITRATION 	637
In arbitration proceedings, strict rules of evidence do not apply and, typically, arbitrators are
liberal in accepting evidence. This permits an easier and faster presentation of records, correspon-
dence, documents, photographs, and live testimony (direct and cross-examination). In fact, the AAA
Construction Rules encourage arbitrators to accept any and all evidence that may shed light on the
dispute. This approach to receiving evidence can result in a very prolonged (read: expensive) arbi-
tration. In the more relaxed environment of arbitration, substantive legal defenses, such as statute of
limitations, no damages for delay clauses, and notice requirements may be given less weight than in
a trial setting.
In addition to the arbitrators being granted considerable latitude in their conduct of hearings and
rendering of awards,17 the right of appeal by means of challenging an award is extremely limited in
scope. 18 This limited scope of judicial review of arbitration awards is yet another trade-off. Although
it certainly curtails a party’s rights compared to the scope of appealing a jury verdict, the limited
scope tends to reduce the number and length of appeals from arbitration awards. This is, of course,
in contrast to the court system with its lengthy and expensive appellate procedures.
D. 	Enforceability of Agreements to Arbitrate
In addition to the contract’s arbitration clause, a party’s right to arbitration may depend on its ability
to go to court and enforce the agreement to arbitrate. In earlier times, the courts historically were
jealous of their jurisdiction and very protective of a person’s right of access to the courts. Today,
however, the overburdened court system has made alternative dispute resolution a contractual right
and a necessity. Most states have attempted to broaden the right to arbitration either by statute or
court decision.
In addition to state laws, construction arbitration agreements are often enforceable under the
Federal Arbitration Act (FAA), 19 which is an expression of a strong federal policy favoring arbi-
tration. 20 The FAA applies only if the arbitration clause in a contract “evidences” a transaction
involving commerce, meaning interstate commerce. Generally, transactions involved in a large con-
struction project often satisfy this interstate commerce requirement (out-of-state subcontractors,
equipment lessors, and material suppliers) and come within the FAA’s scope.21 If the interstate

corruption in the arbitrators, or either of them; (3) where the arbitrators were guilty of misconduct in refusing to postpone
the hearing, upon sufficient cause shown, or in refusing to hear evidence pertinent and material to the controversy, or of any
other misbehavior by which the rights of any party have been prejudiced; or (4) where the arbitrators exceeded their powers,
or so imperfectly executed them that a mutual, final, and definite award upon the subject matter submitted was not made.

After signing a contract including an arbitration provision, some parties will attempt either to
avoid or to enforce an arbitration clause contained in the contract. The United States Supreme Court
has held that questions of arbitrability, such as whether a party is bound by an arbitration clause and
disagreements about the application of an arbitration clause are questions for the court to decide. 24
However, procedural questions arising out of the dispute, as well as the merits of the dispute, are left
to the arbitrator. 25
Regarding arbitrability, a common question for the courts to decide is whether a nonsignatory
to a contract, such as a supplier, seeking to enforce or avoid an arbitration provision, is bound
by the provision. The United States Supreme Court has held that traditional principles of state
law allow a contract to be enforced by or against nonparties to the contract through assumption,
piercing the corporate veil, alter ego, incorporation by reference, third party beneficiary theories,
waiver, and estoppel.26 Although each case depends on its specific facts, the majority rule regard-
ing nonsignatories is that courts are willing to estop a signatory from avoiding an arbitration clause
where the nonsignatory is seeking to enforce an arbitration clause. However, the courts are reluctant
to enforce an arbitration clause against a nonsignatory who is trying to avoid it.27 In most cases,
where a nonsignatory initiates a claim under the contract or for some injury based on negligence
(known as a tort) that is related to contract performance, the courts have found that the nonsigna-
tory is seeking a direct benefit under the contract and should be bound by an arbitration provision in
that contract.

E. 	Special Problems Involving Multiple Parties to Arbitration
A recurring issue in administering construction arbitrations is the consolidation of separate arbitra-
tions and multiple parties on the same project into one proceeding. Common fact patterns involve an
owner’s claim against a contractor in which the contractor seeks to assert liability against the owner’s
architect-engineer design firm, or a subcontractor asserts a claim against the general contractor which
in turn blames another subcontractor.
The potential for problems and the desirability of consolidation need to be considered when the
arbitration clause is being drafted prior to award of the contract, long before any claim develops.
Although consolidating court proceedings involving numerous parties is common, few construction
contracts specifically provide for such consolidated proceedings in arbitration. Even without con-
tractual authorization, a minority of courts have required consolidation as an expeditious means to
resolve construction disputes.28 However, the traditional and majority rule appears to be that, with-
out express contractual consent to multiparty arbitrations, courts will not require consolidation.29
Notwithstanding the absence of specific contractual provisions authorizing consolidation, several
state legislatures have enacted statutes to empower their respective state courts to address multi-
party arbitration through either consolidation or joinder of parties.30 The AAA’s Construction Rules
currently provide a mechanism for consolidation or joinder of related arbitrations if the parties can-
not agree to consolidate. A single arbitrator is appointed under Rule R-7 for the limited purpose of
deciding whether related arbitrations should be consolidated or the parties joined. If not specifically
provided for in a contract or contracts, the parties can mutually agree to consolidation or joinder.
For example, the arbitration clause contained in AIA A201 provides the following:

methods for selecting arbitrator(s).

F. 	Med-Arb
Med-Arb is a term of art meaning mediation followed by arbitration if the mediation is unsuccessful.
In Med-Arb, the parties may elect to have the same person serve as both the mediator and arbitra-
tor. Such an arrangement has its advantages in that the mediator becomes familiar with the parties,

understanding of the issues. The disadvantage in the mediator serving as the arbitrator is that infor-

arbitration. Consequently, Med-Arb may be most useful in cases where the stakes are not that high
and the parties want a quick resolution of the dispute.
G. 	Arbitration Agreements and Procedures
Courts in the United States recognize the rights of parties to contractually bind themselves to an
arbitration process for dispute resolution. The parties are free to select the method, manner, and
timing of arbitration.
A number of organizations provide for the administration of formal arbitration proceedings that
parties may choose to reference in their project contracts or in subsequent arbitration agreements. The
suitability of one organization over another depends upon the nature of the parties, the underlying
transaction, and personal preference.
1. 	American Arbitration Association and JAMS Rules and Procedures
The American Arbitration Association (AAA) 35 is the most widely used organization in the United
States for administering the resolution of construction disputes through arbitration. JAMS36 is the
largest private alternative dispute resolution (ADR) provider in the world. JAMS specializes in medi-
ating and arbitrating complex, multi-party, business/commercial cases.
The AAA is a public service, not-for-profit organization that offers a broad range of dispute res-
olution procedures, including arbitration. As previously mentioned, the AAA’s Construction Rules
provide a framework for the resolution construction disputes of any size or complexity, whether
national or international in scope. The applicable rules and procedures vary depending on the size
and complexity of the dispute, with larger and more complex construction disputes being subject to
a higher degree of subject-matter discovery and procedural management. The AAA’s Construction
Rules also include fast-track procedures for resolution of disputes less than a set dollar amount. As
mentioned in a note referenced in Section VIII.A of this chapter, administrative fees are determined
on a sliding scale in relation to the size of the claims in dispute. Arbitrators are selected from a large
panel of industry professionals and construction lawyers and are paid based on individual hourly or
daily rates. All AAA rules and procedures can be found online.
Historically, the AIA, the Associated General Contractors of America, and the EJCDC have
favored arbitration administered by the AAA. However, a recent trend, especially with the involve-
ment of state court systems to implement ADR programs and to certify mediators and arbitra-
tors, has been to let the contracting parties select their own means for arbitration including the
entity, if any, administering these processes. Even if the parties do not opt for AAA administra-
tion, they can contractually agree to be bound by AAA procedural rules. AIA A201 provides in
pertinent part:
§ 15.4.1 If the parties have selected arbitration as the method for binding dispute resolution
in the Agreement, any Claim subject to, but not resolved by, mediation shall be subject to
arbitration which, unless the parties mutually agree otherwise, shall be administered by the
American Arbitration Association in accordance with its Construction Industry Arbitration
35 https://www.adr.org/.
36 https://www.jamsadr.com/

Rules in effect on the date of the Agreement . . . . A demand for arbitration shall be made
in writing, delivered to the other party to the Contract, and filed with the person or entity
administering the arbitration. 37
Although the language does not limit arbitration to the AAA, unless otherwise agreed to, the

ConsensusDocs 200 provides the parties to the contract with an expanded menu that specifies a

rules and administration of the AAA.39
More and more, parties are relying on their own counsel to select an arbitrator or arbitrators
and to enter into an arbitration agreement pursuant to remedies and rules either provided for in
their respective state’s Uniform Arbitration Act or pursuant to terms and conditions acceptable to
the parties. See Section VIII.G.4 of this chapter for more information concerning party-drafted
agreements.
2. 	Center for Public Resources Rules and Procedures
The Center for Public Resources (CPR) serves as a vehicle and resource for self-administered arbi-
tration of private and public business disputes in the United States and abroad. CPR rules and
procedures emphasize flexibility in permitting sophisticated business entities to craft dispute resolu-
tion procedures appropriate for their particular dispute without the traditional assistance of outside
organizations. Members of the CPR include multinational corporations, law firms, legal academics,
and public institutions. As with the AAA, the CPR suggests contract language that parties may
include in their arbitration clauses and provides a framework of rules and procedures the parties
may employ in arbitrating a dispute. Additional information on this dispute resolution institute can
be found at CPR’s website.40
3. 	International Chamber of Commerce Rules and Procedures
Established in 1923, the International Court of Arbitration (the Court) organizes and supervises
arbitrations held throughout the world under the Rules of Arbitration of the International Chamber
of Commerce (ICC). The primary function of the Court is to provide for the resolution by arbitration
of business disputes of an international character, although parties are free to invoke the ICC Rules
in non-international cases. The ICC Rules have a particularly international flavor and are designed
to provide a mutually acceptable arbitration framework for adversaries that may not share common
customs, culture, or language.41 The ICC’s rules and procedures vary from those of the AAA and the
CPR. One significant difference is that the arbitrator’s fees (different from initial filing fees) under
the ICC Rules are calculated on a sliding scale in relation to the amount in dispute. It cannot be
overemphasized that before agreeing to an arbitration clause that invokes ICC arbitration, the parties
must understand the applicable arbitration rules and procedures, as well as the fee structure.

39 EJCDC C-800 ¶ SC-17.02 (2018 ed.).

4. 	Party-Drafted Arbitration Agreements: Federal and State Law Considerations
Parties drafting arbitration clauses in private contracts must consider what law will govern the
enforcement and applicability of the agreement to arbitrate. 42 The Federal Arbitration Act was
enacted in 1925, then reenacted and codified in 1947 as Title 9 of the United States Code. It was
“enacted … as a response to judicial hostility to arbitration” and established “a liberal federal policy
favoring arbitration agreements. It requires courts to enforce agreements to arbitrate according to
their terms.”43 The FAA “was enacted to promote the enforcement of arbitration agreements and
to make arbitration a more viable option to parties weary of the ever-increasing cost and delays of
litigation.”44
The United States Supreme Court has further ruled that the FAA was intended by Congress to
create not merely federal procedural law but also a federal substantive law of arbitration. 45 Conse-
quently, arbitration clauses subject to the FAA are to be liberally construed in favor of arbitration,
notwithstanding any state substantive or procedural policies to the contrary.46 This is true in both
federal and state court proceedings. 47
State arbitration statutes have been tailored closely to the Uniform Arbitration Act (UAA) as
drafted by the National Conference of Commissioners on Uniform State Laws in 1955. The UAA
was revised substantially in 2000 in the form of the Revised Uniform Arbitration Act.
IX. 	LITIGATION
When a contract contains no arbitration provision, litigation is the traditional avenue for obtaining
relief. Rules governing court proceedings are quite complex and vary among federal, state, and local
courts from jurisdiction to jurisdiction. For this reason, the discussion here presents only a thumbnail
sketch of what is involved in going to court.
A. 	Profile of the Construction Trial
The trial of a construction contract dispute offers a unique challenge to both sides of the case. Com-
plex antitrust cases are perhaps the closest parallel, since both involve numerous parties and virtual
mountains of documentation. Certain problems, however, are unique to construction controversies.
In contrast to the typical civil dispute or crime where the wrong occurred at a single point in time,
construction claims typically grow out of an accumulation of events developing over many months
or years. To further complicate matters, a single activity constituting a breach of contract may have
a ripple effect on the remainder of the project, expanding the effect of the breach and entitling the
injured party to recover “impact” costs as an additional element of damages. The category of impact
damages includes the cost of inefficiency and lost productivity resulting from out-of-sequence or
accelerated work. Although at times difficult to prove, such damages can often be substantial. (See
Chapter 18.)
An added difficulty in a construction case is the large cast of characters, which can include one or
more prime contractors and/or construction managers, subcontractors at several levels or tiers, sup-
pliers, equipment lessors, the owner, one or more sureties, design professionals, lenders, insurers, and
42 See Section VIII.D of this chapter, discussing enforceability of arbitration agreements under the FAA.
43CompuCredit Corp. v. Greenwood, 132 S.Ct. 665 (2012).
44Dean Witter Reynolds, Inc. v. Byrd, 470 U.S. 213 (1985).
45Preston v. Ferrer, 552 U.S. 346, 349 (2008).
46CompuCredit Corp. v. Greenwood, 132 S.Ct. 665 (2012).
47See CompuCredit Corp. v. Greenwood, 132 S.Ct. 665 (2012); Preston v. Ferrer, 552 U.S. 346 (2008).

644 	CHAPTER 23 RESOLVING CONSTRUCTION DISPUTES
others. As soon as litigation becomes inevitable, the contractor and its counsel must carefully analyze
the list of possible parties from the standpoint of liability, financial responsibility, jurisdiction, venue,
access to facts, and other factual and legal viewpoints.
In a contract action, the most obvious parties are those that have direct contract relations, or “priv-
ity,” with one another: the owner and prime contractor, or the prime contractor and subcontractor.
Yet other parties may become involved. For example, assume that an owner-plaintiff sues a bonded
prime contractor for defective work. The owner also would likely join the contractor’s surety as a
defendant. Assume that the prime contractor believes the defects are not its fault but the responsibil-
ity of one of its subcontractors. Since there was no “privity of contract” between the owner and the
subcontractor, the owner could not sue the subcontractor directly. The prime contractor, by virtue
of the subcontract, has a direct contractual relationship with the subcontractor and therefore may
“join” the subcontractor as a “third-party defendant.” If the subcontractor is bonded, it is likely that
the subcontractor’s surety will be joined in the litigation. This mechanism is commonly referred to
as “third-party practice.”
This scenario often also results in counterclaims by the prime contractor against the owner for
delays, defective plans, or the like. Every party considering whether to file suit should take into
account the defendant’s likely counterclaim, which may make it impossible to withdraw voluntarily
from litigation once suit has been filed.
The subcontractor may repeat the process by bringing counterclaims against the prime contractor
or cross-claims against the owner. In addition, the subcontractor may believe one of its lower-tier
subcontractors or suppliers is actually responsible for the defect and may, in turn, join that party as a
“fourth-party defendant.” What was once a simple, two-party lawsuit can mushroom into one involv-
ing numerous parties and their counsel, with the attendant increase in complexity, delay, and costs.
B. 	The Court System
Concurrent with identifying the parties to the lawsuit is choosing the most desirable court or, in legal
terminology, the “forum.” From the standpoint of strategy and convenience, it is generally a distinct
advantage to be the plaintiff and to select the forum. The plaintiff tells its story first to the judge or
jury. The plaintiff also has some latitude in determining where to initiate the lawsuit. Frequently, this
allows a convenient or hometown location to be selected.
To evaluate the factors that bear on selecting a particular court, it is helpful to have a basic under-
standing of the various court systems. Essentially, there are two court systems within the United
States: one federal court system and a variety of state court systems. The federal judicial system is
composed of approximately 90 United States District Courts; the next level above, 12 United States
Courts of Appeals (not including the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, which handles
appeals from matters arising under or relating to federal government contracts); and, finally, the
United States Supreme Court.
The federal courts are courts of “limited jurisdiction.” In contrast, state courts are courts of
“general jurisdiction.” The term “limited jurisdiction” means that some specific constitutional or
federal statutory basis must exist before a party can have its case heard in federal court. In other
words, jurisdiction is “limited” to those special instances prescribed by law. In contrast, a presump-
tion exists that a state court has jurisdiction over a particular controversy, unless a showing is made
to the contrary.
“Subject matter” jurisdiction refers to the power of a court to hear a particular type of case. The
federal courts’ subject matter jurisdiction in construction cases typically has a “federal question”
or “diversity of citizenship” basis. “Federal question” jurisdiction encompasses disputes arising
“under the Constitution, laws or treaties of the United States.”48 The second basis for subject matter
48See 28 U.S.C. § 1331.

-- 682 of 771 --

IX. LITIGATION 	645
jurisdiction in the federal courts—and by far the more common in construction disputes—is the
“diversity of citizenship” basis. 49 “Diversity” in this sense refers to controversies between citizens
of different states or between citizens of a state and an alien (that is, a resident of a foreign coun-
try). To satisfy the jurisdictional requirement, diversity of citizenship must be complete—that is, all
defendants must be from states different from all plaintiffs. 50
“Diversity” cases must meet a $75,000 threshold on the amount in controversy, exclusive of inter-
est and costs. This means that suits between residents of different states cannot be brought in federal
court where the alleged damages or realistic recovery is less than $75,000.
The second facet of jurisdiction—“personal” jurisdiction—focuses on whether the defendant has
sufficient contact with the forum state to give the court the right to resolve the dispute. The most
common bases for personal jurisdiction include the defendant’s physical presence within the juris-
diction or, in the case of a corporation, transacting business within the area of the court’s control,
such as performing work on a construction project in the forum state.
Venue also presents a preliminary problem in any lawsuit. The term “venue” refers to the proper
geographic location for bringing suit, rather than which court system has appropriate jurisdiction
to hear and decide the case. 51 Venue considerations apply in both federal and state courts, although
they tend to be more complex under state law due to the characteristic focus of state statutes on the
defendant’s county of residence or the county in which the dispute arises.
C. 	Federal Rules of Civil Procedure
The Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, which govern all procedural aspects of federal trials from
initial pleadings to judgment, are the product of years of study, analysis, and recommendations by
attorneys, judges, and scholars. They represent an effort to provide a workable procedural system.
Many states have adopted the substance of the Federal Rules, in whole or in part, for use in their own
state court systems or have developed minor variations to those rules. However, substantial variations
in the rules of civil procedure do exist from state to state. This is in contrast to the standardization
of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure in all federal courts. Although the Federal Rules of Civil
Procedure apply in all U.S. District Courts, many federal courts have their own “Local Rules” that
expand on the federal rules. Although these Local Rules may vary in some particulars, the attorney
familiar with the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure will ordinarily not feel handicapped in a district
court outside of that attorney’s usual geographic area of practice.
D. 	Discovery
Discovery under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and its counterparts at the state level
is designed to eliminate courtroom surprise and to foster settlement. Discovery is particularly
important in construction litigation because most complicated cases are predicated on vast amounts
of files, plans, specifications, engineering data, and other volumes of paper that may not be available
to all parties. Discovery is the statutory means by which a party is able to elicit facts from the
opposing party, and thereby narrow issues, pin down the opposition’s contentions, and prepare for
trial. (Similar discovery techniques are used in many arbitrations, either by agreement of the parties
or as provided in the rules governing the arbitration.) The most important discovery devices for
construction cases are described next.

1. 	Production of Documents and Things
This rule allows a party to compel another person, whether or not a party to the lawsuit, to
furnish designated documents (including writings, drawings, graphs, charts, photographs, and
other data compilations) and electronically stored information or tangible objects having a bearing
on the case and that are in the other party’s possession. 52 A request for production to a party
under this rule frequently accompanies a set of interrogatories, with the requested documents
or objects to be produced or made available for inspection, copying, testing, or sampling at the
same time that the answers are filed. Production of documents and objects at a deposition can also
be required by means of a subpoena duces tecum. A proper discussion of electronically stored
information (ESI), mentioned above, could easily fill the contents of a multivolume treatise, but for
purposes of this chapter, a brief overview will have to suffice. Virtually all disputes will involve
ESI and lots of it. With the increasing use of email and other electronic technologies and the
decreasing costs for data storage, each construction project is leaving behind an ever-increasing
number of electronic documents that are subject to discovery if relevant and proportional to the
dispute’s needs.
Management of all electronic records created over the course of a project needs to be given careful
consideration and carefully drafted policies need to be put into place. In addition, once it is deter-
mined that a dispute might take place, any policies that call for the regular deletion of certain records
need to be suspended. Once a dispute reaches the discovery phase, relevant electronic records will
need to be collected and produced to the other side. Without knowledgeable people in place to coor-
dinate this process, it can quickly get out of hand. Experienced construction attorneys are able to
guide the process all the way from establishing proper collection procedures, through the review
of those documents for relevance and privilege, and finally to production to the other side. Modern
software is capable of making certain aspects very efficient, but handling ESI can still be one of the
costliest aspects of any construction dispute.
While the most common forms of ESI involved in a construction dispute are emails and
typical project records (RFIs, change orders, design drawings, submittals, schedules, and so on),
it is becoming increasingly common for other sources to be considered, which adds additional
complications to the discovery process. Examples include text messages, social media accounts,
and alternatives to email, such as Slack. Each dispute will involve its own wrinkles when it
comes to ESI.
2. 	Interrogatories
Interrogatories 53 are written questions prepared by one party to the lawsuit and directed to another
party. Typically, the respondent prepares written answers with the assistance of their counsel, which
often causes the respondent’s replies to narrowly address the interrogatories. Nonetheless, inter-
rogatories can be a useful tool for initially obtaining information upon which to base subsequent
discovery. The party answering interrogatories is typically required to swear under oath (or verify)
that the answers are true and correct.
3. 	Depositions
A deposition54 is the oral examination (or, rarely, by written questions) of any person (the
“deponent”), whether or not a party to the action, whose knowledge and perspective are important
52 Fed. R. Civ. P. 34(a)(1).
53 Fed. R. Civ. P. 33(a).
54Id. at 30–32.

-- 684 of 771 --

IX. LITIGATION 	647
to the case. The deposition allows the questioner a more effective method of obtaining information,
since questions can be tailored to the deponent’s prior responses, and the questioner has an
opportunity to follow up spontaneously on new avenues of inquiry.
Depositions play a crucial part in the development of trial strategy because the testimony is taken
under oath, recorded by a stenographer and may be video recorded. Because there is an opportunity
for cross-examination during the course of a deposition, a deposition transcript or video may be used
at trial when a witness dies in the interim or is otherwise unavailable for trial. The deposition may
also be used for contradicting, or “impeaching,” a witness’s courtroom testimony whose testimony
contradicts prior deposition statements.
4. 	Requests for Admission
One party can require another party to the lawsuit to admit, in writing, the truth of certain facts, by
means of a formal request for admission. 55 This saves both time and money, and allows the parties
to direct their energies toward those issues or facts that are truly disputed.
5. 	Motion for Entry upon Land
This discovery rule provides a means for one party to request permission to enter onto another’s
property to inspect, survey, photograph, test, or sample the property or any designated object or
operation thereon.56 The value of this procedure is readily apparent if the contractor has relinquished
control over the site and subsequently needs to photograph site conditions or sample the soil in
connection with a differing site conditions claim.
E. 	Judge or Jury?
Another important decision associated with a trial is whether to present the case to a judge or a jury.
This choice lies with the parties. 57
A number of factors enter into the decision. For example, a judge sitting alone may be more likely
to admit disputed evidence, which would normally be excluded by a jury, on the rationale that it is
better to let in doubtful evidence than to face reversal on appeal because relevant evidence was not
admitted. In such a case, the judge is relying on experience and training to give the evidence only
the weight it deserves. However, a judge is less likely to be swayed by sympathy factors and equities
that frequently work in a party’s favor before a jury.
The type of construction project may also have a bearing on this decision. A local jury may
prove disastrous if the case involves construction of a public facility, such as a school or hospital,
particularly one funded by local property taxes or levies or one that is highly controversial. A similar
result may occur if the party being sued is a local business concern—for example, a subcontractor
or supplier—and the plaintiff is an outsider.
The determining factor may be that many construction cases are simply too complex for
the average jury, although some trial attorneys will argue that most judges are likewise not
familiar—through experience or background—with engineering and construction practices and
principles. In any event, the complexity of the matter and the relative advantage that may be gained
by simplification (or by confusion) are factors in deciding whether to proceed before a judge
or jury.

56Id. at 34(a)(2).
57See Fed. R. Civ. P. 38–39.
