of the cost of the components of which is comprised of components mined, produced, or manufac-
tured in the United States. Similarly, a domestic end product is either an unmanufactured end product
mined or produced in the United States or an end product manufactured in the United States, more
than 50 percent of the cost of the components of which is comprised of components mined, produced,
or manufactured in the United States.199
In practice, however, because of the fundamental difference in the nature of the two, the BAA
functions very differently when applied to end products furnished under supply contracts than to
construction materials furnished for construction projects. With regard to end products in supply
contracts, determinations are made on the final items produced by the contractor and supplied to the
government. An end product is an item in its final form; its subparts are not considered individually
(except to the extent that the subparts are the components of the end product). In contrast, construc-
tion materials are considered individually even though they are merely pieces being integrated or
incorporated into a larger project, such as a bridge, a building, a dam, and so on.
For example, a supply contract for end products could be for trucks, truck engines, or truck tires.
In any case, the test is applied only to the end item being acquired: the truck, the engine, or the tire.
The BAA is applied differently, however, to a construction contract for a building. It is not the end
item—the building—to which the test is applied. BAA requirements apply to the materials used to
build the project. According to the FAR:
Construction material means an article, material, or supply brought to the construction site
by a contractor or subcontractor for incorporation into the building or work. The term also
includes an item brought to the site preassembled from articles, materials, or supplies. How-
ever, emergency life safety systems, such as emergency lighting, fire alarm, and audio evacu-
ation systems, that are discrete systems incorporated into a public building or work and that
are produced as complete systems, are evaluated as a single and distinct construction material
regardless of when or how the individual parts or components of those systems are deliv-
ered to the construction site. Materials purchased directly by the Government are supplies, not
construction material. 200
The key is distinguishing between construction materials and components. In S.J. Amoroso Con-
struction Co. v. United States,201 foreign steel beams were considered construction material before
any domestic components were added. Importantly, the steel beams were delivered to the site before
they were modified. As a consequence, the contractor that used the beams was held to be in violation
of the BAA.

Violations of the BAA can result in significant penalties, including debarment or termination for
default. 202 More often, the government may seek an equitable deduction in the contract price203 or
simply require the contractor to pay the additional cost to obtain compliant construction material.204
Willful violations might also subject a contractor to penalties under the False Claims Act.205 To avoid

C. 	Labor Standards—Wage and Hour Requirements
A number of statutes mandate labor standards that government construction contractors must
observe. 206 These statutes regulate minimum wages, overtime wages, multiple affirmative action
programs, employment eligibility verification, and working conditions. Compliance with these
statutes and the implementing regulations is critical because penalties for violations can include
contract termination and even debarment for up to three years. In addition, as discussed in
Chapter 21, Executive Order 13502 encourages federal agencies to consider using union-only
Project Labor Agreements. The policies applicable to federal contracts are set forth in FAR 19,
Subpart 22.5.
Of particular importance, the Construction Wage Rate Requirements statute (formerly known
as the Davis-Bacon Act, though some government publications and websites have not yet been
updated) 207 requires contractors to pay mechanics and laborers a “prevailing wage”208 on federal
construction projects performed in the United States that exceed $2,000. A violation of the Wage
Rate Requirements statute can justify debarment of the contractor if the Department of Labor (DOL)
finds that the contractor disregarded its obligations to employees and subcontractors.209
1. 	Applicability
Traditionally, the Davis-Bacon Act (again, now called the Construction Wage Rate Requirements
statute) has been the most frequent basis for DOL or contracting agency employment-related actions
involving contractors or their subcontractors on construction projects. The statute applies to construc-
tion activity performed on “the site of the work.” Construction activity generally does not include
manufacturing, supplying materials, or performing service/maintenance work. 210 The site of the
work is usually limited to the geographical confines of the construction job site.211 Transportation of
materials to and from the project site is not considered “construction” for the purposes of the Con-
struction Wage Rate Requirements statute.212 The Construction Wage Rate Requirements statute
may also apply to construction work performed under a non-construction contract, for example, an
installation-support contract. If the contract requires a substantial and segregable amount of con-
struction, the statute applies. 213
The prevailing wage is the key to the labor standards issued in accordance with the Construction
Wage Rate Requirements statute. “Wages” includes both basic hourly rates for various classifications
of labor needed for the project and fringe benefits. DOL wage determinations are not subject to

decision on the contractual relationship between the government and its contractors may be the

2. 	Enforcement
Enforcement of the Construction Wage Rate Requirements statute may begin with either the DOL or
the contracting agency. The contracting officer must withhold contract payments if the contracting
officer believes that a violation exists or if requested to do so by the DOL. If an alleged violation is
not resolved at the local level, the DOL resolves the dispute. Disputes related to the interpretation
and enforcement of the Construction Wage Rate Requirements statute are not subject to the disputes
clause (discussed in Section IV of this chapter), even though the contracting officer makes the initial
withholding of funds. 215
Violations of the Construction Wage Rate Requirements statute (Davis-Bacon Act) can lead to
termination and even debarment. For example, consider the ruling in Glazer Construction Co., Inc.
v. United States. 216 In a construction contract with the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), the VA
terminated the contractor for default after significant delays and for failure to complete performance
by the contract completion date.
Subsequent to the issuance of the final decision, violations of the Davis-Bacon Act (as it was
called at the time) by the contractor came to the attention of the VA. While the contractor and its
president were debarred for these violations, the contracting officer had not considered the wage and
hour violations when deciding whether to terminate the contract for default.
The contractor appealed the termination for default to the COFC, arguing that because the VA
had not relied on those violations as a basis for the termination, they could not be used by the VA
to sustain the earlier termination. The court concluded that the decision to terminate the contractor
could be justified by those Davis-Bacon Act violations.

2. 	Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED) and Green Globes
Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED) is a voluntary rating system for sustain-
able building and design. LEED provides building owners and operators a framework for identifying
and implementing practical and measurable green building design, construction operations, and
maintenance solutions. LEED can be applied to any type of building. Federal agencies with a sig-
nificant construction program have adopted policies requiring LEED certification for all agency
construction. The Department of Agriculture, General Services Administration, NASA, and the
U.S. Navy typically require that all new construction and major renovation obtain LEED Silver
certification.
Another voluntary certification program for green building design is the “Green Globes” rating
system, which has been distributed by the Green Building Institute since 2004. Green Globes is a
rating system for new or existing commercial and residential buildings that is designed to measure
the overall sustainability of buildings. The program certifies a rating of one to four “green globes”
based on a percentage of points attained on a scale of 1000 available points. The points are attained
using a web-based program for green building guidance and Green Globes’ third-party assessors
who interface with project teams and building owners to review documentation and conduct on-site
building assessments.221 To be certified at the lowest rank of one green globe, a building must obtain
at least 35% of applicable points on the 1000-point scale, while four green globes requires at least
85% of applicable points.
For more information on environmentally friendly construction, see Section V of Chapter 19.
IV. 	RESOLUTION OF CONTRACT DISPUTES
A. 	Introduction
The Contract Disputes Act (CDA) is the basic federal law governing the resolution of government
contract claims. 222 It describes the process for the assertion of a claim by the contractor or the gov-
ernment and provides time frames for contracting officer’s decisions on contractor claims. The CDA
encompasses nearly all post-award disputes related to a government contract, including both mone-
tary and nonmonetary claims. However, while the CDA provides that all claims related to a contract
shall be submitted to the contracting officer for a decision, the act also states that it does not address
“a claim or dispute for penalties or forfeitures prescribed by statute or regulation which another
federal agency is specifically authorized to administer, settle, or determine.” For example, a dispute
arising under the prevailing wage requirements of the Construction Wage Rate Requirements statute
(formerly known as the Davis-Bacon Act) 223 is not subject to the CDA.
219 FAR § 23.202.
220 FAR § 23.203.
221See www.thegbi.org/green-globes-certification/how-to-certify/.
222 41 U.S.C. §§ 7101–09.
223 40 U.S.C. § 3141.

B. 	Contractor Claims under the CDA
1. 	Elements of a CDA Claim
The term claim has multiple meanings in federal government contracting. A contractor’s submission
of a change order proposal to the contracting officer may be a claim under the False Claims Act224
even though it is not a CDA claim. The basic elements of a CDA claim are as follows:
• A written demand or written assertion by one of the contracting parties seeking, as a matter
of right, the payment of money in a “sum certain,” the adjustment or interpretation of contract
terms, or other relief arising under or relating to this contract.
• A written demand by the contractor seeking the payment of money exceeding $100,000 is not
a CDA claim until it is certified in accordance with the CDA.
• Unless otherwise stated in the contract, the contractor’s written claim must be submitted to the
contracting officer within six years after accrual of the claim.
CDA claims are not limited to monetary claims. Consequently, it is possible to assert a claim over
an interpretation of a specification, as well as claims for time, money, or both. Although the FAR
and law governing government contracts have specific requirements related to submitting claims, the
basic principles and approaches to preparing a claim or a request for an equitable adjustment (REA)
on any construction project apply to a federal government contract. A discussion of the elements of
a claim is addressed in Section V of Chapter 23 and the principles governing the basic pricing of a
claim are addressed in Section II of Chapter 18.
Even though a document labeled a “claim submission” or “request for an equitable adjustment”
is submitted to the contracting officer, it is not automatically considered a claim for the purposes of
the CDA. To invoke the dispute resolution procedures of the CDA, a “claim in dispute” must exist
and the contractor must submit that “claim” to the contracting officer for a final decision. The case
law does not make an express request for a final decision a CDA-claim requirement.225 However,
the absence of a specific request for a final decision creates a risk that a board or the COFC will hold
that there was no dispute between the parties sufficient to constitute a CDA claim. 226
The written demand for payment, or statement of the monetary relief, can present a trap for the
unwary. A monetary claim exists only when the amount sought is set forth as a “sum certain”227
or may be determined by a simple mathematical calculation from the information provided by the
contractor. 228 For example, a claim in “an amount of no less than $1,072,957.05” was not a demand
for a “sum certain.”229
A change order proposal, termination settlement proposal, or request for an equitable adjustment
may not be considered a CDA claim when it is first submitted if there has been no impasse between
the parties.230 However, if there is no action on it within a reasonable period of time, that delay may,
by itself, operate to change the status of the submission to a CDA claim. 231

2. 	CDA Claim Submissions—Frequently Asked Questions
Who may submit a CDA claim?
Generally, only a prime contractor may assert claims against the government. The CDA refers
to “contractor’s claims”232 and states that the term “contractor means a party to a Federal Gov-
ernment contract other than the Federal Government.”233 As a general rule, a subcontractor
is not considered a party to the contract and may not assert claims directly against the gov-
ernment. 234 Similarly, a non-completing performance bond surety is not a contractor for the
purposes of the CDA. 235
What are the critical timing considerations?
¤ Notice requirements: Most contractor claims for time, and/or money reference one of three
key clauses: Changes, 236 Differing Site Conditions,237 or Suspension of Work. 238 Each of
these clauses contains a notice requirement, which may, under certain circumstances, bar
a contractor’s claim as untimely. To help avoid the potential loss of rights, the project staff
should develop a notice checklist for each project. (See Chapter 15 for a sample notice
checklist.)
¤ Releases and reservations of rights—modifications and final payment: FAR § 43.204(c)
provides that contracting officers “should” include a release in every supplemental agree-
ment or change order and sets forth a recommended release form. Consequently, a contractor
should carefully review the language of every release in any contract modification. Failure
to appreciate the possible effect of a release on a contractor’s rights may result in the denial
of subsequent REAs or claims. 239 Additionally, final payment on the contract may bar the
later presentation of any claim that is not specifically reserved from the release provided in
conjunction with the request for final payment.240 The description of the claim reserved by
a contractor can be critical because a general, or broad-brush, reservation of rights may be
ineffective. 241 If a claim is properly reserved, the contractor may later increase the dollar
value of that claim. 242
¤ CDA statute of limitations: When enacted, the CDA did not contain a statute of limitations.
However, the CDA now states that “each claim” relating to a contract shall be submitted
“within six years after the accrual of the claim.”243 The accrual concept applies to claims
by either the contractor or the federal government, except for government claims based on
a fraud by the contractor. 244
Contractors also need to consider the distinction between a CDA claim and a change order pro-
posal/REA. Note that submitting a change order proposal/REA may not satisfy the six-year submis-
sion requirement if it is later determined that the REA was not a CDA claim.245 The CDA statute

3. 	Claim Submission Preparation and Elements
a. 	Written Submission Requirement For purposes of the CDA, a claim must be in writing
and submitted by the contractor 248 to the contracting officer for a written decision. Verbal demands
seeking compensation are not CDA claims. Similarly, a written demand that is submitted to a per-
son who is not the contracting officer is not a CDA claim. If there is doubt regarding whether
the submission to the contracting officer’s subordinate is appropriate, the contractor should copy
the contracting officer. No particular wording or format is needed when submitting a claim. 249
However, the contractor must provide sufficient information so that the contracting officer has ade-
quate notice of the claim’s basis (entitlement) and the sum certain amount (quantum) of a monetary
claim. 250
b. 	Request for Final Decision In Transamerica Insurance Corp. v. United States,251 the Federal
Circuit rejected the assertion that a claim must include a specific request for a final decision so long
as the claim sets forth a clear indication that a decision was desired.252 Notwithstanding this decision,
the failure to make a specific request for a final decision may be viewed as evidence that there was
no dispute between the parties sufficient to constitute a “claim” under the Act.
c. 	Certification Requirements
(1) Contract Disputes Act claim certification. The CDA currently requires that a claim in excess
of $100,000 be certified. 253 A contractor may not avoid this requirement by dividing a single
claim into a series of separate claims of $100,000 or less.254 If the contractor’s certification
is defective or improper, that deficiency no longer requires a board or court to dismiss the
appeal or suit. However, the contractor remains obligated to correct the “defective” certifica-
tion before a board or court can render a decision. In addition, a contracting officer is excused
from issuing a final decision on a defectively certified claim if, within 60 days of the date of
receipt of the claim, the contracting officer advises the contractor in writing of the basis for the
conclusion that the certification was inadequate. The total absence of the required certification
is not treated as the equivalent of a defective certification. 255 That omission cannot be cured by

4. 	Subcontractors and the CDA Claims Process
a. 	Standing to Pursue a Claim The existence of a contractual relationship between the claimant
and the government is an essential element in the CDA claims process. Consequently, a subcon-
tractor seldom has the right to assert a claim directly against the government even though a large
percentage of the work typically is subcontracted by the prime contractor. However, a prime con-
tractor may assert a claim against the government on behalf of a subcontractor that has been damaged
(for example, incurred additional cost) due to government action or inaction. 262 A prime contractor
may maintain the claim on behalf of its subcontractor only if it has reimbursed the subcontractor
for its costs or remains liable for such reimbursement. 263 In government contracts, this require-
ment is known as the Severin doctrine. 264 In Severin, the contract between the prime contractor and
the subcontractor contained an exculpatory clause, which the court concluded totally absolved the
prime contractor from liability to the subcontractor for any claim caused by actions of the govern-
ment. Consequently, prime contractors and subcontractors need to consider that doctrine’s potential

b. 	Pass-Through Agreements Sponsorship of a subcontractor’s claim in the disputes process
can present a risk for inconsistent results between a decision in the federal claims process and one in

The Miller Act also addresses the time of any waiver of the right to sue on the payment bond. 40
U.S.C. § 3133(c) provides:
A waiver of the right to bring a civil action on a payment bond required under this subchapter
is void unless the waiver is—
(1) In writing;
(2) Signed by the person whose right is waived; and
(3) Executed after the person whose right is waived has furnished labor or material for use in
the performance of the contract.
Many prime contractors seek to address the risk of potentially inconsistent results and the cost of
multiple legal actions over the same claim through the mechanism of a “Pass-Through” or “Claims
Cooperation Agreement.”268 The intent of this type of agreement is to provide the framework for
a cooperative effort on the claim and to address the potential for inconsistent results. There is no
standard form Claims Cooperation Agreement because it must be tailored to reflect the applicable
subcontract/purchase order provisions and the facts of the specific situation.
c. 	Certification of Subcontractor Claims Certification of a subcontractor’s claim can present
problems for prime contractors. To varying degrees, the prime contractor may not agree with the
subcontractor’s positions. In addition, it is likely that the prime contractor must, to some extent,
rely on factual and cost data developed outside of its organization. Both circumstances need to be
carefully considered in determining if the prime contractor can make a good-faith submission and
certification of the subcontractor’s claim. Notwithstanding these problems, the subcontractor’s claim
must be certified by the prime contractor and contain all of the required elements.269 The prime con-
tractor is not entitled to qualify its certification by stating that it is “based on” a certificate provided
by the subcontractor270 or that it was “subject to review.”271 However, absolute agreement with the
subcontractor’s claim is not essential; the prime contractor may certify the subcontractor’s claim if
it concludes that it is made in good faith and is not frivolous.272

5. 	Government Claims
The CDA also covers government claims. The CDA states, “Each claim by the Federal Government
against a contractor relating to a contract shall be the subject of a written decision by the contracting
officer.”273 The one clear exception to the requirement for a final decision is where the government
asserts an affirmative fraud claim against a contractor. That type of claim need not be the subject of
a contracting officer’s final decision.274
The assessment of liquidated damages has been called the “quintessential government claim.” 275
But when the contractor challenges the liquidated damages assessment on the basis that the govern-
ment caused the delay, there can be both a government claim and a contractor claim. 276 And some
board decisions require the contractor to submit a CDA claim to receive CDA interest on any remis-
sion of liquidated damages. 277 Many government claims may result in a withholding of funds. Even
if the government’s position is determined to have no merit, the contractor is not entitled to CDA
interest on those funds unless it submits a CDA claim.278
6. 	Contracting Officer’s Decision
Following the submission of a valid CDA claim, the next step is the issuance of a contracting officer’s
decision. In general, the issuance of a contracting officer’s decision, or the failure to issue a decision
within the time allowed by the Act, is a prerequisite to the contractor bringing suit on the claim in
the COFC or filing a board appeal.279
a. 	Time Allowed for Issuing the Decision The CDA provides that, in the case of claims of
$100,000 or less, the contracting officer shall issue a decision within 60 days of receipt of a written
request from the contractor that a decision be issued within that period. 280 For claims over $100,000,
the Act provides that, within 60 days of receipt of a certified claim, the contracting officer shall issue a
decision or notify the contractor of the time within which a decision will be issued.281 The Act states
that contracting officer’s decisions on claims over $100,000 are to be issued “within a reasonable
time.”282
b. 	Failure to Issue a Decision and Deemed Denied Appeals If the contracting officer
unduly delays issuing a decision, a contractor may petition the appropriate board of contract appeals
or the COFC to direct that a final decision be issued in a specified period of time, 283 commence a

c. 	Contents of the Decision 	The CDA requires that each contracting officer’s final decision
“state the reasons for the decision reached and … inform the contractor of [his] rights as provided
in [the Act]. Specific findings of fact are not require[d, but, if made, shall not be] binding in any
subsequent proceeding.”288 However, the FAR requires that every final decision contain a paragraph
reading substantially as follows:
This is the final decision of the Contracting Officer. You may appeal this decision to the agency
board of contract appeals. If you decide to appeal, you must, within 90 days from the date you
receive this decision, mail or otherwise furnish written notice to the agency board of contract
appeals and provide a copy to the Contracting Officer from whose decision this appeal is taken.
The notice shall indicate that an appeal is intended, reference this decision, and identify the
contract by number. With regard to appeals to the agency board of contract appeals, you may,
solely at your election, proceed under the board’s (1) small claim procedure for claims of
$50,000 or less, or in the case of a small business concern (as defined in the Small Business
Act and regulations under that Act) $150,000 or less; or (2) accelerated procedure for claims
of $100,000 or less. Instead of appealing to the agency board of contract appeals, you may
bring an action directly in the United States Court of Federal Claims (except as provided in
[the Contract Disputes Act of 1978,] 41 U.S.C. 7102(d), regarding Maritime Contracts) within
12 months of the date you receive this decision.289
A final decision that fails to contain this paragraph is considered defective. 290 However, a contrac-
tor may treat a clear written assertion by the contracting officer of the government’s right to payment
of a sum certain as a final decision even if that document fails to include the otherwise required final
decision and statement of appeal rights. 291 Disregarding a defective final decision can be risky, as a
defective statement of the contractor’s appeal rights does not automatically toll (stop) the period for
filing an appeal or suit. To excuse a late appeal, the contractor must demonstrate detrimental reliance
on the defective statement of its appeal rights. 292

e. 	Final Decision Appeal Deadlines 	The CDA provides that a final decision on a claim
(whether a contractor or a government claim) is “final and conclusive and is not subject to review by
any forum, tribunal, or Federal Government agency unless an appeal or suit is timely commenced
as authorized by [the Act].” 295 Upon receipt of a contracting officer’s final decision, a contractor
has two options: (1) take no action and the decision becomes binding on both parties; or (2) appeal
the decision.
Under the CDA, a contractor has two avenues for appealing a final decision. Within 90 days of
the date of receipt of the decision, the contractor may appeal to the appropriate board of contract
appeals 296 or, within 12 months of the date of receiving the decision, the contractor may initiate
an action in the COFC. 297 Neither a board nor the COFC can consider an appeal that is not timely
presented to it.298
The boards’ rules provide that filing of the notice of appeal occurs when it is mailed or other-
wise furnished to the board. 299 “Mailing” has been interpreted as meaning the United States Postal
Service.300 If the appeal notice is sent in a different manner (for example, commercial carrier or
facsimile), the date of receipt at the board is the filing date. 301
A contracting officer cannot waive the filing deadlines.302 However, reconsideration of final deci-
sion by a contracting officer can have the effect of starting a new appeal period, which would allow
the board to assume jurisdiction over a timely appeal of the second final decision 303 or, under certain
circumstances, even the lack of a second final decision.304 However, relying on post-final decision
communications to extend the appeal deadline(s) is very risky because these communications do not
revive appeal rights unless they clearly constitute and document the contracting officer’s reconsid-
eration of the final decision. 305

Once a contractor files at a board or the COFC, it may not switch to the other forum. The term
election doctrine refers to the body of law related to the contractor’s right to initially select the forum
in which to challenge a final decision. However, the Act does not allow the contractor to pursue
its claim in both forums.306 A binding election occurs when a contractor timely files an appeal or
initiates a suit in a “forum with jurisdiction over the proceeding.”307
8. 	Contract Disputes and Alternative Dispute Resolution
The purpose for using alternative dispute resolution (ADR) procedures is to increase the opportunity
for relatively inexpensive and expeditious resolution of issues. Essential elements of an ADR in
government contract disputes include: (1) the existence of an issue in controversy; (2) a voluntary
election by both parties to participate in the ADR process; (3) an agreement on alternative procedures
to be used in lieu of formal litigation; (4) participation in the process by officials of both parties
with the authority to resolve the controversy; and (5) contractor certification of claims in excess of
$100,000.308
ADR procedures may be used any time where the contracting officer has authority to settle the
matter and may be applied to a portion of a claim. When ADR procedures are used subsequent
to issuance of a final decision, their use does not alter any of the time limitations or procedural
requirements for filing an appeal of the final decision; nor does it constitute a reconsideration of the
final decision. If the contracting officer rejects a request to use ADR, the FAR requires the contracting
officer to set forth a written explanation for that decision and to provide it to the contractor. 309
9. 	Recovery of Attorney’s Fees in Government Contract Claims
Generally, the FAR precludes the recovery of attorney’s fees and expenses, or claim consultant’s
fees and expenses, associated with preparing and prosecuting claims.310 However, the Equal Access
to Justice Act (EAJA), 311 provides a statutory basis for certain contractors to recoup some or all of
their legal costs and expenses of litigation with the government.
An EAJA application for recovery of legal fees and expenses is filed within 30 days after the
conclusion of the primary appeal or suit. 312 To recover its fees and expenses, the claimant must meet
the following criteria:
• Have a net worth of not more than $7 million.
• Have no more than 500 employees.313
• Be the prevailing party in the litigation with the government.314

V. 	STANDARDS OF CONDUCT FOR CONTRACTORS
Government contractors are expected to conduct business with a high degree of integrity and
ethics. 316 Failing to meet these expectations of integrity can be extremely serious. The government’s
remedies include contract cancellation, fines, damages, forfeiture of claims, suspension, and
debarment, as well as criminal sanctions.
A. 	Importance of Certifications
Central to government contracting is the requirement that contractors and subcontractors must deal
honestly with the government. Consistent with the expectation of a high standard of ethics and con-
duct, contractors are routinely required to provide certifications during all phases of the contracting
process, ranging from the initial solicitation, monthly progress payment applications, and payroll
data317 to the resolution of claims. Often, these certifications provide the initial foundation of the
government’s assertion of wrongdoing by a contractor. Consequently, no certification or affirmation
of fact should be dismissed as “just another government form.”
B. 	Procurement Integrity/Standards of Conduct
Whether competing for or performing a government contract, every contractor needs to appreciate
the broad legislation intended to protect the government (that is, the public) from a variety of prohib-
ited activities. These laws prescribe a range of improper actions and the applicable civil and criminal
sanctions. Additionally, the government perceives that the task of inspecting work and determining
compliance with the contract requirements for billions of dollars in contracts every year is extremely
difficult.
Three different approaches have been adopted to address this difficulty. One approach involves
the use of contractor-furnished certifications and representations. These certifications and represen-
tations can serve at least three purposes, as follows:
• Alert the contractor signing the certification or representation to the significance of its
signature.
• Simplify the government’s proof in establishing a violation of an underlying statute.
• Create the basis for an action based solely on the false nature of the certification.
The final two approaches involve multiple civil and criminal statutes addressing prohibited con-
duct and the provision of economic incentives to those who report wrongdoing. In that regard, federal
law provides substantial bounties for individuals to disclose fraudulent conduct by government con-
tractors. In 1986, Congress amended the Civil False Claims Act, 31 U.S.C. §§ 3729–33 to encourage
third parties to identify and institute civil qui tam actions 318 involving allegations of fraudulent con-
duct, and to share in the recovery of those actions.
315R. C. Constr. Co., Inc. v. United States, 42 Fed. Cl. 57 (1998).
316See FAR § 3.1002(a) (contractors are expected to conduct themselves with the “highest degree of integrity and honesty”).
317 Per the Construction Wage Rate Requirements statute (formerly the Davis-Bacon Act).
318 Essentially means private attorney general actions.

V. STANDARDS OF CONDUCT FOR CONTRACTORS 	695
C. 	Civil False Claims Act Actions
Fraudulent statements and certifications to the government can result in considerable penalties for
violators. Federal laws provide for both civil319 and criminal 320 mechanisms to pursue potential
offenses, which the government will often use at the same time for parallel prosecution.321 The civil
component of these enforcement actions is governed by the False Claims Act (FCA).322 The FCA
allows the cases to be brought by either the Department of Justice (DOJ) 323 or private individuals
as “whistleblowers” on behalf of the government (otherwise called qui tam actions).324 The FCA is
often invoked by the government as the preferred statutory basis for an action rather than the parallel
criminal FCA statute or other anti-fraud statutes. From 2000–2018, an average of 606 new FCA
matters were initiated each year.325 In 2018, there were 767 new FCA matters, resulting in the DOJ
recovering more than $2.8 billion from government contractors. 326 The FCA is often used because
of its qui tam provisions, its proof of knowledge standard, and its assessment of damages.
1. 	Qui Tam Provisions of the FCA
Included in the 1986 revisions of the False Claims Act, the qui tam provisions allow for private
individuals to bring suits as “whistleblowers” against entities that may be liable under the False
Claims Act. 327 These suits are brought on behalf of the federal government. The individual bringing
suit, whether a person or corporate entity (called a relator in the litigation), is entitled to share in any
recovery that results from the suit. Individuals in positions to know of potentially unlawful conduct
have an incentive to bring the allegations to light primarily because of the prospect of sharing in
any recovery from the contractor. The government benefits from the qui tam provisions because
the individual bringing the FCA suit is often in a position to know a great deal more information
concerning a contractor’s or subcontractor’s activities than the government agency administering
the contract or the Department of Justice.
As a continuing trend in the last two decades, whistleblower qui tam actions make up the majority
of FCA actions filed. For example, in 2018, of the 767 new FCA matters 645 were brought by qui
tam whistleblowers. 328
2. 	Elements of an FCA Action
The FCA prohibits eight forms of conduct, as follows:
(1) Knowingly submitting or causing the submission of a false or fraudulent payment or approval
claim329
(2) Knowingly creating, using, or causing the creation or use of a false record or statement material
to a false or fraudulent claim330

prevents a defendant from denying their guilt in a later civil suit).

(3) Possessing or being in control of money or property intended for the Government and provid-

(4) Making or providing a receipt to the government without a complete knowledge of a receipt’s
accuracy, with the intention to defraud the government 332
(5) Knowingly buying or receiving a debt or property from a government official who is not autho-

(6) Knowingly creating, using, or causing the creation of a false record or statement material to

property to the Government335
(8) Conspiring to commit a violation of the FCA under any of the above listed categories 336
The most commonly litigated issues result from violations of the first two prohibitions and relate
to the submission of false or fraudulent claims or supporting documentation. In fact, for the purposes
of the FCA, claims include any requests or demands for payment if presented to an “officer, employee
or agent of the United States” or even “a contractor, grantee or other recipient,” if the payment is made
on behalf of the government or for the government’s purposes and has or will be at least partially
reimbursed by the government. 337 For instance, on a typical construction project, each bill or invoice
submitted by a prime contractor to the government or a subcontractor to a prime will amount to a
claim and could result in liability if it’s false or fraudulent. 338
False claims under the FCA also do not require any actual knowledge or proof of specific intent
to defraud.339 Violations of the FCA will be found when claims are made with deliberate ignorance
or reckless disregard for the truth or falsity of the information provided.340
3. 	Theories of Liability under the FCA
Courts have applied the FCA broadly. Indeed, contractors have been found to be in violation of the
FCA for a wide range of actions. As can be expected, the FCA has been used to punish companies
that have explicitly made false or fraudulent assertions to the government to either receive more than
they were owed by the government or to provide less than they owed to the government. Practices
of this sort have been termed “direct false claims” to describe their explicit nature.341
a. 	False Certifications Companies have been held liable for other practices as well. As described
above for example, problems with erroneous certifications could serve as a basis for a violation. For
that matter, case law suggests that there are at least two ways that a contractor can get into trouble
with a certification, as follows: 342
• Express false certifications have been defined to include any instance of an entity deceitfully
and explicitly certifying compliance with a statute, regulation or contract despite the fact that
actual compliance was a basis of payment.343

• Implied false certifications in contrast, do not require an explicit indication of compliance,
and merely necessitate that a contractor imply their entitlement to payment when submitting a
claim. 344
Because of the vague nature of the definition for implied false certifications, until recently, the
courts have struggled to interpret what exactly a contractor must do to imply their entitlement to pay-
ment and whether such actions would even qualify as a violation. In 2016, however, the Supreme
Court issued a decision in Universal Health Servs., Inc. v. United States, which clarified the sub-
ject substantially. In Universal Health Servs., the parents of a deceased child filed a qui tam action
against a health clinic, where their child was treated, for employing unlicensed medical professionals
who submitted fraudulent reimbursement claims to Medicaid for services they were not admitted to
provide. 345 In a unanimous decision, the Supreme Court ruled that implied false certifications could
create liability under the FCA.346 The Court noted that violations could be found only on that basis,
when a claim for payment makes “specific representations about the goods or services provided, but
knowingly fails to disclose the defendant’s noncompliance with a statutory, regulatory, or contrac-
tual [requirement, although] the omission renders those representations misleading.”347 The Court
further indicated that the misrepresentation must be material to the government’s payment decision
for a violation and must be of the kind that would have led the government to refuse payment if they
knew the truth. 348
Since the Universal Health Servs. decision, courts have focused on what the government does
after finding out about the wrongful certification.349 For that reason, awareness and documentation
of industry practices can be particularly useful in these cases.
b. 	Department of Justice’s “Brand” and “Granston” Memos. 	In 2018, the Department of
Justice (DOJ) issued two internal memoranda indicating a change in the government’s approach
to FCA enforcement. The first (often referred to as “the Granston memo”) was issued by Michael
D. Granston, the Director of the Fraud Section in the Commercial Litigation Branch, on January
10, to other DOJ attorneys handling FCA cases. 350 The Granston memo reminded DOJ staff about
the authority provided to them by 31 U.S.C. § 3730(c)(2)(A), which permits the government to
dismiss qui tam cases brought by individuals. The memorandum noted that while this authority has
been previously used “sparingly” by the government, it is an important tool for the preservation
of limited judicial resources and government interests. The memorandum continued by outlining
several instances that exemplify appropriate uses for this authority, which included:
(1) Curbing meritless claims
(2) Preventing parasitic or opportunistic qui tam actions and controlling litigation
(3) Preventing interference with agency policies and programs
(4) Instances where controlling litigation was brought on behalf of the United States
(5) Safeguarding classified information and national security interests
(6) Preserving government resources
(7) Addressing egregious procedural errors

4. 	Fines and Damages
The monetary penalties for a contractor found liable under the False Claims Act may be fines,
damages, or both. Under the civil False Claims Act, a court may assess a fine of between $10,957
and no more than $21,916353 per violation, plus treble damages may be awarded as “3 times the
amount of damages which the Government sustains” because of the violation.354 Violators are
also liable to the government for the costs of a civil action brought to recover any such penalty
or damages. 355 In United States v. United Technologies Corporation,356 the court found that the
contractor had submitted to the Air Force for payment under its contract 709 invoices that were
tainted by a false claim. In holding that United Technologies was liable under the False Claim
Act, the court considered each invoice to be a separate claim and assessed fines in the amount of
$7,090,000. 357 The basis for the false-claim action was the contractor’s explanation of the factual
basis for its contract pricing. Although the contractor stated to the government that it had used
certain data in predicting future costs and prices, it did not in fact use that data and the court
found that the contractor was obliged to have followed through with its representation.358 There
were no damages because the court additionally found that the contractor reduced the price of
the engines so that the government saved money over the term of the contract. 359 A contractor
should recognize that even if the government is unharmed or even benefits from a false statement,
as in United Technologies, the contractor can still be held liable for civil penalties under the False
Claims Act.
However, the false claim in a case may not be each voucher submitted to the government. In United
States ex rel. Longhi v. Lithium Power Technologies, Inc., 360 the court disagreed with the govern-
ment’s contention that the defendant submitted 54 vouchers, each of which should incur the $10,000
penalty. Rather, the court looked at the defendant’s “causative act” and awarded the penalty only for

to be an issue that may be given wide interpretation by a trial court.
For the treble damages that may be awarded to the government in addition to the fines, the deter-
mination of the extent of the damages that the government suffered will vary depending on the type
of contract and the circumstances of an individual case. In United States v. Lithium Power, the defen-
dants misrepresented information about their history and qualifications in order to obtain a contract
under the Small Business Innovation Research Program (SBIR). In assessing damages, the court dis-
regarded the argument that the government received benefit in the research done by the defendants.
Rather, it found that the purpose of the SBIR was to award contracts to foster entrepreneurship by,
and the development of, eligible small businesses. Since the defendants were not eligible to partici-
pate in the program because they had misrepresented their capabilities and resources, 362 the purpose
of the program was not met and the government received no benefit. The court then assessed damages
equal to the value of each of the four contracts awarded to the defendants.363
In instances where the case is brought by a qui tam whistleblower, the individual whistleblower
plaintiff may receive a portion of the overall damages awarded or amount of settlement. 364 If the
government joins the qui tam suit, the individual plaintiff can receive between 15% and 25% of the
proceeds or settlement of the claim, “depending [on] the extent to which the person substantially
contributed to the prosecution of the action.” 365 If the government does not join the qui tam suit,
the amount awarded to the plaintiff increases to a range of 25% to 30% of the proceeds or settle-
ment. Plaintiffs also receive “an amount for any reasonable expense[s,]” reasonable attorney’s fees
and costs, all of which are paid by the defendant. 366 The incentive approach has made the FCA a
popular tool for whistleblowers and, in fact, the majority of FCA cases today are brought by private
individuals. As a result of such prosecutions, the DOJ recovered more than $20 billion from 2014
to 2018.367
5. 	Potential Subcontractor Liabilities
The language of the FCA is broad enough to allow the government to reach subcontractors despite the
lack of a direct contractual relationship. However, the government’s ability to pursue subcontractors
directly does not necessarily release prime contractors from responsibility. Prime contractors can
be held responsible along with subcontractors where their own actions qualify as violations under
the act. Violations will certainly be found in cases where the prime contractor is aware of the false
claim or fraudulent representation submitted by the lower-tier contractor when the prime contractor
forwards it to the government.368 Further, even a lack of due diligence in evaluating a subcontractor
claim against the government can result in penalties for the prime contractor.369 The requirements
for those good-faith reviews are particularly crucial to remember given the prime contractor markup
often incorporated on top of subcontractor costs.
6. 	Defendant Recovery of Attorney’s Fees
FCA defendants may be able to recover attorney’s fees following a successful defense and resolution
to the FCA case. But the FCA provisions are not as generous to defendants in an FCA action as they

D. 	Contractor Business Ethics and Conduct
1. 	FAR Requirements
The FAR provisions detailing a contractor’s business ethics obligations are found in FAR Subpart
3.10, Contractor Code of Business Ethics and Conduct; FAR Subpart 9.4, Debarment, Suspension,
and Ineligibility; and the implementing FAR clauses.372 These provisions combine a statement of
expectations applicable to all contractors; differing mandatory requirements depending on a com-
pany’s size, the dollar value and duration of a government contract; and potential sanctions applicable
to any contractor that fails to make required disclosures to the government.
a. 	Contractor Standards of Conduct 	The FAR addresses contractor codes of business ethics
and conduct with a combination of a statement of expectations applicable to any contractor and
mandatory requirements that vary with the size of the contractor and the value and duration of the
contract.
(1) Statement of Expectations
• All contractors “must conduct themselves” with the “highest degree of integrity and honesty.”
• All contractors “should have” a written code of business ethics and conduct.
• As part of an effort to promote compliance with the written code, all contractors “should have”
an employee business ethics and training program suitable for the size of the company that will
“facilitate discovery and disclosure of improper conduct” and “ensure corrective measures” are
carried out.
• If the contractor is aware that the government has overpaid on a contract financing or invoice
payment, the contractor is expected to remit the overpayment amount to the government. A
contractor may be suspended and/or debarred for knowing failure by a principal to “timely”
disclose “credible evidence” of a significant overpayment.373
(2) Mandatory Requirements
Any contractor receiving a government contract in excess of $5.5 million 374 and a duration of
120 days or more (“Covered Contract”) shall do the following:
• Have a written code of business ethics and conduct.
• Make a copy of that code available to each employee engaged in the performance of a covered
contract.

e. 	Self-Reporting of Potential Violations and Investigations 	A contractor must make a

2. 	Potential Nondisclosure Sanctions: Suspension and Debarment

explicit requirements for certain contractor disclosures, that clause does not contain an express state-

found in FAR § 3.1003(a)(2) and (3) 382 and are included in the grounds for contractor suspension or
debarment found in FAR §§ 9.407–2 and 9.406–2, respectively. These two provisions set forth the
following as grounds for contractor suspension or debarment:
• “Knowing failure” by a “principal” of the contractor to make a “timely” written disclosure to
the government in connection with a government contract awarded to that contractor when the
contractor has “credible evidence” of:
¤ Violation of federal criminal law involving fraud, conflict of interest, bribery or gratuity
violations
¤ Violation of the civil False Claims Act (31 U.S.C. §§ 3729–33)
¤ “Significant overpayments” on a contract other than those resulting from contract financing
as defined in FAR § 32.001383
• The disclosure obligation relates to the award, performance, or closeout of the contract or a
subcontract under that contract.

➣ 	POINTS TO REMEMBER
• Federal government construction contracts can be an excellent opportunity because of the con-
sistently large volume of new work each year and the adoption of standard contract provisions
that, in general, provide a balanced set of conditions related to changes, differing site condi-
tions, delays, project inspection and acceptance, and termination.
• When contracting with the federal government, contractors need to appreciate that there are a
few overriding public-policy considerations that can fundamentally alter a contractor’s rights.
These include policies related to the authority of government employees to bind the government
and the application of contract provisions reflecting a fundamental public policy, such as the
right to terminate a contract for the convenience of the government.
• “Best value,” not low price, is now the predominant procedure to award federal government
construction contracts. The determination of the offeror providing the best value can be heavily
influenced by the past performance reports that the federal government develops and retains on
its contractors. Any contractor working for a federal agency needs to understand the importance
of the past performance reports on their ability to secure new work.
• The federal government uses its purchasing power to implement a variety of social and eco-
nomic policies and programs including preferences for small businesses, domestic construction
materials and products, labor standards, and environmental regulations. Any firm interested in
competing for government construction contracts needs to determine both the opportunities
presented by and obligations imposed by each of these policies.
• The process of resolving disputes and claims on government construction contracts is con-
trolled by the Contract Disputes Act. This act provides a detailed set of requirements and
procedures related to the submission of claims, consideration of claims by government agen-
cies and, if necessary, the disposition of disputes in boards of contract appeals or the U.S. Court
of Federal Claims.
• In accordance with the Contract Disputes Act, contractors must certify any claim in excess of
$100,000, which is then submitted to the contracting officer for consideration. This certification
requirement includes claims submitted on behalf of subcontractors or vendors. The submission
of the certification is necessary for the resolution of the claim.
• The federal government expects its contractors to conduct themselves with the “highest degree
of integrity and honesty.” Consistent with that expectation, contractors are expected to adopt
and publish codes of ethics. Most contractors must also adopt programs to ensure compliance
with the expected standards of conduct, report wrongdoing, and certify their compliance with
numerous regulations and contract obligations. Risks of noncompliance can result in fines, civil
damages, criminal sanctions, and debarment.
• Every contractor needs to adopt system-wide protocols to obtain a complete understanding of
the special requirements in government contracts before undertaking to compete for or perform
a government construction contract.

APPENDIX 24.1 INTERNET RESOURCES FOR FEDERAL
GOVERNMENT CONSTRUCTION CONTRACTS
I. 	SYSTEM FOR AWARD MANAGEMENT (SAM)
Currently, to participate in most federal agency contracting programs, a contractor must be listed in
the System for Award Management (SAM), which includes the following:
• Central Contract Registry (CCR)
• Online Representations and Certifications Application (OCRA)
• Excluded Parties List (EPLS)
• Federal Agency Registration (Fedreg)
According to the SAM website (www.sam.gov/SAM), a firm’s existing CCR and OCRA data
was moved to SAM and there is no need to update the information prior to its expiration.
II. 	FEDERAL BUSINESS OPPORTUNITIES (FED BIZ OPPS)
For firms and individuals desiring to do business with the various agencies of the government, many
agencies maintain websites that provide information regarding solicitations, both pending and con-
templated (that is, pre-solicitation notice). The primary source, however, for all federal contracting
opportunities, including the U.S. Postal Service, is Fed Biz Opps—Federal Business Opportunities
website (fedbizopps.gov/).
III. 	INFORMATION ON REGULATIONS AND AGENCIES
Websites that provide information on several aspects of federal contracting, including laws and reg-
ulations, are listed below.
A. 	Regulations
1. To search in the most current FAR, as well as the agency supplements, point your browser to
the Electronic Code of Federal Regulations website (www.ecfr.gov).
2. From the Browse pull-down menu, select Title 48—Federal Acquisition Regulations Sys-
tem, and click Go. The FAR table of contents page is displayed.
3. In the Browse Parts column, click on the subpart you want to view.
B. 	Government Standards, Guidance, and Other Reference Materials
• Agency reference materials, standards, and design guides can be obtained on the respective
agency’s website. Websites such as those maintained by the Corps of Engineers, NAVFAC, the
VA, and GSA’s Public Buildings Service, have links to “publications” or “libraries.”
